The Political Economy of the ASEAN Green Deal
v
Foreword
Every country needs a strategy to address the great challenges of our age: rapid 
technological advance, the urgent need for advanced education and skills, the 
rapid transformation to green technologies, the need for regional solutions that 
transcend national borders, and the need for diplomacy in order to operate 
effectively in a multipolar world. In sum, every country needs a strategy for 
Sustainable Development.
This volume proves that Cambodia is undertaking an intensive transformation 
to an advanced knowledge economy that aims to utilize science, technology, and 
innovation (STI) to address the many dimensions of sustainable development. In 
this exceptionally strong compendium of essays, Cambodian scientists, scholars, 
policymakers, and thought leaders, as well as co-authors from other ASEAN 
nations, explore every dimension of Cambodia’s sustainable development 
challenges, from considerations of the local environment to the opportunities for 
global diplomacy. This expansive perspective – ranging across issues, scientific 
disciplines, and scales of action – is just what is needed for Cambodia to meet 
its national objective of becoming a high-income and sustainable society by mid-
century, if not sooner.
What is most impressive to me is Cambodia’s recognition that all success 
will depend on the quality of education of Cambodia’s young people, and their 
preparation for an interconnected, knowledge-intensive, and digitally driven 
world economy. Cambodian scholars and policy leaders recognize that every 
sector of the Cambodian economy will soon have to be a “high-skilled” sector, 
including even the so-called traditional sectors such as textiles, tourism, and 
agriculture. Each sector of the economy, and all successful enterprises, will 
be digitally empowered, linked to artificial intelligence and other machine 
learning, and in need of continual innovations in order for Cambodia to remain 
globally connected and competitive. In short, Cambodia must prepare to thrive 
in an age of rapid technological advancement.
If the digital age were all that is challenging Cambodia, that alone would be a 
major challenge. But Cambodia faces even greater challenges. As a remarkable 
tropical environment of unique biodiversity and ecosystems, Cambodia depends 
on its natural capital for its sustenance, culture, and global competitiveness. Yet 
Cambodia’s vital natural capital is already under deep stress, both because of 
past poor practices in land use, waste management, and industrial pollution 
and because ongoing global environmental changes (most importantly, global 
warming) will create major new risks for Cambodia regarding water management, 
agricultural production, urban habitability, and protection of biodiversity.
As the essays here underscore, the Royal Government of Cambodia, 
together with Cambodia’s leading universities and scientific centers, have 
turned their curricula, research priorities, and operating budgets to face these 
new challenges. The returns will be enormous. Cambodia’s investments in 
Green Ideals
vi
STI will result in enormous advances in Cambodian productivity, efficiency of 
energy and materials use, and sustainability. These advances in turn will enable 
Cambodia to achieve rapid economic growth in the decades ahead, also taking 
advantage of the overall rapid growth of East Asia.
The essays here touch on every dimension of the STI agenda: water resource 
management, agricultural productivity, circular economy, and achievement of 
a zero-carbon energy system. In each area, the urgency is clear. Cambodia is 
already facing the risks of intensified droughts and floods, heatwaves, and land 
degradation. Yet the opportunities are even greater. Through smart technologies, 
Cambodia will be able to raise agricultural productivity, reduce food wastes, 
build a regional power grid based on renewable energy, and enhance Cambodia’s 
standing as a global destination for sustainable tourism.
One of the great innovations ahead lies in Cambodia’s future Universities 
4.0, meaning Cambodian universities that are technologically enabled and 
organizationally structured to train young people to become national and 
global leaders of sustainable development. A University for Sustainability will 
teach the interconnections among the Earth’s physical systems, the engineered 
infrastructure systems, and the socio-politico-economic systems. It will train 
students and researchers in the policy methods needed to achieve sustainable 
development. It will guide students through the ethical underpinnings needed for 
a high-income sustainable society. And it will train future problem solvers in the 
diplomatic arts of regional and global collaboration.
The essays in this volume recognize at every juncture that Cambodia is not 
alone in facing these great challenges, and that indeed, Cambodia can meet its 
national objectives only through extensive diplomacy and global cooperation. 
International cooperation will be needed at many scales. The ASEAN countries 
working together will need to build an interconnected zero-carbon power grid 
extending across ASEAN and connecting ASEAN with neighbors including 
Australia, China, and others. ASEAN countries will need to coordinate on the 
protection of ASEAN’s rainforests, fisheries, coastal areas, and river sheds. 
ASEAN nations will need to join together in fruitful diplomacy with other 
regions of the world, such as with the European Union. In this regard, ASEAN’s 
Green Deal will be an important diplomat counterpart to the European Green 
Deal and will enable the EU and ASEAN to set mutually agreed rules for trade, 
finance, and technological change.
ASEAN will also need to play a major global leadership role as well, in the 
UN General Assembly, the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, the 
UN Convention on Biological Diversity, the G20, the BRICS, and other global 
venues. As the chapter on Climate Finance makes clear, Cambodia’s success 
will also depend on access to high-quality international financing – long-term 
loans, green bonds, foreign direct investments, and various kinds of grants from 
international institutions – in order for Cambodia to invest at the scale needed 
to achieve rapid growth combined with sustainable development. Cambodia’s 
The Political Economy of the ASEAN Green Deal
vii
leadership, both through the national government and as a leading member of 
ASEAN, will be very important in forging the needed reforms of the Global 
Financial Architecture.
In sum, the coming years will be a period of rapid global change. With 
leadership, vision, ethics, good governance, and strong national institutions 
working in collaboration with other nations, Cambodia is poised for very exciting 
advances. The volume’s lead editors are Prof. Chhem Kieth Rethy, a scientist, 
physician, and former UN diplomat, Dr. Chem Phalla, an engineer specializing 
in water resources management, hydrology, and hydraulics and Dr. Khieng 
Sothy, an accomplished scholar, educator, and higher education administrator. 
Their dedicated partnership during the past decade has focused on development 
and foreign policy research and has emphasized the interconnected dynamics of 
environmental, social, and economic dimensions. The editors and the authors 
of this volume deserve high praise and careful attention to their many important 
insights and recommendations, which together provide an important framework 
for Cambodia’s path to sustainable development.
Prof. Jeffrey Sachs
President of the UN Sustainable Development Solutions Network

Preface
Cambodian Scholars’ Vision of the Green Deal
In an era defined by unprecedented environmental challenges and the urgent need 
for sustainable solutions, the world’s attention has turned towards the ambitious 
concept known as the “Green Deal.” This comprehensive framework has since 
captured the imaginations of policymakers, scholars, and citizens around the globe. 
The Green Deal represents a holistic approach to addressing pressing issues related 
to climate change, environmental sustainability, and socio-economic development.
The “Green Deal” concept encompasses practical policies, frameworks, and 
strategies aimed  at mitigating the consequences of climate change and promoting 
sustainable development.  Conversely, “Green Ideals” are the aspirational objectives, 
principles, and visions that serve as the  impetus for these pragmatic initiatives. The 
Green Ideals are the visionary foundation that propels  these endeavours, while the 
Green Deal concentrates on implementation. It is imperative for  ASEAN to adopt 
Green Ideals as a Green Deal aspiration, as this ensures that practical actions are 
consistent with high standards and long-term environmental objectives, thereby 
promoting a more  comprehensive and unified approach to sustainability. In 2022, 
former Samdech Prime Minister  Hun Sen introduced the concept of the green 
deal. To strengthen early efforts from governments  to further define the ASEAN 
Green Deal—currently a vision and early regional initiative—this  book aims to 
clarify the concept. By offering diverse perspectives, it endorses the critical mission 
of the 2022 Green Deal and underscores the region’s need to take it seriously, 
thereby transforming  ideals into actionable ideas and impactful outcomes.
As we embark on this journey through the perspectives and insights of 
Cambodian scholars and experts, we explore a diverse array of topics, each 
intertwined with the overarching theme of the Green Deal. From the intricate 
geopolitics of this transformative initiative to the vital connections between 
Sustainable Development Goal 13 (SDG 13) and circular economy principles, this 
book offers a multifaceted exploration of the Green Deal’s far-reaching impact. 
In our exploration, we uncover the intricate connections between international 
trade and the circular economy, demonstrating how economic policies can either 
reinforce or hinder our progress toward a greener future. We investigate the realms 
of climate and water diplomacy, shedding light on the crucial role of diplomacy 
in addressing shared environmental challenges. As technology continues to 
shape our world, we examine the concept of Green Digital Transformation and 
how it can revolutionize our approach to sustainability. The book looks into 
the complexities of energy diplomacy within the Green Deal framework and 
explores the nexus between food systems, security, and sustainable agriculture. 
We also highlight the critical intersections of science, technology, and 
innovation, including the advent of Industry 4.0, in driving forward the 
Green Deal’s objectives. Environmental scientists, as well as their invaluable 
Green Ideals
x
contributions, take center stage in this discourse, emphasizing the pivotal role 
they play in shaping a greener future.
The Green Deal is not just about the environment; it is about global health 
too. Climate change’s impact on public health is a pressing concern, and we 
investigate how it intertwines with this grand endeavor. The concept of a 
University for Sustainability is presented as a potential game-changer in 
educating and equipping the next generation of leaders with the tools to navigate 
the challenges of our time.
Financing is at the heart of any transformative initiative, and we explore the 
various mechanisms and strategies for funding Green Deal programs. Sustainable 
tourism, as a key economic sector, is examined in-depth, considering its potential 
to drive sustainable development.     Lastly, we explore the creation of a green-
built environment, showcasing innovative architectural and design approaches 
that prioritize sustainability. 
The chapters within this book offer a panoramic view of the Green Deal’s 
multifaceted dimensions, weaving together the perspectives of Cambodian 
scholars and experts with global implications. Through these insightful 
contributions, we hope to inspire discussions, spark innovation, and foster a 
deeper understanding of the transformative potential of the Green Deal on both 
local and global scales. It is our collective hope that this book will serve as a 
valuable resource for policymakers, academics, students, and anyone passionate 
about building a sustainable and resilient future for our planet.
In practice this book was conceived as a compilation of chapters contributed by 
a diverse group of scholars, practitioners, and policy researchers. All of them are 
thoughtful and clear-thinking researchers. The intention was not to impose a strict 
formatting style on the individual chapters. Instead, the editors chose to provide 
authors with the freedom to express their research and ideas creatively. Our goal was 
to encourage each author to explore the urgent need for a Green Deal in their own 
unique way.
By doing so, we aimed to foster brainstorming and gather the most innovative, 
unrestrained ideas and solutions to address the pressing challenges posed by climate 
change and its far-reaching impacts on both humanity and the environment. In 
summary, the aim was to create a book that is both approachable and thorough, serving 
as the starting point for our intellectual exploration of the intricate and captivating 
aspects of the Green Deal. The wide array of ideas from diverse perspectives can 
serve as a foundation for conducting comprehensive interdisciplinary research on 
the Green Deal that aims to inform future policies that transcend national borders, 
emphasizing a more systematic and globally relevant approach. 
CHHEM Kieth Rethy
CHEM Phalla
KHIENG Sothy
The Political Economy of the ASEAN Green Deal

Editors and Contributors
CHEA Angela is a Cambodian dual degree student at Barnard College and 
Columbia University’s School of International and Public Affairs (SIPA). 
She holds a BA in History with a minor in Economics, and is pursuing 
a MPA concentrating in Economic and Political Development with a 
specialization in Data Analytics and Quantitative Analysis. She has a strong 
academic background in economic development, sustainable development, 
statistical analysis, international relations, and public policy. She offers a 
unique perspective on youth and sustainable development, informed by her 
interdisciplinary studies and practical research experience.
CHEA Vatana was a Vice President of Cambodia University of Technology 
and Science and holds a master’s and a doctoral degree in demography. His 
research interest includes population projection, migration and development, 
human capital development, and the economics of household. Dr. Chea has 
authored and co-authored more than thirty scientific articles, including book 
chapters and journals in ISI and SCOPUS databases.
CHEM Phalla, an Adjunct Professor at Cambodia University of Technology 
and Science and an esteemed scholar holding a Ph.D. in Water Resources 
Management from the University of Sydney, delves into the transformative 
realm of water diplomacy in transboundary river basins and is also a co-editor 
of this book. Serving as the Vice-Chairman, with the rank of Minister, at the 
Economic, Social, and Cultural Council office of the Council of Ministers 
in the Kingdom of Cambodia, Dr. Phalla brings unparalleled expertise in 
climate change and water governance, water resources management and 
sustainability, and policy design and implementation in the water resources 
sector. His dedication to fostering connections among societies through water 
highlights the critical intersection of diplomacy, sustainability, and societal 
well-being in our shared water resources.
CHHEANG Vannarith, a distinguished scholar with a Ph.D. in Asia Pacific 
Studies from Ritsumeikan Asia Pacific University, expertly explores the 
ASEAN Green Deal’s political economy landscape. As the visionary Founder 
and Chairman of Angkor Social Innovation Park (ASIP), he pioneers initiatives 
at the intersection of ASEAN, geopolitics, and geoeconomics in the Asia 
Pacific region. Dr. Vannarith’s dedication to research and policy development 
shapes the conversation on sustainability and regional cooperation, driving 
impactful change for a greener and more prosperous future.
CHHEM Kieth Rethy is a distinguished medical doctor, scientist, educator, and 
historian with expertise in Digital/AI, Nuclear Technology, Nuclear Disaster 
Management and Science Diplomacy. He is a Distinguished Professor of AI 
and Humanities at CamTech University. He holds a MD, a PhD in Education, 
The Political Economy of the ASEAN Green Deal

and a PhD in History. Dr. Chhem has extensive experience in leadership roles, 
including Director of the Division of Human Health at the International Atomic 
Energy Agency (IAEA). He is currently a member of the Leadership Council 
of the UNSDSN (Sustainable Development Solutions Network) and Fellow of 
the AETDEW (Academy of Engineering and Technology of the Developing 
World). His diplomatic contributions include serving as a UN Diplomat at 
the IAEA, Minister Attached to the Prime Minister (Foreign Affairs) and as 
Secretary of State at the Ministry of Industry, Science, Technology & Innovation 
Recently, he is a Senior Minister in charge of the Economic, Social and Cultural 
Council of the Royal Government of Cambodia. His insights in the book on 
Green Ideals will offer valuable perspectives on sustainable practices and 
policies, particularly in ASEAN.
CHHEM Sirika, who holds a PharmD and an MD from Université Libre 
de Bruxelles, is a Visiting Research Fellow at the University Puthisastra, 
Cambodia. With an interdisciplinary academic background in astrophysics, 
paleoradiology, and stem cell research, she offers a unique perspective on the 
impacts of climate change on global health.
CHHEM Siriwat is an Adjunct Assistant Professor at CamTech University and 
a trailblazer in digital transformation for AI and sustainability. He holds a 
Bachelor’s degree in Physics, Chemistry, and Environmental Sciences from 
the University of British Columbia, a Master’s degree in Digital Technology 
Management (Artificial Intelligence) from the University of Bologna and 
a Master’s degree in Diplomacy from Pannasastra University. Currently 
pursuing PhD research at the intersection of Leadership, AI, and Comparative 
Philosophy. Mr. Chhem is a driving force in leveraging technology for the 
betterment of our planet through active Science Diplomacy. He is sought after 
for his expertise in global governance AI by international organizations such 
as the UN and the International Science Council. He currently serves as a 
Board Member of the World Digital Chamber and is the Strategic Advisor to 
the Asian Vision Institute. Through his unparallel expertise in the inclusive 
digital economy, artificial intelligence, and cyber diplomacy, Mr. Chhem is 
committed to fostering impact and responsibility. Mr. Chhem’s qualifications 
and innovative approaches to digital transformation make his contributions 
to “Green Ideals” significant. His insights on leveraging digital technology 
for sustainable development are essential for understanding how to harness 
technology for a more sustainable world.
CHHORT Chhorravuth, an International Master of Management graduate 
from Audencia Business School, explores the intricate realm of the ASEAN 
Green Deal’s political economy. As the Executive Director of Angkor 
Social Innovation Park, he combines his social innovation and sustainable 
development expertise to drive positive change in the ASEAN region. 
Chhorravuth is passionate about exploring the intersection of business, 
Green Ideals
xiv
politics, and environmental sustainability to foster a greener, more inclusive 
future for all.
GOUSHCHI Adonis, who holds an M.D. from Université Libre de Bruxelles, 
is a dedicated medical professional with a focus on internal medicine and a 
subspecialization in infectious diseases. He is in charge of infection control. 
He is committed to advancing global health initiatives and currently serves as 
attending physician at Iris South Hospital in Brussels.
GUPTA Aditya, who holds a Master of Corporate Law from the University 
of Cambridge, United Kingdom, brings a wealth of expertise to Cambodia’s 
decarbonization landscape. As a Research Fellow at the Centre for Advanced 
Research and Legal Studies at the Asian Vision Institute, he focuses on 
corporate governance, ESG practices, and green financing. Aditya is dedicated 
to advancing sustainable initiatives and driving positive change through 
innovative legal frameworks and responsible business practices.
HING Vutha, a lecturer in International Trade at the University of Adelaide 
and an Adjunct Professor at Cambodia University of Technology and Science 
and a Ph.D. holder in Economics from the University of Adelaide, shines 
as a Senior Project Advisor at CDRI, where he channels his expertise in 
International Trade, Productivity, Economic Growth, and the Economics of 
Digitalization. With a keen focus on the implications of the European Union 
Green Deal for Cambodia, Dr. Hing navigates the intersection of economics 
and sustainability with finesse.
HUL Seingheng is an Adjunct Professor at Cambodia University of Technology 
and Science and holds a Ph.D. in Environmental Engineering from the 
University of the Philippines and Shizuoka University in Japan. He is a faculty 
member at the Cambodia University of Technology and Science (CamTech) 
with expertise in optimization algorithms, water treatment technologies, 
communication science, STI policy development and implementation, and 
national innovation system assessment.
KEO Piseth, a distinguished scholar with a Doctor of Philosophy from the 
National University of Singapore and the Harvard-Yenching Institute, 
spearheads Cambodia’s decarbonization journey. A seasoned expert in 
navigating the complexities of sustainable development, Dr. Keo specializes 
in environmental management, climate change mitigation and adaptation, 
biodiversity conservation, governance, and institution building. With a 
passion for preserving nature and pioneering renewable energy solutions, Dr. 
Keo is a driving force in shaping Cambodia’s eco-friendly future.
KHIENG Sothy, founding President of Cambodia University of Technology 
and Science and advisor to the National Council of Science, Technology, 
and Innovation, is an accomplished scholar, educator, and higher education 
administrator. Previously, he served as Vice President (Research and 
The Political Economy of the ASEAN Green Deal
xv
Administration) at Kirirom Institute of Technology and spent a decade 
at Cambodia’s leading research think tank, the Cambodia Development 
Resource Institute (CDRI). At CDRI, Dr. Khieng co-founded and led the 
Education Unit, co-edited several books on Cambodian education and science 
and technology, and authored the book “The Dawn of Social Enterprise in 
Cambodia,” based on his doctoral research. His interdisciplinary research 
interests include post-secondary education, social entrepreneurship and 
innovation, and science and technology. Dr. Khieng has held research 
fellowships at Griffith University and the University of Melbourne (Australia), 
and the Swiss Federal University for Vocational Education and Training. 
He is a co-founder and President of the Comparative Education Society of 
Cambodia (CESCam) and serves on the boards of CESCam and Compare: A 
Journal of Comparative and International Education (UK).
KUOK Fidero served as the Under-Secretary of State and oversaw the National 
Institute of Science, Technology & Innovation (NISTI) under the Ministry of 
Industry, Science, Technology & Innovation (MISTI). Dr. Fidero obtained a 
Ph.D. in Environmental Engineering from the Tokyo Institute of Technology 
(TIT) in Japan. He has been working over ten years on Waste Management 
and Environmental Pollution Control. Moreover, Dr. Fidero is recognized as 
an alumnus of ASEAN Science Diplomat, ASEAN Science & Technology 
Fellow, and the American Association for the Advancement of Science. Dr. 
Fidero’s research interests extend to supporting STI Policy and Roadmap 
by focusing on decision-making modeling, technology foresight, and carbon 
neutrality. He is also a dedicated environmental advocate and science 
diplomat, driving sustainability through strong leadership in science-based 
policy and science diplomacy.
LIM Seakleng is currently pursuing a master’s degree in Western Philosophy 
at Wuhan University, China under the ASEAN-China Young Leaders 
Scholarship. His work experience began in 2018 as an intern at the Centre 
for Educational Research and Innovation of the Cambodia Development 
Resource Institute (CDRI). After graduating with a bachelor’s degree in 
International Relations from the Royal University of Phnom Penh, Seakleng 
worked as a Research Assistant at the Cambodia University of Technology 
and Science (CamTech). From 2021 to 2023, he also served as member of 
secretariat of the Comparative Education Society of Cambodia. His research 
interests include political philosophy, philosophy of technology and higher 
education development.
NATH Kananda, a dedicated professional, holds a bachelor’s degree in 
Architecture and Urbanism from the esteemed Royal University of Fine Arts 
in Cambodia. Currently serving as a Lecturer in Architecture and Interior 
Design at CamTech, he is passionate about Sustainable Construction 
Materials and Technologies in the field of Architecture.
Green Ideals
xvi
NORN Samnangseymony possesses a dual master’s degree in public and 
international law (LL.M.) from the Université Paris Vincennes – Saint-Denis 
and the Royal University of Law and Economics. He is affiliated with the 
Asian Vision Institute as a Program Coordinator at the Centre for Advanced 
Research and Legal Studies as well as a Research Fellow at the Centre for 
Culture and Peace Studies. His research interests include comparative law, 
administrative law, international trade law, youth diplomacy, and the United 
Nations Sustainable Development Goals.
PROMENTILLA Michael Angelo B, with a doctoral degree in Socio-
Environmental Engineering from Hokkaido University, Japan, is a 
distinguished figure at De La Salle University, specializing in decision

INTRODUCTION 
As global temperatures rise, the future existence of humans and other living 
species is called into question. Climate change and the environment have emerged 
as global concerns. The United Nations (UN), as a global governance actor, 
has played a critical role in developing and promoting policies to decrease and 
influence the norm in response to climate change. For example, the majority UN 
of member states have supported the United Nations Sustainable Development 
Goals, which are scheduled to be fulfilled by 2030. It is important to highlight that 
although development is vital and the state must seek to provide a better quality 
of life for its residents, it should be carried out or at the very least, considered 
a long-term option. In other words, if a country continues to use coal and fuel 
as a source of energy for houses, businesses, and daily life, it will have long-
term consequences; thus, sustainable development is critical. However, although 
it is a great notion, implementing sustainable development is not as simple as 
expected. For one thing, the notion of sustainability may be greenwashed by 
many actors, notably a lack of good faith on the part of the superior, including 
governments or corporate actors, towards the weak. In addition, actors with less 
capability are more likely to face and be harmed by climate change. In light of the 
above, it is critical to investigate the green development funding model to learn 
how it functions and how much it contributes to mitigation efforts. Knowing the 
possible effects, risks, and repercussions in each area is also crucial for matching 
the budget allocation.
However, it should not be assumed that there is a generally applicable solution 
to this dilemma; rather, it is critical to situate the issue in its appropriate local 
context. With this immediate need for action in mind, the ASEAN Green Ideals

dilemma while also providing a chance for additional intellectual research into 
the Green Deal’s numerous and interesting features. To provide a thorough 
understanding and introduce a wide range of ideas from diverse perspectives

interdisciplinary research on the Green Deal with the goal of informing future 
policies that transcend national borders, emphasizing a more systematic and 
globally relevant approach. To  ensure a comprehensive yet holistic approach

1. Introduction 
The standard economic system of “business as usual (BAU)” has been unsuccessful 
in achieving comprehensive growth or social progress and has frequently resulted in 
damage to the environment and shortages (United Nations Economic Commission 
for Africa [UNECA], 2020). To address these issues, it is necessary to create a 
“green economy” that can promote the structural transformation of the economy, 
increase productivity and value-added, and address distributional impacts 
(UNECA, 2020). In 2011, the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) 
defined a “green economy” as an economic system that leads to better human 
welfare and fairness while significantly minimizing environmental hazards and 
ecological scarcity (UNECA, 2020). Similarly, the Organisation for Economic Co-
operation and Development (OECD) defined a “green economy” as an economic 
development that ensures that natural assets continue to provide the resources and 
environmental services on which development relies (OECD, 2011).
In 2022, as the rotating Chair of ASEAN, Cambodia proposed the ASEAN 
Green Deal to harness the green economy and combat climate change in the 
region. The deal is based on the European Green Deal, which aims to make the 
European Union carbon-neutral by 2050 (Chheang, 2023). The ASEAN Green 
Deal is a framework that aims to promote sustainable, inclusive, and resilient 
development in Southeast Asia. This chapter aims to shed light on the green 
economy, the objectives and driving forces of the ASEAN Green Deal, and 
potential implications on political and economic transformations.
2. Green Economy: A New Game in Town 
The concept of a green economy has gained momentum over the past decade 
due to the increasing global concern over climate emergency and environmental 
degradation caused by rapid, unsustainable economic growth. The green 
economy aims to promote sustainable development by minimizing the adverse 
impacts of economic activities on the ecosystem while maximizing the positive 
impact on social and economic well-being. There are several key indicators to 
measure the green economy, including the following: 
•	 Environmental and resource productivity
•	 Economic and environmental assets
•	 Environmental quality of life
•	 Economic opportunities and policy responses (OECD, 2011).

Green Ideals

A green economy should embed the five following principles (Green Economy 
Coalition, 2020):
First, the Wellbeing Principle aims to provide all individuals with the ability 
to generate and enjoy prosperity. 
Second, the Justice Principle strives for fairness and equity both for current 
and future generations through an impartial system that ensures that 
decisions, benefits, and costs are distributed equally. 
Third, the Planetary Boundaries Principle emphasizes the significance of 
safeguarding, repairing, and investing in nature. 
Fourth, the Efficiency and Sufficiency Principle promotes sustainable 
consumption and production through various means. 
Fifth, the Good Governance Principle is based on the idea of having institutions 
that are inclusive, transparent, and accountable. 
3. Driving Factors 
There are three main driving factors. First, political factors play a significant 
role in the emergence and development of the green economy. Governments 
are adopting policies to promote it. For a green economy transformation to 
take place effectively and successfully, it is necessary to establish a conducive 
political framework for negotiating institutional and legal reforms. Without 
such a framework, there is a risk that influential stakeholders may impede the 
process or push it in conflicting directions (UNECA, 2020). There are instances 
where green growth policies may compel countries to revise their national 
strategies in manners that can increase the financial burden and production 
costs for local economic players (Resnick et al., 2012).
Second, a market-based approach is crucial to the green economy. The transition 
to a green economy involves restructuring production and consumption patterns, 
which can have significant economic impacts. Market-based mechanisms can 
encourage flexibility in discovering solutions to enhance resource utilization, 
environmental quality and justice, as well as provide incentives to minimize the 
expenses of achieving green objectives. Moreover, they foster innovation that 
reduces the expense of implementing environmental sustainability criteria (Asian 
Development Bank, 2021).
Third, social factors also play a role in the green economy. Public attitudes and 
consumer behavior toward sustainability can influence political and economic 
decisions (Gugushvili, 2021). The political economy of the green economy is 
complex and shaped by a range of political, economic, and social forces. While 
the emergence of sustainable policies and practices has gained momentum in 
recent years, there are still challenges that need to be addressed to fully realize the 
potential of the green economy.

4. The EU Green Deal: A Source of Inspiration for ASEAN 
The European Green Deal is a comprehensive plan introduced by the European 
Union (EU) to tackle climate change and create a more sustainable future for 
Europe. The plan was announced by the European Commission in December 
2019 and aims to make Europe carbon-neutral by 2050. The EU Green Deal covers 
a wide range of topics, including energy, transport, agriculture, biodiversity, and 
waste management, and sets out a roadmap for achieving a more sustainable and 
environmentally friendly Europe (Fetting, 2020).
One of the primary goals of the EU Green Deal is to reduce greenhouse 
gas emissions. The EU aims to cut emissions by at least 55 percent by 2030, 
compared to 1990 levels, and reach net-zero emissions by 2050 (European 
Commission [EC], 2021). Another key element of the EU Green Deal is the 
protection of biodiversity. The European Union’s biodiversity strategy for 
2030 is an extensive, ambitious, and long-term blueprint for safeguarding the 
environment and reversing the deterioration of ecosystems. The objective of 
the plan is to lead Europe’s biodiversity towards recovery by 2030 and includes 
specific measures and commitments (EC, 2020). Furthermore, the Commission 
recommends reducing the use and hazards of chemical pesticides by 50 percent 
by 2030 (EC, 2022).
The EU Green Deal also includes plans to transition to a circular economy. 
This means reducing waste and increasing the use of recycled materials. By 
2030, the European Union intends to cut residual municipal waste by 50 percent, 
and the recycling goals for municipal waste are inherently related (European 
Environment Agency, 2023).
The EU Taxonomy Legislation came into effect on July 12, 2020, with 
the aim of promoting sustainable investment, which will contribute to the 
realization of the European Green Deal. Moreover, it is a significant tool for 
encouraging and facilitating changes and transitions towards sustainability. 
The Taxonomy Regulation outlines six fundamental environmental objectives, 
including (a) “mitigating climate change”; (b) “adapting to climate change”; 
(c) “sustainably utilizing and protecting water and marine resources”; (d) 
“transitioning towards a circular economy”; (e) “preventing and controlling 
pollution”; and (f) “protecting and restoring biodiversity and ecosystems” (Keo 
& Chheang, 2022, p. 126). 
5. Green Development in Southeast Asia 
Over the past few decades, Southeast Asia’s economy has grown significantly, but 
there are a myriad of economic, social, and environmental issues and challenges 
that need to be tackled. The current growth model relies heavily on exploiting 
natural resources, particularly in the least developed economies. To tackle these 
challenges, it is important to strengthen public and private institutions, structurally

8
reform the economic systems, integrate green growth into national policy design 
and implementation, and steer sustainable growth to ensure the well-being and 
prosperity of the people (OECD, 2014). In other words, a people-centric approach 
needs to be adhered to.
Notably, green development is becoming increasingly important as the region 
faces mounting environmental challenges such as climate change. One of the 
main benefits of green development in Southeast Asia is the potential to reduce 
environmental degradation and promote sustainability. Southeast Asia is home to 
some of the world’s most biodiverse ecosystems, but these ecosystems are under 
threat due to unsustainable practices, such as deforestation and mining. Green 
development can help to protect these ecosystems by promoting sustainable land 
use, such as agroforestry and sustainable forestry practices. Another potential 
benefit of green development in Southeast Asia is the creation of green jobs and 
economic growth. Green industries, such as renewable energy and sustainable 
agriculture, have the potential to create new jobs and stimulate economic growth. 
The growth of green industries can also help to reduce poverty and improve 
social equity.
However, there are also challenges to implementing green development 
in Southeast Asia. One of the main challenges is the lack of political will and 
institutional capacity. Many governments in the region have not yet prioritized 
environmental sustainability, and there is often a lack of political will to 
implement green policies. In addition, many countries in the region lack the 
institutional capacity to enforce environmental regulations and promote 
sustainable development.
Another challenge is the lack of funding for green development projects. 
Many green projects require significant investments, and there is often a lack of 
funding from both public and private sources. In addition, the high costs of green 
technologies, such as renewable energy, can make it difficult for Southeast Asian 
countries to transition to a more sustainable economy.
To conclude here, green development is an important concept for Southeast 
Asia as the region faces significant environmental challenges. Green development 
has the potential to reduce environmental degradation, promote sustainability, 
and create new jobs and economic growth. A green recovery from the COVID-19 
pandemic could transform Southeast Asia into an “economic powerhouse” 
(Argyriou, 2020). However, there are also challenges to implementing green 
development in the region, including the lack of political will and institutional 
capacity and the lack of funding for green projects. To promote green development 
in Southeast Asia, governments and international organizations can take several 
steps to support sustainable practices and invest in green technologies and 
industries.

6. The ASEAN Green Deal 
The ASEAN Green Deal is a framework that aims to promote resilient, inclusive 
and sustainable development in Southeast Asia. Overall, the ASEAN Green Deal 
should (a) promote knowledge sharing and capacity building on green economy 
and green innovation; (b) generate new opportunities from the adoption of green 
technologies and improved production capacity; (c) generate new opportunities 
for investment in green infrastructure through public-private partnerships 
and innovation in new sustainable technologies, as well as new programs for 
ecological maintenance; (d) promote sustainable production and consumption; 
and (e) develop integrated and innovative solutions to green economy and green 
transformation.
Some of the key elements of the ASEAN Green Deal might include (a) green 
energy, infrastructure, and logistics to support the global transition to a zero-
carbon, affordable, and resilient energy system; (b) green production and green 
consumption by harnessing new technologies and applications that reshape value 
chains to improve efficiency, lower costs and reduce environmental impact; and 
(c) green finance platform to mobilize public and private investment for green 
transformation in energy and infrastructure1. 
The ASEAN Green Deal will contribute to the ASEAN region’s transition 
to a green future, sustainability, resource efficiency, resilience, and economic 
competitiveness. It covers a wide range of areas, from infrastructure, energy, and 
manufacturing to consumption and agriculture. The detailed concept and action 
plan of the ASEAN Green Deal have yet to be developed, but generally it seeks 
to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, enhance energy security and efficiency, and 
promote sustainable agriculture and circular economy practices.
Although ASEAN and its member states have shown strong commitment 
to climate action, the region’s emissions are among the fastest growing 
in the world. Southeast Asia has experienced rapid population growth, 
urbanization, industrialization, rising income levels, and development gains 
over the past few decades, resulting in a significant increase in emissions. 
While region-wide action, especially around initiatives related to renewable 
energy deployment and energy efficiency, has been increasing, it is essential 
to transition to clean energy sources to mitigate the impacts of these trends. 
Without such efforts, energy-related emissions in ASEAN are predicted to 
nearly double by 2040 (ASEAN Green Future, 2021).
Various ASEAN Member States (AMS) have set targets for reducing 
greenhouse gas emissions. For instance, Cambodia has committed to reducing 42 
percent of emissions below “business as usual (BAU)”  levels by 2030. Indonesia

The ASEAN Green Deal has the potential to have a significant impact on

However, there are challenges to implementing the ASEAN Green Deal. The 
deal relies on the cooperation of all ASEAN Member States, and some countries 
may be reluctant to adopt sustainable policies that could impact their economic 
growth. Additionally, the costs of transitioning to a more sustainable economy 
could be high, particularly for the less developed economies. At the national 
level, governments play a crucial role in the implementation of the Green Deal. 
National governments will need to develop and implement policies to achieve 
the objectives of the Green Deal. 
Local governments also play a crucial role in the implementation of the Green 
Deal. Local governments can implement policies to reduce emissions from 
transport, such as promoting the use of bicycles and public transportation and 
promoting energy-efficient buildings. Local governments can also implement 
policies to protect biodiversity and promote sustainable land use.
One of the main benefits of domestic politics in promoting green development 
is the ability to create policies and regulations that incentivize sustainable 
practices and penalize unsustainable practices. Governments can use a range of 
policy tools, such as taxes, subsidies, and regulations, to promote sustainable 
practices. For example, governments can provide subsidies for renewable energy, 
tax incentives for energy-efficient buildings, and regulations to reduce emissions 
from industries.
Another benefit of domestic politics in promoting green development is the 
potential to create green jobs and stimulate economic growth. Green industries, 
such as renewable energy and sustainable agriculture, have the potential to create 
new jobs and stimulate economic growth. Governments can create policies and 
programs to support the growth of green industries, such as providing funding for 
research and development or creating training programs for workers.
However, there are also challenges to promoting green development 
through domestic politics. One of the main challenges is the lack of political 
will and institutional capacity. Governments may not prioritize environmental

In addition, governments may lack the institutional capacity to enforce

To address these challenges, governments should prioritize environmental

The following are key areas to focus on for achieving a zero-carbon, affordable,

Agenda for Sustainable Development:
•	 Advancing the decarbonization of the energy system to provide reliable 
and affordable access to zero-carbon energy for all.
•	 Developing smart, low-carbon, water-secure, and climate-resilient cities, 
infrastructure, and mobility to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and 
enhance water security.
•	 Developing blended finance for sustainable investments in energy, 
infrastructure, logistics, food production, and water supply.
•	 Accelerating and scaling up innovations in sustainable development by 
implementing new business models and solutions to reduce environmental 
impact.
•	 Transitioning towards a more circular economy to maximize resource 
efficiency and minimize environmental impact, which will create new 
business and employment opportunities (UNESCAP, 2022).
To achieve the policy objectives mentioned earlier, several strategic 
interventions need to be implemented. These include developing green and clean 
energy system; building green infrastructure and logistics for smart, green, and 
climate-resilient cities and buildings; promoting green finance to mobilize public 
and private investment for innovation in the energy sector, infrastructure, logistics, 
and other sectors of a green and circular economy; promoting green innovation 
and scaling up new technologies and applications to reduce environmental 
impact; and promoting a circular economy with new business and employment 
opportunities (UNESCAP, 2022).
Green Ideals
12
The ASEAN Framework on Circular Economy adopted in 2021 aims to 
achieve three strategic goals which are to promote resilient economy, resource 
efficiency, and sustainable growth. There are five strategic priorities, including 
(a) “standard harmonization and mutual recognition”, (b) “trade openness and 
trade facilitation”, (c) “innovation, digitalization and emerging technologies”, (d) 
“sustainable finance and innovative investments”, and (e) “efficient use of energy 
and other resources”. Additionally, there are six guiding principles, namely (a) 
encouraging the integration of ASEAN and the development of value chains 
within the region; (b) taking into account the overall impact on the economy 
and society; (c) acknowledging the distinctive circumstances of each ASEAN 
Member State; (d) fostering collaboration across ASEAN for the sharing of 
knowledge and technology; (e) assessing the financial and institutional viability 
and sustainability before implementing initiatives; and (f) operating within the 
context of international production connection (ASEAN Secretariat, 2021). The 
Circular Economy Framework presents a forward-thinking, far-reaching goal for 
the circular economy, leveraging the advantages of current ASEAN programs 
and projects. It also pinpoints crucial areas of emphasis and factors that will 
facilitate the advancement of a circular economy in ASEAN, with the aim of 
hastening its realization.
The green transition transformation cannot be realized without significant 
international support. ASEAN and its member states need financial and technical 
support from the dialogue partners to develop and implement the ASEAN Green 
Deal. For instance, ASEAN and the EU have closely cooperated on green 
economy and climate change. At the national level, it is important to establish a 
national-level cross-ministerial governance body in order to build political buy-in, 
build political consensus, formulate a holistic transition strategy, and strengthen 
inter-agency coordination to implement the ASEAN Green Deal.
The ASEAN region has the potential to expedite the transition to a low-
carbon economy and gain significant economic advantages. Leveraging its 
history of working together to address shared issues, the region can benefit from 
a coordinated approach to tackle one of the most pressing challenges of our 
era. By collaborating to recognize and tackle common obstacles, ASEAN can 
speed up its transition to a low-carbon future and facilitate the establishment 
of priority projects relating to green and circular economy across the region. 
ASEAN Member States have identified the establishment of a regional climate 
fund, carbon market, and power grid as the top three collective opportunities to 
accelerate the shift to a low-carbon economy (ASEAN Green Future, 2021).
In 2021, the ASEAN Taxonomy on Sustainable Development was introduced 
as a comprehensive guide for all ASEAN Member States to complement 
their respective national sustainability initiatives, and to serve as a common 
language for sustainable finance in the ASEAN region. It will cover capital 
markets, banking, and insurance sectors and will be multi-tiered and inclusive, 
The Political Economy of the ASEAN Green Deal
13
facilitating an orderly and effective transition towards a sustainable ASEAN. 
The development of the ASEAN Sustainable Finance Taxonomy will benefit all 
ASEAN Member States, providing an overarching guide that complements their 
national sustainability initiatives (Keo & Chheang, 2022).
7. Conclusion
The ASEAN Green Deal is an important framework for promoting resilient, 
inclusive, and sustainable development in Southeast Asia. By promoting clean 
and renewable energy, circular economy, green production, and green innovation, 
the deal has the potential to contribute to the global effort to mitigate climate 
change, while promoting regional transition into a green economy. However, 
there are challenges to implementing the deal, and it will require the cooperation 
of all ASEAN Member States and the private sector to achieve its objectives. 
International support is essential to assist ASEAN and its members to develop 
and carry out the ASEAN Green Deal.
Five strategic policy interventions are recommended to make the ASEAN 
Green Deal a reality. First, it is critical to invest in a carbon-neutral, dependable, 
affordable, and resilient energy system. Second, more emphasis should be placed 
on developing smart, green, and climate-resilient infrastructure. Third, public 
and private funds for green investment and transformation should be raised. 
Fourth, stakeholders should continue to accelerate and scale up green innovation. 
To implement UNESCAP’s Asia Pacific Green Deal and the Framework for 
Circular Economy for the ASEAN Economic Community, all parties should 
promote multi-stakeholder consultation and partnership building, as well as 
develop a green economic zone. In addition to green economy development, 
we require a holistic approach to wellbeing that integrates economic, social, and 
environmental solutions.

The message is not only loud but very clear. Only sincere, concrete and diligent 
global efforts can limit temperature increase to 1.5°C. The Intergovernmental 
Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Sixth Assessment Report, largely a confirmation 
of the previous five reports, reiterates the scientific consensus on global warming, 
greenhouse gases, and the climate change impact. The very recent Conference of 
Parties (COP) 28’s global stocktake on the situation, however, revealed a slow 
progress across different areas including greenhouse gas emissions, resilience 
to climate change, and lack of financial & technological support to vulnerable 
nations (United Nations Climate Change [UNCC], n.d.). As Kennedy said, 
“First is danger of futility” (Kennedy, 1966, para 32), the global initiatives don’t

The European Green Deal’s aims to reach net-zero greenhouse emissions 
within the European Union (EU) and deliver a pollution-free environment by 
2050 (EU-ASEAN, 2022b). Following commitments by other nations such as 
India, the United States, Japan, and China keep the hopes alive. Cambodia, a 
nation known for its remarkable resilience, not only in South East Asia but all 
over the world, has resolved to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by about 42 per 
cent by 2030 and by 2050, decarbonize its rapidly growing economy. 
This chapter discusses the ongoing global debate around climate change in 
light of decarbonization strategies, forest conservation, and renewable energy.

actions and to increase the insistence on renewable energy (Say, 2022).

2. Climate Change
Climate change is real. The overall increase in earth’s temperature (global 
warming) can be attributed to the significant increase in the greenhouse gases1 
due to human activities. These are produced by the burning of fossil fuels2, 
agricultural activities, wastes from production and consumption, refrigeration 
and air conditioning, and other activities3.
The Climate Change 2023 (‘Synthesis Report’) brings home the fact that 
humans have greatly contributed to the global heating for more than 195 
years leading to a current temperature increase of  1.1°C above pre-industrial 
levels. This in-turn has led to hazardous and frequent weather events that are 
extremely detrimental to the people and the planet (United Nations Environment 
Programme, 2023). The seven years from 2014-20 rank as the warmest years 
since 1880 (United Nations Environment Programme, 2023, p. 108). Lakes have 
shrunk, glaciers have melted, and the sea level has risen. Around 3.3 billion people 
live in areas vulnerable to climate change (Chatterley et al., 2023). According 
to the World Health Organization (2023), climate change could cause 250,000 
additional deaths per year from malaria, malnutrition, heat stress, and diarrhoea, 
between 2030-50. Fires, floods, and droughts in various parts are some other 
consequences of change being felt in different parts of the world. Hans Joachim 
Schellnhuber, one of the leading climate researchers whilst underscoring the 
gravity of the problem has warned about a civilisational collapse (Moses, 2020).

Cambodia’s climate change vulnerability as one of high disaster-prone countries 
globally makes it a priority contender for sustained actions (Climate Change 
Knowledge Portal, 2021). Between 2011 and 2018, droughts have affected 
nearly over seven and a half million hectares of land, and floods and storms have

3. Decarbonization or Carbon Neutrality
Carbon neutrality is expressed as the balance sought to be achieved between 
emitting carbon and absorbing carbon emissions by carbon sinks such as forests, 
soils and oceans. It is a term used interchangeably with ‘net zero’ which envisages 
a situation where no carbon is emitted at the very outset. The Paris Agreement 
was a breakthrough for achieving the common consensus for carbon neutrality to 
limit global warming to below 2°C (preferably 1.5°C). Signatories to the Accord 
were required to submit Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC’s). 
Speaking of Cambodia’s resolve towards decarbonization, it has already 
ratified the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change 
(UNFCCC), acceded to the Kyoto Protocol and subsequently has adopted the 
Paris Climate Agreement in 2016. It presented a long-term strategy in 2021 to 
reflect its firm commitment towards the Paris Agreement and to achieve the goal 
of carbon neutrality in the next 30 years10.  The strategy presents the institutional 
arrangements for development of a monitoring and evaluation framework, long-
term planning, and analysis of socioeconomic impacts and financial options of 
selected actions that need to be prioritized (NCSD, 2021). Based on rules for 
reporting and review under the Enhanced Transparency Framework of the Paris 
Agreement, Cambodia also put in place the NDC tracking tool, which traces the 
progress towards achieving and implementing its NDC11. 
Since the early 2000s, the country has pro-actively been involved in, and 
has implemented voluntarily, projects for mitigation of Green House Gasses 
(GHG’s) including Angkor Bio Cogen Rice Husk Power Project, a methane fired 
power generation plant in Samrong Thom, Animal Husbandry Biogas, TTY 
Cambodia Biogas Project and Kampot Cement Waste Heat Power Generation 
Project (KCC-WHG)12. In 2013, the Climate Change Strategic Plan (CCCSP) 
(2014-2023) was adopted to steer the country towards achieving a green, 
climate resilient, low-carbon, sustainable, equitable, and knowledge-oriented 
society. According to the First Biennial Update report to the UNFCCC (2020), 
Cambodia emitted an average of 163.59 megatons of CO2-equivalent in 2016, 
285 per cent more than that in the year 1994 (NCSD, 2020b). Forest and Other

4. Forest Conservation
Forests are fundamental components for the planet’s recovery (Fothergill et al., 
2020). They are nature’s carbon sinks and their importance in maintaining the 
ecological balance is acknowledged from time immemorial. Forests are not only 
essential for wildlife but people as well. Over 1.6 billion people need forests for 
food, timber, fuel, shelter and jobs (United Nations Department of Economic 
and Social Affairs, 2020), most importantly, for oxygen. Forests play an integral 
role in maintaining the Earth’s water cycle. Plant and tree roots keep soil from 
washing away in heavy rainfall and clogging rivers (National Geographic Kids, 
2016, p. 288). World’s forests could provide ecosystem services worth 16.2 
trillion USD annually (National Geographic Kids, 2016, p. 26). Afforestation 
could absorb 66 per cent of the carbon emissions in the atmosphere (Fothergill 
et al., 2020).
A crucial factor responsible for high vulnerability in the ASEAN region 
in relation to climate change is massive deforestation that leads to negative 
implications for environmental feedback effects and most importantly local 
resilience. The ASEAN Joint Statement on Climate Change to COP 28 
reaffirms the commitment of the ASEAN Member States to promote sustainable 
management of forests through Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and 
Forest Degradation and the role of conservation, sustainable management of 
forests and enhancement of forest carbon stocks in developing countries (REDD+) 
(ASEAN, 2023). Due to persistent droughts and climatic disturbances, around 4 
million hectares of lowland forests, especially in the southwest and northeast, are 
likely to be affected which may result in serious repercussions. High deforestation

5. Renewable Energy
The changing geopolitical dynamics following the Ukraine war have tilted the 
balance in favor of clean energy and the European nations greatly acknowledge 
its importance. Germany’s energy strategy (Energiewiende) aims to achieve 80 
per cent renewable energy target by 2050. State of the art fossil-free technologies 
such as green hydrogen, sustainable aviation fuels, fossil-free steel coupled with 
carbon capture and storage capabilities are set to change the ways in which the 
markets function and operate.
ASEAN too has identified its key areas- renewable energy diffusion and 
energy efficiency improvement. Ensuring energy efficiency would entail proper 
management of advanced coal and gas power plants whilst offering a greater 
impetus to renewable energy portfolio diversification (i.e., solar, wind, large 
scale hydroelectricity, geothermal etc.). The ASEAN Power Grid project aims 
to prioritize rural electrification and ensure energy security, transborder energy 
interconnection and renewable power penetration in the future - so much so that 
an aspirational target has been set to increase the share of renewable energy in 
the ASEAN energy mix to 23% and the total installed power capacity to 35% by 
2025 (ASEAN Centre for Energy, 2020). 
As Cambodia embarks upon its growth journey, the demand for energy has 
increased at an unprecedented rate.  The per capita electricity consumption has 
risen around 18 per cent year-on-year during 2010-2019, whilst electricity demand 
has increased more than four-fold over the same period (Open Development 
Mekong, 2022). Investments in clean energy projects are extremely important 
to meet the increased energy requirements to ensure sustained, balanced, and 
efficient growth. The National Energy Efficiency Policy provides the long-term 
vision to transform the consumption of energy in Cambodia to create a strong 
vibrant economy whilst fostering sustainable development. It also envisages the 
policy, regulatory and sector specific intervention programs and a mechanism to 
facilitate coordination amongst various governmental agencies. 
Extraordinary times call for extraordinary measures. Specific measurable 
targets to achieve energy efficient goals are the key. The national target for

Keeping in mind, Cambodia’s rivers and highlands in its geographical

6. ESG, Green Financing, and Sustainable Financial Inclusion 
The focus of investments should be the emerging and developing nations. It is 
extremely important that ESG compliant companies (or seemingly so) walk the 
talk rather than just talking the talk. Transformative greenification of businesses 
is seen with scepticism by some corporations and investors. Profit is certainly 
not a dirty word. However responsible, businesses are expected to be profitable 
ones. Green washing may thus be preferred to risk taking.  The Securities and 
Exchange Commission in the United States has adopted rules to standardise and 
enhance climate related disclosure for investors (US Securities and Exchange 
Commission, 2024). The European Union’s Corporate Sustainability Reporting 
Directive (CSRD) entered into force on 5 January 2023 aims to bring around 
50,000 companies under its ambit (European Parliament, 2022). 
Financing forest action is needed to address climate crisis. Green Climate 
Fund (GCF) has been set up to scale up financing and catalyse investment for

Foreword
Every country needs a strategy to address the great challenges of our age: rapid 
technological advance, the urgent need for advanced education and skills, the 
rapid transformation to green technologies, the need for regional solutions that 
transcend national borders, and the need for diplomacy in order to operate 
effectively in a multipolar world. In sum, every country needs a strategy for 
Sustainable Development.
This volume proves that Cambodia is undertaking an intensive transformation 
to an advanced knowledge economy that aims to utilize science, technology, and 
innovation (STI) to address the many dimensions of sustainable development. In 
this exceptionally strong compendium of essays, Cambodian scientists, scholars, 
policymakers, and thought leaders, as well as co-authors from other ASEAN 
nations, explore every dimension of Cambodia’s sustainable development 
challenges, from considerations of the local environment to the opportunities for 
global diplomacy. This expansive perspective – ranging across issues, scientific 
disciplines, and scales of action – is just what is needed for Cambodia to meet 
its national objective of becoming a high-income and sustainable society by mid-
century, if not sooner.
What is most impressive to me is Cambodia’s recognition that all success 
will depend on the quality of education of Cambodia’s young people, and their 
preparation for an interconnected, knowledge-intensive, and digitally driven 
world economy. Cambodian scholars and policy leaders recognize that every 
sector of the Cambodian economy will soon have to be a “high-skilled” sector, 
including even the so-called traditional sectors such as textiles, tourism, and 
agriculture. Each sector of the economy, and all successful enterprises, will 
be digitally empowered, linked to artificial intelligence and other machine 
learning, and in need of continual innovations in order for Cambodia to remain 
globally connected and competitive. In short, Cambodia must prepare to thrive 
in an age of rapid technological advancement.
If the digital age were all that is challenging Cambodia, that alone would be a 
major challenge. But Cambodia faces even greater challenges. As a remarkable 
tropical environment of unique biodiversity and ecosystems, Cambodia depends 
on its natural capital for its sustenance, culture, and global competitiveness. Yet 
Cambodia’s vital natural capital is already under deep stress, both because of 
past poor practices in land use, waste management, and industrial pollution 
and because ongoing global environmental changes (most importantly, global 
warming) will create major new risks for Cambodia regarding water management, 
agricultural production, urban habitability, and protection of biodiversity.
As the essays here underscore, the Royal Government of Cambodia, 
together with Cambodia’s leading universities and scientific centers, have 
turned their curricula, research priorities, and operating budgets to face these 
new challenges. The returns will be enormous. Cambodia’s investments in 
Green Ideals
vi
STI will result in enormous advances in Cambodian productivity, efficiency of 
energy and materials use, and sustainability. These advances in turn will enable 
Cambodia to achieve rapid economic growth in the decades ahead, also taking 
advantage of the overall rapid growth of East Asia.
The essays here touch on every dimension of the STI agenda: water resource 
management, agricultural productivity, circular economy, and achievement of 
a zero-carbon energy system. In each area, the urgency is clear. Cambodia is 
already facing the risks of intensified droughts and floods, heatwaves, and land 
degradation. Yet the opportunities are even greater. Through smart technologies, 
Cambodia will be able to raise agricultural productivity, reduce food wastes, 
build a regional power grid based on renewable energy, and enhance Cambodia’s 
standing as a global destination for sustainable tourism.
One of the great innovations ahead lies in Cambodia’s future Universities 
4.0, meaning Cambodian universities that are technologically enabled and 
organizationally structured to train young people to become national and 
global leaders of sustainable development. A University for Sustainability will 
teach the interconnections among the Earth’s physical systems, the engineered 
infrastructure systems, and the socio-politico-economic systems. It will train 
students and researchers in the policy methods needed to achieve sustainable 
development. It will guide students through the ethical underpinnings needed for 
a high-income sustainable society. And it will train future problem solvers in the 
diplomatic arts of regional and global collaboration.
The essays in this volume recognize at every juncture that Cambodia is not 
alone in facing these great challenges, and that indeed, Cambodia can meet its 
national objectives only through extensive diplomacy and global cooperation. 
International cooperation will be needed at many scales. The ASEAN countries 
working together will need to build an interconnected zero-carbon power grid 
extending across ASEAN and connecting ASEAN with neighbors including 
Australia, China, and others. ASEAN countries will need to coordinate on the 
protection of ASEAN’s rainforests, fisheries, coastal areas, and river sheds. 
ASEAN nations will need to join together in fruitful diplomacy with other 
regions of the world, such as with the European Union. In this regard, ASEAN’s 
Green Deal will be an important diplomat counterpart to the European Green 
Deal and will enable the EU and ASEAN to set mutually agreed rules for trade, 
finance, and technological change.
ASEAN will also need to play a major global leadership role as well, in the 
UN General Assembly, the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, the 
UN Convention on Biological Diversity, the G20, the BRICS, and other global 
venues. As the chapter on Climate Finance makes clear, Cambodia’s success 
will also depend on access to high-quality international financing – long-term 
loans, green bonds, foreign direct investments, and various kinds of grants from 
international institutions – in order for Cambodia to invest at the scale needed 
to achieve rapid growth combined with sustainable development. Cambodia’s

In sum, the coming years will be a period of rapid global change. With 
leadership, vision, ethics, good governance, and strong national institutions 
working in collaboration with other nations, Cambodia is poised for very exciting 
advances. The volume’s lead editors are Prof. Chhem Kieth Rethy, a scientist, 
physician, and former UN diplomat, Dr. Chem Phalla, an engineer specializing

Their dedicated partnership during the past decade has focused on development

environmental, social, and economic dimensions. The editors and the authors 
of this volume deserve high praise and careful attention to their many important 
insights and recommendations, which together provide an important framework 
for Cambodia’s path to sustainable development.

Preface
Cambodian Scholars’ Vision of the Green Deal
In an era defined by unprecedented environmental challenges and the urgent need 
for sustainable solutions, the world’s attention has turned towards the ambitious 
concept known as the “Green Deal.” This comprehensive framework has since 
captured the imaginations of policymakers, scholars, and citizens around the globe. 
The Green Deal represents a holistic approach to addressing pressing issues related 
to climate change, environmental sustainability, and socio-economic development.
The “Green Deal” concept encompasses practical policies, frameworks, and 
strategies aimed  at mitigating the consequences of climate change and promoting 
sustainable development.  Conversely, “Green Ideals” are the aspirational objectives, 
principles, and visions that serve as the  impetus for these pragmatic initiatives. The 
Green Ideals are the visionary foundation that propels  these endeavours, while the 
Green Deal concentrates on implementation. It is imperative for  ASEAN to adopt 
Green Ideals as a Green Deal aspiration, as this ensures that practical actions are 
consistent with high standards and long-term environmental objectives, thereby 
promoting a more  comprehensive and unified approach to sustainability. In 2022, 
former Samdech Prime Minister  Hun Sen introduced the concept of the green 
deal. To strengthen early efforts from governments  to further define the ASEAN 
Green Deal—currently a vision and early regional initiative—this  book aims to 
clarify the concept. By offering diverse perspectives, it endorses the critical mission 
of the 2022 Green Deal and underscores the region’s need to take it seriously, 
thereby transforming  ideals into actionable ideas and impactful outcomes.
As we embark on this journey through the perspectives and insights of 
Cambodian scholars and experts, we explore a diverse array of topics, each 
intertwined with the overarching theme of the Green Deal. From the intricate 
geopolitics of this transformative initiative to the vital connections between 
Sustainable Development Goal 13 (SDG 13) and circular economy principles, this 
book offers a multifaceted exploration of the Green Deal’s far-reaching impact. 
In our exploration, we uncover the intricate connections between international 
trade and the circular economy, demonstrating how economic policies can either 
reinforce or hinder our progress toward a greener future. We investigate the realms 
of climate and water diplomacy, shedding light on the crucial role of diplomacy 
in addressing shared environmental challenges. As technology continues to 
shape our world, we examine the concept of Green Digital Transformation and 
how it can revolutionize our approach to sustainability. The book looks into 
the complexities of energy diplomacy within the Green Deal framework and 
explores the nexus between food systems, security, and sustainable agriculture. 
We also highlight the critical intersections of science, technology, and 
innovation, including the advent of Industry 4.0, in driving forward the 
Green Deal’s objectives. Environmental scientists, as well as their invaluable 
Green Ideals
x
contributions, take center stage in this discourse, emphasizing the pivotal role 
they play in shaping a greener future.
The Green Deal is not just about the environment; it is about global health 
too. Climate change’s impact on public health is a pressing concern, and we 
investigate how it intertwines with this grand endeavor. The concept of a 
University for Sustainability is presented as a potential game-changer in 
educating and equipping the next generation of leaders with the tools to navigate 
the challenges of our time.
Financing is at the heart of any transformative initiative, and we explore the 
various mechanisms and strategies for funding Green Deal programs. Sustainable 
tourism, as a key economic sector, is examined in-depth, considering its potential 
to drive sustainable development.     Lastly, we explore the creation of a green-
built environment, showcasing innovative architectural and design approaches 
that prioritize sustainability. 
The chapters within this book offer a panoramic view of the Green Deal’s 
multifaceted dimensions, weaving together the perspectives of Cambodian 
scholars and experts with global implications. Through these insightful 
contributions, we hope to inspire discussions, spark innovation, and foster a 
deeper understanding of the transformative potential of the Green Deal on both 
local and global scales. It is our collective hope that this book will serve as a 
valuable resource for policymakers, academics, students, and anyone passionate 
about building a sustainable and resilient future for our planet.
In practice this book was conceived as a compilation of chapters contributed by 
a diverse group of scholars, practitioners, and policy researchers. All of them are 
thoughtful and clear-thinking researchers. The intention was not to impose a strict 
formatting style on the individual chapters. Instead, the editors chose to provide 
authors with the freedom to express their research and ideas creatively. Our goal was 
to encourage each author to explore the urgent need for a Green Deal in their own 
unique way.
By doing so, we aimed to foster brainstorming and gather the most innovative, 
unrestrained ideas and solutions to address the pressing challenges posed by climate 
change and its far-reaching impacts on both humanity and the environment. In 
summary, the aim was to create a book that is both approachable and thorough, serving 
as the starting point for our intellectual exploration of the intricate and captivating 
aspects of the Green Deal. The wide array of ideas from diverse perspectives can 
serve as a foundation for conducting comprehensive interdisciplinary research on 
the Green Deal that aims to inform future policies that transcend national borders, 
emphasizing a more systematic and globally relevant approach.

INTRODUCTION 
As global temperatures rise, the future existence of humans and other living 
species is called into question. Climate change and the environment have emerged 
as global concerns. The United Nations (UN), as a global governance actor, 
has played a critical role in developing and promoting policies to decrease and 
influence the norm in response to climate change. For example, the majority UN 
of member states have supported the United Nations Sustainable Development 
Goals, which are scheduled to be fulfilled by 2030. It is important to highlight that 
although development is vital and the state must seek to provide a better quality 
of life for its residents, it should be carried out or at the very least, considered 
a long-term option. In other words, if a country continues to use coal and fuel 
as a source of energy for houses, businesses, and daily life, it will have long-
term consequences; thus, sustainable development is critical. However, although 
it is a great notion, implementing sustainable development is not as simple as 
expected. For one thing, the notion of sustainability may be greenwashed by 
many actors, notably a lack of good faith on the part of the superior, including 
governments or corporate actors, towards the weak. In addition, actors with less 
capability are more likely to face and be harmed by climate change. In light of the 
above, it is critical to investigate the green development funding model to learn 
how it functions and how much it contributes to mitigation efforts. Knowing the 
possible effects, risks, and repercussions in each area is also crucial for matching 
the budget allocation.
However, it should not be assumed that there is a generally applicable solution 
to this dilemma; rather, it is critical to situate the issue in its appropriate local 
context. With this immediate need for action in mind, the ASEAN Green Ideals 
Book was created to analyze the region’s sustainable or green development 
dilemma while also providing a chance for additional intellectual research into 
the Green Deal’s numerous and interesting features. To provide a thorough 
understanding and introduce a wide range of ideas from diverse perspectives 
from various authors with multidisciplinary backgrounds, it is important to note 
that the ASEAN Green Ideals book was designed to conduct comprehensive 
interdisciplinary research on the Green Deal with the goal of informing future 
policies that transcend national borders, emphasizing a more systematic and 
globally relevant approach. To  ensure a comprehensive yet holistic approach 
to sustainable development, the book strives to  incorporate the green ideal 
suggestion into each chapter, either as a practical application or as a  framework 
for the green deals. This will be particularly relevant in the development of the 
ASEAN  Green Deals as a structured and implementable document.
