Chapter 1: The Political Economy of the ASEAN Green Deal
CHHORT Chhorravuth* and CHHEANG Vannarith
1. Introduction 
The standard economic system of “business as usual (BAU)” has been unsuccessful 
in achieving comprehensive growth or social progress and has frequently resulted in 
damage to the environment and shortages (United Nations Economic Commission 
for Africa [UNECA], 2020). To address these issues, it is necessary to create a 
“green economy” that can promote the structural transformation of the economy, 
increase productivity and value-added, and address distributional impacts 
(UNECA, 2020). In 2011, the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) 
defined a “green economy” as an economic system that leads to better human 
welfare and fairness while significantly minimizing environmental hazards and 
ecological scarcity (UNECA, 2020). Similarly, the Organisation for Economic Co-
operation and Development (OECD) defined a “green economy” as an economic 
development that ensures that natural assets continue to provide the resources and 
environmental services on which development relies (OECD, 2011).
In 2022, as the rotating Chair of ASEAN, Cambodia proposed the ASEAN 
Green Deal to harness the green economy and combat climate change in the 
region. The deal is based on the European Green Deal, which aims to make the 
European Union carbon-neutral by 2050 (Chheang, 2023). The ASEAN Green 
Deal is a framework that aims to promote sustainable, inclusive, and resilient 
development in Southeast Asia. This chapter aims to shed light on the green 
economy, the objectives and driving forces of the ASEAN Green Deal, and 
potential implications on political and economic transformations.
2. Green Economy: A New Game in Town 
The concept of a green economy has gained momentum over the past decade 
due to the increasing global concern over climate emergency and environmental 
degradation caused by rapid, unsustainable economic growth. The green 
economy aims to promote sustainable development by minimizing the adverse 
impacts of economic activities on the ecosystem while maximizing the positive 
impact on social and economic well-being. There are several key indicators to 
measure the green economy, including the following: 
•	 Environmental and resource productivity
•	 Economic and environmental assets
•	 Environmental quality of life
•	 Economic opportunities and policy responses (OECD, 2011).

Green Ideals
6
A green economy should embed the five following principles (Green Economy 
Coalition, 2020):
First, the Wellbeing Principle aims to provide all individuals with the ability 
to generate and enjoy prosperity. 
Second, the Justice Principle strives for fairness and equity both for current 
and future generations through an impartial system that ensures that 
decisions, benefits, and costs are distributed equally. 
Third, the Planetary Boundaries Principle emphasizes the significance of 
safeguarding, repairing, and investing in nature. 
Fourth, the Efficiency and Sufficiency Principle promotes sustainable 
consumption and production through various means. 
Fifth, the Good Governance Principle is based on the idea of having institutions 
that are inclusive, transparent, and accountable. 
3. Driving Factors 
There are three main driving factors. First, political factors play a significant 
role in the emergence and development of the green economy. Governments 
are adopting policies to promote it. For a green economy transformation to 
take place effectively and successfully, it is necessary to establish a conducive 
political framework for negotiating institutional and legal reforms. Without 
such a framework, there is a risk that influential stakeholders may impede the 
process or push it in conflicting directions (UNECA, 2020). There are instances 
where green growth policies may compel countries to revise their national 
strategies in manners that can increase the financial burden and production 
costs for local economic players (Resnick et al., 2012).
Second, a market-based approach is crucial to the green economy. The transition 
to a green economy involves restructuring production and consumption patterns, 
which can have significant economic impacts. Market-based mechanisms can 
encourage flexibility in discovering solutions to enhance resource utilization, 
environmental quality and justice, as well as provide incentives to minimize the 
expenses of achieving green objectives. Moreover, they foster innovation that 
reduces the expense of implementing environmental sustainability criteria (Asian 
Development Bank, 2021).
Third, social factors also play a role in the green economy. Public attitudes and 
consumer behavior toward sustainability can influence political and economic 
decisions (Gugushvili, 2021). The political economy of the green economy is 
complex and shaped by a range of political, economic, and social forces. While 
the emergence of sustainable policies and practices has gained momentum in 
recent years, there are still challenges that need to be addressed to fully realize the 
potential of the green economy.

7
4. The EU Green Deal: A Source of Inspiration for ASEAN 
The European Green Deal is a comprehensive plan introduced by the European 
Union (EU) to tackle climate change and create a more sustainable future for 
Europe. The plan was announced by the European Commission in December 
2019 and aims to make Europe carbon-neutral by 2050. The EU Green Deal covers 
a wide range of topics, including energy, transport, agriculture, biodiversity, and 
waste management, and sets out a roadmap for achieving a more sustainable and 
environmentally friendly Europe (Fetting, 2020).
One of the primary goals of the EU Green Deal is to reduce greenhouse 
gas emissions. The EU aims to cut emissions by at least 55 percent by 2030, 
compared to 1990 levels, and reach net-zero emissions by 2050 (European 
Commission [EC], 2021). Another key element of the EU Green Deal is the 
protection of biodiversity. The European Union’s biodiversity strategy for 
2030 is an extensive, ambitious, and long-term blueprint for safeguarding the 
environment and reversing the deterioration of ecosystems. The objective of 
the plan is to lead Europe’s biodiversity towards recovery by 2030 and includes 
specific measures and commitments (EC, 2020). Furthermore, the Commission 
recommends reducing the use and hazards of chemical pesticides by 50 percent 
by 2030 (EC, 2022).
The EU Green Deal also includes plans to transition to a circular economy. 
This means reducing waste and increasing the use of recycled materials. By 
2030, the European Union intends to cut residual municipal waste by 50 percent, 
and the recycling goals for municipal waste are inherently related (European 
Environment Agency, 2023).
The EU Taxonomy Legislation came into effect on July 12, 2020, with 
the aim of promoting sustainable investment, which will contribute to the 
realization of the European Green Deal. Moreover, it is a significant tool for 
encouraging and facilitating changes and transitions towards sustainability. 
The Taxonomy Regulation outlines six fundamental environmental objectives, 
including (a) “mitigating climate change”; (b) “adapting to climate change”; 
(c) “sustainably utilizing and protecting water and marine resources”; (d) 
“transitioning towards a circular economy”; (e) “preventing and controlling 
pollution”; and (f) “protecting and restoring biodiversity and ecosystems” (Keo 
& Chheang, 2022, p. 126). 
5. Green Development in Southeast Asia 
Over the past few decades, Southeast Asia’s economy has grown significantly, but 
there are a myriad of economic, social, and environmental issues and challenges 
that need to be tackled. The current growth model relies heavily on exploiting 
natural resources, particularly in the least developed economies. To tackle these 
challenges, it is important to strengthen public and private institutions, structurally 
Green Ideals
8
reform the economic systems, integrate green growth into national policy design 
and implementation, and steer sustainable growth to ensure the well-being and 
prosperity of the people (OECD, 2014). In other words, a people-centric approach 
needs to be adhered to.
Notably, green development is becoming increasingly important as the region 
faces mounting environmental challenges such as climate change. One of the 
main benefits of green development in Southeast Asia is the potential to reduce 
environmental degradation and promote sustainability. Southeast Asia is home to 
some of the world’s most biodiverse ecosystems, but these ecosystems are under 
threat due to unsustainable practices, such as deforestation and mining. Green 
development can help to protect these ecosystems by promoting sustainable land 
use, such as agroforestry and sustainable forestry practices. Another potential 
benefit of green development in Southeast Asia is the creation of green jobs and 
economic growth. Green industries, such as renewable energy and sustainable 
agriculture, have the potential to create new jobs and stimulate economic growth. 
The growth of green industries can also help to reduce poverty and improve 
social equity.
However, there are also challenges to implementing green development 
in Southeast Asia. One of the main challenges is the lack of political will and 
institutional capacity. Many governments in the region have not yet prioritized 
environmental sustainability, and there is often a lack of political will to 
implement green policies. In addition, many countries in the region lack the 
institutional capacity to enforce environmental regulations and promote 
sustainable development.
Another challenge is the lack of funding for green development projects. 
Many green projects require significant investments, and there is often a lack of 
funding from both public and private sources. In addition, the high costs of green 
technologies, such as renewable energy, can make it difficult for Southeast Asian 
countries to transition to a more sustainable economy.
To conclude here, green development is an important concept for Southeast 
Asia as the region faces significant environmental challenges. Green development 
has the potential to reduce environmental degradation, promote sustainability, 
and create new jobs and economic growth. A green recovery from the COVID-19 
pandemic could transform Southeast Asia into an “economic powerhouse” 
(Argyriou, 2020). However, there are also challenges to implementing green 
development in the region, including the lack of political will and institutional 
capacity and the lack of funding for green projects. To promote green development 
in Southeast Asia, governments and international organizations can take several 
steps to support sustainable practices and invest in green technologies and 
industries.
The Political Economy of the ASEAN Green Deal
9
6. The ASEAN Green Deal 
The ASEAN Green Deal is a framework that aims to promote resilient, inclusive 
and sustainable development in Southeast Asia. Overall, the ASEAN Green Deal 
should (a) promote knowledge sharing and capacity building on green economy 
and green innovation; (b) generate new opportunities from the adoption of green 
technologies and improved production capacity; (c) generate new opportunities 
for investment in green infrastructure through public-private partnerships 
and innovation in new sustainable technologies, as well as new programs for 
ecological maintenance; (d) promote sustainable production and consumption; 
and (e) develop integrated and innovative solutions to green economy and green 
transformation.
Some of the key elements of the ASEAN Green Deal might include (a) green 
energy, infrastructure, and logistics to support the global transition to a zero-
carbon, affordable, and resilient energy system; (b) green production and green 
consumption by harnessing new technologies and applications that reshape value 
chains to improve efficiency, lower costs and reduce environmental impact; and 
(c) green finance platform to mobilize public and private investment for green 
transformation in energy and infrastructure1. 
The ASEAN Green Deal will contribute to the ASEAN region’s transition 
to a green future, sustainability, resource efficiency, resilience, and economic 
competitiveness. It covers a wide range of areas, from infrastructure, energy, and 
manufacturing to consumption and agriculture. The detailed concept and action 
plan of the ASEAN Green Deal have yet to be developed, but generally it seeks 
to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, enhance energy security and efficiency, and 
promote sustainable agriculture and circular economy practices.
Although ASEAN and its member states have shown strong commitment 
to climate action, the region’s emissions are among the fastest growing 
in the world. Southeast Asia has experienced rapid population growth, 
urbanization, industrialization, rising income levels, and development gains 
over the past few decades, resulting in a significant increase in emissions. 
While region-wide action, especially around initiatives related to renewable 
energy deployment and energy efficiency, has been increasing, it is essential 
to transition to clean energy sources to mitigate the impacts of these trends. 
Without such efforts, energy-related emissions in ASEAN are predicted to 
nearly double by 2040 (ASEAN Green Future, 2021).
Various ASEAN Member States (AMS) have set targets for reducing 
greenhouse gas emissions. For instance, Cambodia has committed to reducing 42 
percent of emissions below “business as usual (BAU)”  levels by 2030. Indonesia

41 percent depending on international support. Lao PDR has committed to a 60 
percent reduction by 2030, while Malaysia has set a target of a 45 percent reduction 
in carbon intensity by 2030. Thailand has committed to a 40 percent reduction by 
2030, conditional on capacity building, finance, and technological support. 
The ASEAN Green Deal has the potential to have a significant impact on 
the region. By promoting sustainable economic growth and reducing greenhouse 
gas emissions, the deal could contribute to the global effort to mitigate climate 
change. The promotion of renewable energy and sustainable agriculture could 
also enhance energy and food security in the region, while the promotion of 
circular economy practices could reduce waste and promote more sustainable 
consumption and production patterns.
However, there are challenges to implementing the ASEAN Green Deal. The 
deal relies on the cooperation of all ASEAN Member States, and some countries 
may be reluctant to adopt sustainable policies that could impact their economic 
growth. Additionally, the costs of transitioning to a more sustainable economy 
could be high, particularly for the less developed economies. At the national 
level, governments play a crucial role in the implementation of the Green Deal. 
National governments will need to develop and implement policies to achieve 
the objectives of the Green Deal. 
Local governments also play a crucial role in the implementation of the Green 
Deal. Local governments can implement policies to reduce emissions from 
transport, such as promoting the use of bicycles and public transportation and 
promoting energy-efficient buildings. Local governments can also implement 
policies to protect biodiversity and promote sustainable land use.
One of the main benefits of domestic politics in promoting green development 
is the ability to create policies and regulations that incentivize sustainable 
practices and penalize unsustainable practices. Governments can use a range of 
policy tools, such as taxes, subsidies, and regulations, to promote sustainable 
practices. For example, governments can provide subsidies for renewable energy, 
tax incentives for energy-efficient buildings, and regulations to reduce emissions 
from industries.
Another benefit of domestic politics in promoting green development is the 
potential to create green jobs and stimulate economic growth. Green industries, 
such as renewable energy and sustainable agriculture, have the potential to create 
new jobs and stimulate economic growth. Governments can create policies and 
programs to support the growth of green industries, such as providing funding for 
research and development or creating training programs for workers.
However, there are also challenges to promoting green development 
through domestic politics. One of the main challenges is the lack of political 
will and institutional capacity. Governments may not prioritize environmental 
The Political Economy of the ASEAN Green Deal
11
sustainability, and there may be resistance from industries and interest groups. 
In addition, governments may lack the institutional capacity to enforce 
environmental regulations and promote sustainable development. Another 
challenge is the potential for policy to be too rigid or inflexible. Policies and 
regulations can be effective in promoting sustainable practices, but they may also 
be too rigid and not able to adapt to changing circumstances. In addition, policies 
and regulations may have unintended consequences, such as creating negative 
impacts on small businesses or low-income communities.
To address these challenges, governments should prioritize environmental 
sustainability and invest in green technologies and industries. They can also 
create policies and regulations that incentivize sustainable practices and penalize 
unsustainable practices. In addition, governments can engage with businesses, 
civil society, and communities to ensure that policies and regulations are 
effective, fair, and equitable. United Nations Economic and Social Commission 
for Asia and the Pacific (UNESCAP)’s Asia Pacific Green Deal for Business can 
be integrated in the policy framework of the ASEAN Green Deal. 
The following are key areas to focus on for achieving a zero-carbon, affordable, 
and resilient energy system, in line with the Paris Agreement and the 2030 
Agenda for Sustainable Development:
•	 Advancing the decarbonization of the energy system to provide reliable 
and affordable access to zero-carbon energy for all.
•	 Developing smart, low-carbon, water-secure, and climate-resilient cities, 
infrastructure, and mobility to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and 
enhance water security.
•	 Developing blended finance for sustainable investments in energy, 
infrastructure, logistics, food production, and water supply.
•	 Accelerating and scaling up innovations in sustainable development by 
implementing new business models and solutions to reduce environmental 
impact.
•	 Transitioning towards a more circular economy to maximize resource 
efficiency and minimize environmental impact, which will create new 
business and employment opportunities (UNESCAP, 2022).
To achieve the policy objectives mentioned earlier, several strategic 
interventions need to be implemented. These include developing green and clean 
energy system; building green infrastructure and logistics for smart, green, and 
climate-resilient cities and buildings; promoting green finance to mobilize public 
and private investment for innovation in the energy sector, infrastructure, logistics, 
and other sectors of a green and circular economy; promoting green innovation 
and scaling up new technologies and applications to reduce environmental 
impact; and promoting a circular economy with new business and employment 
opportunities (UNESCAP, 2022).
Green Ideals
12
The ASEAN Framework on Circular Economy adopted in 2021 aims to 
achieve three strategic goals which are to promote resilient economy, resource 
efficiency, and sustainable growth. There are five strategic priorities, including 
(a) “standard harmonization and mutual recognition”, (b) “trade openness and 
trade facilitation”, (c) “innovation, digitalization and emerging technologies”, (d) 
“sustainable finance and innovative investments”, and (e) “efficient use of energy 
and other resources”. Additionally, there are six guiding principles, namely (a) 
encouraging the integration of ASEAN and the development of value chains 
within the region; (b) taking into account the overall impact on the economy 
and society; (c) acknowledging the distinctive circumstances of each ASEAN 
Member State; (d) fostering collaboration across ASEAN for the sharing of 
knowledge and technology; (e) assessing the financial and institutional viability 
and sustainability before implementing initiatives; and (f) operating within the 
context of international production connection (ASEAN Secretariat, 2021). The 
Circular Economy Framework presents a forward-thinking, far-reaching goal for 
the circular economy, leveraging the advantages of current ASEAN programs 
and projects. It also pinpoints crucial areas of emphasis and factors that will 
facilitate the advancement of a circular economy in ASEAN, with the aim of 
hastening its realization.
The green transition transformation cannot be realized without significant 
international support. ASEAN and its member states need financial and technical 
support from the dialogue partners to develop and implement the ASEAN Green 
Deal. For instance, ASEAN and the EU have closely cooperated on green 
economy and climate change. At the national level, it is important to establish a 
national-level cross-ministerial governance body in order to build political buy-in, 
build political consensus, formulate a holistic transition strategy, and strengthen 
inter-agency coordination to implement the ASEAN Green Deal.
The ASEAN region has the potential to expedite the transition to a low-
carbon economy and gain significant economic advantages. Leveraging its 
history of working together to address shared issues, the region can benefit from 
a coordinated approach to tackle one of the most pressing challenges of our 
era. By collaborating to recognize and tackle common obstacles, ASEAN can 
speed up its transition to a low-carbon future and facilitate the establishment 
of priority projects relating to green and circular economy across the region. 
ASEAN Member States have identified the establishment of a regional climate 
fund, carbon market, and power grid as the top three collective opportunities to 
accelerate the shift to a low-carbon economy (ASEAN Green Future, 2021).
In 2021, the ASEAN Taxonomy on Sustainable Development was introduced 
as a comprehensive guide for all ASEAN Member States to complement 
their respective national sustainability initiatives, and to serve as a common 
language for sustainable finance in the ASEAN region. It will cover capital 
markets, banking, and insurance sectors and will be multi-tiered and inclusive, 
The Political Economy of the ASEAN Green Deal
13
facilitating an orderly and effective transition towards a sustainable ASEAN. 
The development of the ASEAN Sustainable Finance Taxonomy will benefit all 
ASEAN Member States, providing an overarching guide that complements their 
national sustainability initiatives (Keo & Chheang, 2022).
7. Conclusion
The ASEAN Green Deal is an important framework for promoting resilient, 
inclusive, and sustainable development in Southeast Asia. By promoting clean 
and renewable energy, circular economy, green production, and green innovation, 
the deal has the potential to contribute to the global effort to mitigate climate 
change, while promoting regional transition into a green economy. However, 
there are challenges to implementing the deal, and it will require the cooperation 
of all ASEAN Member States and the private sector to achieve its objectives. 
International support is essential to assist ASEAN and its members to develop 
and carry out the ASEAN Green Deal.
Five strategic policy interventions are recommended to make the ASEAN 
Green Deal a reality. First, it is critical to invest in a carbon-neutral, dependable, 
affordable, and resilient energy system. Second, more emphasis should be placed 
on developing smart, green, and climate-resilient infrastructure. Third, public 
and private funds for green investment and transformation should be raised. 
Fourth, stakeholders should continue to accelerate and scale up green innovation. 
To implement UNESCAP’s Asia Pacific Green Deal and the Framework for 
Circular Economy for the ASEAN Economic Community, all parties should 
promote multi-stakeholder consultation and partnership building, as well as 
develop a green economic zone. In addition to green economy development, 
we require a holistic approach to wellbeing that integrates economic, social, and 
environmental solutions.

3. Decarbonization or Carbon Neutrality
Carbon neutrality is expressed as the balance sought to be achieved between 
emitting carbon and absorbing carbon emissions by carbon sinks such as forests, 
soils and oceans. It is a term used interchangeably with ‘net zero’ which envisages 
a situation where no carbon is emitted at the very outset. The Paris Agreement 
was a breakthrough for achieving the common consensus for carbon neutrality to 
limit global warming to below 2°C (preferably 1.5°C). Signatories to the Accord 
were required to submit Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC’s). 
Speaking of Cambodia’s resolve towards decarbonization, it has already 
ratified the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change 
(UNFCCC), acceded to the Kyoto Protocol and subsequently has adopted the 
Paris Climate Agreement in 2016. It presented a long-term strategy in 2021 to 
reflect its firm commitment towards the Paris Agreement and to achieve the goal 
of carbon neutrality in the next 30 years10.  The strategy presents the institutional 
arrangements for development of a monitoring and evaluation framework, long-
term planning, and analysis of socioeconomic impacts and financial options of 
selected actions that need to be prioritized (NCSD, 2021). Based on rules for 
reporting and review under the Enhanced Transparency Framework of the Paris 
Agreement, Cambodia also put in place the NDC tracking tool, which traces the 
progress towards achieving and implementing its NDC11. 
Since the early 2000s, the country has pro-actively been involved in, and 
has implemented voluntarily, projects for mitigation of Green House Gasses 
(GHG’s) including Angkor Bio Cogen Rice Husk Power Project, a methane fired 
power generation plant in Samrong Thom, Animal Husbandry Biogas, TTY 
Cambodia Biogas Project and Kampot Cement Waste Heat Power Generation 
Project (KCC-WHG)12. In 2013, the Climate Change Strategic Plan (CCCSP)

Cambodia has been a beacon of hope for achieving the global goal of carbon

4. Forest Conservation
Forests are fundamental components for the planet’s recovery (Fothergill et al., 
2020). They are nature’s carbon sinks and their importance in maintaining the 
ecological balance is acknowledged from time immemorial. Forests are not only 
essential for wildlife but people as well. Over 1.6 billion people need forests for 
food, timber, fuel, shelter and jobs (United Nations Department of Economic 
and Social Affairs, 2020), most importantly, for oxygen. Forests play an integral 
role in maintaining the Earth’s water cycle. Plant and tree roots keep soil from 
washing away in heavy rainfall and clogging rivers (National Geographic Kids, 
2016, p. 288). World’s forests could provide ecosystem services worth 16.2 
trillion USD annually (National Geographic Kids, 2016, p. 26). Afforestation 
could absorb 66 per cent of the carbon emissions in the atmosphere (Fothergill 
et al., 2020).
A crucial factor responsible for high vulnerability in the ASEAN region 
in relation to climate change is massive deforestation that leads to negative 
implications for environmental feedback effects and most importantly local 
resilience. The ASEAN Joint Statement on Climate Change to COP 28 
reaffirms the commitment of the ASEAN Member States to promote sustainable 
management of forests through Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and 
Forest Degradation and the role of conservation, sustainable management of 
forests and enhancement of forest carbon stocks in developing countries (REDD+) 
(ASEAN, 2023). Due to persistent droughts and climatic disturbances, around 4 
million hectares of lowland forests, especially in the southwest and northeast, are 
likely to be affected which may result in serious repercussions. High deforestation

Cambodia has lost an average of 132,733 hectares and 579,280 hectares of 
forest cover every year from 1994-2009 and 2010-2016 respectively (NCSD, 
2020b). Relying on sustainable forest management to maintain at least 60 per 
cent forest cover could massively reduce GHGs from FOLU. Approximately, 
41 percent of Cambodian land was covered by forests in 2016, 97 or more of 
which were semi-evergreen, deciduous and evergreen forests whilst flooded, 
mangrove and planted forests covered only a small percentage (Chou & Chinh, 
2023; Ministry of Environment, 202014).
During 1965-2014, Cambodia’s forest cover declined from a mighty 73.04 per 
cent to 49.48 per cent (Open Development Cambodia, 2022a, p. 14; 2022b, p. 
39). This figure remains the highest in terms of forest coverage. Around 9 million 
hectares of forests are under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Environment 
(MoE) and the Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries (MAFF). 
The Royal Government of Cambodia has also taken a decision to integrate 
Cambodia’s national REDD+ institutional arrangements with the MoE and the 
NCSD (Royal Government of Cambodia [RGC], 2017). 
Large scale reforestation and afforestation efforts are essential to reverse 
deforestation that contributes to increased CO2 emissions. Cambodia’s REDD+ 
program is in conformity with the decisions adopted the United Nations 
Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) (RGC, 2017). Both 
local governments and community participation is vital for the success of REDD+ 
Program. Once full financed, the program is likely to reduce the deforestation by 
50 per cent in 2030 in comparison to the REDD+ baseline set in the updated 
NDC (reducing 50 per cent of historical emission) (NCSD, 2021).
Cambodia has long since assumed the role of a leader in the ASEAN region 
when it comes to initiatives concerning community involvement. Community-
Based Natural Resource Management (CBNRM) was introduced in Cambodia 
as early as 1991 as a new system of collectivization aimed to empower local 
people to manage their own common resources. The co-author has elucidated 
the successes of the CBNRM and the Sahak Khom in his doctoral thesis and 
other distinguished works (Piseth, 2017).  
From the early 2000s, the government has welcomed and considered the 
local community as one of the key actors for forest conservation and protection. 
Currently, there are more than 500 community-based institutions being formed 
and recognized by the government for forest protection and protected areas

has proven to be more cost effective, better protects forests, and addresses local

While the REDD+ initiative is bearing fruit and the recovery of the forest cover 
is under way, Cambodia could well be an important participant in the carbon credit

5. Renewable Energy
The changing geopolitical dynamics following the Ukraine war have tilted the 
balance in favor of clean energy and the European nations greatly acknowledge 
its importance. Germany’s energy strategy (Energiewiende) aims to achieve 80 
per cent renewable energy target by 2050. State of the art fossil-free technologies 
such as green hydrogen, sustainable aviation fuels, fossil-free steel coupled with 
carbon capture and storage capabilities are set to change the ways in which the 
markets function and operate.
ASEAN too has identified its key areas- renewable energy diffusion and 
energy efficiency improvement. Ensuring energy efficiency would entail proper 
management of advanced coal and gas power plants whilst offering a greater 
impetus to renewable energy portfolio diversification (i.e., solar, wind, large 
scale hydroelectricity, geothermal etc.). The ASEAN Power Grid project aims 
to prioritize rural electrification and ensure energy security, transborder energy 
interconnection and renewable power penetration in the future - so much so that 
an aspirational target has been set to increase the share of renewable energy in 
the ASEAN energy mix to 23% and the total installed power capacity to 35% by 
2025 (ASEAN Centre for Energy, 2020). 
As Cambodia embarks upon its growth journey, the demand for energy has 
increased at an unprecedented rate.  The per capita electricity consumption has 
risen around 18 per cent year-on-year during 2010-2019, whilst electricity demand 
has increased more than four-fold over the same period (Open Development 
Mekong, 2022). Investments in clean energy projects are extremely important 
to meet the increased energy requirements to ensure sustained, balanced, and 
efficient growth. The National Energy Efficiency Policy provides the long-term 
vision to transform the consumption of energy in Cambodia to create a strong 
vibrant economy whilst fostering sustainable development. It also envisages the 
policy, regulatory and sector specific intervention programs and a mechanism to 
facilitate coordination amongst various governmental agencies. 
Extraordinary times call for extraordinary measures. Specific measurable 
targets to achieve energy efficient goals are the key. The national target for

and 2050, of the Long-Term Strategy for Carbon Neutrality, the power sector 
will increase its decarbonization efforts by increasing the share of renewable 
energy in the generation mix, to 35 per cent (12 per cent to come from solar) in 
2050 (NCSD, 2021). The Cambodian energy mix in 2030 is projected to have 
hydropower (55 per cent), coal/gas (35 per cent) and renewable energy (biomass, 
solar, and wind) (10 per cent)15. Statistics indicate that 6.7 per cent of the electricity 
generated in Cambodia comes from solar energy, and around 53 per cent from 
hydropower16. As a developing economy with increasing energy requirements, 
Cambodia imports about 59 per cent of its total energy requirements. Increased 
capacity for solar, hydropower and other renewable energy projects would 
augment the existing supply and help in making the nation self-reliant whilst 
catering to the carbon neutrality goal. 
Keeping in mind, Cambodia’s rivers and highlands in its geographical 
makeup, the potential is enormous potential for the better development of 
hydropower capabilities alongside advanced research and development in 
renewable technologies. 
6. ESG, Green Financing, and Sustainable Financial Inclusion 
The focus of investments should be the emerging and developing nations. It is 
extremely important that ESG compliant companies (or seemingly so) walk the 
talk rather than just talking the talk. Transformative greenification of businesses 
is seen with scepticism by some corporations and investors. Profit is certainly 
not a dirty word. However responsible, businesses are expected to be profitable 
ones. Green washing may thus be preferred to risk taking.  The Securities and 
Exchange Commission in the United States has adopted rules to standardise and 
enhance climate related disclosure for investors (US Securities and Exchange 
Commission, 2024). The European Union’s Corporate Sustainability Reporting 
Directive (CSRD) entered into force on 5 January 2023 aims to bring around 
50,000 companies under its ambit (European Parliament, 2022). 
Financing forest action is needed to address climate crisis. Green Climate 
Fund (GCF) has been set up to scale up financing and catalyse investment for 
sustainable forests and enabling environments needed for countries to take forest 
action. GCF has been proactive in supporting countries in the implementation 
of the REDD+ to mainstream the role of forests in climate resilient development 
processes whilst ensuring benefits for indigenous people. Mobilization of private

The Enhanced Transparency Framework (ETF) under the Paris Accord aims

the ASEAN region in supporting a greener sustainable tomorrow. The EU under 
the ASEAN Green Finance Facility would commit 50 million EUR to encourage 
private investments in green infrastructure projects in ASEAN Member States (EU-
ASEAN, 2022a). Strategic actions for green growth in Cambodia would involve 
policy level reforms to facilitate public private partnerships and capacity building 
for resilient, sustainable and environment friendly solutions (RGC, 2013). 
Climate mitigation and adaptation requires enough funds to be available 
for technology development, human capacity building and climate change 
intervention (RGC, 2013). Green bonds might act as important pillars for clean 
growth and instruments of sustained financial inclusion in the Cambodian 
financial markets. They could be backed by the government for public private 
ESG projects and offer fixed returns to investors with issuers making a non-
binding voluntary commitment to utilize the funds for green projects. Around 
269.5 billion USD worth of green bonds were issued worldwide in 2020. 
Recently, the European Union (EU) has also agreed upon the Carbon Border 
Adjustment Mechanism levy to equalize the price of carbon paid for EU products 
and non-EU products. A similar arrangement could be envisaged by considering 
the introduction of an ASEAN-wide carbon tax or working out an inter-regional 
mechanism for pricing carbon (Nurdianto & Resosudarmo, 2016). Cambodia 
has vast reserves of carbon credits estimated to be around 15 million and is an 
important trading partner of the US and the EU. Initiatives such as establishment 
of global marketplaces, such as Climate Impact X in Singapore, could go a long 
way in the monetization of carbon credits. The price that the carbon credits 
would fetch would be much greater in the developed countries’ markets.   
The essential elements of legislation such as the Inflation Reduction Act in the 
US merit consideration for adoption in the Cambodian legislative framework.

7. Conclusion and Policy Recommendations
In light of the above discussion, it is essential to ponder upon whether we owe 
the youth a better planet - what David Attenborough calls “a rich, diverse and 
sustainable future in the world.” (Fothergill et al., 2020).
•	 We recommend for community-based natural resource management/
gender inclusive climate change responses to ensure that farmlands can 
turn into wilderness again to restore the ecological balance - an initiative in 
which Cambodia already has the first mover advantage. 
•	 Embarking upon environmentally sustainable projects for promoting the 
use of renewable energy using the Public Private Partnership (PPP) model.
•	 Effective legislative measures could be introduced by the Ministry of 
Environment and Ministry of Commerce in consultation with the Ministry 
of Industry, Science, Technology & Innovation to ensure seamless 
technology transfer with stringent anti-dumping measures in place. With 
the fast-paced developments waiting to see the light of the day including 
carbon capture and storage technologies and fusion technology, Cambodia 
should not remain bereft of these developments. 
•	 Strengthening the existing ESG framework by ensuring accountability 
mechanisms and penalties for companies indulging in green washing or 
window dressing the ESG expenditure18.
•	 We also recommend that the financial system and the markets should be 
more resilient and conducive for green projects that aim to greenify every 
sector. In this regard, the Government could consider issuing green bonds 
with attractive interest rates to bring citizens in the mainstream19.

1. Introduction
In the past, trade and development policies have prioritized promoting economic 
growth and eradicating poverty over the long-term health of the environment. 
However, this strategy has resulted in gradual environmental degradation and 
resource depletion, both of which pose a threat to the economic growth and 
poverty reduction that these policies aim to achieve. As the effects of climate 
change worsen, there is a growing recognition of the need for sustainable 
development policies that strike a balance between economic growth and 
environmental protection; consequently, climate change and environmental 
sustainability appear to be the primary focus of the development strategies of 
the majority of countries. The emergence of green industries and technologies, 
which foster not only economic growth but also lessen environmental impact, is 
a result of the shift towards sustainable development policies. 
Furthermore, international programs like the Paris Agreement have pushed 
nations to cooperate for a more sustainable future. As of March 2023, 127 
nations, including the United States, China, and the European Union (EU) — 
the three largest emitters — have committed to achieving net-zero emissions 
by 2050 (United Nations, n.d.-b). A concerted effort from all facets of society, 
including governments, corporations, and individuals, is necessary to achieve 
this goal of net-zero emissions, which is a significant step in the direction of 
reducing the effects of climate change. To ensure sustainable development for 
future generations, it is essential that we keep sustainable development policies 
as a top priority and continue to invest in green businesses and technologies.
The EU, the third-largest greenhouse gas emitter and responsible for 
approximately 8% of the world’s greenhouse gas emissions (European Parliament, 
2018), has made significant efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, particularly 
through its climate and energy policies. The EU Green Deal (hereinafter referred 
to as EGD) is one of the most important and integral components of the EU’s 
strategy to implement the 2030 Agenda and the sustainable development goals 
of the United Nations. The EGD was adopted in December 2019 and became a 
comprehensive plan to transform the EU’s economy and society towards a more 
sustainable and resilient future while also addressing the urgent need to combat 
climate change and biodiversity loss. It also aims to create new job opportunities 
and ensure a just transition for workers in sectors that will be impacted by the

the majority of countries. The emergence of green industries and technologies, 
which foster not only economic growth but also lessen environmental impact, is 
a result of the shift towards sustainable development policies.

nations to cooperate for a more sustainable future. As of March 2023, 127 
nations, including the United States, China, and the European Union (EU) — 
the three largest emitters — have committed to achieving net-zero emissions 
by 2050 (United Nations, n.d.-b). A concerted effort from all facets of society, 
including governments, corporations, and individuals, is necessary to achieve 
this goal of net-zero emissions, which is a significant step in the direction of 
reducing the effects of climate change. To ensure sustainable development for 
future generations, it is essential that we keep sustainable development policies 
as a top priority and continue to invest in green businesses and technologies.

approximately 8% of the world’s greenhouse gas emissions (European Parliament, 
2018), has made significant efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, particularly 
through its climate and energy policies. The EU Green Deal (hereinafter referred 
to as EGD) is one of the most important and integral components of the EU’s 
strategy to implement the 2030 Agenda and the sustainable development goals 
of the United Nations. The EGD was adopted in December 2019 and became a 
comprehensive plan to transform the EU’s economy and society towards a more 
sustainable and resilient future while also addressing the urgent need to combat 
climate change and biodiversity loss. It also aims to create new job opportunities 
and ensure a just transition for workers in sectors that will be impacted by the 
transition to a greener economy (Fetting, 2020). The EGD includes a wide range

legally binding reduction targets for greenhouse gas emissions. In addition,

scientific advice and monitor progress towards the targets. The climate law

time, ensures that the energy supply needs to be secure and affordable for 
consumers and businesses. The clean energy transition will require smart 
infrastructure. In this direction, the EU will foster the deployment of 
innovative technologies and infrastructure such as smart grids, hydrogen 
networks or carbon capture, storage and utilization and energy storage.

sustainable production and consumption practices. The circular economy

waste and pollution. It also encourages innovation and the development of 
new technologies that can help achieve more sustainable production and 
consumption. By promoting a circular economy, the EGD can create new 
business opportunities and jobs in sustainable industries. The Commission 
has issued a new ‘circular economy action plan’ to guide the transition of 
all sectors on various issues including the sustainable and circular design 
of products, reducing and reusing materials, measures on the release of 
plastics, and the packaging (EC, 2020a). The circular economy has the 
potential to reduce waste significantly and contribute to greenhouse gas 
emission reduction. Furthermore, the circular economy action plan will 
help the EU modernize its economy and stimulate the development of lead 
markets for climate-neutral and circular products in the EU and beyond.

greenhouse gas emissions, the EGD aims to promote sustainable and 
clean transport by increasing the use of low-emission vehicles, improving 
public transport, and supporting cycling and walking. This will not only

greenhouse gas emissions from transport by at least 55% by 2030 and

the use of sustainable fuels, and improving public transport services.

measures for sustainable food production, sustainable food processing

food labelling and increase consumer awareness of the environmental 
impact of their food choices. Additionally, the strategy aims to promote 
the adoption of sustainable farming practices and reduce food waste 
throughout the supply chain.  It is anticipated that these actions will not 
only lead to a more sustainable and resilient food system in the region and 
benefit the environment but will also support the economic viability of the 
European agriculture sector.

health and sustainability of Europe’s ecosystems and food systems. The

new  commitments, measures, targets, and governance mechanisms  to

3. Implications of the EU Green Deal for Cambodia 
While the EGD is primarily focused on the EU’s internal social, economic, 
and environmental affairs, its impact will be felt beyond European borders. 
Cambodia, in particular, is likely to be affected in several ways. One of the major 
implications is that the EGD will present Cambodia with a number of potential 
opportunities to transition to a more sustainable economy while promoting 
environmental conservation and social development. More precisely, Cambodia 
can leverage the EU’s commitment to promoting sustainable production and 
consumption practices such as organic farming and agroforestry by adopting 
sustainable agricultural practices, which could help the country both reduce 
Green Ideals
36
its carbon emissions and attract environmentally conscious consumers and 
investors. Furthermore, it is expected that the EGD will increase the demand 
for agricultural goods especially sustainably produced foods. This presents a 
significant opportunity for Cambodia to tap into the EU market and increase its 
agricultural exports.
Access to funding is yet another opportunity presented by the EGD. The 
EU has committed to mobilizing at least €1 trillion in investment over the next 
decade to support the transition to a more sustainable economy (EC, n.d.-a). 
This funding will be directed towards projects that aim to reduce greenhouse 
gas emissions and increase energy efficiency, creating new job opportunities 
and boosting economic growth in the process. As promoting global cooperation 
and encouraging other countries to adopt similar measures to combat climate 
change is part of the EGD’s strategic action (Fetting, 2020), the EU is likely 
to expand the development aids, and further strengthen diplomatic efforts and 
partnerships involving funding for projects that promote economic growth, 
job creation, and environmental sustainability.  This could potentially lead 
to increased cooperation between the EU and Cambodia on environmental 
and sustainable issues. In fact, the EU has already started cooperating with 
Cambodia on environmental issues, including extending support for sustainable 
forest management and the promotion of renewable energy. However, the EGD 
will open up additional avenues for financial and technical assistance, including 
waste management, renewable energy sources, sustainable agricultural practices, 
and a circular economy. These efforts will not only assist Cambodia in lowering 
its carbon footprint and reducing the effects of climate change, but they may 
also generate new employment opportunities and stimulate economic growth. 
Further collaborations and partnerships on the issues essential to the EGD could 
strengthen the relationship between Cambodia and the EU, leading to an increase 
in trade and investment opportunities in sustainable industries.
Although the EGD offers Cambodia opportunities to further develop its trade, 
investment, and development partnerships, it also presents Cambodia with many 
challenges, especially with respect to adhering to EU rules. As part of the EGD, 
the new Circular Economy Action Plan (CEAP) introduces new regulations, non-
regulatory measures, and sustainability standards for imports to accelerate the 
transition to a circular economy. A few examples of more stringent requirements 
include sustainable product design with an emphasis on circularity, durability, 
and repairability, and a production process requiring the use of sustainable 
materials (EC, 2020a). As  these changes may require significant investments 
in new technologies, as well as changes in business models and supply chain 
management practices, it is  likely to increase costs and responsibilities  for 
businesses exporting into the EU. Apart from that, adhering to these rules might 
be challenging for Cambodia, and as a result, it could affect its ability to export 
goods to the EU.
The European Union Green Deal and Its Implications
37
CEAP also imposes a comprehensive set of measures for the textiles industry, 
the fourth most-pressurized sector for the use of primary raw materials and water 
and the fifth for greenhouse gas emissions (EC, 2020a). It specifically calls for 
the application of a sustainable product framework by the producers, along 
with environmental standards for the collection of textile waste, to guarantee 
that textile products are suitable for circularity. The implementation of CEAP in 
Cambodia’s textile industry may result in higher production costs, which could 
reduce their ability to compete in the EU market. However, compliance with 
these regulations could allow Cambodia to enhance its sustainability practices 
and attract environmentally conscious consumers.
4. Conclusion
In summary, the EGD is a comprehensive and critical policy initiative that seeks 
to combat climate change and sustainable development globally. As the EGD 
underscores the importance of global cooperation and leadership in promoting 
sustainable development, it represents a significant shift in global trade and 
development cooperation landscapes. Given that the EU is one of Cambodia’s 
largest trading partners and providers of development assistance, a shift in 
trade and development financing under the Green Deal framework could have 
a substantial impact on Cambodia’s economy. Cambodia can benefit from the 
EU’s growing demands and support for environmentally friendly products in 
promoting sustainable agricultural practices and exporting sustainable products 
to the EU. Cambodia could also benefit from the technical and financial assistance 
that the EU can provide to promote sustainable development and address the 
challenges of climate change.
To maximize the benefits of the EGD, Cambodia may need to invest more 
in green initiatives, such as sustainable production methods, renewable energy, 
waste management, and recycling systems. In addition, Cambodia may need to 
collaborate closely with the EU to increase policy coherence. This requires the 
nation to develop a green growth strategy and align its policies and programs with 
the EGD.  To ensure compliance with the new regulations, Cambodia may need 
to invest in strengthening its institutional capacity, regulatory framework, and 
research and development capabilities. At the same time, Cambodian businesses 
must immediately begin preparing for and adapting to these changes in order to 
remain competitive in the EU market.

1. Introduction 
This chapter explores the water diplomacy framework considering the three-
dimensional interaction between (1) the natural domain or river nodes, (2) the 
social domain, and (3) the political domain that creates water problems linking 
water-user communities from upstream to downstream through hydrological 
connectivity (Islam & Susskind, 2013).
Figure 4.1 Interactions Between Natural and 
Social Processes Within a Political Domain
Source: Islam and Susskind (2013)
This paper hypothesizes that to manage the complex water problems involved 
in transboundary-river basin management, such as the Mekong River basin, 
riparian states require a water diplomacy framework that would help solve 
problems through robust cooperation. Dealing with such management involves 
interactions that are usually unknowable and unpredictable due to many 
variables, including economic, political, and environmental factors, and requires 
much feedback. The engineering approach, which water managers have relied on 
for decades, needs to work better because hydrological processes and social and 
political boundaries significantly shape water problems.
According to Islam and Susskind (2013), water networks are interconnected nodes 
representing natural (ecological), societal, and political variables. Therefore, information 
and data sharing between nodes is vital to enable managers to regulate and 
coordinate the use of shared water resources (Islam & Susskind, 2013). The most 
challenging aspect of water management as a common pool resource is how best 
to share the information among riparian stakeholders to formulate a policy that 
meets the desired outcomes.

Chapter 4: 	Connecting Societies Through Water: The Potential of Water 
Diplomacy in Transboundary River Basins
CHEM Phalla*
1. Introduction 
This chapter explores the water diplomacy framework considering the three-
dimensional interaction between (1) the natural domain or river nodes, (2) the 
social domain, and (3) the political domain that creates water problems linking 
water-user communities from upstream to downstream through hydrological 
connectivity (Islam & Susskind, 2013).
Figure 4.1 Interactions Between Natural and 
Social Processes Within a Political Domain
Source: Islam and Susskind (2013)
This paper hypothesizes that to manage the complex water problems involved 
in transboundary-river basin management, such as the Mekong River basin, 
riparian states require a water diplomacy framework that would help solve 
problems through robust cooperation. Dealing with such management involves 
interactions that are usually unknowable and unpredictable due to many 
variables, including economic, political, and environmental factors, and requires 
much feedback. The engineering approach, which water managers have relied on 
for decades, needs to work better because hydrological processes and social and 
political boundaries significantly shape water problems.
According to Islam and Susskind (2013), water networks are interconnected nodes 
representing natural (ecological), societal, and political variables. Therefore, information 
and data sharing between nodes is vital to enable managers to regulate and 
coordinate the use of shared water resources (Islam & Susskind, 2013). The most 
challenging aspect of water management as a common pool resource is how best 
to share the information among riparian stakeholders to formulate a policy that 
meets the desired outcomes.

The water diplomacy framework is suitable because water flow connects society 
upstream and downstream into a complex interaction. Therefore, water problems 
such as conflicts occur when the three dimensions—natural river nodes, societal, 
and political systems—interact (Islam & Susskind, 2013). Therefore, water

In the following sections, the chapter introduces water diplomacy, its 
importance in water management cooperation, and other aspects such as green 
economy, sustainable development, and water sector development in more detail.
2. What is Water Diplomacy?
Water diplomacy employs diplomatic tools to resolve or alleviate disputes and 
conflicts arising from shared water resources to foster cooperation, regional 
stability, and peace (Schmeier & Shubber, 2018). Diplomatic tools encompass 
treaties, conventions, agreements, and protocols. A treaty is a formal agreement 
between cooperating countries, while a convention sets rules for member countries 
in multilateral cooperation. Water diplomacy tools may involve negotiation, 
dispute-resolution methods, and diplomatic discussion platforms.
It is crucial to distinguish between scientific tools and water diplomacy 
instruments. For example, organizing collaborative research trips, which are 
considered a technical tool like creating comprehensive management plans or 
shared monitoring systems, does not fall under the realm of water diplomacy.
Water diplomacy is a strategic approach that focuses on resolving disagreements 
and conflicts over scarce water resources. These conflicts often arise when different 
user groups have competing interests, potentially destabilizing communities, 
countries, or regions. Disputes frequently center around differing views on whether 
water development should prioritize economic gains or mutual benefits, especially 
in shared water basins like the Mekong River Basin. It is crucial for parties involved 
to address these disagreements early on to prevent them from escalating into 
conflicts, highlighting the importance of diplomacy in managing water resources. 
Water diplomacy is a resourceful tool that promotes peace and stability by fostering 
diplomatic engagement and cooperation toward common goals.
Water diplomacy has been previously introduced in the Mekong River Basin, 
with organizations like the Mekong River Commission (MRC) using it to develop 
strategies. However, there is still disagreement among riparian nations on the term. 
A common term needs to be integrated into policies and strategies. Managing the 
Mekong River, a transboundary issue, is complex due to physical, social, and 
political factors. Water diplomacy has been crucial in promoting cooperation and 
peacebuilding for sustainable river basin development and management.
The MRC has played an influential role in policy dialogue and cooperation 
between member states and has engaged with regional partners and stakeholders 
on transboundary water management. For example, it has intensely engaged 
Connecting Societies Through Water
41
with China and Myanmar, organized a basin-wide ASEAN-Mekong forum, and 
incorporated academic and public opinions in its planning. This existing mechanism 
and practice paved the way for a more structural water diplomacy framework 
(MRC, 2021). The role of the regional coordination of the MRC significantly 
impacts the future water diplomacy framework in promoting individual riparian 
members to participate in the regional decision-making process. 
3. Why Water Diplomacy?
The Mekong River provides an enriching aquatic biodiversity. It is vital to the 
social, cultural, environmental, and economic wealth of more than 65 million 
people in the Basin (Soukhaphon et al., 2021). The riparian states have developed 
more infrastructure along the Mekong basin in their territories to gain significant 
benefits. However, such infrastructure development causes adverse effects on 
local livelihoods and the environment. In addition, water management requires 
scientifically supported data and politicians’ commitments in their evidence-
based policymaking to support regional governance decision-making in water 
sharing and allocation. Governments and regional coordination bodies, such as 
MRC, can use water diplomacy to talk about how to fix problems that people 
are worried about because of how climate change and development might affect 
the Mekong basin’s physical, environmental, and ecological processes (Hoanh 
et al., 2010). However, such impacts lead to a potential disagreement, leading to 
a regional conflict between upstream and downstream communities, in which 
stakeholders should use diplomatic tools to mitigate the risks (Kittikhoun & 
Staubli, 2018).
4. What is a Green Economy?
This chapter argues that development leads to economic benefits but alters river 
flows and affects the environment. One approach to dealing with environmental 
degradation is to adopt a green economy—a path of economic growth that 
promotes a sustainable environment and social inclusion. Nevertheless, the 
question is how to translate “green development” into real natural resource 
management. In the case of transboundary river flow, incorporating water 
diplomacy principles into the green economy and development is critical for 
achieving a balance between economic growth and environmental sustainability. 
Water diplomacy also provides a framework for cooperation among riparian 
states, ensuring that development activities do not disturb the ecological balance 
of shared water resources.
With limited experience, attempting to achieve a sustainable environment 
while simultaneously considering economic growth and social harmonization 
is challenging. From an environmental point of view, “greener” economic 
development means supporting resource efficiency, greener tourism and 
markets, and “cleaner” agricultural products (Vuola et al., 2020). Moreover,

the Cambodian government promotes cooperation to achieve sustainable 
development goals. Cambodia could use this to capitalise on water diplomacy as 
a tool for facilitating dialogue and negotiations among stakeholders in order to 
achieve inclusive and sustainable green economy goals throughout the Mekong 
River Basin.
5. Cambodia’s Sustainable Development Goals
Sustainable economic growth must ensure environmental sustainability and 
social harmonization. Therefore, it requires a multidisciplinary approach 
and a high level of multistakeholder support for goals, especially Sustainable 
Development Goal 6 on access to clean water and sanitation and Goal 9 on 
industry, innovation, and infrastructure.
Preserving good environmental health supports sustainable economic growth. 
However, a single state cannot solve environmental problems because of the 
three-dimensional interactions that shape such problems. Therefore, a basin-
wide multistakeholder cooperation approach is required (Charoula, 2015). This 
approach is reinforced by water diplomacy, which facilitates collaboration among 
riparian nations to address water-related challenges, ensuring that economic 
development does not undermine the region’s environmental and social integrity. 
In such regional multistakeholder-approach cooperation, states exercise sovereign 
development policy for sustainable development. Cooperation among states 
occurs through international treaties and ratification procedures. International 
cooperation also takes the form of economic and technological cooperation and 
governance that brings together economic and environmental resolution.
Thus, water diplomacy plays a crucial role in realising Cambodia’s SDGs 
and highlighting Cambodia’s commitment to SDGs by integrating sustainable 
water management into broader development policies and ensuring that 
economic growth aligns with environmental and social sustainability objectives. 
The Cambodian Government has a policy on Development Cooperation 
and Partnership Strategy (DCPS 2014-2018 and now 2019-2023). Through 
this policy, the government considers cooperation financing for economic 
development through promoting technological development in every sector of 
economic and social development. In addition, institutional capacity building 
in science is part of practical cooperation through promoting bilateral, regional, 
and multilateral diplomacy. Using the framework of DCPS (2019-23), Cambodia 
will continue to engage with national and international economic, technological, 
and scientific institutions at regional and global levels. Such an approach will 
establish monitoring, evaluation, and reporting systems that enhance results-
based development cooperation. Development cooperation in the Cambodian 
context has progressively taken a result-based approach. The Rectangular 
Strategy is a comprehensive framework that supports achieving development 
results. Cambodia has integrated its Sustainable Development Goals framework

into its National Strategic Development Plan. At the same time, Cambodia also 
integrates its development cooperation into national budget planning (Cambodian 
Rehabilitation and Development Board, 2020).
6. Water Sector Development 
The source of the Mekong River is the Lancang River on the Tibetan Plateau in 
China. It flows through several countries, including Myanmar, Thailand, Lao 
PDR, and Cambodia, before reaching the South China Sea in Vietnam. This 
river sustains diverse ecosystems, with about 86 percent of Cambodia’s inland 
water draining into the Mekong system, while only 14 percent flows into coastal 
areas. The annual surface water availability is around 75,000 million m3 per 
annum, excluding the portion that drains into the coast. Additionally, there is an 
estimated 17,600 million m3 of groundwater (Ministry of Water Resources and 
Meteorology, 2019). Cambodia’s varied geography supports rich biodiversity 
and allows for growing different crops. The country’s agricultural practices are 
divided into upland, lowland, and floodplain areas, with the central plain having 
high population densities, rich ecological diversity, and significant potential for 
agriculture and fisheries development.
The Tonle Sap Great Lake (known as the ‘Great Lake’) connects to the 
Mekong River through the Tonle Sap River, which meets the Mekong River at 
the Chatomouk confluence in Phnom Penh.

Cambodia utilizes its water for domestic water supply, irrigation, drainage, 
flood protection, recreation, and energy generation (MRC, 2021). The 
government’s vision is to graduate from a low-middle-income to a high-middle-
income country by 2030 and a high-income country by 2050. Such a vision 
requires the government to gain high economic growth. In addition, such 
economic growth must be environmentally sustainable and socially harmonious. 
Therefore, the government supported the Sustainable Development Goals 
(SDGs) at the UN General Assembly in 2015. Since then, Cambodia has 
adopted the Cambodian SDGs. First, the government provides a strategy and 
policy intervention to improve Cambodia’s competitiveness by promoting SMEs 
and attracting Foreign Direct Investment (FDI). Secondly, the government 
fosters Public-Private Partnerships to increase investment projects, including 
BOT (Build Operate Transfer) in economic infrastructure development. Thirdly, 
the government continues to improve connectivity to all corners of the country 
(Ministry of Planning, 2019).
When there is enough water, there are not many social problems. On the 
contrary, when there is not enough water, competition occurs between upstream 
and downstream areas of the basin, which is often intense and can lead to conflict. 
In such a situation, there is often a question: who should get water first, how 
much, and when? With such a scarce resource, while the country needs economic 
growth, we must maintain a good environment and social harmonization, 
nationally and regionally. In such a situation, Islam and Susskind (2013) suggest 
that a negotiation involving diplomats using a collaborative-adaptive technique 
would be a water diplomatic tool, ideal for building informed agreements among 
conflicting interests.
7. A Call to Action in Water Resources Management
The government strives to reduce poverty by diversifying economic activities, 
increasing social expenditure, promoting public administrative reform, and 
improving national food security. The water sector is one of the critical 
prioritized areas contributing to poverty reduction by improving access to safe 
and adequate water for domestic consumption, irrigation, and industry, tackling 
and minimizing all forms of threat, loss of life, and livelihoods according to 
water-related hazards, and sustainably managing water resources. Hence:
•	 The Government fosters effective and sustainable water management 
to improve the national economy and social welfare (Ministry of Water 
Resources and Meteorology, 2007). However, investment in irrigation 
development remains an urgent priority mode with no basin-wide approach 
to irrigation management in a catchment management context (Chem & 
Craig, 2008). Therefore, the Government will consider a scientific approach 
to water management.

irrigation management responsibility for small-scale irrigation operation 
and maintenance (O&M) to the Farmer Water User Community (FWUC). 
However, the FWUC lacks support from the technical departments 
leaving the FWUC to struggle in performing its O&M roles. FWUC plays 
a crucial role in sustainable irrigation development by performing its small-
scale O&M. Therefore, the Government supports them financially and 
technically in performing their roles and responding effectively.
•	 FWUC in downstream areas cannot manage its irrigation schemes in 
isolation from the upstream areas because the hydrological processes have 
connected them spatially and temporarily. The Government will manage 
irrigation schemes following the principle of Integrated Water Resources 
Management (IWRM1).
•	 The Government will facilitate institutional arrangements supporting 
irrigation management, urban water supply, urban sanitation, rural water 
supply and sanitation, and ecological conservation. Strategies, including 
electricity, fisheries, agriculture, forestry, and the environment, are also in 
place in the form of strategic frameworks and action plans.
•	 The Government will define policies and develop water resources 
management and development strategies. Other plans should include 
Research and Development (R&D) in water conservation, such as 
flood control and drought warning, gathering and managing data and 
information about surface and groundwater, and meteorology. Another 
key role is coordinating international collaboration in the Mekong River 
Basin.
•	 The Cambodia National Mekong Committee (CNMC) advises the 
Cambodian representative to the MRC Council on all matters relating to 
the Mekong River Basin activities that could affect Cambodian interests. 
CNMC also examines suggestions that agencies of the Royal Government 
of Cambodia produced considering the Mekong-1995 Agreement and 
collaborates between MRC and the appropriate ministries.
8. Conclusion
In the national context, the central plains around Tonle Sap Lake and the 
Mekong lowland are ideal for irrigation development in Cambodia’s geographical 
condition. However, the above geographical locations pose limitations for 
suitable, cost-effective large-scale reservoir storage sites, with many suitable only

Addressing water scarcity has become a complex issue due to the complexity of 
natural, social, and political systems. Therefore, a new approach to water scarcity 
management must accept the increased interconnectivity and the consequences 
of the political decision and reject the unquestioned authority of the hierarchical 
governance structure. Most importantly, water managers must ask themselves, 
as water is a common pool resource, how to ensure adequate water to support 
(1) sustainable economic growth that can feed the growing population, (2) social 
harmonization, and (3) sustainable ecology.
Additionally, there is a connection between the Mekong Basin and the 
Tonle Sap Lake. Many natural-rainfall phenomena and the Mekong water level 
contribute to water scarcity, affecting the flow of the Tonle Sap Lake. The flow 
from upstream directly impacts the Mekong River’s water levels and flow, which 
in turn affects the water supply of Tonle Sap Lake. Therefore, when responding 
to the question above, we need to consider water diplomacy to solve water issues 
at every level, especially regional river-basin development. Maintaining the 
water level in the Mekong River would increase the flow from the Mekong into 
Tonle Sap Lake. Having enough water level in the Mekong River would provide 
Cambodia with great potential for agricultural production and fishing industries 
while maintaining the unique ecosystems of the Tonle Sap Lake.
Globally, there is widespread adoption of the new approach to water 
management, known as Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM). 
However, water professionals generally lack awareness and knowledge of 
it. Therefore, water professionals and managers must change management 
techniques by accepting the water diplomacy framework according to the 
river’s hydrological-social-political connectivity. Nevertheless, the approach 
is standard; for example, at the national level, there is a need to establish a 
catchment management committee or river basin management committee to 
take responsibility for coordinated multistakeholder catchment management. 
However, Cambodia has not yet established such a catchment management 
committee. Instead, it considers implementing catchment management under 
the water law and sub-decree on river basin management.

Chapter 5: Digital Transformation for Environmental Sustainability: 
Impact and Responsibility 
PRUM Sophea* and CHHEM Siriwat
1. Introduction
The advent of Industry 4.0 (IR4.0) has brought about a significant shift in the 
ways we live, work and interact with each other, largely due to the transformative 
impact of digital technology. This revolution has led to increased efficiency 
and productivity across various sectors, resulting in reduced carbon emissions 
in areas such as agriculture, transport, planning, building, waste management, 
and public services. It is imperative to acknowledge that our usage of digital 
technology has a significant impact on the environment, primarily in terms of 
energy consumption. In this context, it becomes vital to realize the intrinsic 
relationship between environmental health and human wellbeing. According 
to the World Health Organization (Sphera’s Editorial Team, 2020; World 
Health Organization, n.d.), around 24 percent of all worldwide deaths can be 
attributed to environmental factors. Therefore, ensuring access to clean air, 
fresh water, and safe living conditions free from pollutants and hazards assumes 
critical importance for promoting human health and quality of life. While digital 
transformation has the potential to enhance socio-economic progress, it can 
also impose costs on the environment. Therefore, it is crucial to establish clear 
roles and responsibilities for various stakeholders to maintain a balance between 
socio-economic development and environmental sustainability. Moreover, it is 
important to devise digital transformation diplomacy to ensure this equilibrium.
2. The Impact of Digital Transformation on the Environment
According to recent estimates, the number of active internet users worldwide 
has reached around 4.66 billion, which accounts for approximately 60 percent 
of the global population (ESCP Business School, 2021). While digitalization has 
positively impacted on various aspects of our lives, it is important to recognize 
that it also comes with certain costs, particularly in terms of energy consumption 
and greenhouse gas emissions. Recent reports indicate that digital technologies 
are responsible for emitting approximately 1.6 billion annual tons of greenhouse 
gasses, accounting for roughly 4 percent of all GHG emissions (The Shift Project, 
2019; Efoui-Hess, 2019). Furthermore, this energy consumption is increasing at a 
rate of 9 percent per year, and it is expected that by 2025, the digital industry will 
account for 20 percent of the world’s total electricity consumption (Ferreboeuf 
et al., 2021).
