wide multistakeholder cooperation approach is required (Charoula, 2015). This 
approach is reinforced by water diplomacy, which facilitates collaboration among 
riparian nations to address water-related challenges, ensuring that economic 
development does not undermine the region’s environmental and social integrity. 
In such regional multistakeholder-approach cooperation, states exercise sovereign 
development policy for sustainable development. Cooperation among states 
occurs through international treaties and ratification procedures. International 
cooperation also takes the form of economic and technological cooperation and 
governance that brings together economic and environmental resolution.
Thus, water diplomacy plays a crucial role in realising Cambodia’s SDGs 
and highlighting Cambodia’s commitment to SDGs by integrating sustainable 
water management into broader development policies and ensuring that 
economic growth aligns with environmental and social sustainability objectives. 
The Cambodian Government has a policy on Development Cooperation 
and Partnership Strategy (DCPS 2014-2018 and now 2019-2023). Through 
this policy, the government considers cooperation financing for economic 
development through promoting technological development in every sector of 
economic and social development. In addition, institutional capacity building 
in science is part of practical cooperation through promoting bilateral, regional, 
and multilateral diplomacy. Using the framework of DCPS (2019-23), Cambodia 
will continue to engage with national and international economic, technological, 
and scientific institutions at regional and global levels. Such an approach will 
establish monitoring, evaluation, and reporting systems that enhance results-
based development cooperation. Development cooperation in the Cambodian 
context has progressively taken a result-based approach. The Rectangular 
Strategy is a comprehensive framework that supports achieving development 
results. Cambodia has integrated its Sustainable Development Goals framework 
Connecting Societies Through Water
43
into its National Strategic Development Plan. At the same time, Cambodia also 
integrates its development cooperation into national budget planning (Cambodian 
Rehabilitation and Development Board, 2020).
6. Water Sector Development 
The source of the Mekong River is the Lancang River on the Tibetan Plateau in 
China. It flows through several countries, including Myanmar, Thailand, Lao 
PDR, and Cambodia, before reaching the South China Sea in Vietnam. This 
river sustains diverse ecosystems, with about 86 percent of Cambodia’s inland 
water draining into the Mekong system, while only 14 percent flows into coastal 
areas. The annual surface water availability is around 75,000 million m3 per 
annum, excluding the portion that drains into the coast. Additionally, there is an 
estimated 17,600 million m3 of groundwater (Ministry of Water Resources and 
Meteorology, 2019). Cambodia’s varied geography supports rich biodiversity 
and allows for growing different crops. The country’s agricultural practices are 
divided into upland, lowland, and floodplain areas, with the central plain having 
high population densities, rich ecological diversity, and significant potential for 
agriculture and fisheries development.
The Tonle Sap Great Lake (known as the ‘Great Lake’) connects to the 
Mekong River through the Tonle Sap River, which meets the Mekong River at 
the Chatomouk confluence in Phnom Penh.

Cambodia utilizes its water for domestic water supply, irrigation, drainage, 
flood protection, recreation, and energy generation (MRC, 2021). The 
government’s vision is to graduate from a low-middle-income to a high-middle-
income country by 2030 and a high-income country by 2050. Such a vision 
requires the government to gain high economic growth. In addition, such 
economic growth must be environmentally sustainable and socially harmonious. 
Therefore, the government supported the Sustainable Development Goals 
(SDGs) at the UN General Assembly in 2015. Since then, Cambodia has 
adopted the Cambodian SDGs. First, the government provides a strategy and 
policy intervention to improve Cambodia’s competitiveness by promoting SMEs 
and attracting Foreign Direct Investment (FDI). Secondly, the government 
fosters Public-Private Partnerships to increase investment projects, including 
BOT (Build Operate Transfer) in economic infrastructure development. Thirdly, 
the government continues to improve connectivity to all corners of the country 
(Ministry of Planning, 2019).
When there is enough water, there are not many social problems. On the 
contrary, when there is not enough water, competition occurs between upstream 
and downstream areas of the basin, which is often intense and can lead to conflict. 
In such a situation, there is often a question: who should get water first, how 
much, and when? With such a scarce resource, while the country needs economic 
growth, we must maintain a good environment and social harmonization, 
nationally and regionally. In such a situation, Islam and Susskind (2013) suggest 
that a negotiation involving diplomats using a collaborative-adaptive technique 
would be a water diplomatic tool, ideal for building informed agreements among 
conflicting interests.
7. A Call to Action in Water Resources Management
The government strives to reduce poverty by diversifying economic activities, 
increasing social expenditure, promoting public administrative reform, and 
improving national food security. The water sector is one of the critical 
prioritized areas contributing to poverty reduction by improving access to safe 
and adequate water for domestic consumption, irrigation, and industry, tackling 
and minimizing all forms of threat, loss of life, and livelihoods according to 
water-related hazards, and sustainably managing water resources. Hence:
•	 The Government fosters effective and sustainable water management 
to improve the national economy and social welfare (Ministry of Water 
Resources and Meteorology, 2007). However, investment in irrigation 
development remains an urgent priority mode with no basin-wide approach 
to irrigation management in a catchment management context (Chem & 
Craig, 2008). Therefore, the Government will consider a scientific approach 
to water management.

•	 Remarkably, since 1994, the Government has considered transferring 
irrigation management responsibility for small-scale irrigation operation 
and maintenance (O&M) to the Farmer Water User Community (FWUC). 
However, the FWUC lacks support from the technical departments 
leaving the FWUC to struggle in performing its O&M roles. FWUC plays 
a crucial role in sustainable irrigation development by performing its small-
scale O&M. Therefore, the Government supports them financially and 
technically in performing their roles and responding effectively.
•	 FWUC in downstream areas cannot manage its irrigation schemes in 
isolation from the upstream areas because the hydrological processes have 
connected them spatially and temporarily. The Government will manage 
irrigation schemes following the principle of Integrated Water Resources 
Management (IWRM1).
•	 The Government will facilitate institutional arrangements supporting 
irrigation management, urban water supply, urban sanitation, rural water 
supply and sanitation, and ecological conservation. Strategies, including 
electricity, fisheries, agriculture, forestry, and the environment, are also in 
place in the form of strategic frameworks and action plans.
•	 The Government will define policies and develop water resources 
management and development strategies. Other plans should include 
Research and Development (R&D) in water conservation, such as 
flood control and drought warning, gathering and managing data and 
information about surface and groundwater, and meteorology. Another 
key role is coordinating international collaboration in the Mekong River 
Basin.
•	 The Cambodia National Mekong Committee (CNMC) advises the 
Cambodian representative to the MRC Council on all matters relating to 
the Mekong River Basin activities that could affect Cambodian interests. 
CNMC also examines suggestions that agencies of the Royal Government 
of Cambodia produced considering the Mekong-1995 Agreement and 
collaborates between MRC and the appropriate ministries.
8. Conclusion
In the national context, the central plains around Tonle Sap Lake and the 
Mekong lowland are ideal for irrigation development in Cambodia’s geographical 
condition. However, the above geographical locations pose limitations for 
suitable, cost-effective large-scale reservoir storage sites, with many suitable only

for shallow reservoirs. Moreover, without significant storage capacity, we cannot

Addressing water scarcity has become a complex issue due to the complexity of 
natural, social, and political systems. Therefore, a new approach to water scarcity 
management must accept the increased interconnectivity and the consequences 
of the political decision and reject the unquestioned authority of the hierarchical 
governance structure. Most importantly, water managers must ask themselves, 
as water is a common pool resource, how to ensure adequate water to support 
(1) sustainable economic growth that can feed the growing population, (2) social 
harmonization, and (3) sustainable ecology.
Additionally, there is a connection between the Mekong Basin and the 
Tonle Sap Lake. Many natural-rainfall phenomena and the Mekong water level 
contribute to water scarcity, affecting the flow of the Tonle Sap Lake. The flow 
from upstream directly impacts the Mekong River’s water levels and flow, which 
in turn affects the water supply of Tonle Sap Lake. Therefore, when responding 
to the question above, we need to consider water diplomacy to solve water issues 
at every level, especially regional river-basin development. Maintaining the 
water level in the Mekong River would increase the flow from the Mekong into 
Tonle Sap Lake. Having enough water level in the Mekong River would provide 
Cambodia with great potential for agricultural production and fishing industries 
while maintaining the unique ecosystems of the Tonle Sap Lake.
Globally, there is widespread adoption of the new approach to water 
management, known as Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM). 
However, water professionals generally lack awareness and knowledge of 
it. Therefore, water professionals and managers must change management 
techniques by accepting the water diplomacy framework according to the 
river’s hydrological-social-political connectivity. Nevertheless, the approach 
is standard; for example, at the national level, there is a need to establish a 
catchment management committee or river basin management committee to 
take responsibility for coordinated multistakeholder catchment management.

Chapter 5: Digital Transformation for Environmental Sustainability: 
Impact and Responsibility 
PRUM Sophea* and CHHEM Siriwat
1. Introduction
The advent of Industry 4.0 (IR4.0) has brought about a significant shift in the 
ways we live, work and interact with each other, largely due to the transformative 
impact of digital technology. This revolution has led to increased efficiency 
and productivity across various sectors, resulting in reduced carbon emissions 
in areas such as agriculture, transport, planning, building, waste management, 
and public services. It is imperative to acknowledge that our usage of digital 
technology has a significant impact on the environment, primarily in terms of 
energy consumption. In this context, it becomes vital to realize the intrinsic 
relationship between environmental health and human wellbeing. According 
to the World Health Organization (Sphera’s Editorial Team, 2020; World 
Health Organization, n.d.), around 24 percent of all worldwide deaths can be 
attributed to environmental factors. Therefore, ensuring access to clean air, 
fresh water, and safe living conditions free from pollutants and hazards assumes 
critical importance for promoting human health and quality of life. While digital 
transformation has the potential to enhance socio-economic progress, it can 
also impose costs on the environment. Therefore, it is crucial to establish clear 
roles and responsibilities for various stakeholders to maintain a balance between 
socio-economic development and environmental sustainability. Moreover, it is 
important to devise digital transformation diplomacy to ensure this equilibrium.
2. The Impact of Digital Transformation on the Environment
According to recent estimates, the number of active internet users worldwide 
has reached around 4.66 billion, which accounts for approximately 60 percent 
of the global population (ESCP Business School, 2021). While digitalization has 
positively impacted on various aspects of our lives, it is important to recognize 
that it also comes with certain costs, particularly in terms of energy consumption 
and greenhouse gas emissions. Recent reports indicate that digital technologies 
are responsible for emitting approximately 1.6 billion annual tons of greenhouse 
gasses, accounting for roughly 4 percent of all GHG emissions (The Shift Project, 
2019; Efoui-Hess, 2019). Furthermore, this energy consumption is increasing at a 
rate of 9 percent per year, and it is expected that by 2025, the digital industry will 
account for 20 percent of the world’s total electricity consumption (Ferreboeuf 
et al., 2021).

2.2. Impact of Digital Transformation Caused by Manufacturing
The widespread use of digital devices like desktops, laptops, tablets, and 
smartphones has led to a significant increase in energy consumption. According 
to a report by Luna (2023) and Cisco (2020), the number of networked devices 
is expected to reach 29.3 billion by 2023, up from 18.4 billion in 2018, which 
translates to an average of 3.6 networked devices per person. Furthermore, with 
the advent of the Internet of Things (IoT), it is predicted that there will be 55.7 
billion connected IoT devices by 2025, as per International Data Corporation’s 
forecast.
According to the findings presented in Statista (2023), it has stated that 
around 1.5 billion smartphones, nearly 126 million desktop computers, 
and approximately 659 million laptops were sold in 2021. These figures are 
expected to experience an exponential surge in the next five to ten years due 
to the emergence of new advanced technologies that are more intelligent 
and interactive. The extensive production of digital devices has sparked 
environmental concerns due to their significant carbon footprint, water 
consumption, and depletion of resources throughout their entire life cycle, 
from mining to manufacturing processes. 
According to Luna (2023), it has been found that the majority of smartphones 
can accommodate 17 rare-earth elements. However, the process of mining 
these essential materials is highly energy-intensive and results in a significant 
environmental impact, affecting forests, mountains, and water sources. 
Moreover, refining, separating, and purifying these elements is an arduous and 
resource-consuming task. This procedure necessitates the use of several chemical 
treatments and purification methods, which frequently cause the degradation of 
land and water resources.
The process of manufacturing digital devices, particularly semiconductors, 
consumes a significant amount of energy. Additionally, the production of 
these devices has a considerable impact on water resources. This is because the 
creation of complex devices such as smartphones and laptops involve numerous 
intricate steps, each requiring a certain amount of water. According to a report in 
Cisco (2020), it has been estimated that the production of a single smartphone, 
including mining operations, requires a whopping 12,760 liters of water.
3. Designing Responsible Digital Transformation
The environment bears the brunt of digital transformation through two major 
factors: excessive data usage and electronic device production. Video streaming is 
the most data-intensive activity, contributing significantly to this issue especially 
the online video uses. On the other hand, the production of electronic devices 
consumes a substantial amount of resources, accounting for almost half of the 
total electric consumption in the process of digital transformation.
Green Ideals
52
3.1. Responsible Data Consumption and Usage
There are two ways to optimize the use of online videos: regulation by technologies 
and infrastructures, and regulation by content. Regulation by technologies and 
infrastructures ensures that the network infrastructures and their usage comply 
with legal requirements. For instance, a subscription model with unlimited data 
access would not limit the amount of data transferred, whereas offering lower-
priced subscriptions with limited access to data transfer volume could reduce data 
consumption and its impact on the environment. On the other hand, regulation 
by content focuses on regulating how information is made available to users. One 
example is implementing regulations for addictive design techniques to minimize the 
time spent by users on platforms, leading to higher data consumption and transfer.
3.2. Responsible Manufacturing
A study conducted by Statista (2023) suggests that the manufacturing process 
of electronic devices has a significant impact on the environment compared 
to their usage. Hence, it is more environmentally friendly to use a device for 
an extended period rather than producing more devices. Therefore, the act of 
reusing electronic devices, such as laptops, desktops, or mobile phones, can 
significantly reduce our environmental footprint. The process of reusing these 
devices typically involves collecting them through a second-hand agent or a 
remanufacturer and then selling, renting, or redistributing them to another 
user. Companies or organizations may carry out larger-scale reuse operations 
with this aim. In fact, each component in each electronic device has a different 
lifespan. To maximize the benefits of reusing electronic devices, it is important 
to consider the reuse potential of each component. Eventually, after a few years, 
even with component replacements, the device or some of its components will 
become unusable. At this stage, it is appropriate to recycle the device in order to 
extract valuable raw materials. Recycling involves breaking down the device and 
retrieving useful materials from it.
4. Green Artificial Intelligence (AI)
In addition to the primary factors of digital transformation’s impact, it is 
important to consider secondary factors such as distribution, the utilization 
of complex computational algorithms for fields like AI, and the recycling of 
electronic devices.
While AI could be viewed as a potential remedy to address the ongoing 
environmental crisis, it is important to acknowledge that AI and other energy-
intensive algorithms consume significant amounts of energy themselves. Hence, 
it is crucial to factor in the environmental impact when implementing any 
applications of AI.
In today’s digital era, it is important for individuals, industries, and 
governments to play their part in reducing the environmental impact of digital 
Digital Transformation for Environmental Sustainability
53
transformation while maximizing its benefits. To achieve this, there are various 
examples of best practices for green digital transformation that can be adopted:
•	 Green Digital Transformation Awareness: Raising awareness about green 
digital transformation is essential because the digital world may seem 
abstract to most users, and they may not realize the environmental impact 
and carbon footprint it creates. 
•	 Managing Data: As stated previously, data usage accounts for 55 percent 
of energy consumption in ICT, making it crucial to manage data storage 
and transactions efficiently. Organizations and companies should take 
responsibility for undertaking digital data clean-up activities to eliminate 
unused and unnecessary digital data. Furthermore, each country should 
establish policies to regulate data usage, covering technology and 
infrastructure regulations as well as content regulations.
•	 Choose Sustainable Device Providers: Every electronic device, whether 
in use or during manufacturing, contributes to the carbon footprint in 
the environment. Hence, it is crucial to select providers who prioritize 
promoting a green environment as a means of reducing the environmental 
impact.
•	 Reuse and Repair before Replace: The environmental impact of 
manufacturing electronic devices is much greater than their usage. Thus, 
promoting the reuse and repairability of these devices can significantly 
extend their average lifetime, leading to reduced emissions and 
environmental damage by millions of tons.
•	 Support Green AI: It is imperative to not only provide researchers with 
greater support to develop AI algorithms that consume less energy but 
also to focus on developing AI algorithms that can solve environmental 
problems.
5. Conclusion
The fourth industrial revolution heavily relies on technology to advance various 
sectors. Despite its benefits, technology adversely effects on the environment and 
contributes to carbon footprint. By 2025, the digital industry will account for 
up to 20 percent of global energy consumption due to data usage and device 
manufacturing. To reduce this impact, it is essential to adopt best practices such 
as promoting green digital transformation awareness, efficient data usage and 
transactions management, sustainable manufacturing processes, extending the 
average lifetime of devices, and supporting research in green AI.

treatments and purification methods, which frequently cause the degradation of 
land and water resources.
The process of manufacturing digital devices, particularly semiconductors, 
consumes a significant amount of energy. Additionally, the production of 
these devices has a considerable impact on water resources. This is because the 
creation of complex devices such as smartphones and laptops involve numerous 
intricate steps, each requiring a certain amount of water. According to a report in 
Cisco (2020), it has been estimated that the production of a single smartphone, 
including mining operations, requires a whopping 12,760 liters of water.
3. Designing Responsible Digital Transformation
The environment bears the brunt of digital transformation through two major 
factors: excessive data usage and electronic device production. Video streaming is 
the most data-intensive activity, contributing significantly to this issue especially 
the online video uses. On the other hand, the production of electronic devices 
consumes a substantial amount of resources, accounting for almost half of the 
total electric consumption in the process of digital transformation.
Green Ideals
52
3.1. Responsible Data Consumption and Usage
There are two ways to optimize the use of online videos: regulation by technologies 
and infrastructures, and regulation by content. Regulation by technologies and 
infrastructures ensures that the network infrastructures and their usage comply 
with legal requirements. For instance, a subscription model with unlimited data 
access would not limit the amount of data transferred, whereas offering lower-
priced subscriptions with limited access to data transfer volume could reduce data 
consumption and its impact on the environment. On the other hand, regulation 
by content focuses on regulating how information is made available to users. One 
example is implementing regulations for addictive design techniques to minimize the 
time spent by users on platforms, leading to higher data consumption and transfer.
3.2. Responsible Manufacturing
A study conducted by Statista (2023) suggests that the manufacturing process 
of electronic devices has a significant impact on the environment compared 
to their usage. Hence, it is more environmentally friendly to use a device for 
an extended period rather than producing more devices. Therefore, the act of 
reusing electronic devices, such as laptops, desktops, or mobile phones, can 
significantly reduce our environmental footprint. The process of reusing these 
devices typically involves collecting them through a second-hand agent or a 
remanufacturer and then selling, renting, or redistributing them to another 
user. Companies or organizations may carry out larger-scale reuse operations 
with this aim. In fact, each component in each electronic device has a different 
lifespan. To maximize the benefits of reusing electronic devices, it is important 
to consider the reuse potential of each component. Eventually, after a few years, 
even with component replacements, the device or some of its components will 
become unusable. At this stage, it is appropriate to recycle the device in order to 
extract valuable raw materials. Recycling involves breaking down the device and 
retrieving useful materials from it.
4. Green Artificial Intelligence (AI)
In addition to the primary factors of digital transformation’s impact, it is 
important to consider secondary factors such as distribution, the utilization 
of complex computational algorithms for fields like AI, and the recycling of 
electronic devices.
While AI could be viewed as a potential remedy to address the ongoing 
environmental crisis, it is important to acknowledge that AI and other energy-
intensive algorithms consume significant amounts of energy themselves. Hence, 
it is crucial to factor in the environmental impact when implementing any 
applications of AI.
In today’s digital era, it is important for individuals, industries, and 
governments to play their part in reducing the environmental impact of digital 
Digital Transformation for Environmental Sustainability
53
transformation while maximizing its benefits. To achieve this, there are various 
examples of best practices for green digital transformation that can be adopted:
•	 Green Digital Transformation Awareness: Raising awareness about green 
digital transformation is essential because the digital world may seem 
abstract to most users, and they may not realize the environmental impact 
and carbon footprint it creates. 
•	 Managing Data: As stated previously, data usage accounts for 55 percent 
of energy consumption in ICT, making it crucial to manage data storage 
and transactions efficiently. Organizations and companies should take 
responsibility for undertaking digital data clean-up activities to eliminate 
unused and unnecessary digital data. Furthermore, each country should 
establish policies to regulate data usage, covering technology and 
infrastructure regulations as well as content regulations.
•	 Choose Sustainable Device Providers: Every electronic device, whether 
in use or during manufacturing, contributes to the carbon footprint in 
the environment. Hence, it is crucial to select providers who prioritize 
promoting a green environment as a means of reducing the environmental 
impact.
•	 Reuse and Repair before Replace: The environmental impact of 
manufacturing electronic devices is much greater than their usage. Thus, 
promoting the reuse and repairability of these devices can significantly 
extend their average lifetime, leading to reduced emissions and 
environmental damage by millions of tons.
•	 Support Green AI: It is imperative to not only provide researchers with 
greater support to develop AI algorithms that consume less energy but 
also to focus on developing AI algorithms that can solve environmental 
problems.
5. Conclusion
The fourth industrial revolution heavily relies on technology to advance various 
sectors. Despite its benefits, technology adversely effects on the environment and 
contributes to carbon footprint. By 2025, the digital industry will account for 
up to 20 percent of global energy consumption due to data usage and device 
manufacturing. To reduce this impact, it is essential to adopt best practices such 
as promoting green digital transformation awareness, efficient data usage and 
transactions management, sustainable manufacturing processes, extending the 
average lifetime of devices, and supporting research in green AI.

energy transition that is just, inclusive and leaves no one behind, promoting 
energy efficiency, renewable technologies and well-functioning global markets, 
amongst other things (Strategic Communications, 2021).

alter the geopolitics of energy in a variety of ways, including shifting power

decades. Geographical factors can occasionally influence political decisions. As 
a result, the term “geopolitics” refers to the field where political, ideological, and 
economic choices are made based on a country’s geography. The population,

3. Energy Landscape of Cambodia
The energy landscape in Cambodia has been undergoing tremendous changes 
in recent decades, as the country has been attempting to address its growing 
energy demand challenges on the one hand and transitioning towards more 
sustainable and diversified energy sources on the other. The demand for energy 
has constantly increased as a result of rapid economic expansion, population 
growth, industrialization, and urbanization, prompting the government to explore 
various means to ensure a reliable and affordable energy supply. Cambodia 
has historically been heavily dependent on imported electricity, primarily from 
neighboring countries such as Thailand and Vietnam. However, the reliance on 
imported energy has posed many problems, such as price stability and energy 
security. Understanding these challenges, the government has been working hard 
to improve domestic energy generation capacity and minimize dependency on 
imports (Economic Research Institute for ASEAN and East Asia, 2019).
According to the Cambodia Energy Technology Roadmap, published by the 
Ministry of Industry, Science, Technology & Innovation in 2023, Cambodia’s 
primary energy sources are diesel power plants, biomass (agricultural and 
firewood), thermal power plants (coal), hydropower plants, and various renewable 
energy sources. Cambodia’s energy landscape experienced a drastic shift from 
heavily dependent on diesel to diversified sources consisting of about only 10% 
of diesel, while hydropower, coal, and biomass are consistently leveraged as its 
primary energy sources (Mika et al., 2021). Even though these trends improve the 
energy status of Cambodia, the Asian Development Bank (Asian Development 
Bank, 2018) reports that around 5 million citizens were not able to access grid 
electricity and still used old methods to generate electricity, including batteries, 
firewood, and other fuels. Cambodia generated around 73.45% of its energy

domestically and imported around 26.55% from neighboring countries (Thailand, 
Laos, and Vietnam) including non-renewable energy (48.83%) and renewable 
energy (51.17%) from local generation. In short, non-renewable energy comprises 
coal (41.20%) and fuel oil (7.63%); and renewable energy sources ranged from 
hydropower (44.17%), solar power (6.36%) and biomass power (0.64%) in 2021 
(Electricity Authority of Cambodia, 2021). 
Cambodia utilizes renewable energy sources due to its favorable conditions. 
Hydropower, agriculture biomass, wind energy and solar energy are significant 
sources of renewable energy in Cambodia. Located in the Great Mekong sub-
region, hydropower has a great potential for energy production (Poch, 2013). 
Cambodia is also beginning to look into the potential of its offshore wind energy. 
The government has initiated studies for offshore wind farms located in coastal 
areas to explore the potential of this untapped resource. Offshore wind could 
tremendously increase the domestic energy production capacity and reduce its 
dependency on fossil fuels as Cambodia’s wind has the potential to generate up 
to 65 gigawatts in the coastal provinces, southwestern mountainous area and 
southern part of Tonle Sap Lake (Asian Development Bank, 2018). 
4. Energy Security and Geopolitics	
Geographical factors can occasionally influence political decisions. Geopolitics 
was initially utilized in relation to military conceptions. Then, the field of 
international relations also started to undertake geopolitical studies, which 
helped to better understand the interactions in the region and produce better 
future policies. Geopolitics in the framework of international relations defines 
the state economy and energy security. Resource scarcity is a major factor in 
how different countries approach their energy policies. For instance, between 
1949 and 1991, the liberal capitalists, led by the United States, and the social 
communists, led by the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR), engaged in a 
global arms race to forge a bi-polar system of power that would rule the new world 
order and tip the scales in their favor. As the two blocs increasingly established 
their own spheres of influence and divided the world into two antagonistic blocs, 
forcing other nations and regions to pick a side between these two camps, their 
competition had a significant impact on the global political scene. 
Southeast Asia has always been a region of great power struggle, according 
to Percival’s (2007) argument, because of its wealth of natural resources and 
advantageous position. In order to better promote its interests during the Cold War, 
the United States thought it could control supplies from the Communist government 
that were more resilient in terms of their military and economy if it had political 
authority over this region. It was seen that superpowers like the United States (USA) 
and the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR) pushed towards western Asian 
states that were rich in energy resources during the Cold War, forming their strategies 
on this matter and using these nations to suit their demands.

From a realist perspective, it is possible to describe how superpowers will 
act in this situation. As a result, the game of bartering over the allocation of 
scarce interstate resources is played. According to Joseph Nye (2002), who had a 
similar viewpoint, “resource bargaining” was crucial in determining the regional 
energy supply. In other words, during the Cold War, the realism-based idea of 
military power started to be challenged, and under the influence of neorealism, 
the idea of military power, as well as rivalry, alliance relationships, and collective 
security, came to the fore. Energy security has unquestionably become significant 
in this situation (Mohapatra, 2016). The recent invasion of Ukraine by Russia in 
February 2022 had a significant impact on the world energy markets (Thomson, 
2022). The International Energy Agency’s World Energy Outlook 2022 report 
explains the key changes to the energy sector following the invasion, including 
higher energy prices, altered trade flows and supply shortages, changes in energy 
policy, economic impacts of the energy crisis, impacts of emissions, and more 
pushes towards renewable energy sources.
5. Climate Change and Renewable Energy	
Climate change poses significant challenges to Cambodia, as the country is 
considered to be among the most vulnerable countries in the world due to its 
geographic location and socio-economic factors. In recent years, Cambodia has 
recognized the importance of addressing climate change and has actively pursued 
renewable energy as a key component of its mitigation and adaptation strategies. 
For example, the National Strategic Development Plan 2019-2023 encourages 
the expansion of, and investment in, its capacity to generate electricity especially 
from renewable and clean energy sources (Royal Government of Cambodia 
[RGC], 2019). Cambodia’s Sustainable Development Goal aims to achieve the 
set goals under the UN’s 2030 Agenda (RGC, 2018). Cambodia is experiencing 
the effects of climate change, including rising temperatures, changing rainfall 
patterns, and increased frequency and severity of extreme weather events such 
as floods and droughts, which seriously impact agriculture, water resources, 
and food security, all of which are very critical for the Cambodian population, 
especially those in rural areas.

exploring other renewable energy sources. Solar energy also gains popularity in 
Cambodia. The country has abundant sunlight, making solar power an attractive 
renewable energy option in addition to the previous energy option, if not entirely 
replacing oil. In recent years, solar farms and rooftop installations have been 
implemented, particularly in rural areas with limited access to the national 
grid. These solar initiatives provide clean electricity for households, schools, 
and healthcare centers, improving energy access and reducing dependence on 
traditional energy. Furthermore, Cambodia is exploring the potential of other 
renewable energy sources, including wind and biomass.
Realizing that we live in an era of unprecedented scientific and technological 
advancement, where innovative solutions have the potential to tackle energy 
challenges and reshape the energy landscape, the Royal Government of 
Cambodia has rolled out the National Research Agenda (NRA) 2025 to utilize 
research and development to pursue national economic interests and overcome 
the challenges the nation has faced through building a vibrant research ecosystem 
to strengthen science and technology capability and, in turn, leverage national 
innovation performance. NRA has prioritized eight research missions that 
Cambodia has to achieve by 2030, three of which are related to energy, which are 
“Reliable Energy Supply: 90 percent of energy consumption is generated locally”; 
“Electricity and potable water: All Cambodians have access to reliable electricity 
and safe potable water”; and “Carbon neutrality: Cambodia becomes a carbon 
neutral country” (RGC, 2023b, p. VI). To achieve these eight missions, four 
policy priorities have been inaugurated including investing in research to support 
the eight research missions, strengthening the role and capacities of research 
institutions, supporting research careers, and incentivizing research activities and 
collaboration. Moreover, the Energy Technology Roadmap has been rolled out 
as a comprehensive strategic actionable plan navigating the efforts toward the 
dynamic landscape of energy technology in the government’s quest to achieve 
energy security and sustainable development (RGC, 2023a).
In addition to mitigating greenhouse gas emissions, Cambodia is also 
focusing on building resilience and adapting to the impacts of climate change. 
To support the development of renewable energy, the Cambodian government 
has implemented various policies and incentives. International cooperation and 
partnerships have also been established to facilitate knowledge sharing, capacity 
building, and technology transfer in the renewable energy sector.
6. Current Landscape of Regional Frameworks on Energy	
In the globalization era, regional cooperation is more important than ever to 
ensuring national security and promoting sustainable development to drive 
positive change on a regional and global scale. Hence, ASEAN has set ambitious 
targets for renewable energy in the Total Primary Energy Supply (TPES) and 
installed power capacity, aiming for a 23% share of renewable energy in TPES 
Energy Diplomacy and ASEAN Green Deal
61
and a 35% share in installed power capacity (Safrina, 2023). However, each 
ASEAN member state has its own clean energy targets, which vary based on 
their capacity, capability, and performance. Considering the diverse energy 
landscapes, economic conditions, and institutional capacities within ASEAN, it 
is natural for each member state to establish their own clean energy targets that 
align with their specific circumstances, resources, and development priorities.
Within ASEAN, Cambodia stands as an active participant in cross-border 
energy trade with neighboring countries, such as Laos, Thailand, and Vietnam. 
Cambodia has set its own ambitious renewable energy target, aiming to achieve 
a 25% share of renewable energy in its energy mix by 2030. To accelerate the 
transition, Cambodia has set a specific objective to install a minimum of 150 MW 
of solar capacity by 2023. Furthermore, Cambodia is actively pursuing waste-to-
energy projects, focusing on the treatment of municipal solid waste (MSW). In 
terms of energy efficiency, Cambodia has identified several measures, including 
targets for reducing electricity consumption, strategies to mitigate the urban heat 
island effect (UHIE), the adoption of Minimum Energy Performance Standards 
(MEPS), and the implementation of energy labeling schemes (ASEAN Centre 
for Energy, 2023).

Senior Officials Meeting on Energy (SOME) and endorsed by the 38th ASEAN 
Ministers on Energy Meeting (AMEM), there are specific program areas of energy

•	 ASEAN Power Grid: This program focuses on enhancing regional power

•	 Trans-ASEAN Gas Pipeline: This program aims to develop a transnational 
natural gas pipeline network within ASEAN to ensure the reliable supply 
and efficient transportation of natural gas across the region.

7. Cambodia and ASEAN Green Deal	
The Green Deal concept has emerged as a tool, adopted by the EU Commission, 
for climate, energy, transport and taxation policies to reduce the net emissions 
of climate change. The introduction of the ‘ASEAN Green Deal’ concept took 
place during the Opening Ceremony of the 55th ASEAN Foreign Ministers’ 
Meeting and Related Meetings on August 3, 2022, during which Prime Minister 
Hun Sen presented two initiatives for ASEAN leaders to endorse. In addition to 
suggesting the creation of the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership 
(RCEP) Secretariat, he also proposed the establishment of a comprehensive 
Energy Diplomacy and ASEAN Green Deal
63
framework known as the ‘ASEAN Green Deal’. This newly-coined initiative, 
according to the Prime Minister, aims to facilitate a gradual transition towards 
a sustainable, resource-efficient, resilient, and competitive green economy in 
the region, which encompasses various sectors, including infrastructure, energy, 
manufacturing, consumption, agriculture, transport, environment, and finance. 
It would rely on technology, innovation, and circularity as enabling factors (Hun, 
2022; Kunthear & Sochan, 2022).
One of the key objectives of the ASEAN Green Deal is to build new sources 
of competitiveness within the ASEAN Economic Community by 2030. This 
includes strengthening economic resilience and promoting inclusive economic 
community building. Additionally, the establishment of a highly innovative 
digital ASEAN Economic Community is envisioned, which will empower 
citizens, entrepreneurs, and businesses, and enhance ASEAN’s competitive edge 
in terms of skilled labor, professionals, enterprises, and industries. This will be 
achieved through continuous improvement of digital infrastructure, connectivity, 
and bridging the digital divide, as well as creating a secure and trustworthy digital 
space and services. The adoption of digital and innovative technologies, along 
with the promotion of circularity in business models, will support ASEAN’s 
drive towards a more sustainable, greener, carbon-neutral, and circular regional 
economy.
The ASEAN Green Deal also aims to strengthen the resilience of ASEAN’s 
economy by building adaptive capacity to manage systemic threats and emerging 
challenges, particularly those related to climate change, biodiversity loss, and 
health emergencies. This will involve mainstreaming resilience across various 
elements and ecosystems of the ASEAN Economic Community, such as food 
security, energy security, sustainable housing, clean air, macroeconomic stability, 
and economic security. Effective governance, both through regulatory practice 
and transparency, will be promoted, along with public and private investment 
to stimulate employment, income growth, and the creation of green jobs. 
Furthermore, a cohesive and enabling ecosystem and regulatory environment 
will provide the necessary financial, investment, infrastructure, and innovation 
support for the deployment of environmentally sustainable projects across 
sectors. The adoption of, and investment in, innovative and climate-friendly 
technologies will also be encouraged to drive sustainable green growth, integrate 
circular economy concepts, and improve the quality and efficiency of ASEAN’s 
urban and rural areas.
To achieve its objectives, the ASEAN Green Deal emphasizes green 
development and investment across various economic sectors, leveraging 
technology, innovation, and circularity. Drawing from the European Green 
Deal’s success, the ASEAN Green Deal seeks to reduce greenhouse gas emissions 
by at least 55% and increase the share of renewable energy by over 32% by 2030. 
Additionally, improving energy efficiency by at least 32.5% is a key target. 
Green Ideals
64
Similar to the European Green Deal, the ASEAN Green Deal proposes new 
legislation and funding mechanisms to support the transition to a green economy 
(Chheang, 2023).
Prime Minister Hun Sen reiterated his commitment to the ASEAN Green 
Deal during subsequent events. At the Opening Ceremony of the 2022 ASEAN 
Leadership and Partnership Forum on September 12, 2022, he expressed his 
intention to host the inaugural Green Economic Zone (GEZ) with the enactment 
of a new investment law as part of the ASEAN Green Deal framework. The 
Prime Minister further reiterated the importance of the ASEAN Green Deal 
at the opening of the 54th ASEAN Economic Ministers’ Meeting and Related 
Meetings on September 15, 2022 and the ASEAN Business and Investment 
Summit (ABIS) 2022 on November 13, 2022, demonstrating his consistent 
emphasis on promoting the green agenda and its integration into ASEAN’s 
economic strategies. At the latest, this initiative was raised at the Opening 
Ceremony of the 43rd ASEAN Inter-Parliamentary Assembly (AIPA) on 
November 21, 2022. 
Albeit his consistent advocacy in various high-level meetings and forums, 
the ASEAN Green Deal remained in the early stages of development during 
Cambodia’s ASEAN chairmanship. Regrettably, no tangible progress or concrete 
actions were taken to advance the initiative.
8. Challenges and Opportunities	
During Cambodia’s chairmanship of ASEAN, there appeared to be a lack of 
enthusiasm among member states for supporting the proposal of the ASEAN 
Green Deal. Despite the efforts made by Cambodia to promote the initiative, 
the response from other countries within the ASEAN community was relatively 
hesitant and reserved. The lack of tangible progress can be attributed to a 
combination of factors, primarily centered around issues of ownership and 
financial responsibility.
One major hurdle that hindered the advancement of the ASEAN Green Deal 
was the absence of clear ownership amongst ASEAN member states. Without a 
consensus on which country or countries would take the lead in developing and 
implementing the initiative, progress was stymied. Additionally, the question of 
financial resources emerged as a critical obstacle. The successful realization of 
any ambitious initiative requires substantial funding. The lack of commitment 
from member states to allocate the necessary resources further impeded the 
advancement of the ASEAN Green Deal. 
It is important to note that the challenges faced by the ASEAN Green Deal 
were not driven by geopolitical considerations but rather by practical concerns 
related to ownership and financial burden-sharing. Unlike some initiatives, such 
as Singapore’s proposal of the ASEAN Smart Cities Network (ASCN) during 
Energy Diplomacy and ASEAN Green Deal
65
their chairmanship of ASEAN, which have seen significant support from the 
proposed government through financial investments and the hosting of events 
and meetings, the ASEAN Green Deal’s case lacks similar commitments. 
Leadership in multilateralism is often determined by a country’s willingness to 
invest financially and create platforms for other nations to join and support the 
initiative. The absence of a strong financial commitment from member states 
limited the potential for leadership in driving the initiative forward. While the 
idea of the ASEAN Green Deal held promise, its progress was hindered by 
practical challenges that needed to be addressed for there to be any future efforts 
in this direction.
Despite the challenges and lack of progress in the development of the ASEAN 
Green Deal, there are still potential opportunities for advancing the initiative. 
These opportunities can be explored to overcome the existing barriers and pave 
the way for a more sustainable and resilient ASEAN community. Some potential 
opportunities include:
•	 Enhanced collaboration and coordination: Member states can seize the 
opportunity to strengthen cooperation and coordination within ASEAN 
to advance the goals of the ASEAN Green Deal. By sharing best practices, 
exchanging knowledge, and pooling resources, member states can 
collectively address the challenges and work towards a sustainable and 
green future.
•	 Leveraging existing regional frameworks: ASEAN can leverage existing 
regional frameworks and initiatives related to energy, sustainability, and 
climate change to support the ASEAN Green Deal. By aligning the goals 
and actions of the Green Deal with other regional initiatives, such as the 
ASEAN Plan of Action for Energy Cooperation (APAEC) or the ASEAN 
Framework on Sustainable Development, synergies can be created to 
maximize impact and efficiency.
•	 Engaging with international partners: ASEAN can explore partnerships 
and collaborations with international organizations, including the 
European Union (EU), development agencies, and other countries that 
have experience and expertise in green initiatives. For example, during 
the 3rd ASEAN-EU Dialogue on Sustainable Development in November 
2021, the Team Europe Green Initiative collaborated with ASEAN to 
establish a work program aimed at fostering a greener future. To support 
this initiative, the EU has allocated an initial grant of $32.2 million, which 
will be utilized alongside the European Green Deal and the ASEAN 
Community Vision 2025. Additionally, the EU has pledged $53.68 million 
to the ASEAN Catalytic Green Finance Facility, encouraging private 
investments in green infrastructure projects across ASEAN member states 
(Chheang, 2023).

66
•	 Mobilizing financial resources: Member states can explore innovative 
financing mechanisms, such as green bonds, public-private partnerships, 
or dedicated funds, to mobilize the necessary financial resources for 
implementing the ASEAN Green Deal. Also, harmonizing national 
targets and implementing supportive policies, regulatory frameworks, and 
financial assistance mechanisms, such as Build-Operate-Transfer (BOT), 
Public-Private Partnership (PPP) and Feed-in Tariff (FiT), are crucial for 
attracting private investments in clean energy within ASEAN (Safrina, 
2023). The active pursuit of funding and investments from international 
governments and organizations is vital, acknowledging the significant role 
of international financing in achieving national and regional energy targets. 
•	 Promoting capacity building and technology transfer: Capacity building 
and technology transfer play crucial roles in enabling the implementation 
of sustainable practices and technologies. ASEAN can facilitate knowledge 
sharing, training programs, and technology transfer initiatives among 
member states to build the necessary skills and capabilities for implementing 
the ASEAN Green Deal.
•	 Public awareness and stakeholder engagement: Member states can actively 
engage with various stakeholders, including businesses, civil society 
organizations, and the general public, to raise awareness and garner 
support for the ASEAN Green Deal. By fostering a sense of ownership 
and promoting public participation, member states can create a conducive 
environment for the successful implementation of the initiative.
9. Policy Recommendations	
As the government strives to achieve energy security and transition to green and 
sustainable energy sources, bold and transformative action to promote sustainable 
development and regional cooperation are indispensable. Hence, here are some 
recommendations to obtain the goals:
•	 Develop a Sustainable Energy Transition Plan: Cambodia should 
formulate a thorough, long-term energy transition strategy with precise 
objectives for transitioning to a sustainable energy landscape. Strategies for 
eliminating high-carbon sources, increasing the utilization of renewable 
energy sources, and incorporating energy storage technologies should all 
be part of this plan.
•	 Enhance Energy Governance and Regulatory Frameworks: Energy 
governance and regulatory frameworks are critical to promoting 
transparency, accountability, and efficiency in the energy sector. It can 
create a stable and conducive environment for investments, encourage 
competition, ensure consumer protection, and enable the transition to a 
cleaner and more sustainable energy ecosystem.
Energy Diplomacy and ASEAN Green Deal
67
•	 Develop a Comprehensive Energy Diplomacy Strategy: Developing a 
comprehensive energy diplomacy strategy requires understanding the 
holistic view of a country’s energy agenda, geopolitical factors, and global 
energy landscapes and trends. This plan shall cover a range of spectrums 
including energy security, economic interests, environmental sustainability, 
and diplomatic engagements. A comprehensive energy diplomacy plan 
should be flexible and responsive to shifting geopolitical conditions, 
developing technical landscapes, and changing energy demands.
•	 Strengthen Bilateral and Multilateral on Green Deal and Energy 
Partnerships: Cambodia should actively engage in bilateral and regional 
energy cooperation initiatives, such as the Association of Southeast Asian 
Nations (ASEAN) and the Greater Mekong Subregion (GMS) frameworks. 
Collaborative efforts can lead to the development of cross-border energy 
infrastructure, interconnections, technology transfer, joint energy projects, 
trading, collaborative research, fostering regional stability and economic 
integration.
•	 Promote Green Deal and Energy Diplomacy and Dialogue: Cambodia 
should actively participate in regional and international energy dialogues, 
forums, and negotiations. Engaging in energy diplomacy can enhance 
the country’s diplomatic relations, foster knowledge sharing, and enable 
Cambodia to contribute to global energy governance.
•	 Invest in Renewable Energy Research and Development: Investing 
in research and development (R&D) for clean energy technologies, 
energy storage systems, and innovative solutions shall be prioritized. 
Collaboration with research institutions, academia, and the private sector 
to drive scientific and technological advancements and enhance innovation 
performance in the energy sector. Promotion of the commercialization of 
indigenous technologies and supporting startups and entrepreneurship in 
the energy sector shall also be considered.
•	 Enhance Cross-Border Green Deals and Energy Trade: Facilitating cross-
border energy trade with neighboring countries and in the region can 
provide Cambodia with access to diverse energy resources and foster energy 
security. The country can explore opportunities for importing electricity or 
natural gas from neighboring countries with surplus production capacity.
•	 Promote Capacity Building and Knowledge Exchange: Cambodia 
should invest in building institutional capacity and expertise in energy 
planning, regulation, and policymaking. This can be achieved through 
training programs, knowledge exchange platforms, and partnerships 
with international organizations and developed countries in the energy 
sector.	
These policy recommendations aim to guide Cambodia towards a 
sustainable, diversified and dynamic energy landscape and energy security

while fostering regional cooperation and energy diplomacy. Implementing 
these strategies can help Cambodia address its energy challenges and 
leverage its energy resources for economic growth and prosperity.
10. Conclusion
Energy diplomacy and the green deal play a crucial role in addressing energy 
security challenges and achieving sustainable development. The global community 
is confronted with urgent threats of climate change and environmental degradation, 
necessitating a shift toward a modern, efficient, and competitive economy. 
Energy diplomacy serves as a vital tool in fostering cooperation, ensuring energy 
security, and driving sustainable development through international partnerships 
and agreements. Energy security faces risks from geopolitical unrest, natural 
disasters, cybersecurity threats, and volatile energy prices. To mitigate these risks, 
governments must engage in energy diplomacy to establish cooperation, facilitate 
dialogue, and create energy agreements. Collaborative efforts among nations can 
reduce vulnerabilities and establish a stable and resilient energy landscape.
The ASEAN Green Deal, as proposed during the ASEAN Foreign Ministers’ 
Meeting, offers a comprehensive approach to address energy and environmental 
challenges. It aims to promote inclusivity, resilience, and sustainable growth in 
the ASEAN region by encouraging investments in clean energy and emission 
reductions. The Green Deal not only addresses the urgent need for energy 
transition but also supports renewable energy development, energy efficiency, 
and sustainable practices.
Energy diplomacy and the green deal are also essential for achieving the 
United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). By ensuring access to 
clean and affordable energy for all, countries can foster economic development, 
improve living conditions, and protect the environment. Collaborative initiatives 
like the UN-Energy partnership and the ASEAN Plan of Action for Energy 
Cooperation (APAEC) provide frameworks for cooperation and progress 
towards these goals.
Looking ahead, investments in technological advancements, energy 
infrastructure, and energy-efficient practices are critical. Governments, local 
administrations, and community leaders should raise awareness about energy 
security and engage in multilateral diplomacy to amplify their voices and 
level the playing field. By embracing innovative solutions and upholding the 
rule of law, smaller states can effectively contribute to international energy 
cooperation and sustainable development. In the context of the ASEAN region, 
the involvement of member states in the ASEAN Plan of Action for Energy 
Cooperation (APAEC) and ASEAN Green Deal represents a form of energy 
diplomacy. Collaborative efforts and cooperation with various stakeholders can 
help achieve the energy goals set at the regional level. While challenges, such 
Energy Diplomacy and ASEAN Green Deal
69
as unclear ownership and financial responsibility, need to be addressed, there 
are opportunities to be capitalized upon. Enhanced collaboration, leveraging 
existing regional frameworks, engaging with international partners, mobilizing 
financial resources, promoting capacity building and technology transfer, and 
fostering public awareness and stakeholder engagement can drive the progress of 
the ASEAN Green Deal.
The ASEAN Green Deal holds significant promise for shaping the future 
of Southeast Asia. It aligns with the global push for sustainability, drawing 
inspiration from successful initiatives like the European Green Deal. By fostering 
regional cooperation and commitment to environmental goals, the ASEAN 
Green Deal has the potential to drive meaningful change, promoting a greener, 
more resilient, and economically competitive Southeast Asia.

1. Sustainability of Industrial Development
The United Nations has adopted in principle the concept of sustainable 
development, which relies on three pillars, namely environment, society, and 
economy. The concept has faced challenges in achieving the ideal universal goal 
of sustainability. It has been observed that balancing the three pillars for common 
goods has not been met due to the fact that most nations value or materialize 
the concept in different forms based on national and/or aligned interests or 
preferences. As a result, realizing the goals is seen as challenging due to the fact 
that the environment and society are commonly left behind. It is important to 
note that human society and the natural environment are common environments 
in which people perceive no self-belonging in taking care. This falls under the 
concept of the tragedy of the commons, in which overpopulation is one of the 
factors that marginalizes the concerns of sustainability in the current context 
(Candelone et al.,1995; Hardin, 1968; Jonsson, 2012).
The natural changes show a strong correlation with human civilization’s 
development. The records from agriculture to the industrial revolution 
appear to be evidence that scientists have agreed on positive development 
in one dimension and negative facts in another. The severity of the 
environmental damage has been quite obvious in the last 100 years (as 
shown in the Figure 7.1.) (Gibbard et al., 2022). For these reasons, the 
United Nations has called for more efforts to reduce degradation while 
ensuring inclusivity and growth in socio-economic development. Thus, many 
theoretical frameworks in regulation and/or science and technology have 
been articulated to maintain the development of the industrial sector. The 
industrial revolution in Anthropocene informs all players of a new paradigm 
shift in balancing development and environmental conservation (Jonsson, 
2012). The accumulation of heavy metal deposition in human inhabitant 
such as Greenland and ice was attributed to tons of contaminants due to the 
industrial revolution (Candelone et al., 1995). This land pollution could be 
more severe for the atmospheric and water environments.
However, new studies have found some promising trends suggesting 
that Industry 4.0 could help manage environmental degradation in both the 
biophysical and social spaces. Additionally, green technologies are a priority for 
the top manufacturing industries. Studies suggest that environmental technologies 
and environmental industries are key factors in addressing sustainability issues

Cambodia has strived to be a low-carbon economy by boosting renewable 
energy sources in order to reduce greenhouse gas emissions which contribute 
to climate change. The increase in hydropower is a significant development 
in Cambodia’s energy environment. The country is endowed with numerous 
rivers and streams which have potential for hydropower, which offers great 
opportunities for renewable energy generation (Poch, 2013). The government has 
made use of this potential by building many large-scale hydropower plants. These 
projects have contributed to increasing domestic energy production, producing 
clean energy, reducing reliance on imported energy, and providing electricity to 
previously underserved rural areas. In addition to hydropower, Cambodia is also

exploring other renewable energy sources. Solar energy also gains popularity in 
Cambodia. The country has abundant sunlight, making solar power an attractive 
renewable energy option in addition to the previous energy option, if not entirely 
replacing oil. In recent years, solar farms and rooftop installations have been 
implemented, particularly in rural areas with limited access to the national 
grid. These solar initiatives provide clean electricity for households, schools, 
and healthcare centers, improving energy access and reducing dependence on 
traditional energy. Furthermore, Cambodia is exploring the potential of other 
renewable energy sources, including wind and biomass.
Realizing that we live in an era of unprecedented scientific and technological 
advancement, where innovative solutions have the potential to tackle energy 
challenges and reshape the energy landscape, the Royal Government of 
Cambodia has rolled out the National Research Agenda (NRA) 2025 to utilize 
research and development to pursue national economic interests and overcome 
the challenges the nation has faced through building a vibrant research ecosystem 
to strengthen science and technology capability and, in turn, leverage national 
innovation performance. NRA has prioritized eight research missions that 
Cambodia has to achieve by 2030, three of which are related to energy, which are 
“Reliable Energy Supply: 90 percent of energy consumption is generated locally”; 
“Electricity and potable water: All Cambodians have access to reliable electricity 
and safe potable water”; and “Carbon neutrality: Cambodia becomes a carbon 
neutral country” (RGC, 2023b, p. VI). To achieve these eight missions, four 
policy priorities have been inaugurated including investing in research to support 
the eight research missions, strengthening the role and capacities of research 
institutions, supporting research careers, and incentivizing research activities and 
collaboration. Moreover, the Energy Technology Roadmap has been rolled out 
as a comprehensive strategic actionable plan navigating the efforts toward the 
dynamic landscape of energy technology in the government’s quest to achieve 
energy security and sustainable development (RGC, 2023a).
In addition to mitigating greenhouse gas emissions, Cambodia is also 
focusing on building resilience and adapting to the impacts of climate change. 
To support the development of renewable energy, the Cambodian government 
has implemented various policies and incentives. International cooperation and 
partnerships have also been established to facilitate knowledge sharing, capacity 
building, and technology transfer in the renewable energy sector.
6. Current Landscape of Regional Frameworks on Energy	
In the globalization era, regional cooperation is more important than ever to 
ensuring national security and promoting sustainable development to drive 
positive change on a regional and global scale. Hence, ASEAN has set ambitious 
targets for renewable energy in the Total Primary Energy Supply (TPES) and 
installed power capacity, aiming for a 23% share of renewable energy in TPES

and a 35% share in installed power capacity (Safrina, 2023). However, each 
ASEAN member state has its own clean energy targets, which vary based on 
their capacity, capability, and performance. Considering the diverse energy 
landscapes, economic conditions, and institutional capacities within ASEAN, it 
is natural for each member state to establish their own clean energy targets that 
align with their specific circumstances, resources, and development priorities.
Within ASEAN, Cambodia stands as an active participant in cross-border 
energy trade with neighboring countries, such as Laos, Thailand, and Vietnam. 
Cambodia has set its own ambitious renewable energy target, aiming to achieve 
a 25% share of renewable energy in its energy mix by 2030. To accelerate the 
transition, Cambodia has set a specific objective to install a minimum of 150 MW 
of solar capacity by 2023. Furthermore, Cambodia is actively pursuing waste-to-
energy projects, focusing on the treatment of municipal solid waste (MSW). In 
terms of energy efficiency, Cambodia has identified several measures, including 
targets for reducing electricity consumption, strategies to mitigate the urban heat 
island effect (UHIE), the adoption of Minimum Energy Performance Standards 
(MEPS), and the implementation of energy labeling schemes (ASEAN Centre 
for Energy, 2023).

7. Cambodia and ASEAN Green Deal	
The Green Deal concept has emerged as a tool, adopted by the EU Commission, 
for climate, energy, transport and taxation policies to reduce the net emissions 
of climate change. The introduction of the ‘ASEAN Green Deal’ concept took 
place during the Opening Ceremony of the 55th ASEAN Foreign Ministers’ 
Meeting and Related Meetings on August 3, 2022, during which Prime Minister 
Hun Sen presented two initiatives for ASEAN leaders to endorse. In addition to 
suggesting the creation of the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership 
(RCEP) Secretariat, he also proposed the establishment of a comprehensive 
Energy Diplomacy and ASEAN Green Deal
63
framework known as the ‘ASEAN Green Deal’. This newly-coined initiative, 
according to the Prime Minister, aims to facilitate a gradual transition towards 
a sustainable, resource-efficient, resilient, and competitive green economy in 
the region, which encompasses various sectors, including infrastructure, energy, 
manufacturing, consumption, agriculture, transport, environment, and finance. 
It would rely on technology, innovation, and circularity as enabling factors (Hun, 
2022; Kunthear & Sochan, 2022).
One of the key objectives of the ASEAN Green Deal is to build new sources 
of competitiveness within the ASEAN Economic Community by 2030. This 
includes strengthening economic resilience and promoting inclusive economic 
community building. Additionally, the establishment of a highly innovative 
digital ASEAN Economic Community is envisioned, which will empower 
citizens, entrepreneurs, and businesses, and enhance ASEAN’s competitive edge 
in terms of skilled labor, professionals, enterprises, and industries. This will be 
achieved through continuous improvement of digital infrastructure, connectivity, 
and bridging the digital divide, as well as creating a secure and trustworthy digital 
space and services. The adoption of digital and innovative technologies, along 
with the promotion of circularity in business models, will support ASEAN’s 
drive towards a more sustainable, greener, carbon-neutral, and circular regional 
economy.
The ASEAN Green Deal also aims to strengthen the resilience of ASEAN’s 
economy by building adaptive capacity to manage systemic threats and emerging 
challenges, particularly those related to climate change, biodiversity loss, and 
health emergencies. This will involve mainstreaming resilience across various 
elements and ecosystems of the ASEAN Economic Community, such as food 
security, energy security, sustainable housing, clean air, macroeconomic stability, 
and economic security. Effective governance, both through regulatory practice 
and transparency, will be promoted, along with public and private investment 
to stimulate employment, income growth, and the creation of green jobs. 
Furthermore, a cohesive and enabling ecosystem and regulatory environment 
will provide the necessary financial, investment, infrastructure, and innovation 
support for the deployment of environmentally sustainable projects across 
sectors. The adoption of, and investment in, innovative and climate-friendly 
technologies will also be encouraged to drive sustainable green growth, integrate 
circular economy concepts, and improve the quality and efficiency of ASEAN’s 
urban and rural areas.
To achieve its objectives, the ASEAN Green Deal emphasizes green 
development and investment across various economic sectors, leveraging 
technology, innovation, and circularity. Drawing from the European Green 
Deal’s success, the ASEAN Green Deal seeks to reduce greenhouse gas emissions 
by at least 55% and increase the share of renewable energy by over 32% by 2030. 
Additionally, improving energy efficiency by at least 32.5% is a key target. 
Green Ideals
64
Similar to the European Green Deal, the ASEAN Green Deal proposes new 
legislation and funding mechanisms to support the transition to a green economy 
(Chheang, 2023).
Prime Minister Hun Sen reiterated his commitment to the ASEAN Green 
Deal during subsequent events. At the Opening Ceremony of the 2022 ASEAN 
Leadership and Partnership Forum on September 12, 2022, he expressed his 
intention to host the inaugural Green Economic Zone (GEZ) with the enactment 
of a new investment law as part of the ASEAN Green Deal framework. The 
Prime Minister further reiterated the importance of the ASEAN Green Deal 
at the opening of the 54th ASEAN Economic Ministers’ Meeting and Related 
Meetings on September 15, 2022 and the ASEAN Business and Investment 
Summit (ABIS) 2022 on November 13, 2022, demonstrating his consistent 
emphasis on promoting the green agenda and its integration into ASEAN’s 
economic strategies. At the latest, this initiative was raised at the Opening 
Ceremony of the 43rd ASEAN Inter-Parliamentary Assembly (AIPA) on 
November 21, 2022. 
Albeit his consistent advocacy in various high-level meetings and forums, 
the ASEAN Green Deal remained in the early stages of development during 
Cambodia’s ASEAN chairmanship. Regrettably, no tangible progress or concrete 
actions were taken to advance the initiative.
8. Challenges and Opportunities	
During Cambodia’s chairmanship of ASEAN, there appeared to be a lack of 
enthusiasm among member states for supporting the proposal of the ASEAN 
Green Deal. Despite the efforts made by Cambodia to promote the initiative, 
the response from other countries within the ASEAN community was relatively 
hesitant and reserved. The lack of tangible progress can be attributed to a 
combination of factors, primarily centered around issues of ownership and 
financial responsibility.
One major hurdle that hindered the advancement of the ASEAN Green Deal 
was the absence of clear ownership amongst ASEAN member states. Without a 
consensus on which country or countries would take the lead in developing and 
implementing the initiative, progress was stymied. Additionally, the question of 
financial resources emerged as a critical obstacle. The successful realization of 
any ambitious initiative requires substantial funding. The lack of commitment 
from member states to allocate the necessary resources further impeded the 
advancement of the ASEAN Green Deal. 
It is important to note that the challenges faced by the ASEAN Green Deal 
were not driven by geopolitical considerations but rather by practical concerns 
related to ownership and financial burden-sharing. Unlike some initiatives, such 
as Singapore’s proposal of the ASEAN Smart Cities Network (ASCN) during 
Energy Diplomacy and ASEAN Green Deal
65
their chairmanship of ASEAN, which have seen significant support from the 
proposed government through financial investments and the hosting of events 
and meetings, the ASEAN Green Deal’s case lacks similar commitments. 
Leadership in multilateralism is often determined by a country’s willingness to 
invest financially and create platforms for other nations to join and support the 
initiative. The absence of a strong financial commitment from member states 
limited the potential for leadership in driving the initiative forward. While the 
idea of the ASEAN Green Deal held promise, its progress was hindered by 
practical challenges that needed to be addressed for there to be any future efforts 
in this direction.
Despite the challenges and lack of progress in the development of the ASEAN 
Green Deal, there are still potential opportunities for advancing the initiative. 
These opportunities can be explored to overcome the existing barriers and pave 
the way for a more sustainable and resilient ASEAN community. Some potential 
opportunities include:
•	 Enhanced collaboration and coordination: Member states can seize the 
opportunity to strengthen cooperation and coordination within ASEAN 
to advance the goals of the ASEAN Green Deal. By sharing best practices, 
exchanging knowledge, and pooling resources, member states can 
collectively address the challenges and work towards a sustainable and 
green future.
•	 Leveraging existing regional frameworks: ASEAN can leverage existing 
regional frameworks and initiatives related to energy, sustainability, and 
climate change to support the ASEAN Green Deal. By aligning the goals 
and actions of the Green Deal with other regional initiatives, such as the 
ASEAN Plan of Action for Energy Cooperation (APAEC) or the ASEAN 
Framework on Sustainable Development, synergies can be created to 
maximize impact and efficiency.
•	 Engaging with international partners: ASEAN can explore partnerships 
and collaborations with international organizations, including the 
European Union (EU), development agencies, and other countries that 
have experience and expertise in green initiatives. For example, during 
the 3rd ASEAN-EU Dialogue on Sustainable Development in November 
2021, the Team Europe Green Initiative collaborated with ASEAN to 
establish a work program aimed at fostering a greener future. To support 
this initiative, the EU has allocated an initial grant of $32.2 million, which 
will be utilized alongside the European Green Deal and the ASEAN 
Community Vision 2025. Additionally, the EU has pledged $53.68 million 
to the ASEAN Catalytic Green Finance Facility, encouraging private 
investments in green infrastructure projects across ASEAN member states 
(Chheang, 2023).
