•	 Mobilizing financial resources: Member states can explore innovative 
financing mechanisms, such as green bonds, public-private partnerships, 
or dedicated funds, to mobilize the necessary financial resources for 
implementing the ASEAN Green Deal. Also, harmonizing national 
targets and implementing supportive policies, regulatory frameworks, and 
financial assistance mechanisms, such as Build-Operate-Transfer (BOT), 
Public-Private Partnership (PPP) and Feed-in Tariff (FiT), are crucial for 
attracting private investments in clean energy within ASEAN (Safrina, 
2023). The active pursuit of funding and investments from international 
governments and organizations is vital, acknowledging the significant role 
of international financing in achieving national and regional energy targets. 
•	 Promoting capacity building and technology transfer: Capacity building 
and technology transfer play crucial roles in enabling the implementation 
of sustainable practices and technologies. ASEAN can facilitate knowledge 
sharing, training programs, and technology transfer initiatives among 
member states to build the necessary skills and capabilities for implementing 
the ASEAN Green Deal.
•	 Public awareness and stakeholder engagement: Member states can actively 
engage with various stakeholders, including businesses, civil society 
organizations, and the general public, to raise awareness and garner 
support for the ASEAN Green Deal. By fostering a sense of ownership 
and promoting public participation, member states can create a conducive 
environment for the successful implementation of the initiative.
9. Policy Recommendations	
As the government strives to achieve energy security and transition to green and 
sustainable energy sources, bold and transformative action to promote sustainable 
development and regional cooperation are indispensable. Hence, here are some 
recommendations to obtain the goals:
•	 Develop a Sustainable Energy Transition Plan: Cambodia should 
formulate a thorough, long-term energy transition strategy with precise 
objectives for transitioning to a sustainable energy landscape. Strategies for 
eliminating high-carbon sources, increasing the utilization of renewable 
energy sources, and incorporating energy storage technologies should all 
be part of this plan.
•	 Enhance Energy Governance and Regulatory Frameworks: Energy 
governance and regulatory frameworks are critical to promoting 
transparency, accountability, and efficiency in the energy sector. It can 
create a stable and conducive environment for investments, encourage 
competition, ensure consumer protection, and enable the transition to a 
cleaner and more sustainable energy ecosystem.
Energy Diplomacy and ASEAN Green Deal
67
•	 Develop a Comprehensive Energy Diplomacy Strategy: Developing a 
comprehensive energy diplomacy strategy requires understanding the 
holistic view of a country’s energy agenda, geopolitical factors, and global 
energy landscapes and trends. This plan shall cover a range of spectrums 
including energy security, economic interests, environmental sustainability, 
and diplomatic engagements. A comprehensive energy diplomacy plan 
should be flexible and responsive to shifting geopolitical conditions, 
developing technical landscapes, and changing energy demands.
•	 Strengthen Bilateral and Multilateral on Green Deal and Energy 
Partnerships: Cambodia should actively engage in bilateral and regional 
energy cooperation initiatives, such as the Association of Southeast Asian 
Nations (ASEAN) and the Greater Mekong Subregion (GMS) frameworks. 
Collaborative efforts can lead to the development of cross-border energy 
infrastructure, interconnections, technology transfer, joint energy projects, 
trading, collaborative research, fostering regional stability and economic 
integration.
•	 Promote Green Deal and Energy Diplomacy and Dialogue: Cambodia 
should actively participate in regional and international energy dialogues, 
forums, and negotiations. Engaging in energy diplomacy can enhance 
the country’s diplomatic relations, foster knowledge sharing, and enable 
Cambodia to contribute to global energy governance.
•	 Invest in Renewable Energy Research and Development: Investing 
in research and development (R&D) for clean energy technologies, 
energy storage systems, and innovative solutions shall be prioritized. 
Collaboration with research institutions, academia, and the private sector 
to drive scientific and technological advancements and enhance innovation 
performance in the energy sector. Promotion of the commercialization of 
indigenous technologies and supporting startups and entrepreneurship in 
the energy sector shall also be considered.
•	 Enhance Cross-Border Green Deals and Energy Trade: Facilitating cross-
border energy trade with neighboring countries and in the region can 
provide Cambodia with access to diverse energy resources and foster energy 
security. The country can explore opportunities for importing electricity or 
natural gas from neighboring countries with surplus production capacity.
•	 Promote Capacity Building and Knowledge Exchange: Cambodia 
should invest in building institutional capacity and expertise in energy 
planning, regulation, and policymaking. This can be achieved through 
training programs, knowledge exchange platforms, and partnerships 
with international organizations and developed countries in the energy 
sector.	
These policy recommendations aim to guide Cambodia towards a 
sustainable, diversified and dynamic energy landscape and energy security

while fostering regional cooperation and energy diplomacy. Implementing 
these strategies can help Cambodia address its energy challenges and

10. Conclusion
Energy diplomacy and the green deal play a crucial role in addressing energy 
security challenges and achieving sustainable development. The global community 
is confronted with urgent threats of climate change and environmental degradation, 
necessitating a shift toward a modern, efficient, and competitive economy. 
Energy diplomacy serves as a vital tool in fostering cooperation, ensuring energy 
security, and driving sustainable development through international partnerships 
and agreements. Energy security faces risks from geopolitical unrest, natural 
disasters, cybersecurity threats, and volatile energy prices. To mitigate these risks, 
governments must engage in energy diplomacy to establish cooperation, facilitate 
dialogue, and create energy agreements. Collaborative efforts among nations can 
reduce vulnerabilities and establish a stable and resilient energy landscape.
The ASEAN Green Deal, as proposed during the ASEAN Foreign Ministers’ 
Meeting, offers a comprehensive approach to address energy and environmental 
challenges. It aims to promote inclusivity, resilience, and sustainable growth in 
the ASEAN region by encouraging investments in clean energy and emission 
reductions. The Green Deal not only addresses the urgent need for energy 
transition but also supports renewable energy development, energy efficiency, 
and sustainable practices.
Energy diplomacy and the green deal are also essential for achieving the 
United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). By ensuring access to 
clean and affordable energy for all, countries can foster economic development, 
improve living conditions, and protect the environment. Collaborative initiatives 
like the UN-Energy partnership and the ASEAN Plan of Action for Energy 
Cooperation (APAEC) provide frameworks for cooperation and progress 
towards these goals.
Looking ahead, investments in technological advancements, energy 
infrastructure, and energy-efficient practices are critical. Governments, local 
administrations, and community leaders should raise awareness about energy 
security and engage in multilateral diplomacy to amplify their voices and 
level the playing field. By embracing innovative solutions and upholding the 
rule of law, smaller states can effectively contribute to international energy 
cooperation and sustainable development. In the context of the ASEAN region, 
the involvement of member states in the ASEAN Plan of Action for Energy 
Cooperation (APAEC) and ASEAN Green Deal represents a form of energy 
diplomacy. Collaborative efforts and cooperation with various stakeholders can 
help achieve the energy goals set at the regional level. While challenges, such 
Energy Diplomacy and ASEAN Green Deal

as unclear ownership and financial responsibility, need to be addressed, there 
are opportunities to be capitalized upon. Enhanced collaboration, leveraging 
existing regional frameworks, engaging with international partners, mobilizing 
financial resources, promoting capacity building and technology transfer, and 
fostering public awareness and stakeholder engagement can drive the progress of 
the ASEAN Green Deal.
The ASEAN Green Deal holds significant promise for shaping the future 
of Southeast Asia. It aligns with the global push for sustainability, drawing 
inspiration from successful initiatives like the European Green Deal. By fostering 
regional cooperation and commitment to environmental goals, the ASEAN 
Green Deal has the potential to drive meaningful change, promoting a greener, 
more resilient, and economically competitive Southeast Asia.

1. Sustainability of Industrial Development
The United Nations has adopted in principle the concept of sustainable 
development, which relies on three pillars, namely environment, society, and 
economy. The concept has faced challenges in achieving the ideal universal goal 
of sustainability. It has been observed that balancing the three pillars for common 
goods has not been met due to the fact that most nations value or materialize 
the concept in different forms based on national and/or aligned interests or 
preferences. As a result, realizing the goals is seen as challenging due to the fact 
that the environment and society are commonly left behind. It is important to 
note that human society and the natural environment are common environments 
in which people perceive no self-belonging in taking care. This falls under the 
concept of the tragedy of the commons, in which overpopulation is one of the 
factors that marginalizes the concerns of sustainability in the current context 
(Candelone et al.,1995; Hardin, 1968; Jonsson, 2012).
The natural changes show a strong correlation with human civilization’s 
development. The records from agriculture to the industrial revolution 
appear to be evidence that scientists have agreed on positive development 
in one dimension and negative facts in another. The severity of the 
environmental damage has been quite obvious in the last 100 years (as 
shown in the Figure 7.1.) (Gibbard et al., 2022). For these reasons, the 
United Nations has called for more efforts to reduce degradation while 
ensuring inclusivity and growth in socio-economic development. Thus, many 
theoretical frameworks in regulation and/or science and technology have 
been articulated to maintain the development of the industrial sector. The 
industrial revolution in Anthropocene informs all players of a new paradigm 
shift in balancing development and environmental conservation (Jonsson,

synergy.

3. Green Technology for Manufacturing Industries
Industrialization relies heavily on science and technology integration in the 
manufacturing line. Models are seen differently from country to country (Park 
et al., 2021). In the current context of environmental sensitivity, STI must play a 
major role in addressing environmental degradation, and industrial development 
could face challenges as a result. However, STI policies must be rigorously based 
on evidence of climate accountability in order to serve innovation purposes. 
Scholarly, the number of research articles published has been increasing, with 
promising trends from 1995 to 2019 (Usmani et al., 2021). This knowledge 
accumulation on green technologies is the foundation for transforming them 
into technologies that serve the manufacturing sector. This exponential growth 
of articles is projected to increase in the next decade due to environmental 
pressure. It was suggested by some studies that green technological innovation 
efficiently serves the utilization of natural resources, high-tech industries using 
green technological innovation have a correlation with efficient use of resources, 
and green technology transformation is a recommended new trend for resource 
conservation (Miao et al., 2017).

Investing in green technologies is not the direct approach to having 
environmental care among businesses. However, it is an indirect way of 
having social recognition, cost reduction, a new business opportunity, or other 
prerequisites to achieving economic value. Generally, firms attach less value 
to environmental sustainability. Thus, investment by firms in preserving the 
commons is something that policymakers should not underestimate. Incentivizing 
the ecosystem for firms to see beyond the short-term benefits of investment in 
green technologies is necessary. In general, change management toward green 
Green Ideals
78
technology investment among firms is contributed by regulation, commitment, 
customer demand, management concerns, and cost savings (Saunila et al., 2018). 
Governmental policies play a significant role in promoting the integration of 
green technologies to ensure a fast trade-off among firms is possible. Radical 
technological innovation has shown promise, as a means to reshape the current 
industrial landscape. Policy innovation has a strong correlation with industrial 
development and sustainability (Norberg-Bohm, 1999). On the other hand, the 
current trend reveals the need for collaboration by the private sector through 
different forms, viz., public-private partnership investment. Since innovation is 
relatively driven by the private sector, the engagement of the sector with policy 
support by the government sounds promising for future industrial growth and 
sustainability. 
It is important to take note that Environmental, Social, and cooperative 
Governance (ESG) is a set of standards allowing measurement opportunities 
for investors, in which environmental characteristics are undoubtedly the 
major factors that address innovation. This environmental regulatory concept, 
particularly the ESG performance concept, positively impacts the innovation 
ecosystem among manufacturing industries. Furthermore, studies suggest that 
high ESG performance in industrial operations has a strong contribution to 
sustainability and innovation performance. This ESG paradigm has increased 
considerably in the last several years (Zhou et al., 2023). ESG can obviously be 
broken down into the sub-concepts of its three pillars (Clement et al., 2023).
•	 Environment: Impact of businesses on the natural environment and 
its impact on air quality, biodiversity, carbon footprint, greenhouse gas 
emissions, waste, and water quality
•	 Society: Relationships inside the firm among/between employees, 
suppliers, customers, and people in general. Among other things, human 
rights, privacy policies, and efforts to help poor communities are the main 
aspects taken into consideration by this pillar.
•	 Governance: Leadership of firms, internal controls, audits, board 
composition, corruption, executive compensation, and policies.
4.  Conclusion
The United Nations’ sustainable development concept, which is built on three 
pillars: the environment, society, and the economy, has struggled to achieve 
universal goals due to a misalignment of these elements. The tragedy of the 
commons, in which overpopulation trumps environmental concerns, has resulted 
in overexploitation of available resources to fulfill greedy in human populations. 
The Anthropocene’s industrial revolution has ushered in a new paradigm shift in 
the balance between development and environmental conservation. Industry 4.0 
has the potential to help manage environmental degradation in both biophysical 
Science, Technology, and Innovation
79
and social spaces, with green technologies being prioritized by high-value added 
manufacturing industries to address sustainable development agenda. Innovation 
drives social and economic development, particularly green technological 
innovation, which is critical for reducing carbon emissions and increasing natural 
resource use efficiency. Cambodia’s National Policy on STI is based on five 
pillars: improving of governance, building human capital, investment in R&D, 
collaboration, and building ecosystem. These pillars are critical to the country’s 
sustainable industrial development, which should be driven by innovation and 
environmental concerns. Having said that, the policy should be based on evidence 
of climate accountability, which includes high-quality education, innovation-
driven R&D investment, quality infrastructure support, an entrepreneurial 
mindset in the private sector, and sufficient infrastructure. Government policies 
play an important role in building national innovation system by encouraging the 
integration of green technologies and ensuring a quick trade-off between firms. 
Radical technological innovation has shown promise in reshaping the current 
industrial landscape.

1. Introduction
The Prime Minister of Cambodia and Chair of the Association of Southeast 
Asian Nations (ASEAN), Samdech Hun Sen, proposed the “ASEAN Green 
Deal” during the 55th ASEAN Foreign Ministers’ Meeting as a crucial priority in 
response to the challenges faced during the post-pandemic recovery (Han, 2022). 
The primary objective of this comprehensive framework is to motivate ASEAN 
member states to invest in decarbonizing their economies, effectively addressing 
climate change concerns, and fostering collaboration among ASEAN member 
states and external partners. In a previous instance, during the global crises in 
2008 concerning fuel, food, and finances, the United Nations Environment 
Program (UNEP) called upon governments to allocate financial resources 
towards supporting environmentally sustainable sectors and striving towards the 
reduction of carbon emissions and ecosystem degradation (UNEP, 2009). UNEP 
has put forth a series of measures, including mandating high-income countries 
such as the US, EU, and other OECD economies, along with middle- and high-
income G20 economies, to allocate a minimum of one percent of their GDP 
over two years towards carbon emission reduction. Furthermore, developing 
nations should also implement domestic strategies to curtail carbon emissions 
while dedicating at least one percent of their GDP to enhancing access to clean 
water and sanitation for impoverished communities. 
The Green Deal movement seeks to promote sustainable development, reduce 
carbon emissions, and address climate change. It is crucial for environmental 
scientists to provide robust scientific research to the public and policymakers in 
order to shape policies and implement actions throughout the entire process. As 
challenges such as climate change and emerging pandemics become increasingly 
complex, the role of environmental scientists as agents of change in science 
diplomacy is more critical than ever. They provide scientific advice to inform 
foreign policy objectives (Science in Diplomacy), foster international scientific 
collaboration (Diplomacy for Science), and utilize scientific cooperation to 
improve international relations (Science for Diplomacy). Environmental 
scientists communicate scientific facts and discoveries to the public, engaging 
them in discussions to achieve a sustainable future. They also play a significant 
role in monitoring and evaluating the effectiveness of environmental policies and 
regulations, ensuring that the most reliable scientific methods are employed for 
assessment purposes.

Chapter 8: Roles of Environmental Scientists and Engineers in the Green 
Deal Movement
KUOK Fidero* and PROMENTILLA Michael Angelo B.
1. Introduction
The Prime Minister of Cambodia and Chair of the Association of Southeast 
Asian Nations (ASEAN), Samdech Hun Sen, proposed the “ASEAN Green 
Deal” during the 55th ASEAN Foreign Ministers’ Meeting as a crucial priority in 
response to the challenges faced during the post-pandemic recovery (Han, 2022). 
The primary objective of this comprehensive framework is to motivate ASEAN 
member states to invest in decarbonizing their economies, effectively addressing 
climate change concerns, and fostering collaboration among ASEAN member 
states and external partners. In a previous instance, during the global crises in 
2008 concerning fuel, food, and finances, the United Nations Environment 
Program (UNEP) called upon governments to allocate financial resources 
towards supporting environmentally sustainable sectors and striving towards the 
reduction of carbon emissions and ecosystem degradation (UNEP, 2009). UNEP 
has put forth a series of measures, including mandating high-income countries 
such as the US, EU, and other OECD economies, along with middle- and high-
income G20 economies, to allocate a minimum of one percent of their GDP 
over two years towards carbon emission reduction. Furthermore, developing 
nations should also implement domestic strategies to curtail carbon emissions 
while dedicating at least one percent of their GDP to enhancing access to clean 
water and sanitation for impoverished communities. 
The Green Deal movement seeks to promote sustainable development, reduce 
carbon emissions, and address climate change. It is crucial for environmental 
scientists to provide robust scientific research to the public and policymakers in 
order to shape policies and implement actions throughout the entire process. As 
challenges such as climate change and emerging pandemics become increasingly 
complex, the role of environmental scientists as agents of change in science 
diplomacy is more critical than ever. They provide scientific advice to inform 
foreign policy objectives (Science in Diplomacy), foster international scientific 
collaboration (Diplomacy for Science), and utilize scientific cooperation to 
improve international relations (Science for Diplomacy). Environmental 
scientists communicate scientific facts and discoveries to the public, engaging 
them in discussions to achieve a sustainable future. They also play a significant 
role in monitoring and evaluating the effectiveness of environmental policies and 
regulations, ensuring that the most reliable scientific methods are employed for 
assessment purposes.

The ASEAN Green Deal presents a promising framework for addressing 
the urgent environmental challenges in Southeast Asia. There are several 
key considerations to enhance its effectiveness. Firstly, the role of the Penta-
helix partnership, involving academia, industry, government, the media, 
and the community, should be explicitly acknowledged within the ASEAN 
Green Deal. It is essential to incentivize and support such partnerships in 
adopting sustainable and low-carbon practices and technologies. Secondly, the 
significance of international cooperation should be further emphasized. The 
ASEAN region is not immune to climate change and environmental degradation 
impacts, necessitating global collective action. The framework could encompass 
measures to foster international collaboration in climate finance, technology 
transfer, and capacity building. Lastly, promoting education and raising public 
awareness of environmental issues should be integral to the ASEAN Green Deal. 
Building knowledge exchange and increasing awareness among stakeholders 
and the general public is vital for bridging the gap between science and policy 
and garnering support for transitioning to a sustainable and inclusive green 
economy. The framework could establish a platform for knowledge sharing, 
including initiatives, such as sustainability science integration in schools, public 
information campaigns, and community engagement programs.
3. Roles in Policy Formulation and Advocacy
Policy formulation typically follows a series of stages, including problem 
identification, policy analysis, development of policy instruments, consultation, 
coordination, decision-making, implementation, and evaluation (see Figure 
8.3). Civil servants are primarily responsible for carrying out most of the work 
involved in the policy cycle, with input and participation from all stakeholders, 
particularly during public consultation (Althaus et al., 2020). Environmental 
scientists and engineers, due to their training, are naturally inclined to identify 
problems that gain public attention through qualitative or quantitative research. 
This identification of issues often triggers the formulation of policies when 
problems become significant, widespread, and aligned with political priorities. 
In practice, policy actors strategically define policy targets and goals, which may 
evolve over time. Therefore, the creation of policy instruments becomes essential 
to achieving these goals. It is widely recognized that correctly defining the 
problem is the initial step, and critical thinking and language awareness is crucial 
for developing evidence-based policies. Undoubtedly, the role of the expert 
group comprising environmental scientists and engineers is indispensable for the 
success of the Green Deal movement’s policy and advocacy. Academic research 
also highlights the importance of the policy mix framework, where multiple 
goals and complex policy instruments are co-designed with the involvement of 
all stakeholders (Kern et al., 2017). This dialogue between policymakers and 
academia indicates a growing interest in the application of policy mix, which has 
shown positive impacts and incremental development (Rosenow et al., 2016).

4. Monitoring and Evaluation
Environmental scientists and engineers have a significant role to play throughout 
the policy cycle, not only in policy formulation but also during policy 
implementation. During implementation, it is crucial to monitor the progress 
to ensure the achievement of policy goals and to track objectively verifiable 
indicators. Monitoring is typically conducted annually, while evaluation is 
usually carried out at the mid-term or end of the policy implementation period. 
These monitoring and evaluation processes are generally led by specialists who 
assess the efficiency and effectiveness of policy implementation. It is important 
to define the evaluation scope at different policy cycle stages, such as input, 
process, output, outcome, and impact (Waller, 1996). The responsibility for 
monitoring and evaluation can lie within the ministry itself, the supervising 
ministry, agencies, or specialized think tanks with expertise in the relevant policy 
areas. Therefore, it is essential for the Green Deal movement to have evaluations 
conducted by environmental scientists and engineers who possess knowledge of 
both the process and objectives related to the assessment indicators. It should be 
noted that the selection of the evaluation body is critical, as the credibility of the 
evaluators will influence the quality of the conclusions and recommendations for 
potential policy interventions, if necessary (Gerston, 2004).

5. Challenges for the Green Deal Movement 
The Cambodian government has articulated its vision of strengthening the 
national innovation ecosystem by approving the Science, Technology and 
Innovation Roadmap 2030, which aligns with the National Policy on Science, 
Technology, and Innovation 2020-2030. However, Cambodia currently faces 
challenges in research funding, with research expenditure amounting to only 
0.12 percent of GDP in 2015 and 35 percent of that funding relying on support 
from foreign partners and international organizations (Economic and Social 
Commission for Asia and the Pacific, 2022). To address these challenges, it is 
crucial to allocate dedicated funding for research and development related to 
the Green Deal. Additionally, there are other obstacles to overcome, including 
limited financial investment and feasibility, a shortage of specialized personnel 
and training programs, and the need for effective partnerships (Mohammed et 
al., 2013).
6. Policy Recommendations
Given the important role of environmental scientists and engineers including, 
the researchers working in the area of sustainability science and engineering 
to achieve the goal of the ASEAN Green Deal, the following are the policy 
recommendations:
1)	 Invest in environmental science education and training: The ASEAN Green 
Deal requires a skilled workforce of environmental scientists and engineers. 
Therefore, investing in environmental science education and training 
programs at all levels, from primary school to university, is essential.
2)	 Support research and innovation: Investing in research and innovation in 
sustainability science and engineering can help develop new technologies 
and practices that support the goals of the ASEAN Green Deal. 
Governments and the private sector should increase funding for research 
and innovation in this transdisciplinary domain.
3)	 Create opportunities for wider stakeholder engagement: Environmental 
scientists and engineers should engage with a range of stakeholders, 
including the media, policymakers, the private sector, civil society, and 
the general public, to ensure that their work is relevant and effective. 
Governments should create opportunities for stakeholder engagement, 
such as public consultations and expert panels.
4)	 Promote interdisciplinary collaboration: Environmental science and 
engineering are interdisciplinary fields of humanities, economics, social 
sciences, natural sciences and other engineering. National collaborative 
and upskilling platforms and programs should therefore be created to 
promote a specialized T-profile competency with relevant skill blocks: 
expertise, and essential and functional skills for the Green Deal movement.

Chapter 9: Global Health and Climate Change 
GOUSHCHI Adonis* and CHHEM Sirika
1. Introduction
Climate change represents a critical challenge globally and Cambodia is no 
exception to its impacts. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), 
climate change is among the most significant threats of the 21st century, projected 
to result in an additional 250,000 deaths annually between 2030 and 2050 due 
to malnutrition, malaria, diarrhea, and heat stress (WHO, 2021). Its impacts are 
already being felt around the world, affecting the environment, animals, and 
economies. However, one of its most significant impacts is on human health. The 
years 2021 and 2022 witnessed a level of severity in weather events that exceeded

1. Introduction
Climate change represents a critical challenge globally and Cambodia is no 
exception to its impacts. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), 
climate change is among the most significant threats of the 21st century, projected 
to result in an additional 250,000 deaths annually between 2030 and 2050 due 
to malnutrition, malaria, diarrhea, and heat stress (WHO, 2021). Its impacts are 
already being felt around the world, affecting the environment, animals, and 
economies. However, one of its most significant impacts is on human health. The 
years 2021 and 2022 witnessed a level of severity in weather events that exceeded 
anything previously experienced. Globally, record-high temperatures have been 
reported across continents such as China, Europe, Africa, and both North and 
South America, leading to thousands of deaths related to the heat. Meanwhile, 
floods ravaged Australia, Canada, China, Malaysia, Pakistan, western Europe, 
and Cambodia, also causing thousands of deaths as well as displacing hundreds 
of thousands of people. Wildfires were responsible for many injuries and deaths 
in the USA, Greece, Turkey, and Cambodia.
Beyond the direct effects like rising temperatures, severe weather, and 
increasing sea levels, climate change also indirectly influences global health 
in multiple ways. These include the proliferation of vector-borne diseases, the 
spread of food and waterborne illnesses, and the increase in air pollution levels. 
As the world grapples with all these effects, it is critical to both understand the 
link between climate change and health and develop strategies to mitigate its 
impact on global health. This requires a multi-sectoral approach involving a 
collaboration between public health officials, policymakers, climate scientists, 
and other stakeholders. This chapter will provide a comprehensive overview of 
the various ways in which climate change affects human health and the steps that 
can be taken to address this growing threat.

pollution, reduced food and water quality, and changes in vector distribution 
and ecology (see Figure 9.1).

The impacts of climate change on health through exposure pathways are 
largely determined by vulnerability. Indeed, climate change does not affect all 
populations equally. Vulnerability refers to the degree to which individuals or 
communities are susceptible to climate-sensitive health risks (Yu et. al., 2021). It 
determines how severe the impacts of climate change might be. Thus, assessing 
vulnerability is essential for identifying regions and populations that are most at 
risk from the impacts of climate change, and for developing targeted strategies to 
mitigate these specific impacts.
Vulnerability to climate change has three aspects: exposure, sensitivity, and 
adaptive capacity (see Figure 9.2).
•	 Exposure refers to the degree of exposure to climate hazards. For example, 
individuals living in coastal areas are at risk from sea level rise and coastal 
flooding, while individuals living in arid regions may be vulnerable to 
drought and heatwaves. Similarly, people living in urban areas with air 
pollution are more susceptible to respiratory problems.
Global Health and Climate Change 
93
•	 Sensitivity refers to the likelihood of negative impacts. There are several 
factors that determine the sensitivity of a population: 
–– Socio-economic factors: Poverty, housing, access to healthcare, 
and education. For example, low-income people have less access to 
healthcare and resources such as air conditioning during heat waves.
–– Demographic factors: The elderly, children and pregnant women are 
more susceptible to extreme temperatures.
–– Health status: Individuals with pre-existing health conditions, such as 
respiratory, cardiovascular and renal disease, are more vulnerable to air 
pollution and heatwaves.
•	 Adaptive capacity refers to the ability to cope with and adapt to those 
impacts. It is determined by factors, such as access to resources, health 
infrastructures, and social support systems.

Reducing vulnerability to climate-sensitive health risks requires addressing 
the underlying social, economic, and environmental factors that contribute to 
vulnerability, and it will prepare individuals and communities to adapt to the 
changing climate and minimize the negative health impacts.
2.1. Heat-Related Illness 
Extreme heat is the first cause of weather-related death (WHO, 2018) and is a 
growing concern for public health, especially in countries like Cambodia where 
extreme temperatures are becoming more common. By 2100, heat waves are 
Green Ideals
94
predicted to increase 25-fold (WHO, 2015) with population exposition increasing 
by several billions. One of the reasons for the increased health risks is that the 
human body has a limited ability to dissipate heat, leading to dehydration, heat 
exhaustion and heat stroke. Heat exhaustion can cause nausea, headaches, fever 
and muscle cramps, while heat stroke can lead to brain damage, organ failure, 
and death. Additionally, extreme temperatures can worsen pre-existing illnesses 
such as cardiovascular, respiratory, cerebrovascular, and renal ones.
Another important factor is the phenomenon of urban heat islands (UHIs). 
Urban areas are often several degrees warmer than their surrounding rural areas 
due to building density, a lack of vegetation, and increased human activity. This 
can exacerbate the effects of heatwaves and increase the risk of heat-related 
illnesses. Cambodian citizens are particularly vulnerable due to the country’s hot 
and humid climate, coupled with high levels of poverty and limited access to 
cooling resources.
To reduce heat-related illnesses and deaths, key actions include: increasing 
access to cooling resources (such as public cooling centers and air-conditioned 
places), implementing heat warning systems for early alerts, reducing the urban 
heat island effect through green spaces and cool roofs/pavements, and conducting 
public awareness campaigns on recognizing symptoms, staying hydrated, and 
keeping cool during extreme heat.
2.2. Air Pollution and Allergens
Climate change is projected to lead to increased concentrations of harmful 
atmospheric pollutants (ground-level ozone and particulate matter) with 
significant human health impacts: increased rates of respiratory and cardiovascular 
diseases and premature death. A reduction in short-lived climate pollutants 
(SLCPs) in Cambodia could prevent almost 5000 premature deaths yearly from 
outdoor air pollution starting from 2030 (WHO, 2015). Ground-level ozone is a 
component of smog and has a detrimental impact on the respiratory system. The 
rise in ground-level ozone concentration has been associated with an increase in 
respiratory diseases such as pneumonia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease 
(COPD) and asthma (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2021). This 
leads to increased hospital admissions and emergency room visits and, therefore, 
increases death rates. Additionally, fine particulate matter concentrations 
(PM2.5: particulate matter < 2.5 µm) will increase due to the smoke emitted by 
wildfire episodes. These small particles cause breathing difficulties for people 
with respiratory diseases but can also increase the risk of cardiovascular events 
(Ebi & McGregor, 2008). 
Another significant concern is household air pollution, primarily caused by 
the combustion of solid fuels such as biomass and coal for cooking. In Cambodia, 
more than 95 percent of the population primarily uses solid fuels for cooking in 
rural areas, while in urban areas, 50 percent of the population does so. Women and 
Global Health and Climate Change 
95
children are at a greater risk for disease from household air pollution, especially 
with rising temperatures and approximately 61 percent of an estimated 2,400 
child deaths due to acute lower respiratory infections in Cambodia is attributable 
to household air pollution. 
One other impact of climate change on the air is the increase in pollen 
release which worsens not only the allergic reactions in asthma and other types 
of allergic diseases but also the risk of allergic sensitization in exposed healthy 
individuals, including children. These factors make the air less breathable leading 
to an increase in premature deaths and hospital admissions for respiratory and 
cardiovascular problems. To mitigate those effects, multiple interventions can be 
implemented such as air quality education for patients with respiratory diseases, 
promotion of renewable energy and reducing greenhouse gas emissions, and 
broadcasting notifications for high pollution levels. 
2.3. Food and Water-Borne Diseases
Climate change has a significant impact on the availability and quality of water 
and, thus, on the occurrence and transmission of water-borne diseases. Heavy 
rainfall and floods can lead to agricultural fields and sewage runoff, contaminating 
water sources and affecting both its consumption, hygiene, and agriculture. Inland 
river flooding is a potential risk in Cambodia, where the number of days of heavy 
rainfall is projected to increase by about 10 days between 1990 and 2100 and 
affect over 30,000 people (WHO, 2015). The effects of climate change on water 
security are especially pronounced in developing countries, where limited access 
to clean water and inadequate sanitation systems can exacerbate the spread of 
waterborne diseases such as cholera and salmonella (Akil et al., 2014). 
Moreover, the rise in water temperature can promote the growth and survival 
of harmful algae, such as cyanobacteria, in both sea and fresh water. This algae 
releases harmful toxins into the water and can also contaminate fish and shellfish 
that consume the algae (Wells et al., 2015). Drinking water or ingesting fish or 
shellfish contaminated by these toxins can cause a range of symptoms, from mild 
stomach pain and skin irritation to more severe reactions affecting the lungs, 
liver, and brain. For instance, in the case of paralytic shellfish poisoning, a type 
of harmful algal bloom can produce a neurotoxin that affects the nervous system 
of those who consume contaminated shellfish, leading to symptoms such as 
tingling, numbness, and paralysis.
To reduce the risk of food and waterborne diseases due to climate change, 
several strategies can be implemented. Governments must develop new 
infrastructures to provide access to clean water and proper sanitation facilities. 
Good hygiene practices, such as frequent handwashing with soap, using clean 
water for drinking and cooking, and safe disposal of waste, are highly effective in 
preventing the spread of microorganisms in water. Improving disease surveillance 
systems and implementing early warning systems can also help detect and 
Green Ideals
96
respond to outbreaks of waterborne diseases promptly. Finally, building flood-
resistant infrastructure may significantly enhance community resilience to the 
impacts of food and water-borne diseases.
2.4. Vector-Borne Diseases
Mosquitoes and ticks are carriers of various diseases that can be transmitted to 
humans, making them significant public health concerns worldwide. For instance, 
malaria, which is transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes, is a major cause 
of morbidity and mortality in tropical countries. It is estimated that there were 
247 million cases of malaria globally in 2022, resulting in 619,000 deaths (WHO, 
2022), and numbers in Cambodia are expected to increase to 22 million by 2070 
(WHO, 2015). Dengue, another mosquito-borne disease, is endemic in over 100 
countries and is a leading cause of illness in tropical regions (WHO, 2002). It is 
the second most worrying infectious threat in Cambodia with similarly increasing 
numbers by 2070 (WHO, 2015). Many other diseases are transmitted by the 
mosquito including West-Nile, Yellow Fever and Chikungunya. 
As the global temperature rises, mosquitoes are expected to expand their 
habitats to more temperate and higher elevated regions of the world. This will 
increase the risk of mosquito-borne diseases spreading to new areas. One of the 
most effective ways to limit vector borne diseases is through mosquito control 
programs that eliminate breeding sites and kill adult mosquitoes. Vaccination 
campaigns play a crucial role in combating mosquito-borne diseases like yellow 
fever. Additionally, adopting preventive measures such as wearing long-sleeved 
clothing and using repellent is essential.
2.5. Mental Health
Extreme weather not only has a physical impact on people but can also affect 
mental health. This situation can result in various psychological disorders, such 
as anxiety, depression, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) (Clayton, 2021). 
These events can also lead to social isolation, job loss, economic instability, 
and displacement, all of which can contribute to poor mental health outcomes. 
Fortunately, there are ways to address these problems. Governments, healthcare 
providers, and community-based organizations can work together to provide 
mental health support and resources to those affected by climate-related events, 
including counseling services and group therapy. We can therefore help reduce the 
psychological impacts of natural disasters and protect the victims’ mental health.
3. Climate Change and Health: Mitigating Impacts on a Global Scale
Addressing the health impacts of climate change presents multiple challenges 
for public health agencies for several reasons. First of all, climate change is a 
relatively new problem, and public health professionals may not have the 
necessary skills and expertise to effectively manage its complexity. Also, the 
scientific understanding of this issue’s underlying mechanisms is still incomplete, 
Global Health and Climate Change 
97
making it difficult to develop effective counterstrategies. Moreover, the necessary 
prevention and adaptation measures go beyond the remit of the health sector, 
requiring engagement with other sectors, such as urban planning, transportation, 
water, energy, agriculture and education. 
The mistake, however, would be to focus solely on human health and forget 
about environmental and animal health, which are intimately linked together. 
Various infectious diseases can be transmitted through either environmental 
sources such as water or animals, as seen with SARS, Ebola, and the West Nile 
virus. The One Health approach recognizes this interdependence (Chhem et al., 
2020), emphasizing the need for a collaborative and holistic approach to address 
climate-related health impacts. By taking this approach, better strategies can be 
developed for human health. For example, a One Health approach could involve 
improving disease surveillance systems that monitor both animal and human 
health, and promoting sustainable agriculture and land use practices that protect 
the environment and reduce the risk of zoonotic diseases. 
Cambodia has already started tackling the health impacts of climate change by 
implementing the Climate Change Strategic Plan 2014–2023 (CCCSP) and working 
on several important adaptations, but much work is still to be done with regards 
to disease surveillance and response, climate resilience, financing and costing 
mechanisms, as well as the analysis of the health benefits from this mitigation. 
3.1. The BRACE Framework
The BRACE Framework, developed in 2010 by the Center for Disease Control 
and Prevention (CDC), is a comprehensive tool that allows health officials to 
identify key health outcomes that are sensitive to climate change and create 
effective strategies to address them. It is regularly updated to reflect the latest 
scientific evidence and best practices. The BRACE Framework is divided into 
five sequential steps (Marinucci et al., 2014) (see Figure 9.3): 
Step 1 of the BRACE Framework involves two important tasks: 
•	 The first task consists of identifying climate-sensitive health outcomes.  
To that end, public health agencies need to access climate data sources 
to identify trends in weather patterns, such as temperature changes, 
precipitation, and extreme weather. Based on these historical data and 
climate mathematical models, and with the collaboration of climatologists, 
climate change can be projected 30 or more years into the future to assess 
the effects of climate change on health. By the end of this task, public health 
agencies will be able to report a list of health outcomes that are most likely 
to be affected by climate change. 
•	 The second task involves identifying vulnerable populations and regions. 
Various methods will be used to identify vulnerable populations, such as the 
analysis of demographic and health status data, and social vulnerability indices.
Green Ideals
98
The climate change projections and vulnerability assessment generated in 
Step 1 will provide a comprehensive understanding of the potential impacts of 
climate change on public health and the populations that are most vulnerable. 
This information can be used by policymakers and stakeholders to develop 
strategies and interventions to mitigate these impacts and protect public 
health.
Step 2 the goal is to estimate the additional disease burden associated with 
climate change. It can be done by linking the projected exposure pathway 
(extreme weather events, heat waves) to the health outcomes. For example, if an 
increase in extreme heat is expected to lead to an increase in heat-related illnesses, 
analysis of historical data and future trend projections are used to calculate the 
numbers incurred by this exposure pathway.
Step 3 concentrates on selecting the most appropriate measures to tackle the 
health issues identified earlier. To do so, the evidence-based public health (EBPH) 
approach can be used, allowing for an assessment of the effectiveness of various 
clinical and public health interventions. This involves a systematic literature 
review to identify relevant interventions and evaluate their efficacy. It is also 
important to evaluate whether interventions are well-matched to the political, 
cultural, and logistical landscape. Additionally, a cost-effectiveness analysis can 
help agencies prioritize interventions based on their cost and benefits.

Step 4 involves formulating a climate and health adaptation strategy that 
amalgamates the insights gathered in preceding phases. This strategy should be 
comprehensive, intersectoral, with a primary focus on public health outcomes. 
It should also harmonize with broader climate change initiatives across different 
sectors to promote collaboration among diverse disciplines and interest groups. 
Furthermore, the strategy should delineate methods for stakeholders to integrate 
adaptations into their existing programs and specify how activities will be assessed. 
Lastly, it should undergo periodic updates and be made publicly accessible.
Step 5 consists of monitoring and evaluating the impacts of interventions 
on public health. By collecting and analyzing data on their outcomes, we can 
learn from previous processes and improve future interventions. This can include 
identifying the most effective interventions, determining which populations 
benefit most from the interventions, and identifying any unintended consequences 
or negative impacts of the interventions. The data collected through monitoring 
and evaluation can also help inform policy decisions and resource allocation.
The framework has been successfully implemented in several countries 
given its numerous advantages. Indeed, it is an adaptive and iterative approach, 
allowing interventions to be refined and adjusted based on ongoing monitoring 
and evaluation. It is also evidence-based and grounded in scientific research and 
data and emphasizes health equity and collaboration between stakeholders. There 
are some potential disadvantages, namely its complexity and need for abundant 
resources, which could limit its feasibility in some contexts. Additionally, its 
focus on long-term outcomes may not provide immediate solutions to urgent 
public health problems. In addition to the use of the BRACE Framework, health 
officials must take into account several considerations to reduce the effects of 
climate change on health. 
Firstly, there is an urgent need for education and training for public health 
and healthcare professionals on climate change. This involves integrating 
climate change-related topics into the existing curricula of these professionals. 
Various training initiatives already exist, such as the Climate and Health Literacy 
Consortium in the US and the Climate and Health Alliance in Australia. By 
incorporating climate change into professional training and education, healthcare 
professionals will be better equipped to identify and manage climate-related 
health issues. 
Secondly, increasing the resilience of health systems is crucial and several 
measures can be undertaken. Hospital designs should include climate-resilient 
aspects with sustainable and resilient building materials, energy-efficient systems, 
and advanced water management systems.  Early warning systems for extreme 
weather events would improve emergency response planning, enhance medical 
supply availability, and increase healthcare system capacity during heat waves or 
disease outbreaks. 
Green Ideals
100
Lastly, it is important to consider the varying vulnerabilities of different 
demographic and socio-economic groups. WHO emphasizes the need for 
health equity in addressing climate-related health threats. However, practical 
implementation of equitable adaptation solutions is rare. Stronger engagement 
of those working on climate change threats with social care providers can help to 
ensure that vulnerable populations, such as the elderly or disabled, have access to 
the support they need to adapt to climate-related challenges. 
3.2. Connecting Global Health and Climate Change through Diplomacy
Climate change is a global phenomenon that is expected to affect every country 
in the world. To effectively address its health impacts, it is essential for all 
countries to take collective action. Global health diplomacy represents the 
convergence of health and international policy, enabling nations to collectively 
tackle global health issues through collaborative negotiations and partnerships. 
It involves a wide range of actors from various sectors, including government 
officials, diplomats, public health professionals, researchers, NGOs, civil society 
groups, and international organizations. These individuals and organizations 
work together to promote international cooperation and coordination on global 
health issues, such as disease outbreaks, natural disasters, and the health impacts 
of climate change.
In recent years, global health diplomacy has played a critical role in addressing 
epidemics such as COVID-19, Ebola, and Zika, by facilitating the sharing of 
information and best practices among countries, helping to coordinate their 
interventions and also by promoting access to medicines and vaccines.  One 
concrete example of global health diplomacy in action is the Westerdam incident 
during the COVID-19 pandemic (Chhem & Chhem, 2020). The Westerdam 
cruise ship was denied entry to several ports due to fears that its passengers and 
crew may have been infected with COVID-19. Eventually, the ship was allowed 
to dock in Cambodia, where its passengers and crew received humanitarian 
assistance. Cambodia’s decision to allow the Westerdam to dock and provide 
assistance to its occupants can be seen as an example of health diplomacy. By 
taking in the ship and its passengers, Cambodia demonstrated its commitment 
to promoting health and protecting vulnerable populations in the face of a global 
health crisis. This decision required diplomacy and negotiation with other 
countries, as well as coordination with public health officials to ensure that 
appropriate measures were taken to prevent the spread of disease.
Similarly, global health diplomacy can play a critical role in addressing the 
impacts of climate change on health by promoting cooperation and collaboration 
between countries. One example is the Paris Agreement on Climate Change 
signed in 2015. Its goal is to maintain the increase in global temperatures below 
2°C relative to pre-industrial levels and to endeavor to limit the rise to no more 
than 1.5°C.  The WHO has also been active in addressing climate change and

101
health through global health diplomacy. The WHO has developed a range of 
strategies and tools to help countries adapt to the health impacts of climate 
change, including the Climate and Health Country Profiles.
4. Conclusion 
To mitigate the health impacts of climate change, urgent and coordinated action 
across sectors and countries is necessary. This requires a multifaceted approach 
that includes reducing greenhouse gas emissions, implementing energy-efficient 
technologies, and promoting sustainable transportation. Adapting healthcare 
systems is crucial, with strengthened disease surveillance, early warning systems, 
and climate-resilient infrastructure. Education campaigns empower individuals 
by raising awareness about the risks of food-borne, water-borne and vector-borne 
diseases, while also providing information on preventive measures to reduce these 
risks and protect public health. Priority must therefore be placed on research, 
policy development, and collaboration among different stakeholders, all the 
while keeping in mind the importance of health equity throughout this whole 
process, as different needs will require different solutions. By working together, 
we can effectively mitigate the detrimental health effects of climate change and 
pave the way for resilient communities, ensuring a better future for all.

1. Introduction
The way that the world is doing business has changed. The evolution from Web 
2.0 to Web 3.0, the increasing domination of Generation Y and Z (tech-savvy 
generation) in the labor market worldwide, the rise of Asian giants like China 
and India as the main engines of economic growth around the world, and the 
increasing global concern over sustainability issues are among the primary 
drivers of these changes (Birkinshaw & Ridderstråle, 2017). These have, without 
a doubt, also altered how the labor market operates and how potential employees 
are recruited in Cambodia. In the past, when industries mainly demanded low-
skilled labor, which was also abundant due to the baby boom in the 1980s 
and early 1990s, the Cambodian labor market was characterized as a “buyer 
market” in which employers could easily hire potential workers. After all, most 
employees then did not need to possess very high competencies to work in a firm 
that predominantly required manual labor.
However, this has started to change as we speak. Since the early 2000s, the 
total fertility rate of Cambodia has continued to decline significantly from 4.0 
in 2000 to 2.4 in 2020  (United Nations Department of Economic and Social 
Affairs, 2022). The number of young Cambodian workers who enter the labor 
market annually decreased from 300,000 in the early 2010s (Ministry of Labour & 
International Labor Organization, 2014) to 270,000 in 20171, while the demands 
for better skills from first-time job seekers are also intensifying, corresponding 
with higher wages and the changing characteristics of the Cambodian economy 
which has begun to compete in terms of workers’ productivity instead of low 
input costs such as salary. Such a change in the nature of competition is true 
even in the case of the garment and footwear industry, which is considered a low-
skilled sector. As a result, young Cambodians must be equipped with the high 
skills necessary to succeed and thrive in an uncertain and unpredictable future 
while the country is on its way towards becoming a more developed country. 
It is in this sense that the way the youth is educated must also be revisited and 
reconsidered. The Cambodian education system cannot be the same as it was 
thirty years ago if the country is to advance further and grab a larger part of the 
global market for its products.

The impacts of climate change on health through exposure pathways are 
largely determined by vulnerability. Indeed, climate change does not affect all 
populations equally. Vulnerability refers to the degree to which individuals or 
communities are susceptible to climate-sensitive health risks (Yu et. al., 2021). It 
determines how severe the impacts of climate change might be. Thus, assessing 
vulnerability is essential for identifying regions and populations that are most at 
risk from the impacts of climate change, and for developing targeted strategies to 
mitigate these specific impacts.
Vulnerability to climate change has three aspects: exposure, sensitivity, and 
adaptive capacity (see Figure 9.2).
•	 Exposure refers to the degree of exposure to climate hazards. For example, 
individuals living in coastal areas are at risk from sea level rise and coastal 
flooding, while individuals living in arid regions may be vulnerable to 
drought and heatwaves. Similarly, people living in urban areas with air 
pollution are more susceptible to respiratory problems.
Global Health and Climate Change 
93
•	 Sensitivity refers to the likelihood of negative impacts. There are several 
factors that determine the sensitivity of a population: 
–– Socio-economic factors: Poverty, housing, access to healthcare, 
and education. For example, low-income people have less access to 
healthcare and resources such as air conditioning during heat waves.
–– Demographic factors: The elderly, children and pregnant women are 
more susceptible to extreme temperatures.
–– Health status: Individuals with pre-existing health conditions, such as 
respiratory, cardiovascular and renal disease, are more vulnerable to air 
pollution and heatwaves.
•	 Adaptive capacity refers to the ability to cope with and adapt to those 
impacts. It is determined by factors, such as access to resources, health 
infrastructures, and social support systems.

Reducing vulnerability to climate-sensitive health risks requires addressing 
the underlying social, economic, and environmental factors that contribute to 
vulnerability, and it will prepare individuals and communities to adapt to the 
changing climate and minimize the negative health impacts.
2.1. Heat-Related Illness 
Extreme heat is the first cause of weather-related death (WHO, 2018) and is a 
growing concern for public health, especially in countries like Cambodia where 
extreme temperatures are becoming more common. By 2100, heat waves are 
Green Ideals
94
predicted to increase 25-fold (WHO, 2015) with population exposition increasing 
by several billions. One of the reasons for the increased health risks is that the 
human body has a limited ability to dissipate heat, leading to dehydration, heat 
exhaustion and heat stroke. Heat exhaustion can cause nausea, headaches, fever 
and muscle cramps, while heat stroke can lead to brain damage, organ failure, 
and death. Additionally, extreme temperatures can worsen pre-existing illnesses 
such as cardiovascular, respiratory, cerebrovascular, and renal ones.
Another important factor is the phenomenon of urban heat islands (UHIs). 
Urban areas are often several degrees warmer than their surrounding rural areas 
due to building density, a lack of vegetation, and increased human activity. This 
can exacerbate the effects of heatwaves and increase the risk of heat-related 
illnesses. Cambodian citizens are particularly vulnerable due to the country’s hot 
and humid climate, coupled with high levels of poverty and limited access to 
cooling resources.
To reduce heat-related illnesses and deaths, key actions include: increasing 
access to cooling resources (such as public cooling centers and air-conditioned 
places), implementing heat warning systems for early alerts, reducing the urban 
heat island effect through green spaces and cool roofs/pavements, and conducting 
public awareness campaigns on recognizing symptoms, staying hydrated, and 
keeping cool during extreme heat.
2.2. Air Pollution and Allergens
Climate change is projected to lead to increased concentrations of harmful 
atmospheric pollutants (ground-level ozone and particulate matter) with 
significant human health impacts: increased rates of respiratory and cardiovascular 
diseases and premature death. A reduction in short-lived climate pollutants 
(SLCPs) in Cambodia could prevent almost 5000 premature deaths yearly from 
outdoor air pollution starting from 2030 (WHO, 2015). Ground-level ozone is a 
component of smog and has a detrimental impact on the respiratory system. The 
rise in ground-level ozone concentration has been associated with an increase in 
respiratory diseases such as pneumonia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease 
(COPD) and asthma (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2021). This 
leads to increased hospital admissions and emergency room visits and, therefore, 
increases death rates. Additionally, fine particulate matter concentrations 
(PM2.5: particulate matter < 2.5 µm) will increase due to the smoke emitted by 
wildfire episodes. These small particles cause breathing difficulties for people 
with respiratory diseases but can also increase the risk of cardiovascular events 
(Ebi & McGregor, 2008). 
Another significant concern is household air pollution, primarily caused by 
the combustion of solid fuels such as biomass and coal for cooking. In Cambodia, 
more than 95 percent of the population primarily uses solid fuels for cooking in 
rural areas, while in urban areas, 50 percent of the population does so. Women and 
Global Health and Climate Change 
95
children are at a greater risk for disease from household air pollution, especially 
with rising temperatures and approximately 61 percent of an estimated 2,400 
child deaths due to acute lower respiratory infections in Cambodia is attributable 
to household air pollution. 
One other impact of climate change on the air is the increase in pollen 
release which worsens not only the allergic reactions in asthma and other types 
of allergic diseases but also the risk of allergic sensitization in exposed healthy 
individuals, including children. These factors make the air less breathable leading 
to an increase in premature deaths and hospital admissions for respiratory and 
cardiovascular problems. To mitigate those effects, multiple interventions can be 
implemented such as air quality education for patients with respiratory diseases, 
promotion of renewable energy and reducing greenhouse gas emissions, and 
broadcasting notifications for high pollution levels. 
2.3. Food and Water-Borne Diseases
Climate change has a significant impact on the availability and quality of water 
and, thus, on the occurrence and transmission of water-borne diseases. Heavy 
rainfall and floods can lead to agricultural fields and sewage runoff, contaminating 
water sources and affecting both its consumption, hygiene, and agriculture. Inland 
river flooding is a potential risk in Cambodia, where the number of days of heavy 
rainfall is projected to increase by about 10 days between 1990 and 2100 and 
affect over 30,000 people (WHO, 2015). The effects of climate change on water 
security are especially pronounced in developing countries, where limited access 
to clean water and inadequate sanitation systems can exacerbate the spread of 
waterborne diseases such as cholera and salmonella (Akil et al., 2014). 
Moreover, the rise in water temperature can promote the growth and survival 
of harmful algae, such as cyanobacteria, in both sea and fresh water. This algae 
releases harmful toxins into the water and can also contaminate fish and shellfish 
that consume the algae (Wells et al., 2015). Drinking water or ingesting fish or 
shellfish contaminated by these toxins can cause a range of symptoms, from mild 
stomach pain and skin irritation to more severe reactions affecting the lungs, 
liver, and brain. For instance, in the case of paralytic shellfish poisoning, a type 
of harmful algal bloom can produce a neurotoxin that affects the nervous system 
of those who consume contaminated shellfish, leading to symptoms such as 
tingling, numbness, and paralysis.
To reduce the risk of food and waterborne diseases due to climate change, 
several strategies can be implemented. Governments must develop new 
infrastructures to provide access to clean water and proper sanitation facilities. 
Good hygiene practices, such as frequent handwashing with soap, using clean 
water for drinking and cooking, and safe disposal of waste, are highly effective in 
preventing the spread of microorganisms in water. Improving disease surveillance 
systems and implementing early warning systems can also help detect and 
Green Ideals
96
respond to outbreaks of waterborne diseases promptly. Finally, building flood-
resistant infrastructure may significantly enhance community resilience to the 
impacts of food and water-borne diseases.
2.4. Vector-Borne Diseases
Mosquitoes and ticks are carriers of various diseases that can be transmitted to 
humans, making them significant public health concerns worldwide. For instance, 
malaria, which is transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes, is a major cause 
of morbidity and mortality in tropical countries. It is estimated that there were 
247 million cases of malaria globally in 2022, resulting in 619,000 deaths (WHO, 
2022), and numbers in Cambodia are expected to increase to 22 million by 2070 
(WHO, 2015). Dengue, another mosquito-borne disease, is endemic in over 100 
countries and is a leading cause of illness in tropical regions (WHO, 2002). It is 
the second most worrying infectious threat in Cambodia with similarly increasing 
numbers by 2070 (WHO, 2015). Many other diseases are transmitted by the 
mosquito including West-Nile, Yellow Fever and Chikungunya. 
As the global temperature rises, mosquitoes are expected to expand their 
habitats to more temperate and higher elevated regions of the world. This will 
increase the risk of mosquito-borne diseases spreading to new areas. One of the 
most effective ways to limit vector borne diseases is through mosquito control 
programs that eliminate breeding sites and kill adult mosquitoes. Vaccination 
campaigns play a crucial role in combating mosquito-borne diseases like yellow 
fever. Additionally, adopting preventive measures such as wearing long-sleeved 
clothing and using repellent is essential.
2.5. Mental Health
Extreme weather not only has a physical impact on people but can also affect 
mental health. This situation can result in various psychological disorders, such 
as anxiety, depression, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) (Clayton, 2021). 
These events can also lead to social isolation, job loss, economic instability, 
and displacement, all of which can contribute to poor mental health outcomes. 
Fortunately, there are ways to address these problems. Governments, healthcare 
providers, and community-based organizations can work together to provide 
mental health support and resources to those affected by climate-related events, 
including counseling services and group therapy. We can therefore help reduce the 
psychological impacts of natural disasters and protect the victims’ mental health.
3. Climate Change and Health: Mitigating Impacts on a Global Scale
Addressing the health impacts of climate change presents multiple challenges 
for public health agencies for several reasons. First of all, climate change is a 
relatively new problem, and public health professionals may not have the 
necessary skills and expertise to effectively manage its complexity. Also, the 
scientific understanding of this issue’s underlying mechanisms is still incomplete, 
Global Health and Climate Change 
97
making it difficult to develop effective counterstrategies. Moreover, the necessary 
prevention and adaptation measures go beyond the remit of the health sector, 
requiring engagement with other sectors, such as urban planning, transportation, 
water, energy, agriculture and education. 
The mistake, however, would be to focus solely on human health and forget 
about environmental and animal health, which are intimately linked together. 
Various infectious diseases can be transmitted through either environmental 
sources such as water or animals, as seen with SARS, Ebola, and the West Nile 
virus. The One Health approach recognizes this interdependence (Chhem et al., 
2020), emphasizing the need for a collaborative and holistic approach to address 
climate-related health impacts. By taking this approach, better strategies can be 
developed for human health. For example, a One Health approach could involve 
improving disease surveillance systems that monitor both animal and human 
health, and promoting sustainable agriculture and land use practices that protect 
the environment and reduce the risk of zoonotic diseases. 
Cambodia has already started tackling the health impacts of climate change by 
implementing the Climate Change Strategic Plan 2014–2023 (CCCSP) and working 
on several important adaptations, but much work is still to be done with regards 
to disease surveillance and response, climate resilience, financing and costing 
mechanisms, as well as the analysis of the health benefits from this mitigation. 
3.1. The BRACE Framework
The BRACE Framework, developed in 2010 by the Center for Disease Control 
and Prevention (CDC), is a comprehensive tool that allows health officials to 
identify key health outcomes that are sensitive to climate change and create 
effective strategies to address them. It is regularly updated to reflect the latest 
scientific evidence and best practices. The BRACE Framework is divided into 
five sequential steps (Marinucci et al., 2014) (see Figure 9.3): 
Step 1 of the BRACE Framework involves two important tasks: 
•	 The first task consists of identifying climate-sensitive health outcomes.  
To that end, public health agencies need to access climate data sources 
to identify trends in weather patterns, such as temperature changes, 
precipitation, and extreme weather. Based on these historical data and 
climate mathematical models, and with the collaboration of climatologists, 
climate change can be projected 30 or more years into the future to assess 
the effects of climate change on health. By the end of this task, public health 
agencies will be able to report a list of health outcomes that are most likely 
to be affected by climate change. 
•	 The second task involves identifying vulnerable populations and regions. 
Various methods will be used to identify vulnerable populations, such as the 
analysis of demographic and health status data, and social vulnerability indices.
Green Ideals
98
The climate change projections and vulnerability assessment generated in 
Step 1 will provide a comprehensive understanding of the potential impacts of 
climate change on public health and the populations that are most vulnerable. 
This information can be used by policymakers and stakeholders to develop 
strategies and interventions to mitigate these impacts and protect public 
health.
Step 2 the goal is to estimate the additional disease burden associated with 
climate change. It can be done by linking the projected exposure pathway 
(extreme weather events, heat waves) to the health outcomes. For example, if an 
increase in extreme heat is expected to lead to an increase in heat-related illnesses, 
analysis of historical data and future trend projections are used to calculate the 
numbers incurred by this exposure pathway.
Step 3 concentrates on selecting the most appropriate measures to tackle the 
health issues identified earlier. To do so, the evidence-based public health (EBPH) 
approach can be used, allowing for an assessment of the effectiveness of various 
clinical and public health interventions. This involves a systematic literature 
review to identify relevant interventions and evaluate their efficacy. It is also 
important to evaluate whether interventions are well-matched to the political, 
cultural, and logistical landscape. Additionally, a cost-effectiveness analysis can 
help agencies prioritize interventions based on their cost and benefits.

Step 4 involves formulating a climate and health adaptation strategy that 
amalgamates the insights gathered in preceding phases. This strategy should be 
comprehensive, intersectoral, with a primary focus on public health outcomes. 
It should also harmonize with broader climate change initiatives across different 
sectors to promote collaboration among diverse disciplines and interest groups. 
Furthermore, the strategy should delineate methods for stakeholders to integrate 
adaptations into their existing programs and specify how activities will be assessed. 
Lastly, it should undergo periodic updates and be made publicly accessible.
Step 5 consists of monitoring and evaluating the impacts of interventions 
on public health. By collecting and analyzing data on their outcomes, we can 
learn from previous processes and improve future interventions. This can include 
identifying the most effective interventions, determining which populations 
benefit most from the interventions, and identifying any unintended consequences 
or negative impacts of the interventions. The data collected through monitoring 
and evaluation can also help inform policy decisions and resource allocation.
The framework has been successfully implemented in several countries 
given its numerous advantages. Indeed, it is an adaptive and iterative approach, 
allowing interventions to be refined and adjusted based on ongoing monitoring 
and evaluation. It is also evidence-based and grounded in scientific research and 
data and emphasizes health equity and collaboration between stakeholders. There 
are some potential disadvantages, namely its complexity and need for abundant 
resources, which could limit its feasibility in some contexts. Additionally, its 
focus on long-term outcomes may not provide immediate solutions to urgent 
public health problems. In addition to the use of the BRACE Framework, health 
officials must take into account several considerations to reduce the effects of 
climate change on health. 
Firstly, there is an urgent need for education and training for public health 
and healthcare professionals on climate change. This involves integrating 
climate change-related topics into the existing curricula of these professionals. 
Various training initiatives already exist, such as the Climate and Health Literacy 
Consortium in the US and the Climate and Health Alliance in Australia. By 
incorporating climate change into professional training and education, healthcare 
professionals will be better equipped to identify and manage climate-related 
health issues. 
Secondly, increasing the resilience of health systems is crucial and several 
measures can be undertaken. Hospital designs should include climate-resilient 
aspects with sustainable and resilient building materials, energy-efficient systems, 
and advanced water management systems.  Early warning systems for extreme 
weather events would improve emergency response planning, enhance medical 
supply availability, and increase healthcare system capacity during heat waves or 
disease outbreaks.
