100
Lastly, it is important to consider the varying vulnerabilities of different 
demographic and socio-economic groups. WHO emphasizes the need for 
health equity in addressing climate-related health threats. However, practical 
implementation of equitable adaptation solutions is rare. Stronger engagement 
of those working on climate change threats with social care providers can help to 
ensure that vulnerable populations, such as the elderly or disabled, have access to 
the support they need to adapt to climate-related challenges. 
3.2. Connecting Global Health and Climate Change through Diplomacy
Climate change is a global phenomenon that is expected to affect every country 
in the world. To effectively address its health impacts, it is essential for all 
countries to take collective action. Global health diplomacy represents the 
convergence of health and international policy, enabling nations to collectively 
tackle global health issues through collaborative negotiations and partnerships. 
It involves a wide range of actors from various sectors, including government 
officials, diplomats, public health professionals, researchers, NGOs, civil society 
groups, and international organizations. These individuals and organizations 
work together to promote international cooperation and coordination on global 
health issues, such as disease outbreaks, natural disasters, and the health impacts 
of climate change.
In recent years, global health diplomacy has played a critical role in addressing 
epidemics such as COVID-19, Ebola, and Zika, by facilitating the sharing of 
information and best practices among countries, helping to coordinate their 
interventions and also by promoting access to medicines and vaccines.  One 
concrete example of global health diplomacy in action is the Westerdam incident 
during the COVID-19 pandemic (Chhem & Chhem, 2020). The Westerdam 
cruise ship was denied entry to several ports due to fears that its passengers and 
crew may have been infected with COVID-19. Eventually, the ship was allowed 
to dock in Cambodia, where its passengers and crew received humanitarian 
assistance. Cambodia’s decision to allow the Westerdam to dock and provide 
assistance to its occupants can be seen as an example of health diplomacy. By 
taking in the ship and its passengers, Cambodia demonstrated its commitment 
to promoting health and protecting vulnerable populations in the face of a global 
health crisis. This decision required diplomacy and negotiation with other 
countries, as well as coordination with public health officials to ensure that 
appropriate measures were taken to prevent the spread of disease.
Similarly, global health diplomacy can play a critical role in addressing the 
impacts of climate change on health by promoting cooperation and collaboration 
between countries. One example is the Paris Agreement on Climate Change 
signed in 2015. Its goal is to maintain the increase in global temperatures below 
2°C relative to pre-industrial levels and to endeavor to limit the rise to no more 
than 1.5°C.  The WHO has also been active in addressing climate change and 
Global Health and Climate Change 
101
health through global health diplomacy. The WHO has developed a range of 
strategies and tools to help countries adapt to the health impacts of climate 
change, including the Climate and Health Country Profiles.
4. Conclusion 
To mitigate the health impacts of climate change, urgent and coordinated action 
across sectors and countries is necessary. This requires a multifaceted approach 
that includes reducing greenhouse gas emissions, implementing energy-efficient 
technologies, and promoting sustainable transportation. Adapting healthcare 
systems is crucial, with strengthened disease surveillance, early warning systems, 
and climate-resilient infrastructure. Education campaigns empower individuals 
by raising awareness about the risks of food-borne, water-borne and vector-borne 
diseases, while also providing information on preventive measures to reduce these 
risks and protect public health. Priority must therefore be placed on research, 
policy development, and collaboration among different stakeholders, all the 
while keeping in mind the importance of health equity throughout this whole 
process, as different needs will require different solutions. By working together, 
we can effectively mitigate the detrimental health effects of climate change and 
pave the way for resilient communities, ensuring a better future for all.

and India as the main engines of economic growth around the world, and the 
increasing global concern over sustainability issues are among the primary

a doubt, also altered how the labor market operates and how potential employees 
are recruited in Cambodia. In the past, when industries mainly demanded low-

market” in which employers could easily hire potential workers. After all, most 
employees then did not need to possess very high competencies to work in a firm 
that predominantly required manual labor.

total fertility rate of Cambodia has continued to decline significantly from 4.0 
in 2000 to 2.4 in 2020  (United Nations Department of Economic and Social 
Affairs, 2022). The number of young Cambodian workers who enter the labor 
market annually decreased from 300,000 in the early 2010s (Ministry of Labour & 
International Labor Organization, 2014) to 270,000 in 20171, while the demands 
for better skills from first-time job seekers are also intensifying, corresponding 
with higher wages and the changing characteristics of the Cambodian economy 
which has begun to compete in terms of workers’ productivity instead of low 
input costs such as salary. Such a change in the nature of competition is true 
even in the case of the garment and footwear industry, which is considered a low-
skilled sector. As a result, young Cambodians must be equipped with the high 
skills necessary to succeed and thrive in an uncertain and unpredictable future 
while the country is on its way towards becoming a more developed country. 
It is in this sense that the way the youth is educated must also be revisited and 
reconsidered. The Cambodian education system cannot be the same as it was 
thirty years ago if the country is to advance further and grab a larger part of the 
global market for its products.
Nevertheless, discussing how the Cambodian educational system should 
evolve would be too broad to discuss in one paper. After all, different educational

must go beyond their traditional teaching-only mission to encompass social

inclusive and sustainable development. This shift is reflected in the concept of 
University 4.0, which emphasizes the importance of higher education institutions 
in shaping the society of the future where technology, social innovation, and 
sustainability converge (Gorina & Polyakova, 2021; Rosak-Szyrocka et al., 2022).
The findings and discussion in this paper derive from an in-depth interview 
with Prof. Jeffrey Sachs, an economist leading the Center for Sustainable 
Development at Columbia University and the United Nations’ Sustainable 
Development Solutions Network (SDSN), and roundtable panel discussions on 
University and Digital Sustainability during the 14th International Conference 
on Software, Knowledge, Information Management and Applications (SKIMA) 
hosted at the Cambodia University of Technology and Science (CamTech) on 
December 2 – 4, 2022. The panel discussions were public and were participated 
by academics in high-level management positions at seven universities across 
five countries. The discussion was recorded in video format and later transcribed 
into text for coding and thematic data analysis.
This research study echoes the concern of Prime Minister Hun Sen, who 
raised an important question during his opening remarks to audiences at the 
Cambodia Outlook Conference 2022, which consisted of leaders from the 
government, private sector, civil society, universities, and think-tanks, asking 
whether Cambodia will be able to achieve its Sustainable Development Goals 
by 2030, especially after the major disruptions caused by the Covid-19 Pandemic 
and the war in Ukraine in recent years. In addition, it seeks to contribute to 
filling in the gap of knowledge of a nascent initiative known as the ASEAN 
Green Deal, which aims to re-orient regional development towards ASEAN’s 
sustainable, inclusive, and resilient green future while continuing to prioritize 
digital transformation. In short, this research is meant to identify the role of 
universities in promoting sustainability. Moreover, it intends to put sustainability 
on the radar of higher education discourse in Cambodia, as currently, only a 
few Cambodian higher education institutions incorporate sustainability into their 
mission, vision, or academic programs.
Regarding academic significance, we develop and extend Fissi et al.’s (2021) 
framework for a sustainable university to include international collaboration. In

2. Understanding Sustainability and Sustainable University
In 1987, the United Nations Brundtland Commission defined sustainability as 
“meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future 
generations to meet their own needs.” (United Nations, 1987). However, such a 
loose definition with the increasing concern over climate issues is less applicable 
to meet the development needs of today’s agenda. It is in this regard that new 
ideas or concepts of sustainable development must be put in place, giving birth 
to the ambitious aspirations for a greener, healthier, more prosperous, equal, 
and peaceful world known as the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in 
2012. Particularly, sustainability, in this sense and in accordance with Prof. 
Jeffrey Sachs, the champion of the SDGs, revolves around four main basic ideas 
as follows:
•	 All societies are striving for material decency and dignity, economic 
prosperity, and meeting the economic needs of their people;
•	 All societies are or should be striving for social inclusion and social justice, 
and that welfare should be shared more evenly among everyone, regardless 
of race and gender;
•	 Societies need to collaborate to confront the multiple and increasingly 
serious environmental crises such as human-induced climate change, 
massive degradation of vital ecosystems, and mega pollution of air, water, 
and soils;
•	 Finally, all societies should strictly adhere to the principles of cooperation, 
partnership, and a multipolar world to promote peace.
2.1. From Teaching to Digital University
Now that we know how sustainability is defined, we are in an easy position 
to understand what it means for a university, whose role should no longer be 
limited to being a mere spectator for global macro-level challenges. In medieval 
times, a university was an institution where only lectures and seminars were given 
Green Ideals
106
to elitist groups of students with a focus on theology and politics. Their tasks 
were mostly cultivating the next generation of leaders and producing competent 
members of the government, and these graduates would then be the agents of 
gods endeavoring to rule the masses and bring prosperity (Scott, 2006).
This was mainly the case until the research function was incorporated in the 
19th century to expand the scope of work of the university. Wissema (2009) calls 
it the University 2.0, with Humboldt University allegedly being the first of such 
entity in Europe. Research was then another essential source of socioeconomic 
development and innovation worldwide. However, academic research has often 
been criticized by the general public as lacking practicality and of little use in 
daily application. It thus does not contribute back to the community directly. 
In fact, research, for a considerably long time, was mainly done to boost faculty 
members’ publications and the university’s prestige. Under the publish-or-perish 
principle, the world of academia has also been plagued by research fraud, including 
plagiarism, data fabrication, data falsification, and other questionable research 
practices done intentionally by academics (Herndon, 2016) or unintentionally by 
those who pretend to know it all influenced by Dunning-Kruger effects (Dunning, 
2011), causing mass confusion. As a result, only a small number of research 
publications find their way into good hands.
The Third-Generation University (University 3.0 or entrepreneurial 
university), with the University of Cambridge as the best example, is seen as 
the cradle of economic and entrepreneurial activities, translating know-how 
to commercial outcomes, supporting business activities within and outside of 
campus, leading innovation, and competing in the market for research contracts 
from the industries (Wissema, 2009). It may also assume the role of an incubator 
and accelerator for startups. The emergence of technology-based enterprises 
incubated by universities worldwide bears witness to this new overhanging role 
of the university, but such economically competitive characteristics of industries 
can be an invitation to the structural exploitation of natural resources (Kuch, 
2020).
There is also the concept of University 4.0 (digital university), which tends 
to further extend the university’s traditional duties (Strielkowski & Wang, 
2020; Wissema, 2009). Such a university is the latest model of higher learning 
institutions, established to reflect the current teaching and learning paradigm 
known as the Education 4.0 (Cottafava et al., 2019). It, in turn, responds to 
the Industry 4.0 framework, the growing number of Generation Z entering the 
labor market and the digital revolution in education. One example of the new 
teaching methods for digital universities is the use of Massive Open Online 
Courses (MOOC), online learning platforms, and technological devices such as 
Virtual Reality (VR) sets, all of which have rendered the traditional pedagogy 
and learning approaches obsolete.

2.2. University for Sustainability
It is worth noting that the evolution of higher learning institutions is conceptualized 
based on the university’s activities, but by the nature of the competitive market 
economy, these activities may not encourage social and economic sustainability. 
On the contrary, it may reinforce economic inequality (Blanden & Machin, 
2004) and eventually lead to the tragedy of the commons (Grinell & Rabin, 2013; 
Hardin, 1968). As a result, one needs to rethink and restructure the university’s 
functions to include the sustainability dimension in addition to the existing 
tasks. That is to say, a university should incorporate SDG principles into its core 
activities and promote such fundamentals in its daily operations. Formally, a 
sustainable university can be defined as a higher education institution that is managed 
in respect of green economic, social, and environmental practices and that fulfills its function 
of teaching, research, and community engagement in ways to favor the transition of society 
toward sustainable lifestyles (Velazquez et al., 2006, p. 812). Sustainable universities 
can also be used interchangeably with green universities or campuses, the notion 
of which encourages university leaders, faculty members, and students to meet 
social and environmental responsibilities (Dagiliūtė et al., 2018; Yuan et al., 
2013). Indeed, there is still a debate on the concept of the terms “sustainable 
university” and “green university” or if they differ in some senses (Santa et al., 
2019; Velazquez et al., 2006). Regardless of that, it is not the same as a university 
for digital sustainability2.
Under the definition above, a sustainable university has a complex 
and closely interlinked system characterized by four components: campus 
operations, teaching, research, and community engagement (Yuan et al., 2013). 
The first component comprises how the university should maintain its campus 
environment, waste, and use of its resources efficiently and economically. Leal 
Filho et al. (2019) mentioned that while teaching and research have always been 
the core parts of a university since the late 19th century, assuming it is, of course, 
not practicing the medieval-European system as a teaching-only university which 
is still prevalent in Cambodia (Khieng et al., 2017). Last but not least, sustainable 
universities must seek to engage and collaborate with the local community, 
government, and industries to increase their awareness of sustainability issues 
which the world is facing. Specific outreach activities include training, seminars, 
partnership building, and generating new business ideas for startups.
Fissi et al. (2021), however, argue that more than these four dimensions are 
needed. Many Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) have failed to become 
sustainable universities because they did not explicitly indicate their mission 
and vision when it comes to sustainability. Simply put, they need a proper 
institutional framework and a clear policy from the top leadership. In addition,

government, private sector, civil society, universities, and think-tanks, asking

and the war in Ukraine in recent years. In addition, it seeks to contribute to 
filling in the gap of knowledge of a nascent initiative known as the ASEAN 
Green Deal, which aims to re-orient regional development towards ASEAN’s 
sustainable, inclusive, and resilient green future while continuing to prioritize 
digital transformation. In short, this research is meant to identify the role of 
universities in promoting sustainability. Moreover, it intends to put sustainability

3. Findings and Discussion
This section presents the findings from the panel discussion during the SKIMA 
conference held in December 2022. When asked how to integrate sustainability 
concepts and practices into the mindset of everyone on campus, ranging from 
the security guard at the gates to the university president, a common theme was 
identified by most participants, namely that a curriculum with an added focus on 
sustainability issues must be developed. It was also suggested that even a teaching 
university should seek every opportunity to promote the students’ awareness of 
environmental and social issues, and that, in turn, will help them influence their 
workplace practices and perhaps also national policies in the future. It can be 
done by integrating sustainability into the curriculum vertically (students should 
take specific sustainability-related courses throughout their educational journey 
at the university) and horizontally (by including sustainability principles in other 
regular courses). Alternatively, universities can generate sustainability-responsible 
citizens through their undergraduate and graduate programs, particularly those 
who major in sustainability or sustainable development. It is worth noting that it 
is not simply a course in a wider curriculum but a degree program.
“The reason is that if it’s just a single course, students will learn a single course 
and forget it. Sustainability needs to be embedded across all courses, across all 
programs. Many curricula are also very jam-packed. It’s very difficult to add 
additional courses. Most of my students are already studying for 10 to 12 hours a 
day. You can just add an extra course, and they study for 14 hours a day.”
Case 6, President of a Cambodian university.
Regardless of that, the university should also be a focal point that actively 
promotes the concept of green-based entrepreneurship and innovation among 
students. This concept refers to the design and implementation of innovative 
methods that aim to solve societal problems and eventually improve individual 
and community welfare. In a broader sense, a university for sustainability should 
pay more attention to fostering ideas and incubating student startups whose 
business activities are related to the Sustainable Development Goals or aim to 
address the SDG problems to assist the host country in achieving them. Despite 
their young age, youth and students should play a part in helping to develop 
solutions, wherever and whenever possible. In fact, many ideas belonging to, 
and deriving from, the youth and students are creative and innovative, allowing 
the country to cope with and approach societal problems in a different way, as 
Green Ideals
110
their minds are not confined to an intelligence-trapping atmosphere such as the 
workplace culture and structure (Walter, 2012). They are also likely to understand 
their peers’ needs more than people from another generation. 
“We wish to provide a holistic education so that those whom we engage, especially 
our students, when they graduate, they have skills, especially transferable skills, 
…, but more than skills are that they become responsible citizens. “Responsible” 
means responsible consumer, responsible employee, or responsible employer if 
they start their own startup… If enterprises just focus on the bottom line, as I 
already mentioned earlier, and the economy is just focused on growth growth 
growth without limits, an issue that we’ve been warned 30 years ago in 1972, 
when hundreds of scholars launched the book on the limits of growth. If we don’t 
learn the lesson of the limits of growth and we continue to focus on this narrow 
definition of development, then it’s not sustainable.” 
Case 7, President of a Cambodian university.
Nevertheless, entrepreneurship should not be an approach to enriching oneself 
at the expense of others directly or indirectly. It never is, and it should not be the 
fundamentally inherent nature of capitalism. It is here that the university itself, as 
an educational institution seeking to promote a good personality, ought to stand 
firm against such a notion and work to develop and shape a student’s character; 
otherwise, having an educated person is even more destructive to the society than 
having many uneducated individuals.
“Now about the course [sustainability], as I mentioned that it can be added as a 
topic in every course, but I believe there must be a course at the first-day level, 
entry-level, that would teach ethics, leadership, and entrepreneurship.”
Case 3, Professor at a university in Australia.
“Should sustainability courses be compulsory for all academic programs? Of 
course, we should in the foundation year so that all students have this mindset 
while they study with a very good positive attitude in terms of sustainability.”
Case 5, Vice President of a Cambodian university.
Establishing partnership and collaboration across universities is another 
common message raised by the top leadership of the universities that participated 
in the panel discussion. Overseas cooperation here also means being a hub 
and acting as an intermediary to create networking opportunities, foster 
communication, and facilitate partnership and collaboration among and between 
local and foreign higher learning institutions and other stakeholders in order to 
promote integrated and holistic approaches to provide solutions to sustainable 
development challenges.
“So, I think we need to push this somehow and either through our academic 
research in such a way that politicians and those who are in power will believe that 
this is a real crisis and that we should act now. Otherwise, we will be in difficult 
situations in the coming years. Also, I think university education systems until 
now had some problems because, as you have talked about, working in silos. For

example, in my time when I studied in universities. I’m a technical guy; I studied

solution would have an impact on the social aspect, political aspect, and all this. 
So this is critical, like [name] mentioned, that there are the political system, social

Case 4, University professor and director of a research center in Scotland.
It should be highlighted that tackling the technical complexity of the problems 
would generally need interdisciplinary understanding and participation from 
scholars of different fields. For example, the climate crisis cannot be solved solely 
by climatologists. They can only tell what will happen if we emit more greenhouse 
gases, but they are not energy engineers. They will be able to advise on which 
type of (clean) energy sources we should utilize to reduce pollution or how we 
should communicate this with the general public in a way that would change 
their environmentally-unfriendly behavior and earn their trust and support and 
not cause panic. International collaboration among universities would also bring 
about the internationalization of higher education, and it is almost certain that 
through such efforts, the university would prepare the students for a globalized 
workforce and improve their cultural tolerance and ability to work and interact in 
a multi-ethnic environment (de Wit et al., 2015), which in turn would encourage 
more collaboration across societies in the future.
“And the second one, to be quick, is about the uncertainty of science, of course,

networks, and things like that, there’s more and more information everywhere. 
So we need to push also our students to be able to have critical thinking and to 
have also a holistic approach in their problem analysis, so that means that I agree 
totally with Professor [Name] about the transdisciplinary approach, which is very 
very very important. Of course, I’m a computer scientist, and I think most of us are 
from the STEM domain, but we need to work hand-in-hand with human science,

Case 2, Professor at a French university.
A university also needs to revisit its missions and stop considering itself as 
just a place, in the eyes of the commoners, where men with glasses spend long 
hours reading books, talking unintelligibly with one another, doing esoteric and 
bizarre research, and publishing incomprehensible texts. However, we have, 
by no means, suggested that the university needs to forfeit its roles, including 
research and entrepreneurship development. In fact, they need to expand their 
scope of work in each of these roles. There should be a much more active pursuit 
of applied research at the university level that responds to policy and industrial

demands. Simply put, research should seek to make an impact on society and 
contribute in terms of policy suggestions to solve sustainability issues, regardless 
of whether or not it would be publishable in a top journal.
“So the third point is quite similar to what [case 6] mentioned, many of our 
faculty members were trained in an era that was very different from the students 
that we are educating. So we need to continue to retrain and rethink, especially 
after Covid, what is the role of the university again. Is it purely to provide skills

moment, we are proud but at the same time humbled to be a member of UN 
Sustainable Development Solutions Network, a member of the university rectors 
and vice-rectors around the world, connecting resources and expertise, but we are 
also partnering with UN agencies such as UNESCAP and International Labor 
Organization to research and to develop a program in social innovation and social 
entrepreneurship because these are the explicit actions that may address the issue 
Professor Sachs has mentioned – a complete change of mindset in terms of how 
we run the economy.”
Case 7, President of a Cambodian university.
Last but not least, as Prof. Jeffrey Sachs suggested, one needs to strictly adhere 
to exercising diplomacy to promote international collaboration to solve global 
issues. A combined effort to strengthen political liaison is, without question, the 
first thing one needs to consider in a world of conflict; otherwise, it will obstruct 
other competition due to the lack of trust, resulting in mutual losses. For instance, 
climate and environmental issues would require international cooperation across 
continents because many sustainable challenges one country faces, are likely 
shared by its neighboring states, such as Cambodia with Lao PDR, Vietnam, and 
Thailand. Economically speaking, it would be equivalent to a public good which 
is both non-rivalrous and non-excludable. That is to say, if Country A manages 
to clean the air, people from neighboring Country B will also benefit, and that 
Country A cannot exclude Country B from breathing in clean air. However, 
Country A would not want to do this alone and would prefer teamwork, but if 
Country B refuses to partner in this situation, Country A will find absolutely no 
incentives to clean the air, not even for themselves.
4. Challenges
Promoting sustainability even internally within the university campus has always 
been challenging (Ávila et al., 2017; Dahle & Neumayer, 2001), let alone promoting 
international collaboration across countries to deal with these issues which have 
not received a strong political will, especially from the developed world, which 
is the main source of greenhouse gas emission. On some occasions, these major 
emitters also announced their withdrawal from the 2015 Paris Agreement on 
University for Sustainability 
113
Climate Change Mitigation. In fact, there are also very few incentives for any 
higher education institution to do so in the first place. Universities are judged 
and given ranks based mostly on the number of their lecturers, students, research 
impacts and activities, including grants received and publications. They receive 
little to no rewards for being a civic and green university, at least in the context 
of the ASEAN region. Therefore, it comes with little surprise that even though 
the ASEAN universities do collaborate, to a certain degree, they do so in order 
to compete for funding, students and faculty members (Chan, 2004) and not to 
solve sustainability challenges, which have also been given low levels of attention 
(Clark et al., 2018).
In Cambodia in particular, only six institutions, namely the Cambodia 
University of Technology and Science (CamTech), University of Puthisastra (UP), 
University of Cambodia (UC), National University of Management (NUM), 
Royal University of Phnom Penh (RUPP), and Asian Vision Institute (AVI), are 
part of the Sustainable Development Solutions Network (SDSN) championing 
sustainable development resolutions as of April 2023. They have yet to be 
recognized for their efforts in taking initiatives and scaffolding sustainability, 
not even locally. Consequently, the university ranking system should give more 
priority or higher weight to the sustainability aspect and related activities which 
generate impacts on society on top of the mainstream academia. There must be 
an incentive system there to stimulate certain pursuits and discourage harmful 
behavior, or universities are likely to resort to detrimental habits just to put on 
a front, the same way that a country can increase GDP by chopping down trees 
and extracting mineral resources uncontrollably. It apparently looks grand from 
the outside, but in reality, it is very unhealthy on the inside.
Another challenge when it comes to the implementation of the model is 
that both lecturers and students typically have a very strong academic interest, 
believing that their priorities should be to embed the students’ attributes in as many 
technical skills as possible (Pham & Soltani, 2021), disregarding other important 
(social) issues, including sustainable development unless their field of study is 
highly relevant with them. For that reason, it is usually difficult to convince 
students to recognize the value of contemporary general knowledge, which may 
help improve their critical and holistic thinking and chances of landing a job 
right after graduation. The students, however, often only realize the importance 
of taking these subjects later when they enter the real world of the labor market 
and come into contact with employers (Pham & Soltani, 2021). Such insufficient 
and poor preparation of employability skills for students eventually causes 
much frustration to both the students themselves and their potential employers 
(National Employment Agency, 2018). It is worth noting that some research has 
also indicated insufficient government policies to encourage the implementation 
of an educational system for sustainability as a part of the problem (Brandli et 
al., 2015; Filho et al., 2015). In this regard, the university needs to revise its 
Green Ideals
114
current curriculum and introduce a revolutionary interdisciplinary approach to 
education. Certain courses relevant to sustainable development should be made 
compulsory for all university students, regardless of their major. Doing so will 
help students grasp today’s complex phenomenon and global issues and scaffold 
sustainability.
Finally, despite the fact that some HEIs have taken some initiatives to support 
the SDGs, such as establishing a center for social innovation to promote social 
enterprise and entrepreneurship and a school for a sustainable built environment 
to improve urban planning and regulations, and conducting policy research 
studies to provide a better and more comprehensive understanding of the current 
issues and solutions, such initiatives often face major resource challenges since 
the environmental and sustainability field of research is not an area of priority 
(Velazquez et al., 2005). In Brazil, Brandli et al. (2015) have also documented a 
substantial lack of financial aid for sustainability projects for universities that are 
being run mainly based on the goodwill of their faculty members and staff and 
the work of volunteers. Similarly, respondents from 27 Canadian universities 
assert that the greatest barrier to sustainable university programs is the lack of 
funding (Elliott & Wright, 2013).
5. Conclusion
Because of their impact on the economy, society, and environment, the role of 
the institutes for higher learning in scaffolding a more sustainable society has 
recently been a research topic that has been increasingly studied by academics 
(Marques et al., 2019). A few models for sustainable universities have been 
proposed, but these models are limited in the sense that they need to include 
an important component of international collaboration and interdisciplinary 
approaches to dealing with sustainability issues. In the age of globalization and 
economic connectivity, the sustainable development challenge is not a single or 
a few countries’ problem. It is a cross-border topic of concern and discussion. 
For example, if we continue to cut down trees in the United States and Canada, 
the temperature in Europe will also rise, while some cities along the coast in 
Asia are also likely to submerge completely. Addressing the issue in one country 
in Asia alone would not be enough. Likewise, in order for the ASEAN Green 
Deal Initiative to have major impacts, involvement from ASEAN universities 
is a must, and they have to collaborate to implement the tasks. It should be 
highlighted that the ASEAN Green Deal is an instrument to address increasing 
concerns over the discussion on climate change, environmental degradation, 
carbon neutrality, circular economy, and green technologies in addition to 
economic competitiveness and education and TVET reform which have always 
been ASEAN’s priorities.
This backdrop gives rise to a framework for a university for sustainability. 
The model, which comprises four components, including campus operation, 
University for Sustainability 
115
teaching, research, and community engagement, is extended to place significant 
importance on international cooperation and concerted efforts while extending 
the conventional roles of a university directly and indirectly beyond just producing 
the next generation of economically driven executives and skilled workers. 
Instead, it aims to generate socially responsible and environmentally friendly civic 
pioneers, leaders, and innovators with transdisciplinary and interdisciplinary 
competencies to effectively cope with both local and global issues and ensure 
sustainability and survival in the Anthropocene era, where human activities 
have led to much damage to the environment and the whole earth. Note that 
the model recognizes that sustainability and economic growth can go hand in 
hand, contrary to what was suggested by the Limits to Growth report in 1972 
(Meadows et al., 1972). It is worth noting that the report has also received much 
criticism regarding methods and assumptions. We have also discussed how to 
incentivize universities to contribute more to sustainability by rearranging how 
they are ranked and recognized for their efforts. The key constraint remains lack 
of financing to implement such visions. University’s revenue comes from several 
sources, namely research, the funding for which is, at the moment, very limited 
to accomplish the tasks at hand and make a serious effect. Therefore, there should 
be more global and national funding for projects aimed at providing solutions 
to SDGs. It should be highlighted that research grants should be provided to 
a consortium of universities from several countries to eliminate the practice of 
universities working in silos and artificial arrangements in academia.
For Cambodia, as the country embarks on emerging technologies and 
digital transformation, accelerated industrialization, and rapid socioeconomic 
development, the university for sustainability model should be put into practice, 
at least in some universities. A very close collaboration between the government, 
the academia, and the industries, is also required. This is to (1) address business 
challenges, (2) encourage and promote industrial R&D and innovation, (3) 
mitigate the negative impacts of industrial development on the environment, and 
(4) promote responsible and green development for a more sustainable world. 
Such complex and multilayered challenges cannot be undertaken without an 
enabling and supportive environment, including human resources and funding 
for universities to realize its vision, missions, and objectives, especially those of 
the ASEAN Green Deal, which was initiated by Cambodia in 2022 the rotating 
chairman of ASEAN. What comes next would be the execution of the model, 
which requires the operationalization of all the components, especially campus 
operations, and the teaching and learning aspects. It involves the design of a new 
curriculum, restructuring the university’s institutional functions, and changing 
faculty, staff, and students’ behavior and perception toward green campuses. The 
latter conventionally takes quite a lot of time to achieve, for there are always 
people who resist changes in their way of living.

1. Introduction 
People have been debating various aspects of development since the beginning of 
time. It is fascinating to observe how people have utilized their environment and 
surroundings to develop the community. Even though the forms of development 
used in the 21st century have been modernized and a significant emphasis 
has been placed on environmental protection, it may be difficult to conceive 
of human development without environmental dependence. In any case, the 
overexploitation of natural resources has sparked widespread environmental 
degradation concerns. As a result, people worldwide are looking for ways to 
reverse, stop, or lessen environmental degradation, which could eventually lead 
to the extinction of the human race. A multilateralism initiative has gradually 
shaped the concept of sustainable development through the numerous initiatives 
undertaken. Sustainable development applies to several industries, including 
tourism. There has been a shift from “mass tourism” to “sustainable tourism,” 
which has moderated the tourism industry’s operations. Green deals in Europe 
can serve as a model for ASEAN to use in unifying the collaborative approach 
among member states, especially in securing green finance, providing clear 
roadmaps, rules, and regulations. Even coordinating the green innovation 
and STI in the region as a means to sustainable tourism can be supported by 
making a conversion to renewable energy, determining a circular economy, or 
enhancing green infrastructure (Ciot, 2021). In light of this, Cambodia, despite 
being a small nation, views its tourism industry as “Green Gold.” Cambodia has 
adopted various tourism development master plans, strategies, and roadmaps 
which clearly outline the plan to strengthen sustainable tourism through a variety 
of measures. This chapter will begin by examining the concept of sustainable 
tourism, followed by a discussion of sustainable tourism’s challenges and potential 
solutions to those challenges. Later in the chapter, Cambodia’s experience with 
sustainable tourism will be discussed.

Sustainable tourism includes activities, management, and development that 
safeguard natural, economic, and social integrity and conserve cultural resources. 
Thus, implementing sustainable tourism principles requires ensuring viable and 
long-term economic operations, making optimal use of environmental resources, 
and respecting the socio-cultural authenticity of host communities (Niedzióka,

3. Findings and Discussion
This section presents the findings from the panel discussion during the SKIMA 
conference held in December 2022. When asked how to integrate sustainability 
concepts and practices into the mindset of everyone on campus, ranging from 
the security guard at the gates to the university president, a common theme was 
identified by most participants, namely that a curriculum with an added focus on 
sustainability issues must be developed. It was also suggested that even a teaching 
university should seek every opportunity to promote the students’ awareness of 
environmental and social issues, and that, in turn, will help them influence their 
workplace practices and perhaps also national policies in the future. It can be 
done by integrating sustainability into the curriculum vertically (students should 
take specific sustainability-related courses throughout their educational journey 
at the university) and horizontally (by including sustainability principles in other 
regular courses). Alternatively, universities can generate sustainability-responsible 
citizens through their undergraduate and graduate programs, particularly those 
who major in sustainability or sustainable development. It is worth noting that it 
is not simply a course in a wider curriculum but a degree program.
“The reason is that if it’s just a single course, students will learn a single course 
and forget it. Sustainability needs to be embedded across all courses, across all 
programs. Many curricula are also very jam-packed. It’s very difficult to add 
additional courses. Most of my students are already studying for 10 to 12 hours a 
day. You can just add an extra course, and they study for 14 hours a day.”
Case 6, President of a Cambodian university.
Regardless of that, the university should also be a focal point that actively 
promotes the concept of green-based entrepreneurship and innovation among 
students. This concept refers to the design and implementation of innovative 
methods that aim to solve societal problems and eventually improve individual 
and community welfare. In a broader sense, a university for sustainability should 
pay more attention to fostering ideas and incubating student startups whose 
business activities are related to the Sustainable Development Goals or aim to 
address the SDG problems to assist the host country in achieving them. Despite 
their young age, youth and students should play a part in helping to develop 
solutions, wherever and whenever possible. In fact, many ideas belonging to, 
and deriving from, the youth and students are creative and innovative, allowing 
the country to cope with and approach societal problems in a different way, as

workplace culture and structure (Walter, 2012). They are also likely to understand 
their peers’ needs more than people from another generation.

our students, when they graduate, they have skills, especially transferable skills,

that both lecturers and students typically have a very strong academic interest, 
believing that their priorities should be to embed the students’ attributes in as many 
technical skills as possible (Pham & Soltani, 2021), disregarding other important 
(social) issues, including sustainable development unless their field of study is 
highly relevant with them. For that reason, it is usually difficult to convince 
students to recognize the value of contemporary general knowledge, which may 
help improve their critical and holistic thinking and chances of landing a job 
right after graduation. The students, however, often only realize the importance 
of taking these subjects later when they enter the real world of the labor market 
and come into contact with employers (Pham & Soltani, 2021). Such insufficient 
and poor preparation of employability skills for students eventually causes 
much frustration to both the students themselves and their potential employers 
(National Employment Agency, 2018). It is worth noting that some research has 
also indicated insufficient government policies to encourage the implementation 
of an educational system for sustainability as a part of the problem (Brandli et 
al., 2015; Filho et al., 2015). In this regard, the university needs to revise its 
Green Ideals
114
current curriculum and introduce a revolutionary interdisciplinary approach to 
education. Certain courses relevant to sustainable development should be made 
compulsory for all university students, regardless of their major. Doing so will 
help students grasp today’s complex phenomenon and global issues and scaffold 
sustainability.
Finally, despite the fact that some HEIs have taken some initiatives to support 
the SDGs, such as establishing a center for social innovation to promote social 
enterprise and entrepreneurship and a school for a sustainable built environment 
to improve urban planning and regulations, and conducting policy research 
studies to provide a better and more comprehensive understanding of the current 
issues and solutions, such initiatives often face major resource challenges since 
the environmental and sustainability field of research is not an area of priority 
(Velazquez et al., 2005). In Brazil, Brandli et al. (2015) have also documented a 
substantial lack of financial aid for sustainability projects for universities that are 
being run mainly based on the goodwill of their faculty members and staff and 
the work of volunteers. Similarly, respondents from 27 Canadian universities 
assert that the greatest barrier to sustainable university programs is the lack of 
funding (Elliott & Wright, 2013).
5. Conclusion
Because of their impact on the economy, society, and environment, the role of 
the institutes for higher learning in scaffolding a more sustainable society has 
recently been a research topic that has been increasingly studied by academics 
(Marques et al., 2019). A few models for sustainable universities have been 
proposed, but these models are limited in the sense that they need to include 
an important component of international collaboration and interdisciplinary 
approaches to dealing with sustainability issues. In the age of globalization and 
economic connectivity, the sustainable development challenge is not a single or 
a few countries’ problem. It is a cross-border topic of concern and discussion. 
For example, if we continue to cut down trees in the United States and Canada, 
the temperature in Europe will also rise, while some cities along the coast in 
Asia are also likely to submerge completely. Addressing the issue in one country 
in Asia alone would not be enough. Likewise, in order for the ASEAN Green 
Deal Initiative to have major impacts, involvement from ASEAN universities 
is a must, and they have to collaborate to implement the tasks. It should be 
highlighted that the ASEAN Green Deal is an instrument to address increasing 
concerns over the discussion on climate change, environmental degradation, 
carbon neutrality, circular economy, and green technologies in addition to 
economic competitiveness and education and TVET reform which have always 
been ASEAN’s priorities.
This backdrop gives rise to a framework for a university for sustainability. 
The model, which comprises four components, including campus operation, 
University for Sustainability 
115
teaching, research, and community engagement, is extended to place significant 
importance on international cooperation and concerted efforts while extending 
the conventional roles of a university directly and indirectly beyond just producing 
the next generation of economically driven executives and skilled workers. 
Instead, it aims to generate socially responsible and environmentally friendly civic 
pioneers, leaders, and innovators with transdisciplinary and interdisciplinary 
competencies to effectively cope with both local and global issues and ensure 
sustainability and survival in the Anthropocene era, where human activities 
have led to much damage to the environment and the whole earth. Note that 
the model recognizes that sustainability and economic growth can go hand in 
hand, contrary to what was suggested by the Limits to Growth report in 1972 
(Meadows et al., 1972). It is worth noting that the report has also received much 
criticism regarding methods and assumptions. We have also discussed how to 
incentivize universities to contribute more to sustainability by rearranging how 
they are ranked and recognized for their efforts. The key constraint remains lack 
of financing to implement such visions. University’s revenue comes from several 
sources, namely research, the funding for which is, at the moment, very limited 
to accomplish the tasks at hand and make a serious effect. Therefore, there should 
be more global and national funding for projects aimed at providing solutions 
to SDGs. It should be highlighted that research grants should be provided to 
a consortium of universities from several countries to eliminate the practice of 
universities working in silos and artificial arrangements in academia.
For Cambodia, as the country embarks on emerging technologies and 
digital transformation, accelerated industrialization, and rapid socioeconomic 
development, the university for sustainability model should be put into practice, 
at least in some universities. A very close collaboration between the government, 
the academia, and the industries, is also required. This is to (1) address business 
challenges, (2) encourage and promote industrial R&D and innovation, (3) 
mitigate the negative impacts of industrial development on the environment, and 
(4) promote responsible and green development for a more sustainable world. 
Such complex and multilayered challenges cannot be undertaken without an 
enabling and supportive environment, including human resources and funding 
for universities to realize its vision, missions, and objectives, especially those of 
the ASEAN Green Deal, which was initiated by Cambodia in 2022 the rotating 
chairman of ASEAN. What comes next would be the execution of the model, 
which requires the operationalization of all the components, especially campus 
operations, and the teaching and learning aspects. It involves the design of a new 
curriculum, restructuring the university’s institutional functions, and changing 
faculty, staff, and students’ behavior and perception toward green campuses. The 
latter conventionally takes quite a lot of time to achieve, for there are always 
people who resist changes in their way of living.

Chapter 11: Sustainable Tourism: How to Make It Work? 
SENG Touch* and ROS Sayumphu
1. Introduction 
People have been debating various aspects of development since the beginning of 
time. It is fascinating to observe how people have utilized their environment and 
surroundings to develop the community. Even though the forms of development 
used in the 21st century have been modernized and a significant emphasis 
has been placed on environmental protection, it may be difficult to conceive 
of human development without environmental dependence. In any case, the 
overexploitation of natural resources has sparked widespread environmental 
degradation concerns. As a result, people worldwide are looking for ways to 
reverse, stop, or lessen environmental degradation, which could eventually lead 
to the extinction of the human race. A multilateralism initiative has gradually 
shaped the concept of sustainable development through the numerous initiatives 
undertaken. Sustainable development applies to several industries, including 
tourism. There has been a shift from “mass tourism” to “sustainable tourism,” 
which has moderated the tourism industry’s operations. Green deals in Europe 
can serve as a model for ASEAN to use in unifying the collaborative approach 
among member states, especially in securing green finance, providing clear 
roadmaps, rules, and regulations. Even coordinating the green innovation 
and STI in the region as a means to sustainable tourism can be supported by 
making a conversion to renewable energy, determining a circular economy, or 
enhancing green infrastructure (Ciot, 2021). In light of this, Cambodia, despite 
being a small nation, views its tourism industry as “Green Gold.” Cambodia has 
adopted various tourism development master plans, strategies, and roadmaps 
which clearly outline the plan to strengthen sustainable tourism through a variety 
of measures. This chapter will begin by examining the concept of sustainable 
tourism, followed by a discussion of sustainable tourism’s challenges and potential 
solutions to those challenges. Later in the chapter, Cambodia’s experience with 
sustainable tourism will be discussed.
2. Definition and Indicator of Sustainable Tourism
Sustainable tourism includes activities, management, and development that 
safeguard natural, economic, and social integrity and conserve cultural resources. 
Thus, implementing sustainable tourism principles requires ensuring viable and 
long-term economic operations, making optimal use of environmental resources, 
and respecting the socio-cultural authenticity of host communities (Niedzióka,

development that can provide socio-economic benefits to all engaged residents, 
privates, and the government through stable employment, income-earning, 
social service provision, and poverty alleviation (Ady et al., 2022; Niedzióka, 
2012; Palacios-Florencio et al., 2021). Sustainable development can also reduce 
environmental damage (Tahiri et al., 2022). In addition, tourism revenue can 
be used to protect and conserve the environment, making it an essential part of 
sustainable development (Baloch et al., 2023; Shien et al., 2022). It also unites the 
government, commercial sector, NGOs, and communities to preserve and monitor 
the ecological environment, natural heritage, and biodiversity (Baloch et al., 2023; 
Niedzióka, 2012). Culturally and socially, sustainable tourism may boost social 
and cultural engagement, especially between visitors and locals. Tourists also help 
residents and the country market their image, reputation, and culture  (Muaini 
et al., 2021). This is a win-win situation for all parties involved. It conserves the 
built and living cultural heritage and traditional values and contributes to a more 
favorable perception of the nation in the long run (Niedzióka, 2012; Palacios-
Florencio et al., 2021). Thus, measuring sustainable tourism requires considering 
the dimensions, indicators and measures in Figure 11.1.

3. Problems of Sustainable Tourism 
Balancing economic, social, cultural, and environmental perspectives is the most 
challenging obstacle to achieving effective long-term management and sustainable 
Sustainable Tourism
121
tourism development strategies (Ene & Baraitaru, 2010; Palacios-Florencio et al., 
2021). The critical success of this effort heavily relies on meaningful participation 
from all stakeholders.  While the government can set rules, regulations, and 
policies, it needs private actors like hotels, transportation services, and locals 
who benefit from tourism to implement and lead in consumer satisfaction and 
environmental protection (Amoako et al., 2022). If a stakeholder only focuses 
on short-term gains or financial gain while ignoring the environment and social 
impacts, then the environment will deteriorate. The sustainable tourism goals, 
particularly the intended long-term sustainability of incomes, the environment, 
and social-cultural norms for future generations, will not be met (Janusz & 
Bajdor, 2013; Khan et al., 2021). In Poland, hotels will only switch to clean 
energy or water-saving equipment if they believe it will lower operating costs 
(Niedzióka, 2012). In order to ensure the efficacy and productivity required to 
provide long-term benefits to future generations, the complexities of sustainable 
tourism must be taken seriously and addressed collaboratively by a broad range 
of relevant stakeholders and actors.
In addition, as soon as the location for sustainable tourism becomes widely 
known, hordes of tourists will begin to visit, which may lead to new issues such as 
water pollution, air pollution, and noise pollution (Roblek et al., 2021). Without 
proper management, this will undermine sustainable tourism and aggravate 
the situation. Local traditions have steadily eroded or even disappeared since 
residents emphasize financial gain and fit their work to international visitors’ 
interests (Poort et al., 2021). 
The revenue generated by tourism activities has been accumulated by foreign 
firms and individuals but not redistributed to locals, which also defeats the 
purpose of sustainable tourism (Garrigós-Simón et al., 2015). This will worsen 
the economic, social, and environmental situation, which may result in a decline 
in the social well-being of the locals and may also contribute to the destruction 
of the environment or natural resources for financial gain (Andries et al., 2021).
4. Science, Technology and Innovation in Sustainable Tourism
Science, technology, and innovation (STI) play a crucial role in bridging the gap 
between the economic, social-cultural, and environmental spheres, as well as in 
enhancing the overall efficacy and effectiveness of the policy (Sharif et al., 2023). 
Various actors, including the state, the private sector, and locals, can utilize the 
currently available technological or digital resources to enhance monitoring, 
generate income, and promote products or destinations (Anderson et al., 
2021). The government may utilize digital formats or scientific technologies to 
enhance a destination’s environmental health, electronically monitor and take 
action against any environmental intrusion, and digitally facilitate international 
tourists (Anderson et al., 2021; Sulistyo et al., 2022). Private hospitality and food 
companies can use technology to save money and the environment. They may 
Green Ideals
122
limit clean water use, generate electricity with solar panels, or stay ahead with 
online marketing (Anderson et al., 2021). 
Over the last decades, it has been remarkably observed that tourism 
development has significantly benefited from the development of innovative 
technologies added to the market (Gössling, 2021). These technologies have 
significantly improved the efficiency and effectiveness of business operations by 
sharing information between different departments in the hotel industry (Koo 
et al., 2015). In fact, the transformation of technology in tourism can be seen in 
different periods from the 1970s to the present, and the tourism industry has been 
transformed accordingly (Table 11.1).

5. Cambodia’s Sustainable Tourism and Policy Supporting
Cambodia’s tourist attractions are impressive despite their size. Tourism drives 
economic development. International visitors climbed gradually from 4.2 million 
in 2013 to 6.6 million in 2019. By 2022, approximately 2.2 million international 
tourists visited this small nation due to Covid-19 (Ministry of Tourism, 2023). The 
Royal Government of Cambodia (RGC) has put efforts into promoting sustainable 
tourism by implementing policies and legal instruments, including Cambodia’s 
2010 National Tourism Policy, Tourism Development Strategic Plan 2012-2020, 
Roadmap for Recovery of Cambodia Tourism During and Post Covid-19 (2021-
2025), Tourism Development Master Plan Siem Reap 2021-2035, and Tourism 
Development Master Plan Siem Reap 2021-2035. These legal instruments 
mainly emphasize the necessity for sustainable tourism and STI action plans to 
attract tourists, smart tourism, smart destinations, and digitalizing tourist firms 
(Ministry of Tourism, 2021). Recently, RGC has just launched the TourismTech 
Roadmap, one of the primary legislative tools that propel Cambodia as the 
Sustainable Tourism
123
top tourist destination in the region by integrating modern technologies with 
sustainability and inclusion and offering strategic advice to diversify and add 
value (Ministry of Industy, Science, Technology & Innovation, 2023). It improves 
goods and services and generates new economic and social possibilities. These 
legal instruments seek to make Cambodia’s tourism industry a “quality, safe, 
and sustainable tourist destination.” New technologies and creative techniques 
will help Cambodia’s tourist sector adapt to the fourth industrial revolution 
(Ministry of Tourism, 2021). Furthermore, services and the digital economy are 
scientific and technical goals; thus, tourism and technology will be long-term 
priorities. Cambodia also developed STI and established sustainable tourism 
efforts, including “Clean City, Clean Resort, Good Service and Good Hospitality 
(Ministry of Tourism, 2021, p. 19).” Despite this optimism, additional resources 
should be allocated to ensure that public tourism infrastructure is both adequate 
and fully functional and that collaboration between private and public entities is 
strengthened (Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific, 2021). 
6. Conclusion and Recommendations 
It is essential to emphasize that sustainable tourism cannot be approached 
uniformly on any level. This strategy will not yield the desired outcomes. If it is 
not effectively resolved, the concept will continue to be fluid and will amass an 
increasing number of potential dangers. Various public and private entities and 
individuals must collaborate to achieve sustainable development. Everyone needs 
to be on the same page and make progress toward the shared long-term objectives 
of generating income, protecting and conserving the environment, and preserving 
social and cultural well-being. Proper education, effective management, and the 
judicious application of science and technology will undoubtedly contribute to 
achieving an effective and efficient sustainable tourism industry and reducing 
undesirable potential risks.
Policies and legal instruments play an integral role in supporting technology 
use in Cambodia’s tourism industry. They should therefore provide clarity and 
transparency about the rules and regulations surrounding the use of technology 
in the tourism industry, encourage innovation and competition among tourism 
operators, enhance technology integration in tourism services to remove any 
hurdles or barriers when using technology, motivate tourism operators to adopt 
certain standards that can enhance the quality of their services, provide assurance 
to potential investors and invest in related tourism businesses in Cambodia. In 
addition, Cambodian tourism operators require technology adaptation and 
adoption in response to the future global tourism trends and tourism technology 
transformation since these technologies will play a crucial role in sustainable 
tourism in Cambodia.

1. Introduction
In the past decades, the planning, design, and construction communities have 
been embroiled in a vigorous discussion of sustainability and green buildings. 
The link between green building and climate change is, in a way, inseparable. 
Many environmental crises greatly influence us to alter the design and practice of 
the built environment. Pollutions caused by human activities from, for instance, 
the burning of fossil fuels or the rise of global warming, show that we are now in 
emergency mode and need to begin to consider reducing our use of energy.
Sustainable architecture is about the assurance of components that will 
strive, structures with prolonged existence and renewable consumptions of both 
electricity and water. A green built environment is more than just about sustaining 
the use of energy. In the early 2000s, it was about doing what was right. From the 
mid-2010s, considerations were given to client demand, market demand, lower 
operation costs, and branding/public relations 2010s (Charles, 2016, p. 2). These 
trends are what mark the rapid movement of green buildings, but how green are 
they really? To explain what a green built environment is and the strategy to 
tackle the issue, I will raise some key features that need to be considered.
Recent studies from the U.S. Energy Information Administration showed 
that the process of constructing buildings is responsible for almost half of total 
energy usage and carbon emissions (Ching & Shapiro, 2014). This is in relation 
to the production of materials and the processes of construction, cooling, and 
lighting of buildings. Thus, architects and designers need to design buildings that 
incorporate effective utilities, natural lighting, as well as air ventilation.
Before diving into a more thorough explanation, we should take a step back 
and ask what a green building is. Do architects and designers need to follow a 
set of rules and regulations to meet the requirements of a sustainable building 
standard? Or does the building need to have zero or close to zero energy 
consumption to be considered a green building? The factors that urge people 
to choose green buildings over a non-green buildings include improving their 
quality of life. At the same time, some consider reducing expenses to keep up 
with building utilities. In contrast, some choose to conserve the importance of 
other historic buildings and to live somewhere that is reasonably priced.
Despite categorizing all the stated goals, there have always been ongoing 
discussions (Rinkesh, 2020) about the purposes and main priorities of green 
building. In general, green building projects support either one or more of the

3. Problems of Sustainable Tourism 
Balancing economic, social, cultural, and environmental perspectives is the most 
challenging obstacle to achieving effective long-term management and sustainable 
Sustainable Tourism
121
tourism development strategies (Ene & Baraitaru, 2010; Palacios-Florencio et al., 
2021). The critical success of this effort heavily relies on meaningful participation 
from all stakeholders.  While the government can set rules, regulations, and 
policies, it needs private actors like hotels, transportation services, and locals 
who benefit from tourism to implement and lead in consumer satisfaction and 
environmental protection (Amoako et al., 2022). If a stakeholder only focuses 
on short-term gains or financial gain while ignoring the environment and social 
impacts, then the environment will deteriorate. The sustainable tourism goals, 
particularly the intended long-term sustainability of incomes, the environment, 
and social-cultural norms for future generations, will not be met (Janusz & 
Bajdor, 2013; Khan et al., 2021). In Poland, hotels will only switch to clean 
energy or water-saving equipment if they believe it will lower operating costs 
(Niedzióka, 2012). In order to ensure the efficacy and productivity required to 
provide long-term benefits to future generations, the complexities of sustainable 
tourism must be taken seriously and addressed collaboratively by a broad range 
of relevant stakeholders and actors.
In addition, as soon as the location for sustainable tourism becomes widely 
known, hordes of tourists will begin to visit, which may lead to new issues such as 
water pollution, air pollution, and noise pollution (Roblek et al., 2021). Without 
proper management, this will undermine sustainable tourism and aggravate 
the situation. Local traditions have steadily eroded or even disappeared since 
residents emphasize financial gain and fit their work to international visitors’ 
interests (Poort et al., 2021). 
The revenue generated by tourism activities has been accumulated by foreign 
firms and individuals but not redistributed to locals, which also defeats the 
purpose of sustainable tourism (Garrigós-Simón et al., 2015). This will worsen 
the economic, social, and environmental situation, which may result in a decline 
in the social well-being of the locals and may also contribute to the destruction 
of the environment or natural resources for financial gain (Andries et al., 2021).
4. Science, Technology and Innovation in Sustainable Tourism
Science, technology, and innovation (STI) play a crucial role in bridging the gap 
between the economic, social-cultural, and environmental spheres, as well as in 
enhancing the overall efficacy and effectiveness of the policy (Sharif et al., 2023). 
Various actors, including the state, the private sector, and locals, can utilize the 
currently available technological or digital resources to enhance monitoring, 
generate income, and promote products or destinations (Anderson et al., 
2021). The government may utilize digital formats or scientific technologies to 
enhance a destination’s environmental health, electronically monitor and take 
action against any environmental intrusion, and digitally facilitate international 
tourists (Anderson et al., 2021; Sulistyo et al., 2022). Private hospitality and food 
companies can use technology to save money and the environment. They may

122
limit clean water use, generate electricity with solar panels, or stay ahead with 
online marketing (Anderson et al., 2021). 
Over the last decades, it has been remarkably observed that tourism 
development has significantly benefited from the development of innovative 
technologies added to the market (Gössling, 2021). These technologies have 
significantly improved the efficiency and effectiveness of business operations by 
sharing information between different departments in the hotel industry (Koo 
et al., 2015). In fact, the transformation of technology in tourism can be seen in 
different periods from the 1970s to the present, and the tourism industry has been 
transformed accordingly (Table 11.1).

5. Cambodia’s Sustainable Tourism and Policy Supporting
Cambodia’s tourist attractions are impressive despite their size. Tourism drives 
economic development. International visitors climbed gradually from 4.2 million 
in 2013 to 6.6 million in 2019. By 2022, approximately 2.2 million international 
tourists visited this small nation due to Covid-19 (Ministry of Tourism, 2023). The 
Royal Government of Cambodia (RGC) has put efforts into promoting sustainable 
tourism by implementing policies and legal instruments, including Cambodia’s 
2010 National Tourism Policy, Tourism Development Strategic Plan 2012-2020, 
Roadmap for Recovery of Cambodia Tourism During and Post Covid-19 (2021-
2025), Tourism Development Master Plan Siem Reap 2021-2035, and Tourism 
Development Master Plan Siem Reap 2021-2035. These legal instruments 
mainly emphasize the necessity for sustainable tourism and STI action plans to 
attract tourists, smart tourism, smart destinations, and digitalizing tourist firms 
(Ministry of Tourism, 2021). Recently, RGC has just launched the TourismTech 
Roadmap, one of the primary legislative tools that propel Cambodia as the 
Sustainable Tourism
123
top tourist destination in the region by integrating modern technologies with 
sustainability and inclusion and offering strategic advice to diversify and add 
value (Ministry of Industy, Science, Technology & Innovation, 2023). It improves 
goods and services and generates new economic and social possibilities. These 
legal instruments seek to make Cambodia’s tourism industry a “quality, safe, 
and sustainable tourist destination.” New technologies and creative techniques 
will help Cambodia’s tourist sector adapt to the fourth industrial revolution 
(Ministry of Tourism, 2021). Furthermore, services and the digital economy are 
scientific and technical goals; thus, tourism and technology will be long-term 
priorities. Cambodia also developed STI and established sustainable tourism 
efforts, including “Clean City, Clean Resort, Good Service and Good Hospitality 
(Ministry of Tourism, 2021, p. 19).” Despite this optimism, additional resources 
should be allocated to ensure that public tourism infrastructure is both adequate 
and fully functional and that collaboration between private and public entities is 
strengthened (Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific, 2021). 
6. Conclusion and Recommendations 
It is essential to emphasize that sustainable tourism cannot be approached 
uniformly on any level. This strategy will not yield the desired outcomes. If it is 
not effectively resolved, the concept will continue to be fluid and will amass an 
increasing number of potential dangers. Various public and private entities and 
individuals must collaborate to achieve sustainable development. Everyone needs 
to be on the same page and make progress toward the shared long-term objectives 
of generating income, protecting and conserving the environment, and preserving 
social and cultural well-being. Proper education, effective management, and the 
judicious application of science and technology will undoubtedly contribute to 
achieving an effective and efficient sustainable tourism industry and reducing 
undesirable potential risks.
Policies and legal instruments play an integral role in supporting technology 
use in Cambodia’s tourism industry. They should therefore provide clarity and 
transparency about the rules and regulations surrounding the use of technology 
in the tourism industry, encourage innovation and competition among tourism 
operators, enhance technology integration in tourism services to remove any 
hurdles or barriers when using technology, motivate tourism operators to adopt 
certain standards that can enhance the quality of their services, provide assurance 
to potential investors and invest in related tourism businesses in Cambodia. In 
addition, Cambodian tourism operators require technology adaptation and 
adoption in response to the future global tourism trends and tourism technology 
transformation since these technologies will play a crucial role in sustainable 
tourism in Cambodia.

goals sensibly. However, in most cases, there will always be parts that contradict 
each other and, in the end, show what is significant to the quality of life that 
people seek.
2. Primary Essence
The first and foremost thing to consider when we start designing sustainable 
buildings is their loads, which refers to how buildings shelter their dwellers from 
various kinds of factors, both externally and internally. Extreme temperatures 
are the main reasons for human heat and cool buildings. Other external factors 
include wind, rain, and the sun’s ultraviolet effects. Surrounding factors such 
as animals, insects, and pollution from human activities are also considered 
loads (International Energy Agency and United Nations Environment Program, 
2019). The basic practice is to shield and embed our buildings with components 
from those loads. In their book, Ching & Shapiro (2014) mentioned that the most 
commonly used method to cut down on the effects of extreme temperatures is the 
installation of thermal insulation between wall cavities or right under the roofs. 
Screenings such as windows, either of glass or mesh net, are selective types that 
designers use to purposely let in chosen elements and leave out others. 
This practice is only fundamental to what green building means. Kriss (2014) 
noted that “green building is a holistic concept that starts with the understanding 
that the built environment can have profound effects, both positive and negative, 
on the natural environment, as well as the people who inhabit buildings every 
day”. The design of the components mentioned earlier completes most of the 
goals to improve human health and comfort. However, if not tackled properly, it 
would lead to further negative effects on the environment. For instance, all those 
thermal insulations need to be manufactured, using raw materials, energy, and 
carbon emissions and produce waste, which in the end only ends up making the 
project less green than it should be. Thus, hereinafter, this chapter will focus on 
the design process itself, material design, other utilities, and waste management 
systems in architectural green built environment.
3. Integrated Design
Alternatively, incorporated design is a new approach to building sustainably 
from the foremost stage to finishing the construction. In order to do this, many 
involved participants need to work collaboratively with each other to confirm 
that every component contributes to green design. In the later stages, architects, 
owners, and other consultants will need to address the true aims and concept of 
the project. The team needs to clarify as much detail as possible on some of the 
components of the building, such as the number of residents and how much of 
the space is needed to have wall insulation or other temperature control methods. 
With early discussions and confirmations on these steps, the expenses on many 
other utilities and materials can be significantly reduced.
Green Built Environment 
129
Contrary to the earlier obstacles, if an assessment can be made prior to these 
assumptions on the operation costs of a sustainable building during its long uses, 
we can confirm that the utility expense of a sustainable building is generally less 
than that of a normal building. For example, Asim et al. (2022) noted that a 
carefully calculated thermal temperature of a room can significantly reduce the 
cost of an air-conditioner. Lowering the ceiling of a building may reduce the cost 
of materials for the construction, and with more natural lighting, it would also 
help reduce the cost of energy needed during the day.
4. How Can We Build a More Efficient Structure?
The primary goal of starting a project is to choose a site location. Leadership in 
Energy and Environmental Design (2020) indicates in their rating system that 
it is vital to consider the impact and effect when constructing buildings on the 
perimeter of sensitive sites, such as conservative historic sites or other fragile 
forests and greenery. Another aspect is to think about the linkage between the 
site and its nearby community to reduce the use of energy for transportation.

a more efficient structure? Besides the site selection and its community, we 
should redirect our focal point to the design of the building shape. Reducing and
