Building materials have an adverse effect on the environment because of their 
energy consumption and emissions, the depletion of limited resources, and the 
unintentional build-up of waste in landfills. An article, Nature Communications, 
by Zhong et al. (2021), shows that the mining and harvesting of raw materials, 
the processing and production of finished goods, the transportation of resources, 
the usage of hazardous compounds, and the production of construction debris 
Green Ideals
130
are the activities responsible for these effects. We may significantly lessen these 
effects by choosing the quality and quantity of building materials wisely when 
designing the building. From a quantitative perspective, using less material is also 
a greener option. Typically, our production processes begin with energy-intensive 
mining, crushing, smelting, refining, and shaping. Next, additional stages of 
treatments, shielding coatings, and adhesives are frequently added. Unfavorably, 
this intense process is different from the manufacturing that occurs in nature. It 
seems like a worthwhile objective to strive to mimic nature’s efficiency in our 
manufacturing processes given our current problems with resource depletion, a 
growing population, and climate change.

Architecture by Pawlyn (2016), studies show that where these issues may be more 
clearly distinguished, and where conventional production methods and drawing 
packages both support this distinction, the idea that structure and materials are 
inseparable in nature requires a fundamentally new way of thinking. Structure 
and materials are grouped together in nature via hierarchy. Visualizing various 
bridge designs could be a useful method to start understanding hierarchy. Two 
sturdy steel beams placed on piers at either end might be used to crossing a minor 
distance. This would be a non-hierarchical monolithic approach. A pair of steel 
trusses would be a more effective approach to cross the distance. That denotes a 
single hierarchy level. Imagine going a step further and turning each compression 
element into a little box truss and each tension member into a cable made of 
stranded steel. That would indicate a hierarchy with two tiers. The structure 
becomes more effective in terms of the quantity of material needed to accomplish 
a particular goal as the hierarchy levels rise.

building itself but rather with its placement and infrastructure, offers a significant 
potential for material savings. One can utilize the infrastructural elements 
that are already in place by placing structures in already established locations. 
Since they are shared, infrastructure like roads and municipal water systems is 
essentially reused, avoiding the potential material consumption of building new 
infrastructure. Opportunities for material reduction may be found when careful 
structural design is done rather than employing rules of thumb or conventional 
wisdom. For instance, as mentioned in the book, Building Structures Illustrated 
(Ching et al., 2013), depending on the load distribution, the amount of beams 
and columns needed can be reduced.

down on material consumption. An example of this method, which is also 
known as “structure as finish” (Canadian Wood Council, n.d.) enables structural 
components to fulfill both the functions of structure and finish. If the exposed 
structure has a low lighting reflectance, trade-offs with the demand for additional 
illumination should be carefully considered. Another strategy for conserving

resources is to leave visible parts like ducting or plumbing. Gypsum board and 
related furring for chases, soffits, and plenums, as well as finishes, are used less 
frequently as a result.

the same transition from a global economy based on fossil fuels to one based on 
solar energy instead of nuclear energy? A statistic from the International Energy 
Agency (2010), reports that every year we receive energy from the sun that is 
around 10,000 times greater than what we now consume. This abundant source 
of energy has kept life on earth going for billions of years and has enough energy 
to last an eternity (MacKay, 2009). Future energy sources should be available 
other than nuclear-powered plants. For instance, we could meet all of our energy 
requirements by erecting concentrated solar power plants across around 5 percent 
of the world’s deserts.

concentrated solar power and direct solar energy, particularly photovoltaics, 
wind, waves, biomass, and infrared radiation from the sun. Tidal and geothermal

substantial improvements in efficiency are necessary, and advancements in 
the built environment provide some of the largest prospects. Even if there are 
still many obstacles to overcome, the solar economy is now conceivable on a 
practical level, and renewable energy technologies are developing and becoming 
significantly more affordable. As a result, tackling our energy concerns might 
launch the most inventive period in human history if done correctly.

more and more divisive on both an environmental and political level. Reducing 
water use, collecting rainfall, and reusing water are three important techniques 
that can assist us in managing our water resources effectively. The most efficient 
way to reduce water usage is to first look at water loads. This is possible because 
of newly developed fixtures and appliances that consume less water while yet 
producing the same results.
Green Ideals
132

with water suffer from a technical laziness that stems from the same belief in an 
endless supply that defined our view of resources at the beginning of the Industrial

by Bergstrom (2020), she explained the management and key issues of waste in

creating closed-loop systems that are highly desirable. Designers tend to overlook 
it, but projects that investigate it show incredible innovation. It uses the term 
“waste,” which may mean both useless material and anything that indicates the 
possibility of something. We should try to reuse materials wherever feasible in 
order to reduce the embodied energy needed to gather and process new materials 
as well as the depletion of raw material sources. It is recommended to use 
recycled-content materials. During production, pre-consumer recycled materials 
are removed from the waste stream. Materials made from post-consumer 
recycled products are derived from garbage produced by end consumers. The 
most popular building material with recycled aggregate is crushed concrete that 
has had the reinforcing and other embedded elements removed (United States 
Green Building Council, 2009).

cycle of all nutrients, so taking a cool, strategic look at this process might have a 
big impact on how we handle “waste” water. Water may now be separated into 
grey and black water from human usage. Grey water is that which accumulates 
from sinks and showers and may be used to maintain the landscaping and 
gardens. Black water, commonly referred to as sewage water, may be processed 
and utilized for agricultural and landscape upkeep.
Green Built Environment 
133

for achieving harmony inside, among, and with the rest of the world is expressed

elements introduced by green design, such as solar panels, must be elegantly 
incorporated into structures. These parts are a thing of beauty for many of us, 
but not everyone may feel the same way. As designers, it is our responsibility 
to make sure that these elements are combined in a way that is both visually 
pleasing and functional.

numerous negative effects of climate change and other environmental challenges.

greenhouse gas emissions as well as a significant potential to minimize these 
emissions. Those in the design and construction industry have to decide whether 
to take responsibility for the climate change effects of buildings or to drive the 
change required to lessen those effects.

Chapter 13: A Farm-To-Fork Strategy: An Approach Towards 
Sustainable Food System 
SRUN Marnick*, SOTH Sereyboth, and CHHEM Kieth Rethy 
1. Introduction 
The interrelationship between climate change and food systems is a complicated 
issue that negatively affects the world. On the one hand, rising temperatures, 
droughts, and heat waves caused a decline in crop yields and livestock, and 
decreased fisheries and agroforestry, which is susceptible to our food systems 
(Food and Agriculture Organization of the United States et al., 2017). However, 
food systems have also contributed to climate change. Anthropogenic activities in 
each stage of the food supply chain, commencing with production, manufacturing, 
distribution, consumption, and disposal, have caused an increase in greenhouse 
gas emissions (GHGs).
Food systems contribute significantly to global GHGs, with industrialized 
countries accounting for 27 percent and developing countries for 73 percent of 
these emissions (Crippa et al., 2021). The main greenhouse gas emissions in the 
agricultural sector are methane, nitrous oxide, and carbon dioxide. Methane is 
generated by activities such as ruminant digestion, rice farming, and managing 
manure. Nitrous oxide is released from natural processes in agriculture and 
manure management. Carbon dioxide emissions result from food processing 
and transportation, which rely on the use of fossil fuels (Sjörs et al., 2016). The 
environmental and health impacts of these emissions highlight the importance 
of incorporating food policies to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals 
(SDGs).
In order to establish a balanced food system, the Farm-to-Fork (F2F) strategy 
should be considered. The Farm-to-Fork strategy is a significant element in the 
EU Green Deal, which examines the issues of sustainable food systems from 
production to consumption. It acknowledges the strong connections among 
healthy individuals, societies, and a healthy planet (Mowlds, 2020). The Farm-
to-Fork Strategy is specially designed to meet six main goals: 1). sustainable 
production; 2). food security; 3). sustainable food processing; 4). promoting 
sustainable consumption; 5). minimizing food waste and loss and 6). reducing 
food fraud along the supply chain. To achieve these goals, the food supply chain 
from production to processing and distribution to consumption must be taken 
into account. Figure 13.1 illustrates the farm-to-fork strategy in more detail.

Chapter 13: A Farm-To-Fork Strategy: An Approach Towards 
Sustainable Food System 
SRUN Marnick*, SOTH Sereyboth, and CHHEM Kieth Rethy 
1. Introduction 
The interrelationship between climate change and food systems is a complicated 
issue that negatively affects the world. On the one hand, rising temperatures, 
droughts, and heat waves caused a decline in crop yields and livestock, and 
decreased fisheries and agroforestry, which is susceptible to our food systems 
(Food and Agriculture Organization of the United States et al., 2017). However, 
food systems have also contributed to climate change. Anthropogenic activities in 
each stage of the food supply chain, commencing with production, manufacturing, 
distribution, consumption, and disposal, have caused an increase in greenhouse 
gas emissions (GHGs).
Food systems contribute significantly to global GHGs, with industrialized 
countries accounting for 27 percent and developing countries for 73 percent of 
these emissions (Crippa et al., 2021). The main greenhouse gas emissions in the 
agricultural sector are methane, nitrous oxide, and carbon dioxide. Methane is 
generated by activities such as ruminant digestion, rice farming, and managing 
manure. Nitrous oxide is released from natural processes in agriculture and 
manure management. Carbon dioxide emissions result from food processing 
and transportation, which rely on the use of fossil fuels (Sjörs et al., 2016). The 
environmental and health impacts of these emissions highlight the importance 
of incorporating food policies to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals 
(SDGs).
In order to establish a balanced food system, the Farm-to-Fork (F2F) strategy 
should be considered. The Farm-to-Fork strategy is a significant element in the 
EU Green Deal, which examines the issues of sustainable food systems from 
production to consumption. It acknowledges the strong connections among 
healthy individuals, societies, and a healthy planet (Mowlds, 2020). The Farm-
to-Fork Strategy is specially designed to meet six main goals: 1). sustainable 
production; 2). food security; 3). sustainable food processing; 4). promoting 
sustainable consumption; 5). minimizing food waste and loss and 6). reducing 
food fraud along the supply chain. To achieve these goals, the food supply chain 
from production to processing and distribution to consumption must be taken 
into account. Figure 13.1 illustrates the farm-to-fork strategy in more detail.

2. Adopting the Farm-to-Fork Strategy in the Cambodian Context 
Cambodia is a country that is highly vulnerable to climate change in Southeast 
Asia. With 79 percent of its population residing in rural areas and depending on 
agriculture for both livelihood and food security, climate change has a significant 
effect on the country. The country undergoes annual droughts and floods, and it 
faced severe droughts that ruined approximately 41,000 hectares of rice fields in 
2015. Similarly, floods in 2011 caused damage to about 171,000 hectares of rice 
fields (Mishra et al., 2018). These events are predicted to increase in frequency 
and intensity in the coming years. If this persists, Cambodia’s agricultural 
productivity, the foundation of its food security, will be impacted, eventually 
leading to a disruption in the country’s entire food system. Therefore, building a 
resilient food system that can adapt to climate change is vital for a country like 
Cambodia. 
The Farm-to-Fork Strategy is in alignment with ASEAN’s and Cambodia’s 
sustainable development goals and food security objectives. It serves as a 
significant mechanism for realizing Cambodia’s vision of attaining high-middle 
income status by 2030 and becoming a high-income country by 2050, while also 
A Farm-To-Fork Strategy
137
contributing to the achievement of its SDGs. As previously mentioned, the farm-
to-fork process encompasses all aspects of food preparation, from production 
to consumption. The following section will provide a brief overview of the six 
components: 1) Sustainable agriculture; 2) Ensuring food security for all; 3) 
Sustainable food processing; 4) Sustainable consumption; 5) Reducing food 
waste; and 6) Diminishing food fraud along the supply chain.
3. Building a Sustainable Agricultural Production
The majority of agricultural practices still rely on rainfall, and most farmers 
cultivate only a single crop annually. Traditional techniques and seeds are still 
widely employed, which makes Cambodia’s rice yields low and impedes the 
improvement of local livelihoods (Ros et al., 2011). Furthermore, the supply 
of other agricultural products, particularly fresh produce, remains limited and 
seasonal, with approximately 70 percent being imported (United States Agency 
for International Development, 2015; Sim et al., 2021). As such, it is essential for 
all relevant stakeholders, particularly the public sector, to consider modernizing 
the agricultural sector through agricultural technology (Agri-Tech) and utilizing 
bio-products.
Agri-Tech is transforming the way farmers operate around the world, including 
in Cambodia. Automated systems and sensors can help farmers monitor crop 
yields, optimize production output, and manage soil health with minimal manual 
labor and human error. For instance, with Agri-Tech, tasks like controlling 
irrigation levels and managing soil health can be accomplished with the click of a 
button, minimizing manual labor and human error as well as reducing labor costs 
(Ahmad & Sharma, 2023). Agri-Tech also has applications for tracking livestock 
health and behavior, enabling farmers to make informed decisions about animal 
welfare. By reducing farmers’ workloads and promoting sustainable practices, 
Agri-Tech has the potential to revolutionize the agricultural industry.
Bioproducts such as biopesticides, biofertilizers, and biostimulants are 
important for sustainable agricultural production. These products are derived from 
plants, animals, and microbial sources and are safer and more environmentally 
friendly than traditional fertilizers that contain potentially toxic chemicals 
(Upadhyay et al., 2020). Bio-products can help maximize crop yields and 
replenish soil health while providing essential nutrients to crops. Incorporating 
Agri-Tech and bio-products into farming practices can help farmers produce 
healthier and better-yielding crops with less risk of contamination or harm to the 
environment, leading to more sustainable practices in the agricultural industry 
(Spanner & Napolitano, 2015).
Incorporating Agri-Tech and bioproducts into farming practices has the 
potential to transform the agricultural industry, in line with the Agriculture 
4.0 roadmap and the agricultural sector’s plan for 2030 (Ministry of Industry, 
Green Ideals
138
Science, Technology & Innovation, 2022), aimed at promoting a sustainable and 
efficient agricultural industry.
4. Ensuring Food Security 
Food security is achieved when all individuals have consistent access to enough 
safe and nutritious food that meets their dietary requirements and preferences, 
allowing them to maintain good health and an active lifestyle. However, 
Cambodia, with its diverse food systems and rich culinary history, faces several 
challenges in achieving food security.
One of the major obstacles is the country’s vulnerability to climate change and 
natural disasters, which frequently disrupt agricultural production and threaten 
food availability. Rice, as the staple food in Cambodia, plays a vital role in 
providing calories and protein to the population. However, droughts and climate 
anomalies pose significant risks to rice farmers, leading to production losses 
and impacting overall food production. Cambodia also grapples with persistent 
inequalities, despite progress in poverty reduction. A significant portion of the 
population remains unable to afford a healthy diet, exacerbating food insecurity. 
Unfortunately, the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic has further heightened these 
challenges. The global food supply chain disruptions have impacted both food 
availability and affordability, affecting the overall food security situation in 
Cambodia. 
In this context, it becomes even more crucial to prioritize the promotion 
of agriculture and the adoption of healthy dietary practices. By strengthening 
Cambodia’s food systems, the country can enhance its resilience to external shocks 
and ensure food security during and after the pandemic. This entails investing 
in climate-resilient agricultural practices, providing support to rice farmers, and 
addressing inequalities in access to nutritious food. Moreover, efforts should be 
made to improve the efficiency and stability of the food supply chain, ensuring 
that safe and nutritious food reaches all segments of the population.
5. Encouraging Sustainable Food Processing
Food processing, an integral part of the farm-to-fork process, includes a range 
of activities that typically use abundant materials and energy. The majority 
of food processors in Cambodia uses traditional processing methods that rely 
on non-renewable energy, contributing significantly to carbon emissions and 
exacerbating the negative environment. To address this challenge and transition 
towards a more sustainable food system, the adoption of the Food Processing 4.0 
concept is increasingly being seen as a viable solution.
The Food Processing 4.0 concept emphasizes the application of Industry 4.0 
technologies to process food in this digital age, with the aim of enhancing food 
quality and safety, decreasing food processing expenses and time, conserving 
A Farm-To-Fork Strategy
139
energy and resources, as well as reducing food loss and waste (Hassoun et al., 
2023). This includes innovative technologies such as robotics, smart sensors, 
artificial intelligence, and the Internet of Things (IoT) that help the food industry 
optimize its processes, improve efficiency and reduce its environmental footprint. 
One such approach is the use of smart sensors and IoT devices throughout their 
production line to monitor and analyze data in real-time, such as temperature, 
pressure, and pH levels. With this information, they are able to fine-tune their 
production processes to reduce energy usage, minimize waste, and improve the 
quality of their products. Integrating the Time-Temperature Indicator (TTI) in 
food packaging, for instance, can monitor the temperature and time that a product 
has been exposed to. This TTI utilizes color changes that are not reversible, which 
allows consumers to quickly check if the product is safe and prevent unnecessary 
food waste due to premature discarding. Additionally, they can promote optimal 
storage and transportation conditions, which can reduce the likelihood of food 
spoilage and waste (Ahmed et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2015). 
Integrating Food Processing 4.0 into Cambodia’s food industry can support 
the government’s Industrial Development Plan (IDP) and the National Strategy 
for Food Security and Nutrition (NSFSN). It promotes industrial growth, 
diversification, and sustainability while facilitating access to technology, credit, 
and markets for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).  
6. Promoting Sustainable Consumption
Our current diet and eating patterns contribute significantly to our carbon 
footprint, making the consumption stage the most impactful in the food 
system. Unfortunately, unsustainable food choices often involve unhealthy 
diets characterized by high consumption of processed, calorie-dense foods and 
animal products, further exacerbating the carbon footprint. By transitioning to a 
sustainable and healthier diet, we can mitigate these impacts and pave the way 
for a more sustainable future, benefiting both our well-being and the planet.
Information dissemination is vital to promote sustainable food consumption. 
Educating consumers about the environmental impacts, local and seasonal food 
options, and benefits of plant-based diets empowers them to make informed 
decisions (Ammann et al., 2023). This knowledge enables individuals to 
understand the broader consequences of their food choices and encourages 
engagement in sustainable practices. Additionally, the farm-to-table movement 
should be widely promoted as part of sustainable food consumption efforts. 
It prioritizes locally sourced and seasonal ingredients and reduces the carbon 
footprint associated with transportation. Restaurants in this movement highlight 
flavors of locally sourced produce, meats, and dairy, supporting nearby farms 
and minimizing GHGs. It encourages organic and sustainable practices, such as 
avoiding synthetic pesticides and fertilizers, minimizing water usage, promoting 
Green Ideals
140
biodiversity, contributing to soil health, water conservation, and ecosystem 
preservation.
A market-based approach promotes sustainable food consumption 
through certifications and labels. Organic and fair trade certifications ensure 
environmental practices and fair labor. Carbon footprint and water usage labels 
aid consumers in selecting low-impact products. These market signals incentivize 
producers to access niche markets. Collaboration between producers, retailers, 
and policymakers is crucial. Retailers promote sustainability through placement 
and partnerships, while policymakers support adoption through regulations and 
incentives.
In conclusion, market-based approaches, through certifications and labeling 
schemes, empower consumers to make sustainable food choices. Collaboration 
between producers, retailers, and policymakers is crucial to creating a supportive 
market environment. By combining information dissemination and market-based 
strategies, we can build a sustainable food system that benefits human health and 
the environment in the Anthropocene era.
6.1. Minimizing Food Waste and Loss
Food waste is a significant contributor to global GHGs, accounting for 8-10 
percent of the total amount (United Nations Environment Programme, 2021). 
In Phnom Penh, research has shown that households, shops, and markets are 
responsible for 70 percent of food waste, with fruits, vegetables, sugarcane, 
coconut shells, and maize comprising 76 percent of this waste (Chinda & Thay, 
2020; Sang-Arun et al., 2011). These findings underscore the importance of 
addressing food waste in Cambodia and highlight the need for stakeholders, 
particularly consumers, to play an active role in reducing waste.
To tackle this issue, Cambodia needs to develop regulations and enhance 
public understanding. Experts recommend implementing incentives for recycling 
in restaurants and strengthening food bank capabilities. Following Europe’s 
example, extending product shelf life can also be beneficial. Raising awareness 
is vital to changing consumer behavior and reducing emissions from waste 
disposal. The government should take part in implementing regulations and 
establishing food banks, while youth groups can lead awareness campaigns. 
Ensuring coordination is crucial for the efficient distribution of food from retail 
shops to those in need.
Moreover, adopting a circular economy model would greatly benefit 
Cambodia’s waste management system. This approach focuses on minimizing 
waste and maximizing resource value through practices like reuse, recycling, and 
recovery. Implementing circular practices such as composting organic waste or 
repurposing food scraps for animal feed or energy generation can move Cambodia 
closer to a zero-waste system.

6.2 Reducing Food Fraud Along the Supply Chain
Food fraud poses a significant obstacle to achieving a sustainable food system, 
as it leads to consumer misinformation and undermines both food safety and 
fair market practices. In Cambodia, the Consumer Protection, Competition and 
Fraud Repression Directorate-General (CCF) is currently tasked with inspecting 
food products available on the market. Consumer protection is a pressing topic 
in Cambodia and the ASEAN region, and existing frameworks governing 
this area include the United Nations Guidelines for Consumer Protection, the 
ASEAN Strategic Action Plan for Consumer Protection (2016-2025), and the 
government’s Rectangular Strategy - Phase IV.
7. Cambodia’s Progress Towards a Sustainable Food System: An 
Overview of the Current Situation
Cambodia has started a great move so far in building some policy frameworks 
and roadmaps to support a resilient, sustainable, and efficient food system, as 
follows: 
•	 Cambodia has adopted Agriculture 4.0, which involves the use of smart 
greenhouses, drone technologies, smart irrigation, and a digital marketing 
platforms. Recently, the AgriTech Roadmap was launched by the National 
Council of Science, Technology & Innovation and aims to fully adopt 
Agriculture 4.0 technologies by 2030.
•	 The Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry, and Fisheries has partnered with 
Agri-Sambath Khmer to build 10,000 smart greenhouses by 2030, aiming 
to produce 400,000 tons of vegetables annually.
•	 Digital marketing platforms like Chamkar, Tonlesap, CamAgriMarket, 
and Angkor Salad Apps connect farmers with customers.
•	 Oxfam has implemented blockchain technology to link small-scale rice 
producers with buyers in the Netherlands.
•	 The International Fund for Agricultural Development supports digital 
technology start-ups through the SAAMBAT project, accelerating 
agricultural value chains in Cambodia.
•	 Cambodia’s Food Systems for Sustainable Development 2030: Cambodia’s 
vision for 2030 focuses on expanding access to health services, sustainable 
agriculture, and empowering youth and vulnerable groups. The four 
priorities are healthy diets, empowerment, resilient livelihoods, and 
inclusive governance. This vision will drive innovation and infrastructure 
development, leading to a sustainable and inclusive food system.
•	 Cambodia’s National Strategic Development Plan (NSDP) (2019-
2023): The plan will encourage sustainability and resource efficiency by 
implementing the concept of sustainable consumption and production.

•	 Cambodian Sustainable Development Goals (CSDGs) Framework (2016-
2030): The framework aims to align national development priorities with 
the global SDGs, guiding the country towards sustainable development 
that leaves no one behind.
•	 Food Safety Law, endorsed by King Norodom Sihamoni, 18th May 2022: 
The Food Safety Law consists of 11 chapters and 43 articles, providing 
the necessary legal framework and mechanisms to regulate and ensure the 
safety, quality, and sanitation of the food production chains and businesses.
8. Recommendations
To enhance the adoption of these policy frameworks and effectively implement 
the Farm-to-Fork Strategy, the Cambodian government should focus on: 
Investing in human resources:
•	 Enhance stakeholders’ understanding and expertise in the farm-to-fork 
approach, sustainability considerations, and their advantages.
•	 Focus on education, awareness, and skill development.
•	 Engage and support the younger generation in STEM subjects.
Allocating resources for research, innovation, technology, and investments:
•	 Speed up the transition to sustainable, healthy, and inclusive food systems.
•	 Direct financial support towards the agri-food sector and the green and 
digital transformation of farms.
•	 Improve technology access and transfer to enhance productivity.
•	 Increase investment in R&D (currently, one percent of GDP is allocated 
for R&D by 2030).
Enhancing communication channels:
•	 Ensure effective communication between national policies, local authorities 
and farmers.
•	 Establish feedback mechanisms to facilitate coordination and collaboration 
between different stakeholders.
•	 Avoid a lack of coordination that can limit the effectiveness of the strategy.
Strengthening policy frameworks and enforcement:
•	 Implement strict regulatory frameworks to support the farm-to-fork 
strategy.
•	 Ensure strict enforcement of the recently endorsed Food Safety Law (2019) 
to safeguard consumers and maximize the strategy’s potential.

Fostering collaboration and avoiding working in silos:
•	 Encourage the government, farmers, and processors to collaborate and 
share information.
•	 Address the mismatch between market demand information and crop 
quality data.
•	 Minimize food waste and seize economic opportunities by promoting 
cooperation among stakeholders.
Improving infrastructure:
•	 Invest in adequate transportation networks, storage facilities, and 
processing plants.
•	 Strengthen infrastructure to support the farm-to-fork strategy effectively.
Ensuring access to clean water and reliable electricity:
•	 Support food processors’ operations and livelihoods by ensuring access to 
clean water and reliable electricity or energy sources.
9. Conclusion
The Farm-to-Fork Strategy is a sustainable and eco-friendly food system that covers 
all aspects of food production, processing, distribution, consumption, and waste 
reduction. In Cambodia, where agriculture is a significant sector, establishing a 
sustainable food system is essential for future generations. Although Cambodia is 
still in the early stages of implementing sustainable measures in its food system, 
it is crucial to continue investing efforts to overcome the challenges imposed 
by climate change. By embracing the Farm-to-Fork Strategy and implementing 
comprehensive measures throughout the entire food supply chain, Cambodia can 
effectively work towards its sustainable development goals, ensure food security, 
and minimize the adverse environmental impacts caused by its food system.

1. Introduction 
Global peace and stability are becoming progressively endangered by both 
human-driven and natural causes such as climate change, resource depletion, 
geopolitical tensions and socioeconomic disparities, amongst others. The 
potential ramifications of these issues will transcend future generations if they 
are not given urgent and serious attention now. Given that their future is at risk, 
young people naturally play a critical role in sustainable development. Rich in 
innovative ideas and brimming with creativity, it is today’s youth population 
that is most capable and has the greatest desire to construct a better world for 
themselves and generations beyond. At the international level, the United Nations 
(UN) has been and continues to be a crucial agent in facilitating sustainable 
development in the twenty-first century, ensuring that processes of sustainability 
are provided with direction and supported with structural means to achieve 
success. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) has also shown 
a strong commitment to empower and onboard youth as a driving force for the 
region’s long-term development. However, there continues to be much untapped 
potential in many areas across the globe, including ASEAN. It is important to 
understand the different contexts in which sustainable development can best 
be advanced, and how today’s youth can contribute within these contexts. It 
is equally crucial to establish settings that empower and equip historically 
marginalized groups with the necessary measures to transform desires to make 
the world a better place into tangible and productive actions. This chapter opens 
with a discussion of the current state of youth and their role within the 2030 
Agenda for Sustainable Development. It then identifies the areas of sustainability 
where youth engagement and leadership can be amplified. Finally, the chapter 
concludes with an assessment of the ASEAN Green Deal, highlighting the 
opportunities in which Southeast Asian youths can further engage as essential 
stakeholders in new processes of sustainable development.

health and behavior, enabling farmers to make informed decisions about animal 
welfare. By reducing farmers’ workloads and promoting sustainable practices, 
Agri-Tech has the potential to revolutionize the agricultural industry.
Bioproducts such as biopesticides, biofertilizers, and biostimulants are 
important for sustainable agricultural production. These products are derived from 
plants, animals, and microbial sources and are safer and more environmentally 
friendly than traditional fertilizers that contain potentially toxic chemicals 
(Upadhyay et al., 2020). Bio-products can help maximize crop yields and 
replenish soil health while providing essential nutrients to crops. Incorporating 
Agri-Tech and bio-products into farming practices can help farmers produce 
healthier and better-yielding crops with less risk of contamination or harm to the 
environment, leading to more sustainable practices in the agricultural industry 
(Spanner & Napolitano, 2015).
Incorporating Agri-Tech and bioproducts into farming practices has the 
potential to transform the agricultural industry, in line with the Agriculture 
4.0 roadmap and the agricultural sector’s plan for 2030 (Ministry of Industry, 
Green Ideals
138
Science, Technology & Innovation, 2022), aimed at promoting a sustainable and 
efficient agricultural industry.
4. Ensuring Food Security 
Food security is achieved when all individuals have consistent access to enough 
safe and nutritious food that meets their dietary requirements and preferences, 
allowing them to maintain good health and an active lifestyle. However, 
Cambodia, with its diverse food systems and rich culinary history, faces several 
challenges in achieving food security.
One of the major obstacles is the country’s vulnerability to climate change and 
natural disasters, which frequently disrupt agricultural production and threaten 
food availability. Rice, as the staple food in Cambodia, plays a vital role in 
providing calories and protein to the population. However, droughts and climate 
anomalies pose significant risks to rice farmers, leading to production losses 
and impacting overall food production. Cambodia also grapples with persistent 
inequalities, despite progress in poverty reduction. A significant portion of the 
population remains unable to afford a healthy diet, exacerbating food insecurity. 
Unfortunately, the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic has further heightened these 
challenges. The global food supply chain disruptions have impacted both food 
availability and affordability, affecting the overall food security situation in 
Cambodia. 
In this context, it becomes even more crucial to prioritize the promotion 
of agriculture and the adoption of healthy dietary practices. By strengthening 
Cambodia’s food systems, the country can enhance its resilience to external shocks 
and ensure food security during and after the pandemic. This entails investing 
in climate-resilient agricultural practices, providing support to rice farmers, and 
addressing inequalities in access to nutritious food. Moreover, efforts should be 
made to improve the efficiency and stability of the food supply chain, ensuring 
that safe and nutritious food reaches all segments of the population.
5. Encouraging Sustainable Food Processing
Food processing, an integral part of the farm-to-fork process, includes a range 
of activities that typically use abundant materials and energy. The majority 
of food processors in Cambodia uses traditional processing methods that rely 
on non-renewable energy, contributing significantly to carbon emissions and 
exacerbating the negative environment. To address this challenge and transition 
towards a more sustainable food system, the adoption of the Food Processing 4.0 
concept is increasingly being seen as a viable solution.
The Food Processing 4.0 concept emphasizes the application of Industry 4.0 
technologies to process food in this digital age, with the aim of enhancing food 
quality and safety, decreasing food processing expenses and time, conserving 
A Farm-To-Fork Strategy
139
energy and resources, as well as reducing food loss and waste (Hassoun et al., 
2023). This includes innovative technologies such as robotics, smart sensors, 
artificial intelligence, and the Internet of Things (IoT) that help the food industry 
optimize its processes, improve efficiency and reduce its environmental footprint. 
One such approach is the use of smart sensors and IoT devices throughout their 
production line to monitor and analyze data in real-time, such as temperature, 
pressure, and pH levels. With this information, they are able to fine-tune their 
production processes to reduce energy usage, minimize waste, and improve the 
quality of their products. Integrating the Time-Temperature Indicator (TTI) in 
food packaging, for instance, can monitor the temperature and time that a product 
has been exposed to. This TTI utilizes color changes that are not reversible, which 
allows consumers to quickly check if the product is safe and prevent unnecessary 
food waste due to premature discarding. Additionally, they can promote optimal 
storage and transportation conditions, which can reduce the likelihood of food 
spoilage and waste (Ahmed et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2015). 
Integrating Food Processing 4.0 into Cambodia’s food industry can support 
the government’s Industrial Development Plan (IDP) and the National Strategy 
for Food Security and Nutrition (NSFSN). It promotes industrial growth, 
diversification, and sustainability while facilitating access to technology, credit, 
and markets for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).  
6. Promoting Sustainable Consumption
Our current diet and eating patterns contribute significantly to our carbon 
footprint, making the consumption stage the most impactful in the food 
system. Unfortunately, unsustainable food choices often involve unhealthy 
diets characterized by high consumption of processed, calorie-dense foods and 
animal products, further exacerbating the carbon footprint. By transitioning to a 
sustainable and healthier diet, we can mitigate these impacts and pave the way 
for a more sustainable future, benefiting both our well-being and the planet.
Information dissemination is vital to promote sustainable food consumption. 
Educating consumers about the environmental impacts, local and seasonal food 
options, and benefits of plant-based diets empowers them to make informed 
decisions (Ammann et al., 2023). This knowledge enables individuals to 
understand the broader consequences of their food choices and encourages 
engagement in sustainable practices. Additionally, the farm-to-table movement 
should be widely promoted as part of sustainable food consumption efforts. 
It prioritizes locally sourced and seasonal ingredients and reduces the carbon 
footprint associated with transportation. Restaurants in this movement highlight 
flavors of locally sourced produce, meats, and dairy, supporting nearby farms 
and minimizing GHGs. It encourages organic and sustainable practices, such as 
avoiding synthetic pesticides and fertilizers, minimizing water usage, promoting 
Green Ideals
140
biodiversity, contributing to soil health, water conservation, and ecosystem 
preservation.
A market-based approach promotes sustainable food consumption 
through certifications and labels. Organic and fair trade certifications ensure 
environmental practices and fair labor. Carbon footprint and water usage labels 
aid consumers in selecting low-impact products. These market signals incentivize 
producers to access niche markets. Collaboration between producers, retailers, 
and policymakers is crucial. Retailers promote sustainability through placement 
and partnerships, while policymakers support adoption through regulations and 
incentives.
In conclusion, market-based approaches, through certifications and labeling 
schemes, empower consumers to make sustainable food choices. Collaboration 
between producers, retailers, and policymakers is crucial to creating a supportive 
market environment. By combining information dissemination and market-based 
strategies, we can build a sustainable food system that benefits human health and 
the environment in the Anthropocene era.
6.1. Minimizing Food Waste and Loss
Food waste is a significant contributor to global GHGs, accounting for 8-10 
percent of the total amount (United Nations Environment Programme, 2021). 
In Phnom Penh, research has shown that households, shops, and markets are 
responsible for 70 percent of food waste, with fruits, vegetables, sugarcane, 
coconut shells, and maize comprising 76 percent of this waste (Chinda & Thay, 
2020; Sang-Arun et al., 2011). These findings underscore the importance of 
addressing food waste in Cambodia and highlight the need for stakeholders, 
particularly consumers, to play an active role in reducing waste.
To tackle this issue, Cambodia needs to develop regulations and enhance 
public understanding. Experts recommend implementing incentives for recycling 
in restaurants and strengthening food bank capabilities. Following Europe’s 
example, extending product shelf life can also be beneficial. Raising awareness 
is vital to changing consumer behavior and reducing emissions from waste 
disposal. The government should take part in implementing regulations and 
establishing food banks, while youth groups can lead awareness campaigns. 
Ensuring coordination is crucial for the efficient distribution of food from retail 
shops to those in need.
Moreover, adopting a circular economy model would greatly benefit 
Cambodia’s waste management system. This approach focuses on minimizing 
waste and maximizing resource value through practices like reuse, recycling, and 
recovery. Implementing circular practices such as composting organic waste or 
repurposing food scraps for animal feed or energy generation can move Cambodia 
closer to a zero-waste system.

6.2 Reducing Food Fraud Along the Supply Chain
Food fraud poses a significant obstacle to achieving a sustainable food system, 
as it leads to consumer misinformation and undermines both food safety and 
fair market practices. In Cambodia, the Consumer Protection, Competition and 
Fraud Repression Directorate-General (CCF) is currently tasked with inspecting 
food products available on the market. Consumer protection is a pressing topic 
in Cambodia and the ASEAN region, and existing frameworks governing 
this area include the United Nations Guidelines for Consumer Protection, the 
ASEAN Strategic Action Plan for Consumer Protection (2016-2025), and the 
government’s Rectangular Strategy - Phase IV.
7. Cambodia’s Progress Towards a Sustainable Food System: An 
Overview of the Current Situation
Cambodia has started a great move so far in building some policy frameworks 
and roadmaps to support a resilient, sustainable, and efficient food system, as 
follows: 
•	 Cambodia has adopted Agriculture 4.0, which involves the use of smart 
greenhouses, drone technologies, smart irrigation, and a digital marketing 
platforms. Recently, the AgriTech Roadmap was launched by the National 
Council of Science, Technology & Innovation and aims to fully adopt 
Agriculture 4.0 technologies by 2030.
•	 The Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry, and Fisheries has partnered with 
Agri-Sambath Khmer to build 10,000 smart greenhouses by 2030, aiming 
to produce 400,000 tons of vegetables annually.
•	 Digital marketing platforms like Chamkar, Tonlesap, CamAgriMarket, 
and Angkor Salad Apps connect farmers with customers.
•	 Oxfam has implemented blockchain technology to link small-scale rice 
producers with buyers in the Netherlands.
•	 The International Fund for Agricultural Development supports digital 
technology start-ups through the SAAMBAT project, accelerating 
agricultural value chains in Cambodia.
•	 Cambodia’s Food Systems for Sustainable Development 2030: Cambodia’s 
vision for 2030 focuses on expanding access to health services, sustainable 
agriculture, and empowering youth and vulnerable groups. The four 
priorities are healthy diets, empowerment, resilient livelihoods, and 
inclusive governance. This vision will drive innovation and infrastructure 
development, leading to a sustainable and inclusive food system.
•	 Cambodia’s National Strategic Development Plan (NSDP) (2019-
2023): The plan will encourage sustainability and resource efficiency by 
implementing the concept of sustainable consumption and production.

•	 Cambodian Sustainable Development Goals (CSDGs) Framework (2016-

8. Recommendations
To enhance the adoption of these policy frameworks and effectively implement 
the Farm-to-Fork Strategy, the Cambodian government should focus on: 
Investing in human resources:
•	 Enhance stakeholders’ understanding and expertise in the farm-to-fork 
approach, sustainability considerations, and their advantages.
•	 Focus on education, awareness, and skill development.
•	 Engage and support the younger generation in STEM subjects.
Allocating resources for research, innovation, technology, and investments:
•	 Speed up the transition to sustainable, healthy, and inclusive food systems.
•	 Direct financial support towards the agri-food sector and the green and 
digital transformation of farms.
•	 Improve technology access and transfer to enhance productivity.
•	 Increase investment in R&D (currently, one percent of GDP is allocated 
for R&D by 2030).
Enhancing communication channels:
•	 Ensure effective communication between national policies, local authorities 
and farmers.
•	 Establish feedback mechanisms to facilitate coordination and collaboration 
between different stakeholders.
•	 Avoid a lack of coordination that can limit the effectiveness of the strategy.
Strengthening policy frameworks and enforcement:
•	 Implement strict regulatory frameworks to support the farm-to-fork 
strategy.
•	 Ensure strict enforcement of the recently endorsed Food Safety Law (2019) 
to safeguard consumers and maximize the strategy’s potential.

Fostering collaboration and avoiding working in silos:
•	 Encourage the government, farmers, and processors to collaborate and 
share information.
•	 Address the mismatch between market demand information and crop

•	 Minimize food waste and seize economic opportunities by promoting 
cooperation among stakeholders.
Improving infrastructure:
•	 Invest in adequate transportation networks, storage facilities, and

•	 Strengthen infrastructure to support the farm-to-fork strategy effectively.
Ensuring access to clean water and reliable electricity:

9. Conclusion
The Farm-to-Fork Strategy is a sustainable and eco-friendly food system that covers 
all aspects of food production, processing, distribution, consumption, and waste 
reduction. In Cambodia, where agriculture is a significant sector, establishing a 
sustainable food system is essential for future generations. Although Cambodia is 
still in the early stages of implementing sustainable measures in its food system, 
it is crucial to continue investing efforts to overcome the challenges imposed 
by climate change. By embracing the Farm-to-Fork Strategy and implementing 
comprehensive measures throughout the entire food supply chain, Cambodia can 
effectively work towards its sustainable development goals, ensure food security, 
and minimize the adverse environmental impacts caused by its food system.

CHEA Angela*, SAY Vithya Arthur, and ROS Sayumphu 
1. Introduction 
Global peace and stability are becoming progressively endangered by both 
human-driven and natural causes such as climate change, resource depletion, 
geopolitical tensions and socioeconomic disparities, amongst others. The 
potential ramifications of these issues will transcend future generations if they 
are not given urgent and serious attention now. Given that their future is at risk, 
young people naturally play a critical role in sustainable development. Rich in 
innovative ideas and brimming with creativity, it is today’s youth population 
that is most capable and has the greatest desire to construct a better world for 
themselves and generations beyond. At the international level, the United Nations 
(UN) has been and continues to be a crucial agent in facilitating sustainable 
development in the twenty-first century, ensuring that processes of sustainability 
are provided with direction and supported with structural means to achieve 
success. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) has also shown 
a strong commitment to empower and onboard youth as a driving force for the 
region’s long-term development. However, there continues to be much untapped 
potential in many areas across the globe, including ASEAN. It is important to 
understand the different contexts in which sustainable development can best 
be advanced, and how today’s youth can contribute within these contexts. It 
is equally crucial to establish settings that empower and equip historically 
marginalized groups with the necessary measures to transform desires to make 
the world a better place into tangible and productive actions. This chapter opens 
with a discussion of the current state of youth and their role within the 2030 
Agenda for Sustainable Development. It then identifies the areas of sustainability 
where youth engagement and leadership can be amplified. Finally, the chapter 
concludes with an assessment of the ASEAN Green Deal, highlighting the 
opportunities in which Southeast Asian youths can further engage as essential 
stakeholders in new processes of sustainable development. 
2. Current State of Play of the UN SDGs and Youth
Adopted in 2015, the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) constitute 
the latest global call for action to address the myriad of development challenges 
facing countries worldwide. The SDGs seek to dissolve the divide between the 
developed and developing worlds by engaging the efforts of countries at all

148
income levels. Building on the momentum of the Millennium Development Goals 
(MDGs), which primarily targeted poverty alleviation, the SDGs set out a much 
more comprehensive global program that focuses on sustainable development. 
Comprising 17 goals, 169 targets, and over 300 indicators that aim to combat 
social, economic, and ecological issues, the SDGs emphasize the importance of 
inclusivity and a united effort to ensure prosperity for all. The precedent for this 
broadened agenda not only comes from a heightened understanding of global 
interconnectivity but also from a newfound recognition that the world has entered 
a modern geological epoch driven by human impact on global environmental 
changes – the Anthropocene (Griggs et al., 2013; Sachs, 2012). At the same 
time, there is an increasing awareness that implementation of the 2030 Agenda 
necessitates the empowerment of youth participation in propelling sustainable 
changes. Leveraging the energies of young people can bring about innovative 
ideas that have the potential to revitalize often stagnant or unimpactful processes 
of development. 
The UN system itself has demonstrated an active commitment to enhance 
youth engagement in the SDGs and relevant processes. In 2018, UN Secretary-
General Antonio Guterres launched ‘Youth2030, the UN Youth Strategy’ to 
strengthen youth participation. Although Youth2030 progress reports since 2021 
have revealed improvements, challenges such as normalizing meaningful and 
continued participation, acknowledging diversity among youth, and engaging 
marginalized young people continue to impede youth involvement (United 
Nations Youth2030, 2023). To combat these persisting obstacles, the UN 
established a Youth Office that aims to empower participation in development 
processes by gathering ideas and insights from young people to better inform 
UN activities. Such a level of commitment by the UN to positioning youth at 
the core of twenty-first century sustainable development is also evident by the 
fact that the SDGs themselves are anchored within a rights-based framework 
promulgated by several international declarations, including the Convention on 
the Rights of the Child (CRC). Effective since 1990, the CRC recognizes the 
capital and potential of young people in tackling pressing global challenges and 
situates them as key stakeholders in development processes (UN Commission on 
Human Rights, 1990). 
The flexibility of the SDGs – in the freedom that it gives states to interpret 
the goals and implement action – provides opportune spaces for young people 
and youth-led initiatives to accelerate sustainable development. Historical trends 
suggest that young people have been generally marginalized from high-level 
decision-making processes (Bastien & Holmarsdottir, 2017, p.7). However, many 
current national development strategies are now underscoring the importance of 
their participation in driving transformative change to socioeconomic systems. 
In 2023, the High-level Political Forum (HLPF) on Sustainable Development 
published a Voluntary National Reviews (VNR) Synthesis Report highlighting 
Youth and Sustainable Development
149
that several countries, including Bahrain, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Brunei 
Darussalam, Cambodia, Iceland, and Lithuania, actively sought youth 
involvement, outlining diverse initiatives in their VNRs. Other countries also 
found creative ways to engage young people in national-level processes. Guyana 
created a Youth Advisory Council, Turkmenistan appointed Young SDG 
Ambassadors, and Timor-Leste solicited advisory messages from youth addressing 
various development issues and their expectations for implementation (High 
Level Political Forum on Sustainable Development, 2023). At present, several 
countries across the globe have placed serious attention towards empowering 
youth participation in decision-making processes related to the SDGs. 
ASEAN member states in particular have shown sustained efforts in 
establishing and implementing development policies and programs that tap into 
the potential of young people. The ASEAN Youth Development Index (YDI) 
was launched in 2017 under the ASEAN Work Plan on Youth 2016-2020 to 
support such efforts. Based on seven domains, including education, health, 
participation and engagement, and more, the YDI serves as a measurement of 
progress in youth-focused initiatives across ASEAN. The most recent report of 
the YDI recorded an increase from 0.535 in 2013 to 0.606 in 2022. Cambodia 
showed the greatest improvement, with its YDI increasing from 0.440 to 0.568 
in the same period (ASEAN, 2023). While we have witnessed improvements to 
youth engagement in sustainable development across all ASEAN member states, 
certain areas continue to hold opportunities for greater progress. 
The state of the world that we see today is one that is unequivocally most 
conducive to successful youth engagement in sustainable development processes. 
Youths have a plethora of opportunities to actively engage in development 
processes. Social media – its proliferation, immediacy and reach – enables 
young advocates to raise awareness and mobilize collective action towards a 
more sustainable and environmentally conscious future. Educational institutions 
at all levels are increasingly integrating sustainability into their programs and 
curricula, equipping youth with the knowledge and skills necessary to address 
contemporary development challenges. Such learning experiences nurture 
both human-human and human-nature relationships that lead to a deeper 
sense of environmental responsibility among young people (Sterling, 2017). 
Social entrepreneurship provides a space for young business leaders to align 
economic activities with sustainable goals. Technology can be leveraged by 
young innovators to develop solutions and products grounded in sustainability. 
These opportunities collectively contribute to building a generation of informed, 
empowered, and proactive individuals dedicated to sustainable development. 
As the contemporary landscape continues to evolve, youths play a vital role in 
shaping a more sustainable future for themselves and the coming generations. 
Although there are many opportunities for youth engagement in sustainable 
development, multifaceted challenges exist that continue to impede progress. A 
Green Ideals
150
significant hurdle lies in the lack of awareness and understanding among youth 
about the technical intricacies and importance of sustainable development. A 
study done by Arnold and Barbara Pabian (2023) revealed that while social media 
serves as a powerful tool to disseminate information, content on sustainability 
circulating across platforms is limited and often superficial or lacking depth. This 
results in a persisting lack of knowledge that subsequently translates to a lack 
of responsibility and action among many young individuals towards engaging 
in sustainability. Moreover, the prioritization of immediate concerns such as 
education, employment, and simply, the trials and tribulations of growing up, 
often takes precedence over long-term goals for sustainable living. In many cases, 
sustainable lifestyles are viewed as costly and difficult to maintain. Research by 
leading consulting firm Deloitte United Kingdom (2022) finds that 52 percent of 
consumers are hesitant to adopt greener purchasing choices due to high costs. 
Eco-friendly products serve as alternative consumption options that are much 
more environmentally and socially beneficial relative to conventional products. 
But these added benefits often come with heftier price tags, making them, on 
average, 75 to 85 percent more costly. The highest price markups can be found 
in fashion, beauty, and food products (Kearney, 2020). Ironically, these are 
the industries that resonate most with the present-day youth demographic. 
Socioeconomic inequalities, coupled with a lack of inclusivity, can further 
deter segments of the youth population from engaging in sustainability. Such 
a phenomenon is ever present across the world, but especially in developing 
countries where those inequalities are more profound. Transformative changes 
need to be made to socioeconomic systems to ensure that young people are 
supported with the financial, educational, and structural means to meaningfully 
contribute to sustainable development. 
3. Areas of Impact: Where Youth Can Lead
Given that they comprise more than 1.2 billion people, around 16 percent of the 
global population, youths aged between 15 and 24 years naturally play a pivotal 
role in the global pursuit of sustainable development (UN, 2020). Their role is 
further emphasized by their inclusion among the nine Major Groups recognized 
by the UN as the main segments of society through which broad participation 
in sustainable development processes would be promoted, alongside women, 
indigenous peoples, non-governmental organizations, local authorities, workers 
and trade unions, business and industry, and the scientific and technological 
community (UN, 2022). 
The desire for environmental action is substantial among youth, with 7 out 
of 10 young people expressing a desire to actively engage in the green transition 
(United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs [UNDESA], 
2023b). The sheer size and enthusiasm of the youth demographic positions them 
as a force capable of instigating meaningful change. Their population is expected 
Youth and Sustainable Development
151
to further grow by seven percent to approximately 1.3 billion by the conclusion 
of the SDGs Agenda in 2030 (UN, 2020). 
Over the past few years, there have been many exemplary youth pioneers 
who have embarked on green initiatives. Nzambi Matee, the founder of Gjenge 
Makers, revolutionized waste management in Kenya by turning plastics into 
bricks to pave roads, thus addressing both plastic pollution and infrastructure 
needs (United Nations Environment Programme, 2022). Fatemah Alzelzela from 
Kuwait co-founded Eco Star, a non-profit recycling initiative aiming to address 
the country’s high trash generation through using social media to educate and 
inspire sustainable waste management practices (United Nations Environment 
Programme, 2022).
Although many young people have demonstrated an active commitment 
to engage in green initiatives, the current level of youth participation is still 
insufficient to mitigate the rapidly developing negative impacts of climate change. 
The urgency of involving youth in sustainable development is underscored by the 
heightened vulnerability of children to the impacts of climate change (Eskenazi 
et al., 2020). The detrimental effects of climate change have and will continue 
to threaten the futures of youth. Its impacts can be both direct and indirect, 
jeopardizing not only young people’s physical health and well-being, but also 
their future educational, social, and economic opportunities (Sanson et al., 
2019). Furthermore, the Paris Agreement’s goal of limiting global temperature 
rise to under two degrees Celsius, which is essential for averting catastrophic 
consequences, is now in jeopardy (Sachs, 2016). It is projected that, at the 
current rate, none of the SDGs will be achieved by the intended year of 2030, 
with less than 20 percent of the associated targets on track for fulfillment (Sachs 
et al., 2023). As such, it is even more imperative that youths actively participate 
in finding innovative solutions to combat climate change and contribute to 
sustainable development overall. 
For these reasons, green skills are essential for young people to succeed in the 
green economy. These competencies comprise the knowledge, abilities, attitudes, 
and values required to support, foster, and live in a society that is resource-efficient 
and sustainable (UNDESA, 2023a). With 40 percent of employment linked to a 
healthy environment under threat due to climate change (UNDESA, 2023b), the 
green transition is expected to generate 8.4 million employment opportunities for 
young people by 2030 (UNDESA, 2023a). However, a concerning trend emerges 
as 60 percent of young individuals are anticipated to lack the skills essential to 
prosper in this evolving green economy (UNDESA, 2023a). 
Therefore, empowerment is crucial to harness the potential of youth in driving 
sustainable development. Educational initiatives should focus on cultivating 
green skills and equipping young individuals with the knowledge and tools 
needed to address environmental challenges. Additionally, mentorship programs, 
Green Ideals
152
partnerships with businesses, and access to funding can foster the entrepreneurial 
spirit among youth, enabling them to initiate and scale green projects.
4. ASEAN Green Deal and Youth
During his chairmanship of ASEAN in 2022, former Cambodian prime minister 
Hun Sen declared the initiation of the ASEAN Green Deal (Khmer Times, 
2022). It has garnered considerable attention and has been lauded as one of 
ASEAN’s most comprehensive overarching green programs. As of yet, no formal 
document detailing the intended activities or itinerary of the ASEAN Green 
Deal has been produced (Chheang, 2023). However, it is crucial to acknowledge 
that the ASEAN Green Deal bears strong resemblance to the European Green 
Deal, a set of policy initiatives that was officially adopted by the European 
Union in 2020. The European Green Deal encompasses the EU’s dedication to 
tackling environmental and global warming issues while concurrently promoting 
sustainable growth in the bloc via a green economy. It also serves as a mechanism 
for promoting sustainability and strengthening security, by specifically focusing 
on addressing Europe’s security concerns, namely in energy (Rybski, 2023). 
On the contrary, although there have not been any written policies laid out, the 
Chairman’s Statement for the 12th ASEAN-United Nations Summit held in 
Phnom Penh, Cambodia on 11 November 2022, provides an overview of the 
objective of the ASEAN Green Deal:
“Aim to gradually transform ASEAN region towards a green future, sustainability, 
effective use of resources, resilience, and economic competitiveness.” 
Chairman’s Statement of the 12th ASEAN-United Nations Summit (2022)
The excerpt above underscores that the ASEAN Green Deal is designed to 
bolster environmentally conscious endeavors within the ASEAN region, while 
simultaneously functioning as an instrument towards achieving the 2030 UN 
SDGs. This vision, which incorporates the ASEAN Green Deal and UN SDGs, 
can also be found in the ASEAN Economic and Socio-Cultural Community and 
the ASEAN Community Blueprint 2025 (Ting & Yongkun, 2023).
Given the potential long-term consequences of climate change and 
environmental degradation, it is essential to consider their impact on future 
generations in ASEAN. Young people have a crucial role in leading the green 
drive by actively contributing to the resolution of the potential intergenerational 
problems mentioned section 1 and 2 of this chapter. Out of the roughly 660 million 
individuals in ASEAN, 224.2 million were young people in 2020 – this accounts 
for one-third of the population. Among these youths, 53 percent fall within the 
age range of 15 to 25, while the remaining 47 percent are between 26 to 35 years 
of age (ASEAN, 2023). With this, despite being the third biggest population in the 
globe, and although ASEAN has enacted various policy measures, as mentioned 
above, the area’s progress toward sustainable development objectives remains 
Youth and Sustainable Development
153
bleak. For example, the ASEAN SDGs snapshot in 2022 showed that climate-
related disasters had a greater effect on people in the region in 2020 compared to 
2016. In 2020, on average, the number of individuals who were reported missing, 
directly affected, or whose lives were taken by climate-related catastrophes was 
2,546.8 per 100,000 population. This is a significant increase compared to the 
rate of 554 per 100,000 population in 2016 (ASEAN, 2022). Furthermore, the 
outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic has been a reason for the reversed financial 
backing in terms of financial assistance for ecologically friendly initiatives (Ahmed 
et al., 2022). Concurrently, the global energy crisis, which began in 2021 in the 
aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, has impeded the capacity of ASEAN 
member states to shift towards renewable energy or provide support in other 
areas of sustainable development such as healthcare and education (Jahanger et 
al., 2023). ASEAN’s insufficient advancement towards the SDGs can potentially 
result in further consequences, one of which is the threat that climate change in 
2023 may affect up to 11 percent decrease of regional economic growth and the 
mortality caused by climate change to increase to 70,000 in 2030 (Jahanger et 
al., 2023).
Although overall progress in ASEAN has been slow in terms of achieving 
the SDGs by the intended year of 2030, there is still indication of favorable, 
albeit modest, progress in the fulfillment of certain goals. These goals include: 
Goal 2) Eradicate Food Insecurity, Goal 3) Overall Physical and Mental Well-
Being, Goal 4) Quality Education, Goal 7) Affordable and Clean Energy, 
Goal 8) Decent Work and Economic Growth, Goal 9) Industry, Innovation, 
and Infrastructure, and Goal 17) Partnerships for the Goals (ASEAN, 2022). 
Young people in ASEAN have played a crucial role in advancing the SDGs 
by actively participating in various ways. Examples of youth initiatives for 
green skills include the Young Forces for Agricultural Innovation (#Y4AGRI) 
of the Southeast Asian Regional Centre for Graduate Study and Research in 
Agriculture (SEARCA), the ASEAN Student Leaders Forum (ASLF) of the 
ASEAN University Network (AUN), and other prominent regional academic 
networks and initiatives (Nelles, 2023). 
Creating opportunities for youth engagement, empowerment, and awareness 
in sustainable development has been a priority for ASEAN. However, it is also 
important to emphasize to all parties involved, particularly young people, that 
sustainable development must focus on human interests and the long history of 
core principles and practices of environmental sustainability in Southeast Asia 
(Sofjan, 2022). Youth must comprehend the significance of recognizing that 
there is no one-size-fits-all solution or standard of conduct for environmental 
sustainability. It is critical to understand the implications of capitalism, which 
may lead to an absence of true commitment to environmental conservation 
and life preservation (Nelles, 2023). By bringing measures for reducing poverty 
into line with the goals of the private sector, the SDGs could represent a move 
Green Ideals
154
towards a more firmly free-market orientation. Particularly, concentrating on 
global markets, global demands, and global consumption in accordance with the 
neoliberal agenda, rather than a real concern for the sustainable development 
goal, may also lead to the abandonment of unique local cultures (Cervantes, 
2013; Lassou et al., 2019).  Therefore, it may be seen that neoliberalism can 
contribute to a phenomenon known as “greenwashing,” in which multinational 
firms exclusively present the positive impacts of their products or operations on 
the environment while hiding, neglecting, or failing to disclose the repercussions 
to nature (Bowen & Aragon-Correa, 2014). Global community and ASEAN 
should exercise caution regarding the phenomenon. 
5. Conclusion
The engagement of youth in sustainable development is a multifaceted and 
crucial aspect of global and regional agendas. The world and ASEAN stand at a 
crossroads, where the choices we make today will inevitably determine the future 
we inherit. Moving forward, it is important to understand that investing in the 
potential of youth for sustainable development at every level is not merely a moral 
imperative, but a strategic necessity. In the endeavor to build a sustainable world 
for all, policies and initiatives should be implemented that empower and equip 
young people with the knowledge, skills, resources, and platforms they need 
to fully realize their potential. So far, AEAN has demonstrated an unwavering 
commitment to youth engagement, as demonstrated by the Youth Development 
Index, the forthcoming ASEAN Green Deal, and the several initiatives already 
in place for youth to contribute to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. 
Economic dynamism, structural improvements to socioeconomic systems, and 
environment cooperation are all positive avenues for the holistic engagement 
and empowerment of youth in sustainable development processes. ASEAN as a 
region is on the right path in facilitating and fulfilling this. However, more can 
always be achieved. We have yet to maximize our fullest capacity in utilizing the 
potential of youths across Southeast Asia in sustainability. The ASEAN Green 
Deal is just one of the many golden opportunities we have to further explore 
and create ways to enhance young people’s participation. It is only when we 
acknowledge and realize the role of youth as key stakeholders in development 
processes that we can construct a more just, equitable, and sustainable future for 
ourselves and generations beyond.

CONCLUSION
ASEAN Green Ideals book aims to bring together perspectives from writers 
in various fields. Through these incisive contributions, the book has proven to 
encourage conversations, creativity, and ideas, as well as develop a broader 
understanding of the Green Deal’s revolutionary potential for Cambodia, the 
region, and the globe. Throughout the book, it is important to note that there 
is no uniform approach to tackling climate change or maintaining sustainable 
development. On the other hand, it is clear that each sector, ranging from 
technology, food, health, energy, water, and architecture, experiences different 
impacts, while actors such as universities, scientists, and even youth will all 
contribute, albeit in different capacities and levels, to mitigating climate change 
and environmental issues. 
As stated in the preface, the objective was not to enforce a particular formatting 
style on each chapter; however, a certain standard must be met.With that said, 
readers should be aware that, due to the issue’s multifaceted nature and the need to 
gather multidisciplinary experts to take a holistic approach to addressing pressing 
issues such as climate change, environmental sustainability, and socioeconomic 
development, it is critical that people from various backgrounds and disciplines 
have the freedom to express their research and ideas creatively. The book aims 
to provide ideas in a new but comprehensive manner to investigate and advocate 
for the urgent need for a green deal. 
Furthermore, the book aimed to be accessible to policy-makers, students, and 
anybody interested in creating a sustainable and resilient future. The 14 chapters’ 
discussions eventually lead to an academic analysis of the Green Deal’s rich and 
intriguing characteristics. The vast range of ideas from many viewpoints may 
serve as a platform for undertaking an extensive multidisciplinary study on the 
Green Deal with the goal of informing future policies that transcend national 
boundaries, stressing a more systematic and global approach.
Aside from establishing the book’s goal and approach, the combined 14 chapters 
have produced a few conclusions worth contemplating. Climate and environmental 
concerns touch all nations and players, regardless of geography, and show that a 
green strategy and sustainable development are the way ahead for a sustainable 
future. However, said can be easier than done. Issues arise at all levels, from local to 
worldwide, owing to political issues, resource constraints, a lack of knowledge and 
education, or a lack of commitment. These concerns seem to arise in every chapter 
of this book. For example, education has been repeatedly emphasized in numerous 
chapters as a crucial instrument for defining the norms of future generations and 
raising public awareness of the possible consequences of climatic and environmental 
issues. On the other hand, resource-related factors such as cultivating technology, 
green energy, and financial resources for green development are ideal; however, 
there are gaps between the powerful and the rest of the world in the aforementioned 
factors, complicating the path to sustainable development. Despite this, the bulk 
Green Ideals
160
of the chapter emphasized the need for collaboration and working together rather 
than working in silos, since preventing climate change can only be accomplished by 
working in solidarity and across all domains of specialty.
Last but not least, the book demonstrated that ASEAN’s Green Deal will be 
an essential diplomatic equivalent to the European Green Deal, emphasizing that 
ASEAN will need and can play a role in promoting sustainable development. These 
perspectives have been shared by largely Khmer writers and some international 
professionals, demonstrating Cambodia’s expertise and vision as a gift to the 
world. As a framework, as a member of ASEAN and a global player, Cambodia, 
via this book, shares the idea that there are diverse approaches to mitigating 
climatic and environmental concerns and that localization of measures is critical 
rather than adopting a certain norm. At the same time, some chapters questioned 
and raised awareness of the prevailing narrative of sustainable development, while 
others used it as a greenwashing tactic to accomplish a specific goal rather than 
the benefit of the whole global population. Such concerns are crucial, particularly 
when participating in an intellectual discussion with the global community, to 
share their modest viewpoint with the world, with the hope that all voices may 
be heard as part of the decolonization of concepts and information. 
Several potential policy suggestions that would be well-suited for the 
implementation of the ASEAN Green Deal have been identified based on 
the comprehensive data collected from all 14 chapters. Nevertheless, the 
community is currently in the process of transforming these ideals into concrete 
and implementable plans, suggesting that they have not yet reached their full 
potential. This book advocates for the ongoing participation of all stakeholders in 
order to broaden perspectives and guarantee a comprehensive approach. While 
also suggesting that specific aspects of the investigation below may be worth 
further investigation in order to substantiate this idea for ASEAN Green Deal:
•	 To ensure equitable participation and benefits for all member states, how 
can ASEAN countries effectively integrate diverse cultural and social 
values into a unified Green Deal framework?
•	 What governance structures and mechanisms promote transparent and 
accountable regional collaboration for ASEAN Green Deal implementation 
despite differing national interests and capacities?
•	 How can ASEAN create innovative financing models for large-scale green 
technology and infrastructure investments while ensuring that developed 
and developing member countries have access to resources?
•	 How can ASEAN use regional diplomacy to align the Green Deal with 
global sustainability initiatives such as the European Green Deal while 
also addressing local environmental and economic concerns?
•	 How can the ASEAN Green Deal be put into action to prevent 
greenwashing and ensure genuine, measurable sustainability efforts that 
benefit the environment and society for the long term?
