The Cambodian Narrative on the South China Sea 
Dispute, The Unfinished Story 

Early this month, George Yeo, former Foreign Minister of Singapore, returned to 
Cambodia after his last visit to the country in 1999. His visit was notable for his well-
received public lectures at both the National Institute of Diplomacy and International 
Relations, under the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation of 
Cambodia, and the Royal University of Phnom Penh. 
Subsequently, on December 8, 2023, the Khmer Times published an op-ed by Mr 
Yeo titled “Why the West Should Not Give Up on Cambodia.” In this piece, Mr Yeo 
provides a balanced analysis of Cambodia’s remarkable transformation. He underscores 
the country’s journey from being ravaged by conflict to achieving a state of peace and 
developing a vibrant economy. 
The article also addresses Cambodia’s foreign policy. Although I noticed its overall 
objectivity, there is one critical issue that I would like to draw readers’ attention which is 
the South China Sea dispute. The issue is one of the most intricate and hotly contested 
geopolitical issues in the Asia Pacific region, involving regional and global powers. 
Cambodia is not immune to this complex dispute. 
In his commentary, Mr Yeo wrote, ‘When Cambodia blocked the issue of a joint 
statement communique by ASEAN foreign ministers in 2012 and 2016, many felt that the 
decision was taken to please China’. 
It is crucial to clarify that the 2016 ASEAN Foreign Ministers’ meeting did manage 
to issue a joint communique after a tense debate. 
Indeed, ASEAN did not succeed in issuing a joint communique in 2012 during 
Cambodia’s tenure as the ASEAN Chair. This period was marked by allegations that 
Cambodia was collaborating with China to obstruct discussions on the South China Sea 
within ASEAN meetings, claims that Cambodia subsequently refuted. 
It is noteworthy, however, that following this impasse, ASEAN foreign ministers 
eventually reached a six-point consensus on the South China Sea issue. This 
breakthrough was largely attributed to the shuttle diplomacy efforts of the then 
Indonesian Foreign Minister, Marty Natalegawa. This development illustrates Cambodia’s 
ability to adapt and approach diplomatically sensitive issues with a pragmatic mindset. 
Contemporary Perspective 
Part I: Cambodia 
P a g e | 36 
Volume IV 
 Challenging the Criticism 
Former Prime Minister Hun Sen has been vocal in questioning why Cambodia 
was singled out for the South China Sea issue when other ASEAN Chairs faced similar 
challenges. 
He characterized the singling out of Cambodia as ‘injustice’. At the graduation 
ceremony at one university in Phnom Penh in February 2016, he said, “Those who 
attacked Cambodia or me personally apologize to me and repay my justice.” 
“Maybe it is time to return justice to me. I told John Kerry I was disappointed when 
the critics said that Cambodia’s closeness to China was the obstacle to realizing the 
Code of Conduct in the South China Sea,” he added. 
He drew attention to the fact that even when Cambodia was no longer the Chair 
of ASEAN, other ASEAN Chairs also failed to make progress on the issue, including an 
attempt to finalize a binding, substantive Code of Conduct (COC). 
“Before Cambodia took its turn, Vietnam and Indonesia were the rotating Chairs 
of ASEAN. Why couldn’t they realize it? Did they do it after Cambodia’s turn, Brunei, 
Myanmar, and Malaysia? What could they say about it?” he literally asked. 
 Cambodia’s Stand on Sovereignty Disputes 
Cambodia has consistently pushed to address the South China Sea issue within a 
regional context, cautioning against its over-internationalization. This stance, articulated 
by then Secretary of State Kao Kim Hourn in 2012, emphasized ASEAN’s role and the 
ASEAN-China mechanism in handling the dispute. 
Cambodia also underscores the importance of direct negotiations between 
concerned parties. This approach aligns with the understanding that ASEAN, while 
instrumental for regional peace and cooperation, is not the arbitrator in sovereignty 
disputes. 
Mr Hun Sen’s statements at various forums, especially in early 2016, reiterated 
Cambodia’s view that ASEAN should not intervene in territorial and sovereign disputes 
between the Member States or between the Member State(s) and other countries, 
advocating for bilateral negotiations between concerned parties. 
“ASEAN does not have rights to divide land among them. Vietnam and China 
would have to sit down and work together. The Philippines and China, or the Philippines 
Contemporary Perspective 
Part I: Cambodia 
P a g e | 37 
Volume IV 
and Vietnam, will have to sit down and work out their differences,” Mr Hun Sen said in 
early 2016. 
 Asserting Independent Foreign Policy 
Then Prime Minister Hun Sen had consistently affirmed Cambodia’s independent 
and sovereign foreign policy, emphasizing the nation’s strategic autonomy from major 
powers like China and the United States. 
This stance is pivotal in understanding Cambodia’s approach to regional issues, 
reflecting its commitment to navigate a course based on national interests and principles. 
In response to the 2016 arbitral tribunal’s decision regarding the South China Sea, 
Mr Hun Sen declared Cambodia’s unwillingness to support the decision, advocating for 
bilateral negotiations to resolve disputes. 
He said the tribunal’s decision is “politically motivated.” The Philippines did not 
consult other ASEAN Member States before bringing the case against China- deviating 
from the spirit of the Declaration on the Conduct of Parties (DOC) in the South China 
Sea 
Cambodia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation issued a 
statement on 9 July 2016 stressing that “Cambodia views this arbitration case is to settle 
dispute brought by the Philippines against China, and this proceeding is not related to all 
ASEAN Member States. Therefore, Cambodia will not join in expressing any common 
position on the verdict.” 
Cambodia’s South China Sea dispute narrative showcases a nation striving to 
balance regional dynamics, uphold sovereignty, and advocate for a realistic and 
pragmatic approach to dispute resolution. While facing criticism and challenges, 
understanding Cambodia’s perspective is key to appreciating the broader context of this 
ongoing complex, volatile geopolitical issue.

In a world fraught with uncertainty, complexity, and volatility, Cambodia finds itself 
at a pivotal inflection point, where global governance, multilateralism, and the rules-
based international order face unprecedented strains and challenges after the end of the 
Cold War. 
The world faces multiple crises, from the protracted war in Ukraine to the 
escalating war in the Middle East. In Asia, a trio of security flashpoints – India-Pakistan 
tensions over Kashmir, a fragile security environment on the Korean Peninsula, and 
deep-rooted complex disputes in the South China Sea and Taiwan Straits – keep the 
world on edge. 
Southeast Asia grapples with a convergence of challenges or a perfect storm 
within this complex geopolitical landscape- a mixture of the US-China power competition, 
sluggish economic recovery, supply chain disruptions, and rising identity politics and 
nationalism. 
The intricate dance between China and the US casts a long shadow over the 
region. Southeast Asian countries are under increasing pressure to choose sides 
although they persistently resist doing so. Maintaining strategic autonomy is an uphill, 
long-term struggle for small states like Cambodia. 
The geopolitical and geoeconomic landscape in the Mekong region is undergoing 
a profound transformation, marked by increasing complex dynamics of power 
reconfiguration. Almost all significant powers have engaged the area through various 
initiatives. 
This region, historically characterized by its natural beauty and rich cultural 
heritage, is now emerging as a pivotal theater for significant power competition on both 
political and economic fronts. China has taken all measures to secure this strategic 
backyard from being influenced by external powers, particularly the US. 
The crisis in Myanmar has invited foreign intervention. ASEAN has not effectively 
responded to the problem due to its limited crisis management capacity and non-
interference principle. The lack of political consensus and united position within ASEAN 
prevents this inter-governmental organization from having a breakthrough in dealing with 
the crisis. 
Contemporary Perspective 
Part I: Cambodia 
P a g e | 39 
Volume IV 
Transboundary water resource management is another critical issue that requires 
a coherent, effective regional response. The Mekong River Commission provides 
technical solutions to the problems related to managing the Mekong River Basin but 
does not have enforcement power. Therefore, the political will of all riverine countries is 
of utmost importance. 
Given these challenges, Cambodia believes confidence-building measures, 
preventive diplomacy, and robust crisis management mechanisms are essential. 
Simultaneously, Cambodia firmly upholds the principles of the rules-based international 
order while promoting open and inclusive multilateralism. 
Cambodia has been proactive in strengthening cooperation and partnerships with 
its immediate neighbours to maintain regional peace and stability and create new 
economic opportunities for the Kingdom and the region. 
Under the leadership of Prime Minister Hun Manet, Cambodia is going to deepen 
regional integration further- believing that Cambodia’s future or destiny cannot be 
detached from that of the region. Transforming Cambodia into a gateway a hub, or a 
bridging state of the Mekong region is a long-term endeavor. 
Cambodia’s neighbourhood diplomacy is rooted in the fundamental principles of 
mutual respect, mutual understanding, mutual trust, and mutual interest for peace and 
prosperity (M4P2). These principles are the bedrock upon which Cambodia’s foreign 
policy strategy is constructed. Neighbouring countries occupy a central and pivotal 
position within Cambodia’s foreign policy framework. 
 Cooperation with Lao PDR 
Cambodia and Lao PDR share a deep history, cultural values, and identity. This 
strong bond has translated into a growing bilateral trade relationship, reaching USD 210 
million in 2022. 
Furthermore, the active participation of 35 Cambodian companies in Laos 
demonstrates a promising trend of bilateral investment cooperation. 
Notably, Laos plays a pivotal role as a “battery” within the Mekong region. 
Cambodia currently imports approximately 445 megawatts of power from Laos. Looking 
ahead, is anticipated that power trade will surge to a remarkable 6,000 MW by 2030. 
Sustaining and enhancing this trajectory will bolster our energy security and foster 
greater economic prosperity and sustainability for Cambodia and Laos.

P a g e | 40 
Volume IV 
 Cooperation with Thailand 
Cambodia and Thailand enjoy a longstanding relationship marked by practical 
cooperation and increasing bilateral trade and investment. 
At a recent bilateral meeting between the two leaders, both sides agreed to 
elevate bilateral trade to $15 billion by 2025. Bilateral trade reached $4.67 billion in 2022, 
demonstrating consistent growth since 2015. 
Thailand’s investments in Cambodia have exceeded $2 billion in 2022, while 
Cambodia’s investments in Thailand have increased to $130 million. These investments 
reflect the strength of economic ties and the potential for further collaboration in various 
sectors, including infrastructure, agroindustry, and tourism. 
 Cooperation with Vietnam 
Cambodia and Vietnam have cultivated time-honored friendship and cooperation 
characterized by profound political trust and functional collaboration across sectors. 
Economic cooperation between Cambodia and Vietnam has flourished. The 
collaborative efforts have borne fruit, manifesting in a bilateral trade volume that surged 
beyond $10 billion in 2022. 
Vietnam is one of the critical sources of foreign direct investment in Cambodia, 
distributed across a diverse array of 200 projects, amounting to a total of over $2.9 
billion. 
Cambodia could better exercise its agency and be more resilient by fostering 
cooperation and collaboration with immediate neighbours. Through such proactive 
engagement, Cambodia can navigate a multiplex world and contribute to regional 
development. 
The Mekong countries must uphold rules-based international order, promote open 
and inclusive regionalism, and ensure that diplomacy and dialogue prevail over conflict 
and confrontation.

Simultaneously, Cambodia firmly upholds the principles of the rules-based international 
order while promoting open and inclusive multilateralism. 
Cambodia has been proactive in strengthening cooperation and partnerships with 
its immediate neighbours to maintain regional peace and stability and create new 
economic opportunities for the Kingdom and the region. 
Under the leadership of Prime Minister Hun Manet, Cambodia is going to deepen 
regional integration further- believing that Cambodia’s future or destiny cannot be 
detached from that of the region. Transforming Cambodia into a gateway a hub, or a 
bridging state of the Mekong region is a long-term endeavor. 
Cambodia’s neighbourhood diplomacy is rooted in the fundamental principles of 
mutual respect, mutual understanding, mutual trust, and mutual interest for peace and 
prosperity (M4P2). These principles are the bedrock upon which Cambodia’s foreign 
policy strategy is constructed. Neighbouring countries occupy a central and pivotal 
position within Cambodia’s foreign policy framework. 
 Cooperation with Lao PDR 
Cambodia and Lao PDR share a deep history, cultural values, and identity. This 
strong bond has translated into a growing bilateral trade relationship, reaching USD 210 
million in 2022. 
Furthermore, the active participation of 35 Cambodian companies in Laos 
demonstrates a promising trend of bilateral investment cooperation. 
Notably, Laos plays a pivotal role as a “battery” within the Mekong region. 
Cambodia currently imports approximately 445 megawatts of power from Laos. Looking 
ahead, is anticipated that power trade will surge to a remarkable 6,000 MW by 2030. 
Sustaining and enhancing this trajectory will bolster our energy security and foster 
greater economic prosperity and sustainability for Cambodia and Laos.

 Cooperation with Thailand 
Cambodia and Thailand enjoy a longstanding relationship marked by practical 
cooperation and increasing bilateral trade and investment. 
At a recent bilateral meeting between the two leaders, both sides agreed to 
elevate bilateral trade to $15 billion by 2025. Bilateral trade reached $4.67 billion in 2022, 
demonstrating consistent growth since 2015. 
Thailand’s investments in Cambodia have exceeded $2 billion in 2022, while 
Cambodia’s investments in Thailand have increased to $130 million. These investments 
reflect the strength of economic ties and the potential for further collaboration in various 
sectors, including infrastructure, agroindustry, and tourism. 
 Cooperation with Vietnam 
Cambodia and Vietnam have cultivated time-honored friendship and cooperation 
characterized by profound political trust and functional collaboration across sectors. 
Economic cooperation between Cambodia and Vietnam has flourished. The 
collaborative efforts have borne fruit, manifesting in a bilateral trade volume that surged 
beyond $10 billion in 2022. 
Vietnam is one of the critical sources of foreign direct investment in Cambodia, 
distributed across a diverse array of 200 projects, amounting to a total of over $2.9 
billion. 
Cambodia could better exercise its agency and be more resilient by fostering 
cooperation and collaboration with immediate neighbours. Through such proactive 
engagement, Cambodia can navigate a multiplex world and contribute to regional 
development. 
The Mekong countries must uphold rules-based international order, promote open 
and inclusive regionalism, and ensure that diplomacy and dialogue prevail over conflict 
and confrontation.

Public Sector Innovation, A Key to Cambodia’s 
Pentagonal Strategy 

Cambodia is on the cusp of a transformative journey, and at its heart lies the 
ambitious Pentagonal Strategy Phase One. With well-defined goals and concrete action 
plans, this strategic blueprint is poised to propel the nation forward, guided by five 
essential pillars: human capital development, economic diversification, and 
competitiveness enhancement, private sector growth, resilient, sustainable, and inclusive 
development, and the nurturing of a digital economy and society. 
At the core of this strategy lies a critical imperative – state institutions’ governance 
and institutional modernization. This transformation hinges on three pivotal words: 
“cleanness,” “integrity,” and “trust” in public administration. These qualities are the 
bedrock upon which Cambodia’s future success is built. 
To realize this vision, Cambodia must continuously robustly enhance its leadership 
capacity within the public sector. It involves creating frameworks for leadership 
development, instituting training programs, and fostering networks of capable leaders in 
public administration. This is a fundamental step towards ensuring that our public 
institutions are efficient and responsive to the changing needs of our dynamic society. 
Moreover, we must embark on a journey of public sector reform. This journey is 
multifaceted, encompassing process innovation in decision-making, a robust civil service 
management system, institutional coordination, decentralization, service integration, and 
digital transformation. These reforms, undertaken with determination, will streamline our 
bureaucracy, making it more responsive and accountable to the citizens it serves. 
The Pentagonal Strategy places considerable emphasis on human resource 
development within the public sector. It seeks to implement meritocracy in recruitment, 
appointment, promotion, and incentives. This focus on merit ensures that the best and 
brightest serve in our public institutions, driving efficiency, accountability, and innovation. 
The problem the public sector faces is a low number of technocrats. We need more 
technocrats to drive positive change. 
Speaking of innovation, it is not just a buzzword but a catalyst for progress. 
Innovation means creating something new, something that can be implemented, and 
something that benefits society. 
Contemporary Perspective 
Part I: Cambodia 
P a g e | 42 
Volume IV 
However, the path to innovation is not a straight line but rather an interactive and 
social endeavor that demands time and effort. 
To foster innovation in the public sector, we must first recognize the need for 
public organizations to embrace new ideas, approaches, and work methods in response 
to evolving challenges and the high expectations of our people. Cambodians expect this 
new administration to deliver concrete public sector reform outcomes. The primary 
source of legitimacy of the government is performance. 
Moreover, we must appreciate the intricate interplay between the individual, the 
organization, public administration, and society. In this context, leadership should be 
innovative, data-driven, and people-centric, mirroring the principles of design thinking, 
which places the needs and aspirations of the people at the forefront. Leaders must 
motivate their teams to explore new ideas and experiment with novel approaches while 
building the capacity to collect and analyze data and share knowledge. Knowledge is 
built through social interaction. 
Cross-sectoral and cross-functional collaboration and creativity are essential to 
driving innovation in the public sector. We must strengthen public-private-people 
partnerships to develop innovative solutions addressing our most pressing issues and 
challenges. By working together, we could deliver more as an African proverb says: “If 
you want to go fast, go alone; if you want to go far, go together”. 
Financial commitment to innovation is vital. Allocating budgets for innovation-
related projects and programs is essential, and recruiting external consultants to assess 
and monitor institutional innovation capacity can provide valuable insights. The 
government must use the budget smartly by investing more resources in building 
innovation capacity. 
Lastly, Cambodia should actively seek international cooperation and support in 
public sector innovation. Capacity-building in leadership for innovation can benefit from 
shared knowledge and global best practices. Multi-stakeholder dialogue and consultation 
on leadership for innovation needs to be aggressively promoted. 
The Pentagonal Strategy sets a bold vision for Cambodia’s future. To realize it, 
public sector innovation is not just a nice-to-have but a must-have. By fostering a culture 
of innovation, Cambodia can usher in a new era of efficiency, transparency, and 
progress, ensuring a brighter future for all its citizens. With the right mix of vision,

leadership, and collaboration, Cambodia’s transformation is within reach, and public 
sector innovation is the key to unlocking this promising future.

Fostering Leadership for Good, A Call to Action 

The world stands at a critical juncture, characterized by a deficit in political and 
strategic trust, a diminishing global governance framework, and a waning commitment to 
the rules-based international order. This challenging landscape has witnessed the 
proliferation of wars and conflicts, extending from the conflict in Ukraine to the turmoil in 
the Middle East. Additionally, security concerns loom large in Asia, with notable 
flashpoints in the South China Sea and on the Korean Peninsula, heightening tensions 
in the region. 
Cambodia is currently grappling with a myriad of both internal and external 
challenges. External challenges include escalating geopolitical rivalries, regional 
conflicts, the looming specter of climate crises, all of which collectively challenge 
Cambodia’s resilience and development prospects. 
Domestically, it faces the task of achieving a more robust and resilient economic 
recovery in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, addressing vulnerabilities in the 
real estate sector and financial institutions, promoting public trust in government, and 
combatting the growing issue of inequality. 
Against this backdrop, it is imperative to infuse leadership and innovation into the 
public sector, nurture an environment conducive to supporting businesses, and cultivate 
a substantial pool of human capital. 
In this connection, it is paramount to create an ecosystem that actively supports 
businesses, with a particular emphasis on nurturing micro, small, and medium-sized 
enterprises (MSMEs). These enterprises are the backbone of Cambodia’s economy, and 
by empowering them through financial and infrastructural support, we can drive 
economic growth, create employment opportunities, and ultimately improve the standard 
of living of the Cambodian people. 
Cambodia must proactively position itself ahead of the curve. We must adopt a 
strategic foresight approach, which involves anticipating future trends and opportunities, 
preparing for potential risks, and formulating innovative and transformative strategies to 
address them. This forward-thinking mindset is crucial to ensuring our nation’s resilience 
and adaptability in the face of evolving global and regional dynamics. 
Contemporary Perspective 
Part I: Cambodia 
P a g e | 45 
Volume IV 
Most importantly, what we need is leadership for the greater good. Leadership for 
good encompasses a fusion of four distinct leadership styles: conscious leadership, 
servant leadership, systems leadership, and resonant leadership. 
Conscious Leadership is grounded in the belief that leadership is at the heart of 
every change initiative. During transformative periods, such as the one Cambodia 
currently experiences, where uncertainty and complexity abound, quality leadership is 
indispensable. It has the power to steer us through both upheaval and opportunity. 
Servant leadership acts as the moral compass guiding our nation through an 
increasingly volatile, uncertain, complex, and ambiguous (VUCA) world. Leaders who 
prioritize the greater good ensure that the fruits of transformative change are accessible 
to all citizens, particularly the marginalized and vulnerable. They instill hope and unity, 
fostering a sense of shared purpose and commitment to collective progress. Ethical 
leadership fosters trust between the government and its people, a fundamental element 
for successful change initiatives. 
Systems leadership skills are vital for comprehending the interconnections of 
issues, addressing root causes, and crafting holistic solutions with an eye on long-term 
sustainability. In times of transformative change, these leadership capabilities and 
intelligences—emotional, spiritual, and systems intelligence—jointly contribute to 
effective governance, social cohesion, and a sustainable path forward for the country, 
ensuring that no one is left behind. 
Resonant leadership nurtures emotional intelligence, enabling leaders to connect 
with citizens, inspire hope, and rally collective efforts toward a shared vision. Resonant 
leadership actively involves diverse stakeholders in decision-making, tapping into the 
wisdom of the crowd and garnering support for transformative policies. 
Engaging transformational leaders understand that ownership, learning and 
engagement are key enablers of high performance. Engaging leaders inspire followers 
to put in discretionary effort- to go the extra mile-transcending self-interest for the good 
of the organization and system. They are characterized by a genuine concern for the 
people, and they prioritize organizational health and development, understanding that 
employee wellbeing and growth is inextricably linked to long-term success and 
sustainability. 
The inaugural Leadership for Good Summit, taking place on November 7-8 in 
Phnom Penh, invites stakeholders from the public, private, and civil sectors to reflect, 
Contemporary Perspective 
Part I: Cambodia 
P a g e | 46 
Volume IV 
contemplate, envision, and take decisive steps toward constructing a more inclusive, 
sustainable, and resilient Cambodia through innovative and transformative leadership. 
This summit endeavors to build a community of leaders dedicated to co-creating 
the Cambodia of their dreams. Through constructive dialogue, we aim to unearth our 
collective aspirations, strengths, and challenges and pinpoint opportunities for 
collaborative projects that will have a transformative impact on Cambodia, moving 
forward. 
Ultimately, the goal of the Summit is to inject wisdom, innovative ideas and action 
plans to realize the Cambodia Vision 2050, which envisions Cambodia to be “a vibrant 
society”, “a high-income and resilient economy”, “highly knowledgeable” society, and a 
county that “enjoys harmony, resilience, and inclusivity of physical and natural 
environment, and has a good balance between development and environmental 
conservation”.

Hun Manet’s ASEAN Engagement Strategy 

As Prime Minister Hun Manet’s administration approaches its 100-day milestone 
this month, notable foreign policy accomplishments stand out as key highlights. This op-
ed aims to shed light on Cambodia’s ASEAN engagement strategy, drawing upon Prime 
Minister Hun Manet’s remarks at the ASEAN Summits and related Summits held in 
Indonesia in September. 
This discourse of power illustrates Cambodia’s well-crafted policy towards 
ASEAN. It delves into the strategic narratives and increasing relevant role of Cambodia 
in shaping and molding regional architecture, while positioning Cambodia in the region 
and beyond. 
Obviously, ASEAN stands at a crossroads. By embracing a strategy of inclusivity, 
cooperation, and forward-looking policies, ASEAN can navigate the complexities of the 
current global landscape full of uncertainties and risks. 
The path ahead is really challenging, but with unity, shared strategic vision, and a 
commitment to the principles of ASEAN Centrality, the region might emerge stronger and 
become more resilient, ready to claim its place as the fourth largest world economy in 
coming years. 
 Addressing Geopolitical and Geoeconomic Challenges 
The rising geopolitical and geoeconomic competition poses significant challenges 
for ASEAN. Against this backdrop, cooperation in areas of common interest like trade, 
investment, green economy, and sustainable development is essential to build trust and 
avoid zero-sum outcomes. 
In this connection, a stable relationship among major powers is crucial for 
advancing global agenda. 
“Without a healthy and stable relation among the major powers, it is extremely 
difficult to advance any global agenda. Cambodia will do our utmost ability to contribute 
to strengthening multilateral systems that are inclusive, open, fair, rules-based, 
transparent, and mutually beneficial,” stated Prime Minister Hun Manet. 
 ASEAN Centrality in a Fragmented World 
Contemporary Perspective 
Part I: Cambodia 
P a g e | 48 
Volume IV 
The principle of ASEAN Centrality must be the cornerstone of our approach. 
Cambodia has called upon our dialogue partners to support ASEAN Centrality and 
ASEAN-led mechanisms, fostering a regional environment where every nation, 
regardless of size, can thrive. In this era of a multiplex world, ASEAN’s role as a unifying 
force is more crucial than ever. 
Moreover, ASEAN’s dialogue partners must support core priorities without 
undermining the principles of the ASEAN Outlook on the Indo-Pacific (AOIP)- including 
openness, transparency, inclusivity, a rules-based framework, good governance, respect 
for sovereignty, non-intervention. Cambodia has consistently advocated for inclusive, 
open, fair, and transparent implementation of these principles. 
 A Strategic Vision for Relevance 
To maintain its relevance, ASEAN must adopt a more strategic, proactive 
approach. This involves proactive engagement with global and regional powers and 
international organizations. By doing so, ASEAN can better exercise its agency and 
assert its position on the global stage. 
 Navigating Transnational Challenges 
ASEAN faces a myriad of transnational challenges, from climate change and 
natural disasters to regional development gap. These challenges necessitate a unified 
approach, as no single nation can effectively address them alone. By fostering unity and 
solidarity, ASEAN can turn these challenges into opportunities for regional cooperation 
and integration. 
 Opposing the Use of Force 
ASEAN and the international community must lead in opposing the use or threat 
of force against sovereign states. A concerted effort in this direction is indispensable for 
maintaining regional stability and peace. 
 The ASEAN Outlook on the Indo-Pacific 
Cambodia emphasizes the importance of the ASEAN Outlook on the Indo-Pacific 
(AOIP). It calls for building synergies between various initiatives and the AOIP, ensuring 
they contribute to regional peace, stability, and prosperity, and support ASEAN Centrality. 
Contemporary Perspective 
Part I: Cambodia 
P a g e | 49 
Volume IV 
Prime Minister Hun Manet proposed that “we should continue to focus on working 
together to advance the four priority areas of the AOIP through practical and concrete 
projects”. 
“We welcome any initiatives to support the AOIP as long as: (1) they contribute to 
regional peace, stability and prosperity, (2) they are not used against any country, and 
(3) they support the ASEAN Centrality, and are in line with the ASEAN Charter and the 
AOIP,” he added. 
 Myanmar’s Path to Peace 
In Myanmar, ASEAN can provide support but should not impose solutions. The 
country must lead its own peace process, with ASEAN supporting decisions emerging 
from a consensus among Myanmar’s parties concerned. This approach requires 
patience, pragmatism, and flexibility. 
Prime Minister Hun Manet stressed that “for the dialogue to succeed, the parties 
concerned must be committed to finding a solution – including those who are key to the 
peace process – and do their utmost to build trust and promote a convergence of views. 
Undoubtedly, the road ahead will be difficult, and require a high degree of patience, 
pragmatism and flexibility”. 
 Leveraging RCEP for Growth 
The Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) is a landmark 
agreement that can catalyze ASEAN’s economic growth. By effectively leveraging this 
partnership, ASEAN can ensure that the benefits of economic integration are equitably 
shared among its people, which in turn would transform region into an epicenter of 
growth and dynamism. 
Cambodia believes that the RCEP is a catalyst for regional economic growth and 
integration. It is crucial that all RCEP members implement this partnership fully and 
effectively, maximizing its potential benefits. 
 The Potential of Digital Economy 
The digital economy presents a remarkable potential for ASEAN and its partners. 
Expected to add $2 trillion to the regional GDP by 2030, this burgeoning sector offers a 
pathway to accelerate development and bridge economic disparities. To fully capitalize 
Contemporary Perspective 
Part I: Cambodia 
P a g e | 50 
Volume IV 
on this, ASEAN must foster practical cooperation, ensuring that its citizens are equipped 
with necessary skills and knowledge to thrive in this digital era. 
Prime Minister Hun Manet underscored that “while the digital economy is 
presenting great potential for ASEAN and its partners, we need to identify and seize this 
opportunity for practical cooperation to accelerate digital development.” 
 Inclusive and Integrated ASEAN 
For ASEAN to become a global growth epicenter, especially against a weakened 
and fragmented global economy, it must explore new sources of growth. This includes 
digital transformation, green transitions, and capitalizing on the blue and creative 
economies. Significantly increasing intra-ASEAN investments in these key sectors is 
crucial for deeper regional integration. 
ASEAN must underscore its commitment to being inclusive and people-centered. 
Effective implementation of initiatives like Work Plan IV for the Initiative for ASEAN 
Integration is vital. These efforts will ensure that the benefits of growth and integration 
are accessible to all ASEAN citizens. 
 The Post-2025 Vision 
The High-Level Task Force working on the Post-2025 Vision for the ASEAN 
Community must propose bold, yet pragmatic, ideas. These ideas should enhance 
cross-sectoral coordination among the community’s pillars, ensuring that ASEAN 
remains forward-looking, future-proofed, and ready for upcoming challenges and 
opportunities. 
 ASEAN’s Role in the Global Supply Chain 
As a key player in the global supply chain, ASEAN presents myriad opportunities 
for businesses of all sizes. From large corporations to small and medium enterprises and 
startups, the region’s vibrant economic landscape offers fertile ground for innovation and 
growth.

The principle of ASEAN Centrality must be the cornerstone of our approach. 
Cambodia has called upon our dialogue partners to support ASEAN Centrality and 
ASEAN-led mechanisms, fostering a regional environment where every nation, 
regardless of size, can thrive. In this era of a multiplex world, ASEAN’s role as a unifying 
force is more crucial than ever. 
Moreover, ASEAN’s dialogue partners must support core priorities without 
undermining the principles of the ASEAN Outlook on the Indo-Pacific (AOIP)- including 
openness, transparency, inclusivity, a rules-based framework, good governance, respect 
for sovereignty, non-intervention. Cambodia has consistently advocated for inclusive, 
open, fair, and transparent implementation of these principles. 
 A Strategic Vision for Relevance 
To maintain its relevance, ASEAN must adopt a more strategic, proactive 
approach. This involves proactive engagement with global and regional powers and 
international organizations. By doing so, ASEAN can better exercise its agency and 
assert its position on the global stage. 
 Navigating Transnational Challenges 
ASEAN faces a myriad of transnational challenges, from climate change and 
natural disasters to regional development gap. These challenges necessitate a unified 
approach, as no single nation can effectively address them alone. By fostering unity and 
solidarity, ASEAN can turn these challenges into opportunities for regional cooperation 
and integration. 
 Opposing the Use of Force 
ASEAN and the international community must lead in opposing the use or threat 
of force against sovereign states. A concerted effort in this direction is indispensable for 
maintaining regional stability and peace. 
 The ASEAN Outlook on the Indo-Pacific 
Cambodia emphasizes the importance of the ASEAN Outlook on the Indo-Pacific 
(AOIP). It calls for building synergies between various initiatives and the AOIP, ensuring 
they contribute to regional peace, stability, and prosperity, and support ASEAN Centrality.

Prime Minister Hun Manet proposed that “we should continue to focus on working 
together to advance the four priority areas of the AOIP through practical and concrete 
projects”.

regional peace, stability and prosperity, (2) they are not used against any country, and

AOIP,” he added.

In Myanmar, ASEAN can provide support but should not impose solutions. The 
country must lead its own peace process, with ASEAN supporting decisions emerging 
from a consensus among Myanmar’s parties concerned. This approach requires 
patience, pragmatism, and flexibility.

concerned must be committed to finding a solution – including those who are key to the 
peace process – and do their utmost to build trust and promote a convergence of views. 
Undoubtedly, the road ahead will be difficult, and require a high degree of patience, 
pragmatism and flexibility”.

The Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) is a landmark 
agreement that can catalyze ASEAN’s economic growth. By effectively leveraging this 
partnership, ASEAN can ensure that the benefits of economic integration are equitably 
shared among its people, which in turn would transform region into an epicenter of 
growth and dynamism.

integration. It is crucial that all RCEP members implement this partnership fully and 
effectively, maximizing its potential benefits.

Cambodia’s Parliamentary Diplomacy in a New Era 

At the dawn of a transformative phase, Cambodia is steering a new course in both 
its domestic reforms and foreign policy dynamics, following a pivotal transition in its 
executive and legislative leadership. In this evolving landscape, the role of parliamentary 
diplomacy emerges as a critical element, especially amidst escalating global geopolitical 
tensions and conflicts. 
Parliamentary diplomacy encompasses the diverse international efforts made by 
parliamentarians aimed at enhancing mutual comprehension among nations, aiding in 
the enhancement of government oversight and people’s representation, and bolstering 
the democratic validity of inter-governmental organizations. 
Compared to executive diplomacy, parliamentary diplomacy holds distinct 
benefits. These include greater adaptability in engaging with a wide range of local 
players and the ability to communicate more freely, even on delicate matters. This 
approach is reshaping the traditional view of diplomacy and helping to bridge the 
democratic gap in foreign policy decision-making. 
Under the leadership of Samdech Khuon Sudary, Cambodia’s parliamentary 
diplomacy is gaining remarkable momentum. This new wave of diplomatic activism is 
evident in bilateral and multilateral interactions and consistent strategic narratives. 
Remarkably, over the past three months, she has met 24 foreign leaders and diplomats. 
Cambodia’s parliamentary diplomacy was at full play when Cambodia hosted the 
President of the Republic of Korea’s National Assembly, Kim Jin Pyo, in early September. 
Both sides amicably, openly, and candidly exchanged views on regional issues of mutual 
interest and underscored a shared political will and commitment to boost comprehensive 
bilateral cooperation, particularly between the two legislatures. 
Moreover, productive discussions with Thai Prime Minister Srettha Thavisin in late 
September highlighted Cambodia’s dedication to nurturing its ‘good neighbor’ diplomacy. 
Immediate neighbors are central to Cambodia’s foreign policy strategy. To further this 
objective, Khuon Sudary will lead a high-level delegation to Vietnam and Lao PDR later 
this month to reinforce traditional ties and deepen the scope of comprehensive 
cooperation between Cambodia and its neighbors. 
Recent interactions and dialogues with foreign leaders and diplomats, coupled 
with the public statements by the President of the National Assembly, highlight the

evolution of Cambodia’s parliamentary diplomacy around seven key pillars. These pillars 
represent Cambodia’s aspirations and its commitment to contribute to international 
peace, harmony and prosperity- driven by a dual focus: to advance Cambodia’s core 
national interests and to contribute meaningfully to the broader goals of humanity. 
Firstly, economic diplomacy stands at the vanguard. In an era where economies 
are increasingly interconnected, Cambodia’s legislature is pivotal in steering the nation 
towards seamless regional and global integration. This approach is not just about 
participating in the global economy; it’s about strategically maximizing the benefits and 
opportunities stemming from globalization and regionalization. By enhancing market 
access and competitiveness, Cambodia can position itself as a dynamic player in the 
international market. 
The forthcoming inaugural Cambodia-Lao PDR-Vietnam Parliamentary Summit, 
scheduled to take place early next month in Vientiane, presents an opportunity for the 
Cambodian parliament to exercise its agency and leadership role. This summit aims to 
bolster the synergy between legislative and executive branches, enhancing their 
combined efforts to meet shared development goals especially in the areas of cross-
border trade, investment, and tourism, the building of resilient regional supply chains 
particularly in the agriculture sector, and the promotion of sustainable development. This 
summit is set to be a landmark event in fostering regional cooperation and connectivity. 
The second pillar, peace diplomacy, combines the quest for economic 
advancement with the preservation of peace. In a global landscape often marred by 
strife, Cambodia’s journey provides valuable insights for managing crises and resolving 
conflicts. The ‘win-win’ approach, championed by ex-Prime Minister Samdech Hun Sen, 
serves as valuable experiences and lessons learned for others. Along this line, the 
National Assembly President frequently emphasizes to international colleagues that 
peace is a prerequisite for development, just as development is essential for sustaining 
peace. The parliament plays increasingly relevant role in promoting peace. 
Cultural diplomacy, the third pillar, underscores the power of cultural exchanges in 
building bridges. In an increasingly polarized world, Cambodia is leveraging the universal 
language of culture to foster understanding and trust between different civilizations. This 
effort goes beyond mere cultural promotion; it’s about creating the relational bedrock 
upon which economic and political alliances can be built. 
Notably, Khuon Sudary also serves as the Chairwoman of the Asian Cultural 
Council- a platform that she utilizes to promote culture as a cornerstone for fostering 
Contemporary Perspective 
Part I: Cambodia 
P a g e | 53 
Volume IV 
peace, spurring development, and igniting innovation. Her leadership emphasizes the 
vital role of cultural understanding and exchange in shaping a more harmonious, 
prosperous, and sustainable future. 
The fourth pillar, people diplomacy, underscores the essential role of 
parliamentarians as the voice of the people. By emphasizing direct connections between 
individuals and communities, Cambodia can promote a more inclusive and participatory 
approach to international relations. This approach is especially crucial in today’s world, 
where the perspectives and voices of ordinary citizens can be overshadowed by high-
level political dialogues. Cambodia’s focus on people-to-people and person-to-person 
diplomacy aims to ensure that the voices of the people and key stakeholders are not only 
heard but are also integral in shaping global discourse and world order. Inter-personal 
relationships and friendships especially between leaders is critical to promoting mutual 
understanding and trust between nations. 
The fifth pillar focuses on gender equality and women’s empowerment. As the first 
female President of the National Assembly, she has significantly amplified her efforts to 
foster international cooperation, particularly among parliamentarians, to advance 
Sustainable Development Goal 5. Addressing the National Forum on ‘Women in 
Leadership and Governance’ this month, she advocated for the expansion of cross-
sectoral partnerships and networks to support women in areas like capacity building and 
leadership development, thereby empowering them to take on more prominent roles in 
governance and decision-making processes. 
The sixth pillar centers on the critical intersection of climate change and the water-
energy-food security nexus. Recognizing the urgency of these interconnected 
challenges, she has emphasized the need for more robust international collaboration to 
address climate change through both mitigation and adaptation strategies while also 
advocating for stronger inter-parliamentary cooperation on climate change. This 
cooperation is key to effectively managing the interconnected issues of water, energy, 
and food security, ensuring a sustainable and resilient future. 
Finally, the development of a digital parliament marks a significant leap towards 
good governance- which includes the principles of transparency and accountability. As 
Cambodia transitions into digital economy and society, the digital transformation of the 
legislative branch is not just a technological upgrade; it’s a commitment to more 
accessible, efficient, responsive, transparent and people-centered governance. By 
equipping parliamentary staff and lawmakers with the tools and knowledge to navigate 
Contemporary Perspective

P a g e | 54 
Volume IV 
the digital landscape, Cambodia is setting a precedent for the future of parliamentary 
work. 
During the meeting with foreign counterparts, the National Assembly President 
has actively sought support and collaboration with international partners to foster the 
development of a digital parliament, encompassing not only the advancement of 
hardware and software but also the cultivation of human capital. 
Cambodia’s embrace of parliamentary diplomacy under the new leadership 
presents a dynamic and proactive approach to international relations, while setting a 
precedent for how nations can engage internationally in a more inclusive, democratic, 
and people-centered manner.

A Multi-Faceted Challenge and Strategic Response

Cambodia’s Fight Against Non-Communicable Diseases, 
A Multi-Faceted Challenge and Strategic Response 

Cambodia’s struggle against non-communicable diseases (NCDs) highlights a 
significant health challenge faced by many developing countries. These chronic 
diseases, which include cardiovascular diseases, cancer, chronic respiratory diseases, 
diabetes, and mental health conditions, are primarily driven by a combination of genetic, 
environmental, and behavioral factors. The prevalence of these diseases is increasing 
globally, and they now account for seven out of the ten leading causes of death 
worldwide. 
In Cambodia, the prevalence of NCDs is not only a health issue but also an 
economic concern. NCDs are responsible for 64 percent of all deaths in Cambodia, and 
the population has a 23 percent probability of dying between the ages 30 and 70 years from 
one of the four main NCDs. The total economic burden of NCDs to the Cambodian 
economy is $1.5 billion per year, equivalent to 6.6 percent of the country’s annual gross 
domestic product (GDP). 
This situation necessitates a multifaceted approach, integrating health 
interventions with broader economic and social policies. 
A multi-faceted and multi-pronged approach is vital for safeguarding the health 
and well-being of the population, sustaining economic growth, fulfilling the 2030 UN 
Sustainable Development Goals, and realizing Cambodia Vision 2050. 
In March 2019, the Cambodian NCD Alliance (CNCDA) was launched to intensify 
efforts against the escalating challenge of NCDs, while fostering a new wave of 
cooperative efforts. This informal alliance brings together 22 diverse entities, including 
civil society organizations, bilateral and multilateral agencies, academic and research 
institutions, relevant governmental departments, and patient advocacy groups. It 
introduced a comprehensive 3-year Strategic Plan (2020-2023), structured around four core 
objectives: advocacy, knowledge exchange, collaboration, and monitoring. 
In 2013, the National Strategy Plan (NSP) for Prevention and Control of NCDs 
was introduced, which seeks to scale up screening, cost-effective care, and treatment. 
Contemporary Perspective 
Part I: Cambodia 
P a g e | 56 
Volume IV 
Targeting at-risk people over 40 with routine check-ups can provide early detection before 
diseases become unmanageable and untreatable. 
The National Assembly of Cambodia has been active in campaigning against 
NCDs. In a recent address at the consultation workshop on preventive measures on 
NCDs and gender Gap reduction in Phnom Penh, the President of the National 
Assembly, Samdech Khuon Sudary, called for a comprehensive national campaign to 
mitigate NCD risk factors through societal behavioral changes and lifestyle modifications. 
President Sudary outlined a strategic ten-point action plan as following: 
First, acknowledging complexity: Recognize NCDs as multifaceted challenges 
that intersect various sectors, including healthcare, education, the economy, agriculture, 
trade, society, culture, environment, and gender. 
Second, elevating public awareness: Intensify public education on NCD risk 
factors and prevention, with a special focus on women. This involves a holistic health 
promotion strategy that goes beyond basic awareness to include environmental 
modifications, technological integration, and community mobilization for reaching hard-
to-reach populations. 
Third, launching “Healthy Life, Healthy Cambodia”: Initiate a campaign to educate 
citizens about maintaining a healthy lifestyle, emphasizing nutritious diets and regular 
physical activity. 
Fourth, fostering Multi-Stakeholder Partnerships: Encourage collaboration across 
various entities for data collection, research, knowledge sharing, and ensuring healthcare 
accessibility, particularly for women. 
Fifth, strengthening Public-Private Partnerships: Enhance collaboration between 
the public sector and the private sector on research, development and innovation in 
medicine, aiming to improve affordability and accessibility, especially within the context 
of health crises or emergencies. 
Sixth, implementing the Ministry of Health’s Multi-Sectoral Action Plan: Advocate 
for the promotion and effective execution of the Ministry of Health’s Multi-sectoral Action 
Plan for NCD Prevention and Control (2018-2027), with an emphasis on gender-specific 
health issues. 
Contemporary Perspective 
Part I: Cambodia 
P a g e | 57 
Volume IV 
Seventh, implementing the National Salt Reduction Action Plan: Ensure the 
successful implementation of the 2021-2027 National Action Plan for Salt Reduction. This 
includes public education on the dangers of high salt consumption, regulatory measures 
to lower salt in processed foods, and partnerships with the food industry to promote low-
salt products. 
Eight, enforcing health-related laws and regulations: Urge the Ministry of Health 
and other relevant ministries to rigorously enforce regulations pertaining to food safety 
and public health, including the control of alcohol and tobacco consumption. 
Ninth, developing legal frameworks: Propose comprehensive studies to establish 
legal frameworks governing alcohol consumption, focusing on aspects such as the 
minimum age for purchase and consumption, restrictions on sale times, and regulation 
of advertising for alcoholic and high-sugar beverages. 
Tenth, increasing taxes on harmful substances: Collaborate between the Ministry 
of Health and the Ministry of Economy and Finance to raise taxes on alcohol, tobacco, 
and sugar-rich drinks, aiming to reduce consumption of these harmful substances. 
These proposals reflect a robust, multidimensional approach to combatting NCDs 
in Cambodia, highlighting the need for integrated efforts across various sectors and 
levels of governance. Health promotion extends beyond informing the community on 
what they can or cannot do to improve their own health – it calls for a holistic approach 
that encompasses modifying the built environment, leveraging data and technology, and 
rallying communities and volunteers to support the health of the hard-to-reach community 
members. 
While Cambodia’s response to the NCD crisis is evolving, there is a clear need for 
more coordinated, comprehensive strategies that transcend healthcare boundaries. This 
includes enforcing public health regulations, developing legal frameworks for alcohol and 
tobacco control, and increasing taxes on harmful substances including sugar-rich 
beverages. 
Success in this endeavor will not only improve health outcomes but also contribute 
to sustainable economic growth and the realization of Cambodia Vision 2050- to become a 
high-income country.

What to Expect in 2024? 

We are not out of the woods yet. The year 2024 remains in a state of a perfect 
storm. 
The global economy and geopolitical landscape are in a state of flux, with old 
paradigms being challenged and new ones emerging. This will undoubtedly be a period 
of multiple transitions, a time for cautious navigation through the choppy waters of global 
affairs. 
It is a moment for policymakers, businesses, and individuals alike to be agile, 
adaptable, and prepared for a journey through uncharted waters. 
The emergence of the new COVID-19 variant JN.1 is causing a new wave of 
infections worldwide. The pandemic, which has stretched over several years now, 
continues to exert unprecedented pressure on healthcare systems, with new infections 
and the need for ongoing vaccination and booster campaigns. 
The impacts of the pandemic have been far-reaching, exacerbating existing 
inequalities. In 2023, we witnessed how the crisis deepened disparities across various 
spheres. The economic fallout disproportionately affected the lower-income groups, 
widening the income gap. Job losses and reduced incomes became more prevalent 
among the less privileged. 
Environmental degradation and climate-related disasters have hit the poorer 
communities harder, who often lack the resources and infrastructure to deal with such 
calamities. 
Conflicts and wars have added complexity to the crisis. Geopolitical tensions and 
internal strife in various parts of the world have led to humanitarian crises, with millions 
of people displaced from their homes, adding to the global burden of inequality and 
suffering. 
Geopolitical instability emerges as a key global threat, casting a long shadow over 
global economic growth, with ramifications that transcend national borders. 
In this global chess game, certain regions are emerging as critical theaters. The 
Asia Pacific region, with its three security hotspots – the Taiwan Straits, the Korean 
Peninsula, and the South China Sea – is set to become more complex and volatile this 
year. 
Contemporary Perspective 
Part I: Cambodia 
P a g e | 59 
Volume IV 
The US-China competition further complicates the existing intricate geopolitical 
map. The relationship between these two global powerhouses is anticipated to be 
increasingly unpredictable, unstable, and volatile, underpinned by the extensive 
interconnectedness of the current global system. 
While the risk of a full-scale military confrontation between these two competing 
giants remains minimal, the undercurrents of this rivalry will have far-reaching 
implications for global stability and economic growth. 
This perfect storm has catalyzed a seismic shift in international trading patterns 
and growth prospects. The quest for national security and greater economic resilience 
has become a driving force, reshaping global trade and capital flows. 
This new world order is opening up novel investment frontiers across emerging 
markets and Asia, offering a silver lining in the midst of global challenges. China – is 
likely to regain its footing after a year of slower growth. The stabilization of the Chinese 
economy in 2024 will be a crucial factor in the global economic recovery. 
The world economic outlook is projected to achieve a modest growth of 2.7% in 
2024 and rebound to 3% in 2025. 
Democracies worldwide are bracing for an acid test as authoritarian inclinations 
and populist movements gain momentum, challenging the established order and 
potentially altering the global geopolitical landscape. 
Populist movements, often characterized by their appeal to the general populace 
over the elite and their emphasis on nationalistic policies, are gaining momentum across 
the globe. 
The rise in protectionism, a byproduct of this populist surge, further complicates 
the global economic and political landscape. Countries are more frequently looking 
inward, focusing on protecting their own industries and workforce, often at the expense 
of international trade and cooperation. 
The upcoming elections in the U.S. are anticipated to be among the most 
contentious and polarized in its history. Some have called it the “poisonous” elections. 
The US will be more protectionist, inward-looking. As a result, the US will be weaker, not 
stronger. 
For Cambodia, the economic outlook is quite resilient, with a projected growth 
rate surpassing 6 percent, supported by several key sectors. 
Contemporary Perspective 
Part I: Cambodia 
P a g e | 60 
Volume IV 
One of the most significant contributors to Cambodia’s robust growth has been 
the resurgence of its tourism sector. Cambodia has witnessed a substantial increase in 
tourist arrivals, and the trend will continue. 
The country’s rich cultural heritage, exemplified by the iconic Angkor Wat, coupled 
with its natural beauty, has once again made it a popular destination. This revival has not 
only boosted revenues but also stimulated associated sectors such as hospitality, retail, 
and transportation. 
Another key driver of growth has been the rise in domestic consumption. As the 
Cambodian economy recovers, consumer confidence has rebounded, leading to 
increased spending on goods and services. This upswing in domestic consumption 
reflects the growing purchasing power of the Cambodian populace, a positive indicator 
of economic health and stability. 
The diversification of the manufacturing sector has also played a pivotal role. 
While Cambodia has traditionally been known for its garment manufacturing, there has 
been a notable expansion in non-garment sectors. This diversification has made the 
economy more resilient. 
The influx of FDI has been another cornerstone of Cambodia’s economic success. 
Attracted by the country’s stable political environment, competitive labor costs, and 
strategic location in Southeast Asia, foreign investors have been keen to capitalize on 
the opportunities present in various sectors such as manufacturing and agro-industry. 
Lastly, substantial investments in infrastructure have significantly contributed to 
Cambodia’s growth. The government’s focus on improving roads, ports, and power 
supplies has made the country more attractive to foreign investors and has played a 
crucial role in supporting the other growth drivers, like tourism and manufacturing. 
While we continue to walk in the dark woods entering 2024, we must always stay 
hopeful. It is an invitation for us to reimagine the future, to build a world that is more 
resilient, inclusive, and sustainable. 
We can chart a course towards a brighter, more prosperous horizon. Cambodia 
needs to boost up reform momentum, with concrete results. People are waiting to see 
reform outcomes. We need to speed up before it is too late. 
Governance and leadership reforms are expected to gain new momentum. More 
corrupt officials are expected to be punished.

The Evolving Landscape of Nation-Building 

Nation-building represents a dynamic process wherein the institutional and 
cultural elements continually interact and evolve. The success of this endeavour hinges 
on the harmonious alignment of these dimensions, with mutual reinforcement. 
A robust and effective state institution relies on a unified national identity to secure 
the loyalty and social contract- people’s trust in the state institutions. Conversely, a 
strong and cohesive national identity is best preserved and celebrated within the 
framework of a well-functioning state. 
In an era defined by technological revolution, the traditional concept of nation-
building is undergoing a profound transformation. 
The core elements of nation-building, encompassing identity, legitimacy, 
penetration, participation, and distribution, continue to hold relevance in this evolving 
landscape. 
Originally conceived as a process of national integration and consolidation leading 
to the establishment of the modern nation-state, nation-building now grapples with new 
challenges and opportunities in the digital age. 
Within this digital age, it is crucial to encourage and empower active engagement 
and inputs from individuals in matters pertaining to state governance by allowing citizens 
to have a voice and leverage in the decision-making process. A people-centred 
governance is fundamental to advancing nation-building. 
Moreover, the notion of “Smart Nation” has become an integral part of nation-
building, where technology empowers citizens to impact changes and connect. The 
Smart Nation represents a future where boundaries are transcended, and digital 
solutions benefit people and businesses across borders. 
Singapore launched “Smart Nation” strategy in 2014 aiming to “support better 
living, stronger communities, and create more opportunities, for all”, focusing on three 
pillars: digital society, digital economy, and digital government. 
In Cambodia, a nation that has endured prolonged periods of war and internal 
conflict, the process of nation-building took a unique path. After achieving peace and 
national reunification in the late 1990s, Cambodia embarked on a journey of economic 
and social integration, bringing together people from diverse backgrounds. As a result, 
Contemporary Perspective 
Part I: Cambodia 
P a g e | 63 
Volume IV 
peace and order, cultural identity, social harmony, and economic development are the 
key elements of nation building. 
According to Cambodian academician Gaffar Peang-Meth, Khmer values, such 
as korup (respect), kaowd-klach (admiration and fear), smoh trang (loyalty), bamreur 
(service), and karpier (defense), persist as pillars of Cambodian society, shaping its 
character and guiding its interactions even in the contemporary context. 
He added, for the Khmer people, the process of nation-building can be aptly 
described as a continuous journey of “re-building”, “reviving”, and “rebranding”. It entails 
preserving and revitalizing their national and cultural identities, adapting to change, and 
ensuring the enduring legacy of the Khmer nation. 
Technology is driving the next phase of nation-building. Cambodia is forced to 
harness digital technology to its advantage, enhancing its strengths and overcoming 
challenges. The transformation brought by digitalization is pervasive, necessitating 
policies, legislations, and public-private cooperation to ensure success. 
In this digital era, businesses are spurred to invest in technology and talent, while 
individuals are empowered to cultivate their talents and embrace digital technologies for 
better lives. The state needs to adapt and respond to these changes. 
As we navigate the digital frontier, it is evident that nation-building is no longer 
confined to the traditional parameters of statehood and identity. 
For instance, the Smart Nation concept and Cambodia’s unique journey 
underscore the importance of adaptability and innovation in the face of evolving 
challenges and opportunities. In this digital age, the path to nation-building is very much 
shaped by technology. 
Cambodia launched the Digital Economy and Society Policy Framework 2021-
2035 in 2021 aimed at fortifying digital ecosystem, ensuring its resilience in the face of 
crises, and enabling agile responses to the ever-evolving digital technology landscape. 
Moreover, Digital Government Policy 2022-2035 was introduced in 2022 to 
establish a digital government that enhances citizens’ quality of life and fosters public 
trust through the provision of excellent public services. 
In Cambodia, the trajectory of nation-building in a digital age is driven by the four 
unfolding initiatives. 
Contemporary Perspective 
Part I: Cambodia 
P a g e | 64 
Volume IV 
First, the digital economy has emerged as a potent force, propelling businesses to 
redirect their investments into cutting-edge technology and the acquisition of top-tier 
talent. 
Businesses, fuelled by the digital revolution, have the potential to expand their 
horizons, forging regional and global connections. Digital trade, e-commerce and digital 
payments are gaining pace. 
Second, within the realm of the digital society, individuals find themselves 
empowered by possessing the tools and opportunities to cultivate their skills and harness 
the latest technological advancements. 
As a collective force, individuals in this digital era can elevate their voices and 
opinion, using technology to address societal challenges, and create a more inclusive 
future. But the government and the private sector need to promote inclusive digital 
economy to ensure that no one is left behind in digital transformation. 
Third, concerning digital government, it is important to enhance the efficiency, 
accountability, and transparency of the state institutions – delivering better public 
services and ensuring that the voices of the people are valued and integrated into the 
decision-making processes. 
Fourth, the development of a digital parliament – still in a nascent stage – aims to 
overhaul and modernize the legislative body and process, ensuring efficiency, 
accountability, and transparency through digital adoption and transformation. 
Digital parliament is designed to better serve the evolving needs and aspirations 
of the people. It is expected that through technology and digital platforms the lawmakers 
will be able to engage with their constituents more effectively and swiftly, leverage data-
driven policy design and decision making, and streamline legislative procedures to 
address emerging social, economic, and environmental issues. 
To realise the four pillars above, Cambodia needs to invest more resources in 
research and development, innovation, and human capital development, while promoting 
robust multi-stakeholder dialogues and consultations and developing strategic foresight. 
Moreover, data accessibility, cybersecurity, and data privacy occupy a pivotal role 
in safeguarding digital transformation. Public agencies should make data sets accessible 
to the public, fostering a collaborative environment for digital solutions that benefit 
society at large.

Cambodia’s Economic Diplomacy Gains Momentum 

Economics determines politics. Economic security is national security. Economic 
performance defines regime legitimacy. 
As a small and open economy, open and inclusive regionalism and international 
economic integration are the strategic compass of the Kingdom. 
Against this backdrop, the new administration in Cambodia has exhibited a 
noticeable shift in its foreign policy priorities, focusing on economic considerations. It can 
be argued that economic pragmatism is one of the key features of Cambodia’s foreign 
policy in a new era. 
Cambodia’s economic diplomacy has been remarkably gaining momentum under 
the leadership of Prime Minister Hun Manet. His relentless efforts to achieve national 
economic interests can be seen in numerous overseas visits and his meetings with 
foreign guests in the capital, all with the primary objective of economically connecting 
Cambodia with the world. 
Each overseas visit demonstrates Cambodia’s economic pragmatism and 
strategic diversification strategy to extract the maximum benefits from existing bilateral 
and multilateral mechanisms to advance Cambodia’s economic interests. In other words, 
how to transform the international environment and partnerships into a source of national 
growth and strength. 
In 2021, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation unveiled a 
comprehensive economic diplomacy strategy (2021-2023). This strategy sets ambitious 
goals, including the promotion of international trade, attracting foreign direct investment, 
boosting tourism, and promoting Cambodia’s cultural identity. 
The strategy underlines the importance of establishing a robust and efficient 
mechanism that would sustain and further enhance the country’s economic growth by 
fostering multi-sectoral and multi-stakeholder collaboration on both national and 
international fronts. Systemic approaches are required. 
The key challenges identified in the strategy include insufficient qualified human 
resource, insufficient financial resource to carry out the implementation of relevant action 
plans, lack of cross sectoral coordination and an effective information sharing platform 
Contemporary Perspective 
Part I: Cambodia 
P a g e | 67 
Volume IV 
between the relevant actors, and lack of nation branding campaigns and lobbying 
activities. 
Looking ahead, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation is in 
the process of crafting a new economic diplomacy framework- being designed to adapt 
to evolving national and international situations while aligning with the strategic 
objectives of the Pentagonal Strategy. Despite strong backing from top-level political 
leadership, the effective implementation of economic diplomacy still presents challenges 
at the working level. 
The linchpin of Cambodia’s economic diplomacy lies in domestic reforms. To fulfil 
its vision of attracting more investments, it is important to keep improving investment and 
business environment. Only through these results-based reforms and substantial 
improvements can the nation fully realize its economic potential and its vision to become 
a high-income country by 2050. 
Notably, good governance takes centre stage in the Pentagonal Strategy Phase 
One, making it the core element of Cambodia’s economic diplomacy. Ensuring clean, 
smart, and efficient public institutions, and a fair, just and efficient legal system is critical 
here. 
The Pentagonal Strategy underscores the importance of improving the quality of 
public institutions at both national and sub-national levels to ensure efficiency of public 
services, strengthening private sector governance, and fostering favourable environment 
for business, investment, and trade. More concrete results are expected. 
The new investment law adopted in 2021 provides new incentives, better 
guarantees, and easier procedures to attract more investments. Sectors entitled to 
investment incentives include those related to high-tech industries, digital technology, 
green technology, manufacturing, agriculture, agro-industry, education, health, and 
infrastructure. 
Cambodia recognizes that expanding international trade requires a multifaceted 
strategy. In recent years, the Kingdom has actively pursued this goal through strategic 
trade negotiations, achieving significant milestones such as the conclusion of two free 
trade agreements with China and the Republic of Korea. 
Moreover, Cambodia played a crucial role in the negotiation of the Regional 
Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) which was launched during its 
Contemporary Perspective 
Part I: Cambodia 
P a g e | 68 
Volume IV 
chairmanship of ASEAN in 2012. After eight years of intensive negotiation, RCEP was 
concluded in 2021 and entered into force in 2022. 
To further this endeavour, Cambodia is now working on instituting robust trade 
promotion policies, underpinned by an effective implementation mechanism. This 
strategic move aims to create an environment conducive to fostering trade relationships 
and removing barriers that impede the flow of goods and services. 
In the wake of Cambodia’s ambitious journey towards digital transformation, 
digital trade is emerging as a component of the nation’s foreign trade strategy. Digital 
trade, relatively new to Cambodia, refers to commercial activities facilitated through 
electronic means, relying on telecommunications and information and communication 
technology (ICT) services. It encompasses a broad spectrum, including trade in goods 
and services. 
It needs to be noted that the success of Cambodia’s international trade strategy 
hinges not only on negotiations and policies but also on the development of a supportive 
ecosystem for Cambodian entrepreneurs and exporters. This ecosystem is indispensable 
for nurturing local businesses and enabling them to penetrate and thrive in the highly 
competitive international market. 
Small and medium-sized enterprises play an important role in this regard. SMEs 
need more government’s support in access to finance and market, capacity building 
digital literacy and digital marketing, and innovation capacity enhancement such as 
product, service, and process innovation. 
Cambodia’s economic diplomacy is on an upward trajectory, guided by a 
comprehensive strategy and driven by visionary, transformative leadership. However, to 
fully unlock its potential, Cambodia must continuously, robustly implement public sector 
reforms especially-with a focus on good governance and the war on corruption- and 
continue to foster an environment conducive to business, investment, and trade. 
More resources are needed to invest in economic intelligence- collecting and 
analysing economic data, leadership development and capacity building in relation to 
economic diplomacy, nation branding, and strategic lobbying.

Cambodia with the world.

strategic diversification strategy to extract the maximum benefits from existing bilateral 
and multilateral mechanisms to advance Cambodia’s economic interests. In other words, 
how to transform the international environment and partnerships into a source of national 
growth and strength. 
In 2021, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation unveiled a 
comprehensive economic diplomacy strategy (2021-2023). This strategy sets ambitious 
goals, including the promotion of international trade, attracting foreign direct investment, 
boosting tourism, and promoting Cambodia’s cultural identity. 
The strategy underlines the importance of establishing a robust and efficient 
mechanism that would sustain and further enhance the country’s economic growth by 
fostering multi-sectoral and multi-stakeholder collaboration on both national and 
international fronts. Systemic approaches are required. 
The key challenges identified in the strategy include insufficient qualified human 
resource, insufficient financial resource to carry out the implementation of relevant action 
plans, lack of cross sectoral coordination and an effective information sharing platform

objectives of the Pentagonal Strategy. Despite strong backing from top-level political 
leadership, the effective implementation of economic diplomacy still presents challenges 
at the working level. 
The linchpin of Cambodia’s economic diplomacy lies in domestic reforms. To fulfil 
its vision of attracting more investments, it is important to keep improving investment and 
business environment. Only through these results-based reforms and substantial 
improvements can the nation fully realize its economic potential and its vision to become 
a high-income country by 2050. 
Notably, good governance takes centre stage in the Pentagonal Strategy Phase 
One, making it the core element of Cambodia’s economic diplomacy. Ensuring clean, 
smart, and efficient public institutions, and a fair, just and efficient legal system is critical 
here. 
The Pentagonal Strategy underscores the importance of improving the quality of 
public institutions at both national and sub-national levels to ensure efficiency of public 
services, strengthening private sector governance, and fostering favourable environment 
for business, investment, and trade. More concrete results are expected. 
The new investment law adopted in 2021 provides new incentives, better 
guarantees, and easier procedures to attract more investments. Sectors entitled to 
investment incentives include those related to high-tech industries, digital technology, 
green technology, manufacturing, agriculture, agro-industry, education, health, and 
infrastructure.

strategy. In recent years, the Kingdom has actively pursued this goal through strategic

trade, relatively new to Cambodia, refers to commercial activities facilitated through
