Funan Techo Canal: Connecting the Past, Present and 
Future 

The Funan Techo Canal project is the symbol of national pride and progress, 
harkening back to the historical glory of the Khmer civilization during the Funan era. This 
era marked a golden age when Cambodia was the key commercial and cultural gateway 
of the Mekong region, facilitating trade and cultural exchanges that enriched the region 
and the world. 
By undertaking the Funan Techo Canal project, Cambodia aims to revive and 
build upon this glorious history. This ambitious endeavor is not just an infrastructure 
project; it is a symbol of our nation’s enduring spirit and potential- it can be regarded as 
a national rejuvenation project. 
The canal seeks to recreate the dynamic role that ancient Funan played, 
transforming Cambodia once again into a pivotal hub of commerce, culture, and 
innovation. The project’s vision is rooted in a deep respect for our history and an 
unyielding commitment to our future. 
This transformative project rests on four fundamental pillars: national pride, 
economic interests, political independence, and national unity. 
 Promoting National Pride and Historical Glory 
The Funan Techo Canal project is a testament to the ingenuity, resilience, and rich 
cultural heritage of the Khmer civilization which is mainly based on river system and 
waterway. 
It serves as a living monument to our ancestors’ achievements, reminding us of 
the times when Cambodia was a center of trade, culture, and influence. 
By reviving this historical glory, the canal project aims to instill a sense of pride 
among the Cambodian people. It reinforces our national identity, celebrating our unique 
heritage and historical contributions. 
The project is a clarion call to embrace and honor our past while paving the way 
for future generations to take pride in their roots and the progress they contribute to the 
nation. 
 Economic Interests and Development 
Contemporary Perspective 
Part I: Cambodia 
P a g e | 112 
Volume IV 
The economic potential of the Funan Techo Canal project is relatively high. By 
creating a direct link between our inland waterways and the sea, the canal will 
revolutionize logistics and transport in Cambodia. 
This enhanced connectivity will not only facilitate smoother and more efficient 
movement of goods but also attract significant investment. The development of economic 
zones and industrial parks along the canal will spur industrial growth, leading to the 
creation of numerous job opportunities. 
This, in turn, will drive urbanization, bringing modern infrastructure, better 
services, and an improved quality of life to local communities. The canal is envisioned as 
a catalyst for sustainable economic growth, ensuring that the benefits of development 
are widely shared across the communities living along the canal. 
Strengthening Political Independence 
The Funan Techo Canal project is a strategic initiative that enhances Cambodia’s 
political independence. 
By developing our own waterway transport system, we reduce our reliance on 
external entities and increase our self-reliance. 
This move towards self-sufficiency strengthens our sovereignty, enabling us to 
assert greater control over our national infrastructure and resources. 
The canal project embodies our commitment to national ownership and the 
principle of self-determination. It is a bold statement of our ability to chart our own 
course, safeguard our interests, and navigate the complexities of global politics with 
confidence and autonomy. 
 Inspiring National Unity and Strength 
Perhaps one of the most profound impacts of the Funan Techo Canal project is its 
potential to inspire national unity and strength. 
This project is a collective endeavor that transcends regional and social divides, 
bringing together people from all walks of life in a shared vision of progress and 
prosperity. 
It serves as a powerful symbol of what we can achieve when we unite with a 
common purpose- it is part of institutional imagination.

The canal project is a source of hope and pride, fostering a sense of belonging 
and shared destiny. As we work towards the successful completion of this project, we are 
reminded of our national strength and the boundless potential that lies within our unity. 
The Funan Techo Canal is more than just an infrastructural development; it is a

By promoting national pride, driving economic development, strengthening

what we can achieve as a nation. 
As we embark on this journey, let us draw inspiration from our history and look 
forward to a future of prosperity and strength, united in our shared vision for a better 
Cambodia.

Cambodia’s Green Energy Transition Needs Reforms 

Cambodia is at a critical juncture in energy transition. The nation faces rapid 
energy demand growth and high electricity prices due to its reliance on fuel imports. 
Simultaneously, Cambodia’s vulnerability to climate change, particularly from increased 
flooding risks, threatens critical infrastructure. 
Cambodia has embarked on a clean and resilient energy transition, led by the 
power sector. However, significant constraints remain: the institutional capacity for long-
term, data-driven energy sector planning and target-setting, particularly concerning 
climate risks, is still developing, and some institutional and technical constraints relating 
to the development of solar and wind energy. 
In 2004, Cambodia’s electricity grid was a bastion of fossil fuels, primarily relying 
on heavy-fuel oil and diesel. However, by 2013, a remarkable transformation took place, 
with 82% of the nation’s electricity coming from renewable sources, predominantly 
hydropower. 
This significant shift marked a milestone in Cambodia’s energy sector, highlighting 
the country’s potential for green energy leadership. However, there are remaining 
challenges to need to be addressed. 
Regulatory frameworks necessary for new solutions are lacking, and the energy 
transition has not yet permeated sectors such as transport, industry, and buildings. 
Additionally, technical capacities to adopt climate-resilient and clean energy technologies 
are only just emerging. 
The solution lies in mainstreaming renewable energy and energy efficiency while 
adopting innovative technologies and business models. The Energy Transition Sector 
Development Project, approved for financing by the Asian Development Bank (ADB) in 
December 2022, represents Cambodia’s first comprehensive policy reform package for 
the energy sector. 
This project aims to help the energy sector mainstream renewable energy and 
efficiency, transition away from fossil fuels, adopt data-driven regulation, and plan for a 
flexible and resilient power system. 
By combining policy issuance, efficiency standards, and guidelines with 
government-led programs and investment projects, the program seeks to accelerate the 
Contemporary Perspective 
Part I: Cambodia 
P a g e | 115 
Volume IV 
transition toward an energy-efficient economy, reduce greenhouse gas emissions, and 
create green jobs. 
The goals are ambitious: a 25% increase in renewable energy generation and an 
8.6% reduction in annual electricity demand through improved efficiency, all by 2027. 
Renewable energy is not just viable for Cambodia; it is essential. With up to eight 
hours of sunlight per day, Cambodia boasts some of the richest solar resources in 
Southeast Asia. 
A bottom-up energy transition is already underway, with farmers and business 
owners in rural areas adopting solar power to enhance productivity and incomes. Yet, a 
stronger policy push from the government is necessary to fully tap into the country’s high 
solar potential. 
Programs like EnergyLab’s SWITCH to Solar support Cambodian entrepreneurs 
and startups, promoting solar power in the agriculture and fishery sectors and connecting 
them to farmers and rural businesses. 
Such initiatives have already yielded significant results, with solar companies 
selling products worth over $1.4 million and promoting solar technologies to more than 
3,000 micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises. 
However, to maximize the use of clean energy, more policy changes are needed. 
According to the EnergyLab study, increased adoption of Solar PV over 
conventional generation technologies could yield significant economic benefits for 
Cambodia. 
Modelling shows that replacing conventional plants with a higher uptake of Solar 
PV could reduce the overall cost of generating electricity, lower associated externality 
costs, and stimulate GDP growth. 
An ambitious scenario replacing some coal, gas, and hydro with 9,702 MW of 
Solar PV backed by 2,500 MW of Battery Energy Storage System could save Cambodia 
$2.04 billion by 2040 and reduce power system emissions by 117 megatonnes of CO2. 
Even a realistic scenario of 14% solar PV generation could save $250 million in 
total power system costs and reduce externality costs by $1.5 billion, translating to a 
cumulative GDP gain of 0.82% over 20 years.

Cambodia’s robust solar PV resources remain largely untapped and can be 
rapidly developed with significant economic benefits. The time to act is now. By 
embracing renewable energy and energy efficiency, Cambodia can secure a sustainable 
and prosperous future, reducing its reliance on imports and ensuring greater energy 
security. 
The path is clear: a greener Cambodia is within reach, and the government must 
take decisive steps to realize this vision. 
Yet, the development of solar energy faces certain regulatory and bureaucratic 
challenges, including difficulties in obtaining licenses for solar energy farms and a lack of 
legal support to encourage direct solar energy investments for factory supply. 
In neighboring Vietnam, the government has issued a new decree allowing 
factories to directly purchase electricity from power suppliers. This move aims to harness 
the country’s abundant renewable energy potential. 
Under the new regulations, power consumers can buy electricity directly from 
renewable energy generators via private transmission lines at negotiated prices, 
according to a government statement. 
Vietnam, a regional manufacturing hub, has been striving to increase the share of 
solar and wind power in its energy mix. By allowing more space and flexibility for the 
private sector to get involved in the production and distribution of electricity, Vietnam can 
attract more foreign direct investments. 
Cambodia can learn from Vietnam’s regulatory reforms to boost its own renewable 
energy production. This would facilitate easier access to clean power sources for 
multinationals, which is particularly important for exporters to avoid higher tariffs and 
meet environmental, social, and governance (ESG) requirements. 
As a result, Cambodia-based manufacturers could purchase electricity directly 
from producers, effectively ending the monopoly of Electricite du Cambodge (EDC).

Cambodia is at a critical juncture in energy transition. The nation faces rapid 
energy demand growth and high electricity prices due to its reliance on fuel imports. 
Simultaneously, Cambodia’s vulnerability to climate change, particularly from increased 
flooding risks, threatens critical infrastructure. 
Cambodia has embarked on a clean and resilient energy transition, led by the 
power sector. However, significant constraints remain: the institutional capacity for long-
term, data-driven energy sector planning and target-setting, particularly concerning 
climate risks, is still developing, and some institutional and technical constraints relating 
to the development of solar and wind energy. 
In 2004, Cambodia’s electricity grid was a bastion of fossil fuels, primarily relying 
on heavy-fuel oil and diesel. However, by 2013, a remarkable transformation took place, 
with 82% of the nation’s electricity coming from renewable sources, predominantly 
hydropower. 
This significant shift marked a milestone in Cambodia’s energy sector, highlighting 
the country’s potential for green energy leadership. However, there are remaining 
challenges to need to be addressed. 
Regulatory frameworks necessary for new solutions are lacking, and the energy 
transition has not yet permeated sectors such as transport, industry, and buildings. 
Additionally, technical capacities to adopt climate-resilient and clean energy technologies 
are only just emerging. 
The solution lies in mainstreaming renewable energy and energy efficiency while 
adopting innovative technologies and business models. The Energy Transition Sector 
Development Project, approved for financing by the Asian Development Bank (ADB) in 
December 2022, represents Cambodia’s first comprehensive policy reform package for 
the energy sector. 
This project aims to help the energy sector mainstream renewable energy and 
efficiency, transition away from fossil fuels, adopt data-driven regulation, and plan for a 
flexible and resilient power system. 
By combining policy issuance, efficiency standards, and guidelines with 
government-led programs and investment projects, the program seeks to accelerate the

P a g e | 115 
Volume IV 
transition toward an energy-efficient economy, reduce greenhouse gas emissions, and 
create green jobs. 
The goals are ambitious: a 25% increase in renewable energy generation and an 
8.6% reduction in annual electricity demand through improved efficiency, all by 2027. 
Renewable energy is not just viable for Cambodia; it is essential. With up to eight 
hours of sunlight per day, Cambodia boasts some of the richest solar resources in 
Southeast Asia. 
A bottom-up energy transition is already underway, with farmers and business 
owners in rural areas adopting solar power to enhance productivity and incomes. Yet, a 
stronger policy push from the government is necessary to fully tap into the country’s high 
solar potential. 
Programs like EnergyLab’s SWITCH to Solar support Cambodian entrepreneurs 
and startups, promoting solar power in the agriculture and fishery sectors and connecting 
them to farmers and rural businesses. 
Such initiatives have already yielded significant results, with solar companies 
selling products worth over $1.4 million and promoting solar technologies to more than 
3,000 micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises. 
However, to maximize the use of clean energy, more policy changes are needed. 
According to the EnergyLab study, increased adoption of Solar PV over 
conventional generation technologies could yield significant economic benefits for 
Cambodia. 
Modelling shows that replacing conventional plants with a higher uptake of Solar 
PV could reduce the overall cost of generating electricity, lower associated externality 
costs, and stimulate GDP growth. 
An ambitious scenario replacing some coal, gas, and hydro with 9,702 MW of 
Solar PV backed by 2,500 MW of Battery Energy Storage System could save Cambodia 
$2.04 billion by 2040 and reduce power system emissions by 117 megatonnes of CO2. 
Even a realistic scenario of 14% solar PV generation could save $250 million in 
total power system costs and reduce externality costs by $1.5 billion, translating to a 
cumulative GDP gain of 0.82% over 20 years. 
Contemporary Perspective

P a g e | 116 
Volume IV 
Cambodia’s robust solar PV resources remain largely untapped and can be 
rapidly developed with significant economic benefits. The time to act is now. By 
embracing renewable energy and energy efficiency, Cambodia can secure a sustainable 
and prosperous future, reducing its reliance on imports and ensuring greater energy 
security. 
The path is clear: a greener Cambodia is within reach, and the government must 
take decisive steps to realize this vision. 
Yet, the development of solar energy faces certain regulatory and bureaucratic 
challenges, including difficulties in obtaining licenses for solar energy farms and a lack of 
legal support to encourage direct solar energy investments for factory supply. 
In neighboring Vietnam, the government has issued a new decree allowing 
factories to directly purchase electricity from power suppliers. This move aims to harness 
the country’s abundant renewable energy potential. 
Under the new regulations, power consumers can buy electricity directly from 
renewable energy generators via private transmission lines at negotiated prices, 
according to a government statement. 
Vietnam, a regional manufacturing hub, has been striving to increase the share of 
solar and wind power in its energy mix. By allowing more space and flexibility for the 
private sector to get involved in the production and distribution of electricity, Vietnam can 
attract more foreign direct investments. 
Cambodia can learn from Vietnam’s regulatory reforms to boost its own renewable 
energy production. This would facilitate easier access to clean power sources for 
multinationals, which is particularly important for exporters to avoid higher tariffs and 
meet environmental, social, and governance (ESG) requirements. 
As a result, Cambodia-based manufacturers could purchase electricity directly 
from producers, effectively ending the monopoly of Electricite du Cambodge (EDC).

Cambodia’s Path Forward: Embrace Futures 
Thinking 

In an era marked by rapid change and global uncertainties, Cambodia stands at a 
pivotal juncture. To foster meaningful and sustainable development, our nation must 
embrace a forward-thinking strategy that reimagines the future to reshape the present. 
While the past is immutable, our current actions hold the power to define 
tomorrow. The traditional approach of addressing current challenges by relying on past 
experiences has served us well, but it limits our capacity to innovate and adapt in an 
increasingly complex world. 
 Why Futures Thinking Matters 
Futures thinking is more than a theoretical exercise; it’s a practical approach that 
equips us to anticipate emerging issues, navigate uncertainties, and craft resilient 
strategies. 
This method involves identifying trends, exploring various scenarios, and building 
a shared vision for the future through inclusive dialogue. By focusing on what could be, 
rather than just what is, futures thinking fosters innovation and helps design policies that 
are adaptable to change. 
Foresight, the actionable component of futures thinking, employs tools and 
methodologies to project potential futures, manage risks, and seize opportunities. 
This proactive stance allows us to create strategies that are not just reactive but 
anticipatory, positioning Cambodia to better handle the challenges and opportunities of a 
dynamic global landscape. 
 Design Thinking and Systems Thinking: Essential Tools 
To complement futures thinking, we must integrate design thinking and systems 
thinking. Design thinking offers a user-centered, iterative approach to problem-solving, 
encouraging us to question assumptions, redefine challenges, and develop creative 
solutions through continuous experimentation. This approach is crucial for crafting 
practical and innovative pathways to our desired future. 
Systems thinking provides a holistic perspective, focusing on how different 
elements of a system interact and impact each other over time. It emphasizes 
Contemporary Perspective 
Part I: Cambodia 
P a g e | 118 
Volume IV 
understanding the interconnectedness within systems rather than isolating components. 
This comprehensive view is vital for addressing complex issues that cut across multiple 
sectors and governance levels. 
 Beyond Traditional Forecasting 
Futures thinking and foresight go beyond merely analyzing historical data and 
trends; they also incorporate diverse perspectives and imaginative inputs from a wide 
range of stakeholders, including government officials, industry leaders, civil society 
members, and academics. 
Unlike traditional forecasting, which often focuses narrowly on what is feasible, 
futures thinking emphasizes what is aspirational and desirable. This participatory 
approach not only fosters stronger cross-sectoral connections but also promotes 
integrated solutions and empowers individuals to shape their preferred future. 
By expanding the scope to include emerging issues and trends and exploring 
various future scenarios, futures thinking encourages the development of innovative 
solutions and robust policies. 
This forward-looking approach ensures that projects and programs are designed 
with tools and insights that will remain relevant and effective in the future. 
 The Role of Innovation Labs 
Globally, innovation labs have emerged as vital hubs for tackling policy challenges 
with fresh approaches. These labs act as experimental arenas where new models can 
be tested, helping to avoid short-term, narrow-minded policies and investments. They 
apply futures thinking and foresight to map evolving landscapes, analyze uncertainties, 
and uncover development opportunities. 
In Cambodia, the upcoming InnoLab, spearheaded by Angkor Social Innovation 
Park (ASIP) and Sequoia Group, represents a strategic move towards embracing futures 
thinking. Focused on Healthcare and Wellbeing, Sustainable Food Systems, and 
Inclusive Digital Transformation and Women Empowerment, InnoLab will also provide 
training in futures thinking, design thinking, systems thinking, leadership for innovation, 
and change management. 
 InnoLab’s Vision and Core Values 
Contemporary Perspective 
Part I: Cambodia 
P a g e | 119 
Volume IV 
InnoLab will drive progress in key areas: (1) Healthcare and Wellbeing enhances 
preventative healthcare to improve public health outcomes; (2) Sustainable Food 
Systems advances agricultural practices that are environmentally sustainable and 
socially equitable; (3) Inclusive Digital Transformation and Women Empowerment aims 
to address the digital gender gap and empowering women through technology. 
Guided by the values of Resilience, Resourcefulness, Community, and Continuity 
(2R2C), InnoLab celebrates the strength of the Cambodian people, fosters creativity and 
adaptability, emphasizes collaborative progress, and aims to create a lasting positive 
legacy. 
 Aligning with Cambodia Vision 2050 
InnoLab’s initiatives are closely aligned with Cambodia Vision 2050, which 
envisions a nation that is robust, prosperous, and high-income by mid-century. This 
vision includes: a vibrant society, a resilient, high-income economy, a populace with 
knowledge and skills, a commitment to dignity, equality, and social protection, and a 
balanced approach to development and environmental conservation. 
By anchoring its work in this vision, InnoLab aims to catalyze enduring positive 
change. The process of exploring, discovering, and co-creating solutions will not only 
enhance civic engagement but also build a collective commitment and multi-stakeholder 
partnerships to shape and realise Cambodia’s future. 
Embracing futures thinking and foresight is not just an option for Cambodia; it is 
an imperative. By doing so, we position ourselves to navigate uncertainty, drive 
innovation, and build a resilient future for our nation.

Cambodia’s Path to Innovation: Inspirations from 
China 

In recent years, China has undergone a monumental shift in its economic strategy, 
transitioning from a growth-maximizing model to an innovation-led approach. 
This evolution, marked by the introduction of the “Innovation-Driven Development 
Strategy” in 2012, emphasizes the need for technological advancement to sustain long-
term growth. 
As Cambodia looks toward achieving upper-middle-income status by 2030 and a 
high-income country by 2050, there are valuable lessons to be drawn from China’s 
model of innovation-led growth. 
China’s innovation journey can be broken down into three major stages. 
In the late 20th century, China focused on leveraging technological advancements 
to modernize industries. This phase aimed to enhance productivity and create a more 
diversified economy by moving away from reliance on traditional heavy industry. 
In the early 2000s, China pivoted towards making innovation the centerpiece of 
economic growth. The 2005 Medium- and Long-Term Plan for Science and Technology 
Development emphasized indigenous innovation, marking China’s move towards 
technological self-sufficiency. Sectors such as energy, biotechnology, and information 
technology were identified as critical for the future. 
In 2012, the formal Innovation-Driven Development Strategy was launched. China 
acknowledged that economic growth could no longer rely solely on low-cost 
manufacturing and exports. Instead, the country sought to become a leader in cutting-
edge industries like biotechnology, renewable energy, and artificial intelligence. By 
focusing on disruptive technologies, China positioned itself at the forefront of global 
innovation, with the goal of becoming a world leader in science, technology and 
innovation by 2050. 
The Chinese government has been instrumental in promoting innovation by 
channeling resources into specific sectors, offering financial incentives, and fostering 
collaboration between the public and private sectors. 
Contemporary Perspective 
Part I: Cambodia 
P a g e | 121 
Volume IV 
This focus on “lead innovation”—which emphasizes the development of high-tech 
industries capable of transforming existing markets—has enabled China to evolve from 
a manufacturing hub into a global leader in technological innovation. 
President Xi Jinping has emphasized the critical role of scientific and technological 
advancements in achieving Chinese modernization and promoting high-quality 
development. He has advocated for comprehensive planning and high-level scientific 
independence to help China reach its goal of becoming a world leader in science and 
technology by 2035. 
In recent years, China has made significant progress in frontier research, 
advanced in strategic high-tech areas, and seen innovation-driven results contributing to 
its overall development. 
Additionally, the country has taken steps to reform its science and technology 
systems while enhancing international cooperation in these fields. 
Cambodia has experienced impressive economic growth over the past few 
decades, but it remains largely reliant on traditional sectors like garment manufacturing 
and agriculture. To secure long-term prosperity and achieve the ambitious goal of 
becoming an upper-middle-income economy by 2030, Cambodia must embrace an 
innovation-led development model similar to China’s. 
Here’s how Cambodia can apply China’s lessons. 
First, Cambodia should develop a similar “innovation-driven development 
strategy”, taking into consideration national context. In 2019, Cambodia adopted the 
National Science, Technology, and Innovation (STI) Policy 2020–2030, which aims to 
strengthen the country’s innovation capacity. Cambodia should focus on targeted sectors 
such as advanced manufacturing, modern agriculture, digital economy, and green 
economy, which have the potential to drive future economic growth. 
Second, Cambodia should encourage the development of cutting-edge 
technologies. China’s focus on lead innovation helped it become a global leader in 
industries like artificial intelligence and electric vehicles. Cambodia can similarly identify 
and promote technologies that have the potential to create new markets and disrupt 
traditional industries. For instance, investing in agritech and green energy could provide 
Cambodia with a competitive edge while promoting sustainability. 
Contemporary Perspective 
Part I: Cambodia 
P a g e | 122 
Volume IV 
Third, China’s innovation success is due, in large part, to effective collaboration 
between the government, private enterprises, and research institutions. Cambodia’s 
government should foster similar partnerships to accelerate technological advancements 
and invest more resources in research and development. This can include initiatives like 
creating innovation clusters, where universities, startups, and established companies 
collaborate to develop new technologies, products, and services. 
Fourth, China’s rise as a global innovation leader would not have been possible 
without a strong emphasis on education and research. Cambodia needs to invest heavily 
in its education system, especially in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics 
(STEM) fields, to cultivate a skilled workforce capable of driving innovation. Scholarships, 
research grants, and partnerships with foreign institutions can help improve the quality of 
education and research in Cambodia. 
Fifth, China’s innovation ecosystem is supported by a centralized structure that 
coordinates efforts across different sectors. Cambodia’s Ministry of Industry, Science, 
Technology, and Innovation (MISTI) plays a similar role, but there is room for 
improvement. Creating a more robust national innovation system that encourages 
collaboration and knowledge sharing will be essential for achieving the country’s 
innovation goals. 
Cambodia has made significant strides in its economic development, but to reach 
the next level, it must transition from a reliance on traditional sectors to becoming an 
innovation-driven economy. China’s experience offers valuable lessons, particularly in 
the areas of government leadership, public-private partnerships, and investment in high-
tech industries. 
By adopting a focused innovation-led strategy, Cambodia could achieve its 
development vision 2030 and 2050. Strengthening the national STI ecosystem, investing 
in human capital, and investing in research and development will be essential in this 
transformation. The future of Cambodia’s economy lies in its ability to innovate.

Ten Pillars of Hun Sen’s Peace Theory 

Former Prime Minister Samdech Techo Hun Sen, now serving as the President of 
the Senate, has been awarded 24 honorary doctorates from institutions around the world 
in recognition of his contributions to peace, leadership, and development. These 
accolades are based on objective assessments of his impact on Cambodia’s history and 
future. 
Peace is often understood in its simplest form as the absence of war or conflict, 
known as negative peace. However, a deeper and more comprehensive view transcends 
the mere cessation of violence. This broader concept, called positive peace, involves the 
active pursuit of justice, equality, and the well-being of society. Positive peace seeks to 
address structural inequities and injustices, creating conditions where all individuals can 
thrive. 
In Cambodia, both negative and positive peace have been achieved largely due 
to the leadership of Hun Sen and his visionary Win-Win policy. This policy not only ended 
decades of civil war but also laid the foundation for sustainable peace through national 
reconciliation, unity, and development. 
The 1991 Paris Peace Agreement was a crucial turning point for Cambodia, as it 
established a framework to end decades of war and conflict. However, it did not fully 
bring about lasting peace. 
True and enduring peace was only realized in the late 1990s, following the 
implementation of Hun Sen’s Win-Win policy. This policy effectively dismantled the 
remaining Khmer Rouge forces, fostering national reconciliation and leading to total 
peace in the Kingdom. 
The success of the Win-Win policy was anchored in dialogue, trust-building, and 
strategic guarantees that facilitated the full dissolution of the Khmer Rouge and the 
reintegration of its forces into the Royal Cambodian Armed Forces by 1999. 
Three key guarantees—protection of defectors’ lives and safety, assurance of 
employment and livelihoods, and respect for personal property—were instrumental in 
addressing the fundamental human security needs of former combatants. These 
guarantees allowed the Khmer Rouge’s military and political structures to be peacefully 
dismantled, offering defectors a path to reintegration into society. 
Contemporary Perspective 
Part I: Cambodia 
P a g e | 124 
Volume IV 
Moreover, Hun Sen recognized that the lack of infrastructure in remote areas was 
a major factor in sustaining insurgencies. In response, he led efforts to build roads, 
bridges, and other essential infrastructure in former Khmer Rouge strongholds. As he 
often highlighted, the aim was “to connect these areas to the central administration of the 
country,” ensuring that even the most isolated regions were integrated into national 
development. This holistic approach is grounded in a profound understanding of what 
true peace entails. 
As Johan Galtung’s concept of “structural violence” suggests, true peace involves 
more than simply halting active conflict; it requires addressing the underlying inequities 
and power imbalances that perpetuate unrest. Hun Sen’s Win-Win policy did exactly that, 
promoting national unity and giving former adversaries a stake in Cambodia’s future. 
Hun Sen’s peace theory is built on ten conceptual pillars, extending beyond 
military disarmament and the cessation of violence. It includes strategies for social and 
economic integration, as well as fostering justice and international cooperation. His 
theory embodies both negative and positive peace. 
First, ending the war through dialogue. Despite having the upper hand over his 
enemies, Hun Sen prioritized dialogue and trust-building as the foundation of his 
strategy. Through the DIFID approach—’Divide, Isolate, Finish, Integrate, and Develop’—
he successfully divided and defeated opposing forces, ultimately fostering national 
reconciliation. 
Second, promoting social and economic integration. The Win-Win policy 
emphasized that peace is not just about ending violence, but also about integrating all 
factions into a cohesive society. 
Former Khmer Rouge fighters were welcomed back and provided with 
opportunities for livelihoods. This social and economic integration has been crucial to 
Cambodia’s long-term stability, preventing the Kingdom from relapsing into conflict. 
Third, promoting political and military integration. Genuine peace requires 
addressing the root causes of conflict. By incorporating the Khmer Rouge’s political 
ideology and military forces into the broader national framework, Hun Sen ensured these 
factions would have a place in Cambodia’s future, minimizing the risk of future conflict. 
Fourth, forging the peace-development nexus. Hun Sen’s peace theory is 
inextricably linked to economic growth. Cambodia’s aspirations to become an upper-
middle-income country by 2030 and a high-income country by 2050 demonstrate that 
Contemporary Perspective 
Part I: Cambodia 
P a g e | 125 
Volume IV 
peace and development are mutually reinforcing. A stable society attracts investment, 
spurs development, and improves living standards, which in turn strengthens social 
cohesion. 
Sixth, connecting peace with social harmony. The successful integration of former 
adversaries has allowed Cambodia to rebuild its social fabric. By ensuring that all 
citizens, regardless of past affiliations, races or religions, have a place in the new

Former Prime Minister Samdech Techo Hun Sen, now serving as the President of 
the Senate, has been awarded 24 honorary doctorates from institutions around the world 
in recognition of his contributions to peace, leadership, and development. These 
accolades are based on objective assessments of his impact on Cambodia’s history and 
future. 
Peace is often understood in its simplest form as the absence of war or conflict, 
known as negative peace. However, a deeper and more comprehensive view transcends 
the mere cessation of violence. This broader concept, called positive peace, involves the 
active pursuit of justice, equality, and the well-being of society. Positive peace seeks to 
address structural inequities and injustices, creating conditions where all individuals can 
thrive. 
In Cambodia, both negative and positive peace have been achieved largely due 
to the leadership of Hun Sen and his visionary Win-Win policy. This policy not only ended 
decades of civil war but also laid the foundation for sustainable peace through national 
reconciliation, unity, and development. 
The 1991 Paris Peace Agreement was a crucial turning point for Cambodia, as it 
established a framework to end decades of war and conflict. However, it did not fully 
bring about lasting peace. 
True and enduring peace was only realized in the late 1990s, following the 
implementation of Hun Sen’s Win-Win policy. This policy effectively dismantled the 
remaining Khmer Rouge forces, fostering national reconciliation and leading to total 
peace in the Kingdom. 
The success of the Win-Win policy was anchored in dialogue, trust-building, and 
strategic guarantees that facilitated the full dissolution of the Khmer Rouge and the 
reintegration of its forces into the Royal Cambodian Armed Forces by 1999. 
Three key guarantees—protection of defectors’ lives and safety, assurance of 
employment and livelihoods, and respect for personal property—were instrumental in 
addressing the fundamental human security needs of former combatants. These 
guarantees allowed the Khmer Rouge’s military and political structures to be peacefully 
dismantled, offering defectors a path to reintegration into society.

country,” ensuring that even the most isolated regions were integrated into national 
development. This holistic approach is grounded in a profound understanding of what 
true peace entails. 
As Johan Galtung’s concept of “structural violence” suggests, true peace involves 
more than simply halting active conflict; it requires addressing the underlying inequities

A New Chapter of Cambodia-China Parliamentary 
Cooperation 

Cambodia-China relations stand as a model of international cooperation between 
a large and small country based on the principles of mutual respect, non-interference, 
and equality. 
As Cambodia and China move forward in building their community with a shared 
future, the deepening of parliamentary cooperation will play an increasingly important 
role in fostering people’s participation and people-centred strategic partnership. 
National Assembly President Khuon Sudary’s visit to China has opened a new 
chapter in this historic milestone of the parliamentary cooperation and diplomacy, 
illustrating deep strategic trust and friendship. 
Both nations have reaffirmed their political will to enhance bilateral cooperation, 
further aligning their efforts toward realizing a people-centered Community with a Shared 
Future, guided by the consensus of the leadership of the two countries. 
A central focus of Sudary’s visit was the further strengthening of parliamentary 
diplomacy between Cambodia and China. 
During the bilateral meeting, Zhao Leji emphasized that the National People’s 
Congress is ready to work closely with Cambodia to coordinate various forms of 
parliamentary cooperation, exchange experiences in legislation and supervision, and 
provide the legal framework necessary for pragmatic cooperation. 
Zhao, Chairman of the Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress, 
highlighted that the construction of a China-Cambodia community with a shared future 
has entered a new era of high-quality, high-level, and high-standard cooperation. This 
transformation is guided by the strategic vision of both countries’ leaders, further 
deepening the bond between Cambodia and China. 
Noting that China has always placed Cambodia in a special, important position in 
its neighborhood diplomacy, Zhao said China is willing to maintain high-level strategic 
communication and work with Cambodia to support each other firmly on issues 
concerning the two countries’ core interests. 
Wang Huning, Chairman of the the Chinese People’s Political Consultative 
Conference (CPPCC) National Committee, said that China is willing to work with 
Contemporary Perspective 
Part I: Cambodia 
P a g e | 128 
Volume IV 
Cambodia to implement the important consensus reached by the leaders of the two 
countries and continuously consolidate their ironclad friendship. 
The CPPCC National Committee is willing to strengthen exchanges and 
cooperation with Cambodia and make positive contributions to promoting greater 
development of the China-Cambodia community with a shared future, Wang added. 
Sudary stressed that the comprehensive strategic partnership and ironclad 
friendship are built on a strong, resilient foundation. Despite changes at the regional and 
international levels, ironclad friendship is unbreakable, unshakeable. 
Cambodia’s commitment to this partnership is exemplified by its consistent 
support for China on critical issues, including the consistent, firm upholding of the one-
China policy and one-China principle. 
Cambodia is a strong supporter of China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) and other 
China’s global initiatives, including the Global Development Initiative, the Global Security 
Initiative, and the Global Civilization Initiative as these initiatives reflect shared values of 
peaceful co-existence, harmony, shared prosperity—principles that Cambodia has 
embraced in its foreign policy. 
Cambodia views China as an indispensable strategic partner, playing a vital role 
in its socio-economic development as well as the protection of its sovereignty and 
political independence. 
China regards Cambodia as a trustworthy and reliable friend and neighbor. 
China is committed to aligning its engagement strategies with Cambodia’s 
priorities, ensuring that both nations benefit mutually from their cooperation such as the 
promotion of strategic synergies between the BRI with Cambodia’s Pentagonal Strategy 
and the alignment of Cambodia Vision 2050 with China Vision 2049. 
The “Diamond Hexagon” framework is central to the China-Cambodia partnership 
and provides a roadmap for collaboration in key areas such as politics, agriculture, 
energy, production capacities, and people-to-people exchanges. 
The “Industrial and Technological Corridor” and “Fish and Rice Corridor” are other 
practical cooperation frameworks that need more efforts and resources. 
In the exclusive interview with China Global Television Network, Sudary 
emphasized Cambodia’s deep admiration for China’s remarkable achievements in 
Contemporary Perspective

P a g e | 129 
Volume IV 
national governance, particularly in the areas of socio-economic development and 
poverty reduction. 
She underscored that democracy cannot be imported or copied from one country 
to another, as each nation’s democratic model must be rooted in its own unique cultural, 
historical, and social contexts. 
She noted that China’s whole-process people’s democracy is a system tailored to 
its own realities, demonstrating that there is no one-size-fits-all approach to governance 
and that each country must find its own path to meet the needs and aspirations of its 
people. 
Moving forward, parliamentary cooperation and diplomacy will add more values 
and impetus to the realization of a people-centered Cambodia-China Community with a 
shared future.

Cambodia’s Peace Diplomacy 

Cambodia’s foreign policy has undergone a remarkable development over the 
past decade, marked by an increasingly robust and proactive approach to economic 
diplomacy and peace diplomacy. 
These two pillars of modern Cambodian diplomacy reflect the country’s 
transformation from a war-torn nation to an advocate for peace and development, 
underpinned by the principles of mutual respect, mutual understanding, mutual trust, and 
mutual interest for peace and prosperity. 
Independent foreign policy based on international law and the commitment to 
open and inclusive multilateralism and a human-centred approach remains central to 
Cambodia’s foreign policy. 
Cambodia’s peace journey offers valuable lessons for the Mekong region and the 
broader international community. 
One must remember that peace is not given; it needs to be earned. Dialogue is 
key to the peace process. 
 From Conflict to Peace Advocacy 
Once a victim of war and conflict, Cambodia has become a promoter of peace on 
regional and international stages. 
The recent hosting of the 11th Plenary Session of the International Parliament for 
Tolerance and Peace is a case in point. 
The event concluded with the adoption of the Phnom Penh Declaration and the 
Universal Peace Charter, a milestone in fostering global dialogue and cooperation on 
peace. 
Cambodia’s role as a convener of peace-focused discussions is unique. It 
provides a safe and open platform for dialogue among governments, parliaments, 
political parties, experts, and community leaders. 
This approach reflects a core belief that peace can be built through diplomacy and 
dialogue. By positioning itself as a “bridge of trust and cooperation” in the Mekong region 
and beyond. 
Contemporary Perspective 
Part I: Cambodia 
P a g e | 131 
Volume IV 
 The Mekong Region: A New Growth Centre 
The Mekong region is emerging as one of the world’s new growth centers, offering 
immense potential for cooperation, connectivity, and prosperity. 
Cambodia’s peace diplomacy aligns seamlessly with this dynamic, emphasizing 
collaboration over conflict and shared development over division. 
Concerning border negotiations and demarcation with neighboring countries, 
Cambodia remains committed to upholding international law and fostering a spirit of 
friendship and cooperation. 
By fostering trust and cooperation in the Mekong, Cambodia seeks to unlock the 
region’s potential while contributing to international peace and development. 
Cambodia has adopted a proactive stance within the ASEAN framework, actively 
contributing to efforts aimed at achieving a political settlement and delivering 
humanitarian assistance in Myanmar. 
 A Commitment to Global Peace 
Since 2006, Cambodia has underscored its commitment to global peace and 
security by deploying nearly 10,000 peacekeepers to United Nations missions in ten 
countries. These contributions not only highlight Cambodia’s dedication to peace but 
also enhance its international stature as a responsible and proactive member of the 
global community. 
 Leadership and the Win-Win Policy 
Central to Cambodia’s peace diplomacy is the legacy of Hun Sen, often regarded 
as the architect of peace in Cambodia. His Win-Win Policy is a cornerstone of 
Cambodia’s modern history, combining peace negotiation, peacebuilding, and national 
reconciliation. At its heart are trust and confidence-building measures, underpinned by 
Buddhist values of forgiveness, tolerance, and peaceful coexistence. 
Strategic pragmatism has been critical to the success of the Win-Win Policy. By 
being flexible in tactics while remaining firm on principles, Cambodia achieved a durable 
peace that has laid the foundation for its development and international engagement. 
This approach offers a source of inspiration for other nations grappling with conflict and 
post-conflict challenges. 
Contemporary Perspective 
Part I: Cambodia 
P a g e | 132 
Volume IV 
 Transitional Justice and the Rule of Law 
The Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia (ECCC), also known as 
the Khmer Rouge Tribunal, illustrates Cambodia’s commitment to transitional justice. 
By blending international and Cambodian judicial expertise, the ECCC has set a 
global standard for post-conflict justice. Its public outreach programs, which include film 
screenings, study tours, and school lectures, have engaged hundreds of thousands of 
Cambodians, ensuring that the lessons of the past are preserved for future generations. 
The tribunal’s live broadcasts and accessible public gallery have made it a model 
for transparency and civic engagement. Without the Khmer Rouge Tribunal, Cambodia 
would not have been able to record and preserve the history of the Khmer Rouge regime, 
nor establish the critical foundation for the rule of law that now underpins its society. 
 Peace Above All Else 
Cambodia’s peace diplomacy is rooted in a fundamental principle: peace must be 
placed above all else. This ethos, shaped by the country’s painful history, informs its 
foreign policy and domestic governance. By understanding, embracing, and 
implementing the values of peace, Cambodia has charted a path that other nations can 
follow. 
 Looking Ahead 
As Cambodia’s foreign policy continues to evolve, its commitment to peace 
diplomacy will remain central. 
By promoting dialogue, building trust, and emphasizing diplomacy and 
cooperation, Cambodia is not only securing its own future but also contributing to the 
stability and prosperity of the Mekong region and beyond. 
In an era of increasing geopolitical tensions, Cambodia’s model of strategic 
pragmatism, grounded in the values of peace and diplomacy, offers a useful lesson of 
how nations can transform tensions and conflicts into opportunities for peace.

Cambodia’s Parliamentary Diplomacy within ASEAN 

The President of Cambodia’s National Assembly, Samdech Khuon Sudary, led a 
delegation to the 45th General Assembly of the ASEAN Inter-Parliamentary Assembly 
(AIPA) in Vientiane, from October 17 to 23. The focus of the General Assembly is to 
promote parliamentary dialogue and cooperation on regional and international issues, 
with a special emphasis on building a people-centered ASEAN Community. 
The theme of this year underscores the critical role of parliaments in strengthening 
connectivity and fostering inclusive growth across ASEAN. As the region navigates an 
increasingly complex, volatile geopolitical landscape, Cambodia’s parliamentary 
diplomacy has gained renewed momentum, working closely with other legislative bodies 
to promote peace and development for humanity underpinned by the values of mutual 
respect and trust, ensuring that regional cooperation benefits all members of ASEAN 
fairly. 
Looking ahead, Cambodia will demonstrate her proactive parliamentary diplomacy 
by hosting the 11th Plenary Session of the International Parliament for Tolerance and 
Peace (IPTP) next month- it will serve as a platform for multi-stakeholder dialogue on 
peace, while strengthening open and inclusive multilateralism and reinforcing respect for 
international law. A Peace Charter, initiated by Samdech Techo Hun Sen, will be 
elaborated and adopted as a complementary framework to the United Nations Charter, 
further embedding peace as a core value in Cambodia’s international engagement. 
Notably, Cambodia’s approach to parliamentary diplomacy has evolved 
significantly since the start of the seventh legislature, embracing a proactive stance on 
key issues and challenges facing the region. Rooted in principles of mutual respect, 
trust, and common interests, this approach has enabled Cambodia to build stronger 
international cooperation and partnerships, contributing to shape and mold the fast-
evolving regional architecture. 
At the heart of Cambodia’s parliamentary diplomacy are core principles such as 
peaceful co-existence, non-interference in internal affairs, equality, inclusiveness, and 
openness. These values resonate with ASEAN’s broader goal of fostering peace, 
stability, integration, connectivity, and shared prosperity. Central to Cambodia’s strategy 
is the promotion of a people-centered ASEAN Community, ensuring that the interests 
and aspirations of the people are at the core of the regional integration agenda.

Cambodia Needs to Invest in Leadership Development 

Since achieving lasting peace in the late 1990s, Cambodia has made remarkable 
progress in human resource development. 
As emphasized in the Pentagonal Strategy Phase One, human capital 
development is central to Cambodia’s goal of becoming a high-income country by 2050. 
Achieving this vision requires not only the growth of skills and knowledge within 
the workforce but also the establishment of a supportive ecosystem that fosters 
continuous learning, leadership, and innovation. 
For this transformation to be effective, the Cambodian government must prioritize 
strategic investments that cultivate this ecosystem, which goes beyond conventional 
educational and vocational training programs to develop comprehensive pathways that 
incorporate leadership training, critical thinking, and entrepreneurial skills. 
The Ministry of Education, Youth and Sports, along with the Ministry of Labour 
and Vocational Training, has initiated a range of targeted programs aimed at realizing 
this strategic goal. These initiatives, which focus on STEM education, vocational training, 
and skill development, have produced laudable tangible outcomes. 
But in terms of leadership development, Cambodia needs to invest much more. In 
many ways, leadership development is an essential complement to Cambodia’s broader 
human resource initiatives. 
Where technical skills and industry knowledge create the foundation, leadership 
skills fuel the transformative potential of individuals to drive change and innovation within 
organizations and communities. 
Leadership development equips people to navigate challenges and solve 
problems, while strengthening national resilience from the inside out. 
Key aspects of leadership development include a deep understanding of 
organizational dynamics and behavior insights, the ability to build and lead cohesive and 
innovative teams, and the capacity in navigating complex interpersonal and structural 
dynamics. 
Effective leadership development programs should go beyond theoretical learning. 
They should offer practical, hands-on workshops designed to foster self-awareness, 
Contemporary Perspective 
Part I: Cambodia 
P a g e | 137 
Volume IV 
address personal weaknesses, and build on strengths through structured coaching and 
interactive learning sessions. 
These programs should also integrate the expertise of behavioral and leadership 
consultants to help participants identify and overcome internal and external challenges. 
Building these capacities prepares individuals to drive meaningful change in their 
workplaces and communities by aligning their actions with a broader vision. 
At its core, leadership begins at the individual level. A country’s transformation—
whether in the public sector, private sector, or social sector—depends on empowered, 
visionary individuals who are equipped to think critically, act strategically, and foster 
environments of innovation and accountability. 
To drive meaningful and sustainable development, the Cambodian government 
should establish a dedicated fund specifically for leadership and professional 
development programs targeted at public servants at both national and sub-national 
levels. 
Currently, Cambodia has a critical gap in the resources available for cultivating 
leadership skills among those public servants tasked with driving, implementing national 
and sub-national policies. 
The public servants lack the structured support necessary for developing their 
leadership skills and adaptive capacities needed to address Cambodia’s evolving social, 
economic, and administrative challenges. 
To effectively realize Cambodia’s Pentagonal Strategy, with good governance at 
its core, public servants and leaders at all levels must be equipped with a robust set of 
leadership skills. 
These might include team building, futures thinking, coaching, facilitation skills, 
and the ability to foster cross-agency collaboration. Each of these qualities contributes to 
creating a dynamic, agile, and forward-thinking public sector capable of responding to 
complex challenges and driving long-term state building. 
By creating a special fund on leadership development for the public servants, the 
government could support a variety of programs aimed at strengthening leadership 
competencies across key areas such as decision-making, team building, governance, 
and innovative problem-solving. 
Contemporary Perspective 
Part I: Cambodia 
P a g e | 138 
Volume IV 
Structured training sessions, hands-on workshops, and coaching with seasoned 
professionals would provide public servants with opportunities to cultivate skills that are 
not typically acquired through traditional job training or university education. 
Such a focus on professional growth within the public sector would empower 
leaders at every level to take on more complex roles and address challenges with 
confidence and insight. 
Public sector leaders who are well-equipped with leadership skills can act as 
catalysts for change, fostering a culture of life-long learning within government 
institutions. 
By building a sustainable public program or initiative that prioritizes ongoing 
learning and skill development, Cambodia would not only strengthen its public institutions 
but also inspire greater public trust and engagement in government initiatives. 
In the long run, this investment would create a ripple effect throughout Cambodian 
society. Stronger leadership capacity within the government would lead to more effective 
policies, greater public service delivery, more accountable and transparent governance, 
and a more agile response to wicked issues or problems. 
As Cambodia strives to elevate its place in the international arena, investing in the 
leadership potential of its public servants is a critical step toward realizing this vision.

Connecting Khmer Civilization

Contemporary Perspective

P a g e | 139 
Volume IV 
Connecting Khmer Civilization 

The Khmer Empire ruled vast areas of mainland Southeast Asia from around 802 
CE to 1431 CE, reaching its peak between the 11th and 13th centuries. Also known as 
the Kingdom of Angkor, it succeeded the earlier Funan and Chenla kingdoms, shaping 
much of the region’s culture and history. 
Most Khmer people today practice Buddhism, which was first introduced by Indian 
missionaries in the 3rd century BCE, with a significant rise in influence by the 5th century 
CE, coexisting with Hinduism. 
During the Khmer Empire (9th to 15th centuries), Buddhism flourished alongside 
Hinduism. King Jayavarman VII (1181-1218) was a significant proponent, establishing 
Mahayana Buddhism as the state religion. 
By the 13th century, Theravada Buddhism had become the dominant faith in 
Cambodia, eventually establishing itself as the country’s official religion and profoundly 
shaping Khmer culture, art, and architecture. 
The 1993 Cambodian Constitution enshrines Buddhism as the state religion, 
reflecting its central role in national identity. As of now, four countries officially recognize 
Buddhism as their state religion: Bhutan, Cambodia, Myanmar, and Sri Lanka. 
Today, traditional Buddhist festivals like the Kathina festival – originating 2,500 
years ago – are celebrated by Cambodian Buddhists. Held annually in October and 
November, Kathina is the largest alms-giving ceremony in the Buddhist calendar, 
marking the end of the Vassa, or monsoon retreat, when laypeople offer cloth and other 
necessities to monks. 
Following the decline of the Khmer Empire in the mid-15th century, Khmer 
territories gradually contracted as neighboring powers such as Siam (present-day 
Thailand) and Annam (present-day Vietnam) expanded their influence in the region. This 
geopolitical shift led to a dispersal of Khmer communities beyond the borders of present-
day Cambodia. 
Today, Khmer communities can be found in areas such as southern Vietnam, 
where they are known as Khmer Krom (“Lowland Khmer”), and in parts of Thailand, 
where they are called Khmer Loeu (“Upland Khmer”). These communities have 
maintained unique cultural and linguistic ties to Cambodia, preserving aspects of Khmer 
Contemporary Perspective 
Part I: Cambodia 
P a g e | 140 
Volume IV 
heritage despite living under different political systems and often facing pressures to 
assimilate. 
The spread of Khmer communities across the region has created a cultural 
diaspora, linking Cambodian identity with a broader historical region. These dispersed 
communities continue to play an important role in preserving Khmer traditions, language, 
and religious practices, and they form a cultural bridge between Cambodia and its 
neighboring countries. 
The prolonged civil war in Cambodia hindered strong ties between Khmer 
communities across the region. However, following the country’s achievement of total 
peace in late 1998, efforts to rekindle cultural and ancestral bonds are thriving. In a 
recent Kathina ceremony organized at pagodas in the Khmer Krom region of southern 
Vietnam on October 5-6, Cambodian leaders made a clear commitment to preserving 
and revitalizing Khmer cultural heritage and strengthening ties with the Khmer Krom 
people. 
Through the recent Kathina ceremony, led by Samdech Bun Rany Hun Sen, the 
President of the Cambodian Red Cross, Wat Po Kiri Vongsaram, also known as Wat 
Svay Siem Thmey, in Tra Vinh in Southern Vietnam on 5 November 2024, Cambodia has 
opened a meaningful new chapter in its bilateral relations with Vietnam, underscoring the 
values of mutual respect and traditional friendship, allowing Cambodia to honor the 
shared spiritual and cultural ties with Khmer Krom. 
It symbolizes Cambodia’s commitment to fostering people-centered development 
and reconnecting with the Khmer diaspora. By supporting the preservation of Khmer 
culture, language, and heritage, Cambodia is emphasizing these as core pillars of its 
national identity, while also using them to strengthen regional partnerships. This initiative 
aligns with Cambodia’s broader diplomatic approach of using cultural and historical ties 
to build goodwill and harmony with neighboring countries. 
The Khmer Krom, who have long preserved Khmer traditions in southern Vietnam, 
serve as a vital cultural bridge between Cambodia and Vietnam. Their role in maintaining 
Khmer heritage makes them central to Cambodia’s efforts in cultural diplomacy, 
highlighting the interconnectedness of people across borders. By respecting the Khmer 
Krom’s contributions and strengthening these cultural bonds, Cambodia reaffirms its 
vision of being a good neighbor, friend, and partner of Vietnam.

The success of the Kathina ceremony demonstrates that Cambodia’s people

Cambodia’s approach of placing cultural and human values at the center of its diplomatic 
engagements, helping to enhance regional understanding and cooperation.

Empowering Science, Technology and Innovation for 
Peace 

As Cambodia prepares to host a landmark peace forum in Phnom Penh this 
month, bringing together leaders from the legislative and executive branches, political 
parties, international organizations, and peace experts, we must consider a crucial 
question: how can science, technology, and innovation support peace-building efforts in 
an increasingly interconnected, complex, and turbulent world? 
Peace is more than the absence of violence; it is the presence of harmony, social 
well-being, and opportunity. 
Peace serves as the foundation of economic development and social progress, 
yet achieving and sustaining it requires constant efforts. We should never take peace for 
granted. 
In the current era of technological revolution and digital transformation, building a 
resilient “ecosystem of peace” demands that we harness science, technology and 
innovation to support the foundation of peace. 
The synergy between peace and technology grows more pressing each day, 
especially as conflicts multiply and intensify across the globe. 
Science, technology, and innovation hold immense potential to aid in building 
peace – but if used without care, they could also aggravate divisions and vulnerabilities. 
Technology is a double-edged sword. 
 Building a Framework for Science and Technology in Peacebuilding 
A recent study published in the Communications Engineering offers four principles 
essential to creating peace-focused technologies: adopting a common language, 
prioritizing needs-driven innovation, involving diverse stakeholders, and adhering to the 
“do-no-harm” principle. 
These principles offer a practical roadmap to ensure that technology serves as a 
tool for peace, not a source of further harm. 
First, adopting a common language is critical. Too often, researchers, 
policymakers, and peacebuilders speak in silos, hindered by differences in jargon and 
perspective. 
Contemporary Perspective 
Part I: Cambodia 
P a g e | 143 
Volume IV 
By creating a shared language around peace, we can foster solutions that address 
the complex realities of conflict while bridging the divides between disciplines. This 
common understanding allows us to avoid misunderstandings and work together 
effectively. 
Second, promoting needs-driven innovation that centers on designing 
peacebuilding technologies that genuinely serve affected communities. 
When innovation is detached from the lived experiences of those impacted by 
violence, solutions risk being ineffective or even harmful. 
To develop tools that foster peace, we must engage directly with local populations 
and organizations, ensuring our technologies are responsive to real challenges on the 
ground. 
Third, engaging diverse stakeholders. This highlights the importance of 
collaboration. Peacebuilding is a collective effort, requiring insights from international 
organizations, local NGOs, governments, and community leaders. 
Bringing these voices into the design and development stages of peace 
technology ensures that solutions are inclusive, context-sensitive, and scalable. In doing 
so, we draw on the expertise of those who understand the unique dynamics of conflict in 
each community. 
Fourth, commitment to the “do-no-harm”. Emerging technologies can empower, 
but they can also polarize, increase vulnerabilities, and exacerbate violence. 
By conducting thorough risk assessments and implementing ethical safeguards, 
technologists and peacebuilders can work to ensure that new innovations do not 
inadvertently put communities at greater risk. This principle is essential to building trust 
in technology as a force for good. 
 The Growing Field of PeaceTech 
The emerging field of PeaceTech – the use of technology specifically designed to 
prevent violence and support peace – has the potential to transform peacebuilding. 
From artificial intelligence that predicts conflict hotspots to digital platforms 
enabling inclusive peace processes, technological tools are expanding the possibilities 
for effective intervention.

However, along with these possibilities come challenges. We must ensure data 
privacy and security, establish ethical oversight, and address the motivations of 
companies developing these tools to prevent their misuse. 
A new approach, “Peace Innovation,” calls for partnerships across disciplines, 
bringing together researchers, policymakers, technologists, and community leaders to 
design solutions that are informed by context and culture. 
By working across boundaries, peacebuilders and innovators can create 
technologies that address real-world issues, respect cultural sensitivities, and deliver 
tangible results. 
For example, Peace Innovation has already made cities safer through smart city

An Enduring, Resilient Friendship 

This week, the Chairman of the National Assembly of the Socialist Republic of 
Vietnam, H.E. Tran Thanh Man, will embark on a four-day official visit to Cambodia. 
His visit signifies a milestone in strengthening bilateral parliamentary cooperation 
and advancing the deep-rooted ties between the two nations. 
During his time in Cambodia, he will have a bilateral meeting with Samdech 
Khuon Sudary, President of the National Assembly, inaugurate the new administrative 
building of the National Assembly, a generous gift from Vietnam, and participate in two 
major international forums in Phnom Penh. 
This visit is particularly significant as it marks H.E. Tran Thanh Man’s first official 
trip to Cambodia in his capacity as Chairman of the National Assembly, following his 
assumption of the role in May this year. 
The new administrative building, funded by a USD 25 million grant from Vietnam, 
stands as a symbol of the enduring friendship and comprehensive cooperation between 
the two nations. The building reflects the long-term solidarity and friendship shared by 
the two peoples. 
 A Strong and Resilient Partnership 
Cambodia and Vietnam share a stable, healthy, and dynamic relationship 
characterized by deep mutual trust and robust cooperation. 
As good neighbors, trusted friends, and strong partners, the two nations have 
consistently supported one another in all circumstances. 
Economic ties between Cambodia and Vietnam continue to grow at a remarkable 
pace. Bilateral trade is expected to surpass USD 10 billion this year, underscoring the 
vibrant commercial linkages between the two countries. 
Vietnamese investment in Cambodia has reached approximately USD 2.6 billion, 
with notable contributions from enterprises such as Metfone, a subsidiary of Viettel. As 
Cambodia’s leading telecom and digital services provider, Metfone generates over USD 
100 million annually in tax revenue and employs more than 3,000 local staff, further 
solidifying Vietnam’s economic footprint in the Kingdom. 
Contemporary Perspective 
Part I: Cambodia 
P a g e | 146 
Volume IV 
Tourism is another pillar of cooperation. Vietnam ranks as the second-largest 
source of international visitors to Cambodia, with slightly more than one million 
Vietnamese tourists recorded last year. 
 Fostering People-to-People Connections 
Cultural and educational exchanges form the foundation of the strong people-to-
people ties between the two nations. Vietnam annually awards 120 scholarships to 
Cambodian students, while Cambodia reciprocates with 34 scholarships for Vietnamese 
students. 
Educational exchanges deepen mutual understanding and foster long-term 
relationships between future generations. 
 Strengthening Trilateral Cooperation 
While Cambodia recently decided to withdraw from the Cambodia-Laos-Vietnam 
Development Triangle Area (CLV-DTA), its partnership with Vietnam and Laos remains 
unwavering. 
The leadership of the three countries understands that their unity is essential for 
maintaining peace and stability, promoting economic development and poverty reduction 
especially along border areas. 
The metaphor of a tripod aptly captures the interdependence and 
interconnectedness of the three nations – working together ensures collective strength 
and resilience. 
Despite the dynamic changes unfolding at the national, regional, and international 
levels, the trilateral relationship continues to stand firm, characterized by deep trust, 
shared vision, mutual respect, and common interest. 
As the two nations continue to deepen their ties, this new era of parliamentary 
cooperation holds promise for even greater achievements in the years to come. 
While significant progress has been achieved in Cambodia-Vietnam relations, 
there remain untapped potentials that both nations should explore to further deepen their 
partnership. The following recommendations outline key areas for enhanced 
collaboration: 
First, investing in the younger generation is essential to fostering mutual 
understanding and building lasting trust and friendship. 
Contemporary Perspective 
Part I: Cambodia 
P a g e | 147 
Volume IV 
Both countries should expand opportunities for youth exchanges, particularly for 
university students and young leaders. 
Initiatives such as joint academic programs, leadership summits, and cultural 
immersion activities can help bridge generational gaps and cultivate a sense of shared 
destiny. 
Strengthened person-to-person ties are the foundation of a resilient and dynamic 
relationship between the two nations. 
Second, expanding cultural cooperation – through joint celebrations, exhibitions, 
and the study of each other’s rich heritage – will further enrich bilateral relations. 
Exploring the historical connections of Khmer civilization and its influence in the 
region can serve as a unifying narrative that reinforces cultural solidarity. 
Third, unlocking the full potential of cross-border trade, investment, and tourism, 
both governments must work to eliminate existing barriers and obstacles. 
Streamlining customs procedures, harmonizing regulations, and enhancing border 
infrastructure will facilitate smoother economic exchanges. 
Policies that encourage private-sector partnerships and innovation can also drive 
greater economic integration and growth. 
Fourth, jointly addressing transnational crimes such as online fraud, human 
trafficking, and drug smuggling. 
Cambodia and Vietnam should intensify their collaboration through joint task 
forces, intelligence sharing, and capacity-building programs to effectively address these 
threats. 
Enhanced cooperation in law enforcement and judicial coordination is crucial in 
this regard. 
Fifth, cooperating on international issues. In an increasingly complex geopolitical 
landscape, Cambodia and Vietnam must deepen their coordination on regional and 
international matters. 
By working together to advocate for open and inclusive multilateralism, a rules-
based international order, and the Global South, the two nations can amplify their voices 
on the global stage.

Towards 2050, Cambodia Needs a Leapfrog Strategy 

As Cambodia aspires to become a high-income country by 2050, it must adopt a 
leapfrog strategy centered on innovation and technology. 
While the government has set ambitious milestones, including graduating from 
Least Developed Country (LDC) status by 2029 and achieving upper-middle-income 
status by 2030, the one-year gap between these targets highlights a critical challenge. 
Realizing the 2050 vision requires Cambodia to overcome the middle-income 
trap—a complex, structural phenomenon that has stalled many nations on their path to 
prosperity. 
 The Middle-Income Trap: A Challenge to Growth 
The middle-income trap arises when a country loses its competitive edge in low-
cost, labor-intensive goods but fails to transition into higher value-added industries. This 
stagnation leads to sluggish growth, stagnant or declining wages, and an expanding 
informal economy. 
To break free, Cambodia must address the structural issues that underpin this 
trap. Lessons from other countries offer a roadmap: 
• Fostering Innovation: Transforming industries through advanced technologies 
and restructured enterprise practices. 
• Promoting Entrepreneurship: Empowering entrepreneurs to drive economic 
diversification and resilience. 
• Enhancing Education: Expanding access to secondary and tertiary education 
to build a skilled workforce. 
• Building Top-Tier Universities: Establishing world-class institutions to 
advance research and development. 
• Strengthening Institutions: Creating fair, transparent, and accountable 
governance structures. 
• Encouraging Prudent Risk-Taking: Cultivating a culture that embraces 
calculated risks for growth. 
• Prioritizing Sustainability: Embedding environmental considerations into 
economic planning. 
Contemporary Perspective 
Part I: Cambodia 
P a g e | 150 
Volume IV 
• Upholding the Rule of Law: Transitioning from personalized governance to 
rule-based institutional frameworks. 
Cambodia’s path forward demands a concentrated focus on two transformative 
pillars: innovation-driven growth and Artificial Intelligence (AI). 
 Innovation-Driven Growth 
Innovation lies at the heart of escaping the middle-income trap. However, 
Cambodia’s innovation capacity remains limited. According to the Global Innovation 
Index (GII) 2024, Cambodia ranks 103rd out of 133 economies, lagging behind regional 
peers like Thailand (41st) and Vietnam (44th). This highlights the urgency for a robust 
national innovation strategy. 
To strengthen its innovation ecosystem, Cambodia can draw lessons from global 
best practices: 
• Identifying Institutional Structures: Establishing frameworks that prioritize 
innovation outcomes. 
• Developing Common Innovation Infrastructure: Supporting research, higher 
education, and the accumulation of technological knowledge. 
• Strengthening Industry-Science Linkages: Bridging the gap between 
academia and industry to accelerate innovation. 
• Enhancing Efficiency of Support Institutions: Providing entrepreneurs with 
resources to commercialize innovations. 
• Learning from Global Leaders: Adapting successful models from countries 
with high innovation capacity. 
By aligning policies and investments with these priorities, Cambodia can better 
position itself in regional and international supply chains and value chains. 
 Artificial Intelligence 
Artificial Intelligence presents an unparalleled opportunity for Cambodia to 
leapfrog its development. 
Whether a nation fails or grows depends very much on the capacity to develop, 
manage, and govern AI. Southeast Asian countries are competing to become the region’s 
top AI hub. Currently Singapore is leading the race. 
Contemporary Perspective 
Part I: Cambodia 
P a g e | 151 
Volume IV 
Nations leading in AI view it as a strategic tool to address fragmented yet 
interconnected global supply chains. AI is a catalyst of growth. 
For developing countries, AI offers a pathway to accelerate progress in core 
development areas and improve citizens’ lives. 
A well-defined AI strategy should align with Cambodia’s unique strengths, 
challenges, and strategic priorities. Key considerations include: 
• Workforce Development: Addressing STEM talent shortages through re-
skilling, up-skilling, and education reform. 
• Sectoral Prioritization: Targeting AI investments in sectors like agriculture, 
where precision farming can drive productivity, or manufacturing, where 
automation can enhance competitiveness. 
• Ethics and Regulation: Developing a robust regulatory framework that 
integrates data protection, privacy laws, and AI ethics to foster trust and 
accountability. 
• Research Collaboration: Strengthening partnerships between academia, 
industry, and government to create a thriving AI ecosystem. 
International and multi-stakeholder collaboration will also be essential. By learning 
from global leaders and engaging with regional and international partners, Cambodia 
can accelerate its journey toward becoming an AI-ready nation. 
To achieve its 2050 vision, Cambodia must make bold, forward-looking 
investments in innovation and AI. These pillars offer not only a means to overcome the 
middle-income trap but also a foundation for long-term, sustainable growth. 
With a clear strategy and long-term commitment, Cambodia can position itself as 
a high-income country by 2050. It is urgent and imperative for the Cambodian 
government to develop national strategies on innovation and AI.
